INTRODUCTION 
  
  
 I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliame ntary Standing Committee on Industry, 
having been authorized by the Committee, hereby pre sent this Two Hundred Sixty First Report on 
Action Taken Note furnished by the Ministry of Micr o, Small and Medium Enterprises on the 
recommendations contained in the Committee’s Two Hu ndred Forty Seventh Report on 
implementation of Interest Subsidy Eligibility Certificate (ISEC) Scheme.  
 
2. I thank the Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises for furnishing the Action 
Taken Note on the recommendations contained in the Committee’s Two Hundred Forty Seventh 
Report. 
  
3. The Committee in its meeting held on 22 
nd  September, 2014 considered and adopted the 
report. 
 
  
 
  
K.C. Tyagi 
                                               Chairman                                                                                   
                Department -related Parliamentary  
                                                                                                     Standing  Committee   on    Industry  
 
New Delhi 
22 
nd  September, 2014 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
(ii) 
 
 
 
 
 

 
REPORT 
 
The Action Taken Report of the Committee deals with  the Action Taken by the Ministry of 
Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises on the recommendations contained in the Committee’s Two 
Hundred Forty Seventh Report on implementation of I nterest Subsidy Eligibility Certificate 
(ISEC) Scheme  pertaining to the Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises. 
 
2.  Action Taken Notes have been received from the Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium 
Enterprises in respect of the recommendations conta ined in the Report. These have been 
categorized as follows:  
 
Chapter –I   The recommendations/observations, which have bee n accepted by the Ministry. 
 
 The Committee is pleased to observe that the Minis try has accepted its recommendations as 
mentioned in the Chapter – I of the Report. 
 
Chapter -II   The recommendations/observations which the Commit tee does not desire to pursue 
in view of the Government's replies. 
 
 In respect of these recommendations the Committee is convinced with the logic and 
explanations advanced by the Ministry and therefore do not want to pursue them for the present. 
 
Chapter -III    The recommendations/observations in respect of w hich the Committee has either 
not accepted replies of the Ministry or has asked the Ministry to review its reply. 
 
 The Committee expresses its concern over the non-i mplementation of recommendations 
contained in Chapter – III and desires that the Min istry should furnish logical explanations 
therefor. 
 
Chapter -IV    The recommendations/observations in respect of wh ich final replies of the Ministry 
have not been received. 
 
 In respect of recommendations placed in Chapter-IV , the Ministry has either furnished the 
interim replies or couched its language in vague te rms like noted for compliance/guidance, 
therefore, the Committee desires that the Ministry should furnish Action Taken Notes in respects 
of recommendations categorized in Chapter-IV in det ail and to the point, as per the intention and 
spirit of the recommendations of the Committee. 
 
3. The details of the ATR are being discussed in the succeeding pages. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
-2- 
 
CHAPTER-I 
 
Recommendations/observations, which have been accepted by the Ministry  
       
Recommendation/Observation  
 
The Committee observes that the banks have not comp lied with the RBI guidelines in this 
regard which were based on the Kalia Committee's re commendations.  A mechanism must be 
created to monitor the implementation of guidelines .  Any breach of such guidelines must be dealt 
with seriously.   
(Para 9) 
Action Taken  
 
As directed by DRPSCI, KVIC has made all efforts to  familiarize the bankers about the 
scheme and placed the details of the scheme on the KVIC website.  CMDs of all 27 Public Sector 
Banks have also been requested to issue necessary i nstruction to the Bank to ensure that adequate 
finances under ISEC scheme are made available to Khadi Institutions. 
According to Department of Financial Services(DFS),  the recommendations of Kalia 
Committee are very specific to Khadi and Village in dustries whereas Nayak Committee are 
general in nature. Therefore the recommendations of  Kalia Committee and formula suggested by 
them for extension of credit by the banks to SSI/MS ME sector is based on empirical research and 
ground realities of MSME sector. Keeping this in vi ew, the requirements of credit to Khadi 
institutions should be based on the recommendations  of Kalia committee which has already been 
accepted by the RBI.  However, the suggestions of t he banks regarding, associations of the banks 
with khadi institutions at state level and monitori ng of the scheme at state level through SLBC is 
agreed to by this Department.  State offices /Zonal  offices of KVIC should be mandated to have 
periodical and regular interactions with the banks in order to help the khadi societies sufficient 
credit availability from the banks as per their req uirements.  The review of the progress of the 
scheme may be a regular agenda in SLBC meetings and quarterly meeting by KVIC with banks 
 
 
 
 

 
-3- 
 
 
CHAPTER-II  
 
Recommendations/Observations which the Committee do es not desire to pursue in view of 
the Government’s replies  
 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
The Committee feels that such conditions of maintai ning a stock of value higher than the 
sanctioned amount, is too stringent a condition which will only make a khadi unit unviable.   
(Para 12) 
Action Taken  
 
KVIC has already directed the field Directors to ta ke-up the issue of the credit requirement 
of Khadi institution in SLBC/DCC. Further, CMDs of all 27 Public Sector Banks have also been 
requested to include banks credit to Khadi Sector under ISEC Scheme as a standing agenda  for the 
meetings of SLDCs/DLBCs and in such other fora and  issue necessary instruction to the Bank to 
ensure that adequate finances under ISEC scheme are made available to Khadi Institutions. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
  In this regard the Committee takes note of the su bmission made by the  representative 
of the State Bank of India, during its meeting on t he issue on 15 
th  April, 2014. It was stated 
that issue was essentially of difference in interest subsidy approved by the KVIC and amount 
actually claimed. 
 
 “ The issue, apparently, is that of a difference in t he interest subsidy approved by the KVIC and 
the amount which is, actually, physically claimed b y the bank on that interest subsidy.  In my view, 
what really happens is that the loans are sanctione d based on certain projections made by 
borrowers.  And the interest subsidy sanctioned by the KVIC is based on the projections made, for 
example, for the first year of operation.  But, act ually, we have seen in many cases, what really 
happens is that after the first year is completed, the projections do not really take place 100 per 
cent; I mean, the projections may be 50 per cent or  60 per cent or 70 per cent.  So, 
correspondingly, the amount of drawing on the loan is also 50 per cent or 60 per cent or 70 per 
cent, and the interest applied is also that much le ss.  One of the major reasons, to my mind, for the 
difference is that the actual performance, especial ly, in the first year does not match with the 
projections made at the time of sanctioning the loa n.  The second thing which I would like to 
submit  is that  it will,  perhaps, be  a good  idea to have, in the State-level Banker ’s Committee, a  

 
-4- 
 
Sub Working Group or a Sub Group of Bankers, KVIC a nd local State-Government functionaries, 
just like they do for PMEGP, to decide on the appli cations, a joint appraisal of these applications, 
and forward them to the banks concerned in that area for approval.   “ 
 
The representative of Punjab national Bank, too, supplemented : 
 
“The gap between financing, as suggested by the KVI C, and those sanctioned by the bank happens 
from two counts.  One is the Margin Money which is supposedly taken by the KVIC at not more 
than 10 per cent.  Banks, normally, finance between  10 and 25 per cent of the margin, which 
results in lesser financing to that extent because the borrower ’s contribution is expected to be a 
little more than ten per cent in such cases.  Secon dly, we have also mentioned in the Report that 
the bank does not finance full stocks.  So, because  of the drawing power, in case the borrower has 
a 25 per cent margin, he is supposed to maintain a stock of, say, 1,33,000 for drawing a D.P. of 
Rs. 1 crore, and this is only because of Margin Mon ey.  It would result in that gap. And, as rightly 
suggested, we can standardize the forum and we can monitor closely.  One of the bankers would be 
a part of this Joint Appraisal between the KVIC and the banks.” 
 
 In views of submission made by the representatives  of Banks, the Committee 
apprehends that resolution of bottlenecks in implem entation has been left to SLDCs/DLBCs.  
But these bodies work under overall policy guidelin es of RBI and respective Banks.  The 
Committee is of the view that first there should be  consensus over policy level between KVIC 
and Bankers, before delegating the powers of resolu tion to SLBCs/DLBCs. The Committee 
notes that the KVIC is engaging the CMDs of Banks t o address the issue. Also,  the 
Department of Financial Services are  also abreast with the issue. There is a need to evolve 
consensus among the relevant stakeholders.  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
-5- 
 
CHAPTER-III  
 
 
Recommendations/Observations in respect of which th e Committee has either not accepted 
the replies of the Ministry or has asked the Ministry to review its replies  
 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
  
 
The Committee notes that the ISEC is a very good scheme.  However, it regrets to note that 
banks are issuing fifty per cent loans to the total  ISEC issued.  The RBI guidelines based on Kalia 
Committee, governing ISEC mandate that if less than  ninety per cent ISEC issued are honoured by 
banks then the tripartite meeting among the bank, b eneficiary and the State level Director must be 
organized.  The Committee notes with concern that hardly any such tripartite meeting is organized.  
It is a very serious matter.  In the absence of suc h tripartite meeting, the ISEC scheme is not being 
implemented  properly and  effectively.  Such  tripartite  meeting would  provide  opportunities  for 
discussing the problems affecting the khadi institutions and for coordinating the implementation of 
the scheme which involves banks, KVIC and the benef iciaries.  The Committee recommends that 
the KVIC must ensure that such tripartite meetings take place in every State.  Besides, the 
Committee recommends that the State level Directors  of KVIC must also take the initiative to 
organize such tripartite meetings.   
(Para 17) 
 
Action Taken  
   
KVIC has already directed the field Directors to ta ke-up the issue of the credit requirement 
of Khadi Institution in SLBC/DCC.  Further, CMDs of  all 27 Public Sector Banks have also been 
requested to issue necessary instruction to the Ban k to ensure that adequate finances under ISEC 
scheme are made available to Khadi Institutions. DFS agreed with the observations of the Ministry 
of MSME. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation  
 
The Committee recommends that the KVIC must take st eps beyond writing routine 
letters  with  much  avail.  The  Committee  suggests that KVIC too  should  make  innovative  
 

-6- 
 
modifications to address the concerns of the Banks.  KVIC may even also explore new 
avenues of funding this Scheme  and negotiate with  institutions like SIDBI, NABARD and 
other similar institutions to provide finance to Kh adi institutions under ISEC scheme.  The 
KVIC has also not replied as to why the tripartite negotiation mechanism has not been used, 
in case of disputes.   
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

-7- 
 
CHAPTER-IV  
 
 
Recommendations/Observations in respect of which fi nal replies of the Ministry have not 
been received 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
The Committee observes that working capital amount under the ISEC as approved by the KVIC 
and actual availed credit have increased over the y ears, however, the difference between the two, 
in percentage terms too has increased to about 50%.  The Committee finds such a situation where 
Banks lend only half the amount of credit what is a pproved by the KVIC, patently unacceptable. 
There is a need for serious efforts to bridge this gap. While the Government has formulated 
enabling scheme to address the credit needs of khad i and polyvastra institutions, the policies and 
guidelines for financing institutions are either no t in sync with Government's policy or the 
guidelines are not being enforced by the Banks and the RBI.  The Committee was also informed by 
the KVIC officials that even though the beneficiari es got the interest at the rate of four per cent, 
actually some banks are charging more interest than prescribed.  This is a very serious matter.  The 
Committee recommends that those banks which do so m ust be investigated upon and appropriate 
action may be taken so that such gross breach of banking norms do not take place.  The Committee 
recommends that the banks must give credit to the k hadi institution under the ISEC slightly above 
the base rate.  The Committee recommends that the b anks must honour the ISEC and strict 
instructions be issued to the bank Managers to honour it.  
(Para 7) 
Action Taken  
KVIC has already directed the field Directors to ta ke-up the issue of the credit requirement 
of Khadi Institution in SLBC/DCC.  Further, CMDs of  all 27 Public Sector Banks have also been 
requested to issue necessary instruction to the Ban k to ensure that adequate finances under ISEC 
scheme are made available to Khadi Institutions. 
 
A letter has been issued again by KVIC on 07.04.201 4 to all the CMDs of Banks enclosing 
recommendations of the DRPSCI [under intimation to Institutional Finance Division of Ministry of 
Finance] and Dy. Governor (RBI) seeking their inter vention in the implementation of the 
recommendation of DRPSCI. 
 

-8- 
 
Further, a Committee has been formed by KVIC as per  the direction of Ministry to review 
and monitor the implementation of Guidelines under ISEC scheme at Central level. Monitoring at 
State level will be done by SLBCs. 
 
A committee of Officers was formed by KVIC under ch airmanship of Financial Adviser, 
KVIC to discuss the issue with Western Council of t he Chartered Accounts of India. The meeting 
is proposed to be held shortly. 
 
Department of Financial Services(DFS), Ministry of Finance is also of the view that the 
credit requirements of Khadi Sector needs to be taken by the banks on priority and credit should be  
extended to Khadi institutions based on ISEC issued  by KVIC. As regards the suggestions of 
banks regarding some modifications in the guideline s in the scheme and its monitoring, KVIC has 
already formed a committee and the committee may su bmit its report in time bound manner to 
MSME so that modifications in the scheme may be discussed with the banks and representatives of 
DFS and amendments/modifications, if any be carried out accordingly. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation  
 
The Ministry of MSME may inform the committee of th e outcome of the said 
Committee. 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
The Committee is aware of the nature of khadi busin ess. Unlike any other business, a 
typical khadi institutions runs an integrated busin ess involving spinning, weaving, wet processing, 
fabric conversion, wholesale distribution and retai ling. Therefore routine banking norms should 
not be applied in the khadi sector.  
(Para 10) 
Action Taken  
There are already guidelines issued by RBI on credi t requirement of Khadi institutions, 
wherein, it was specifically mentioned that KVIC’s assessment may be accepted if it does not 
exceed the assessment made by the banks more than 1 0%. In case the KVIC’s assessment of 
working capital exceeds more that 10%, the quantum of working capital may be arrived at by 
mutual dialogue between the institutions/KVIC and f inancing bank. DFS has conveyed its 
agreement with the observations of the Ministry of MSME. 
 

-9- 
Further Recommendation/Observation  
 
 The Committee would like to know if the mechanism of Tripartite Negotiations in 
case of disputes, has been resorted to, by the KVIC. In context of presentation made before it 
by the Department of Financial Services and represe ntatives of Banks, the Committee would 
like to review the performance of SLBCs in respect of ISEC disbursals.  
 The Committee takes note of the presentation made by the Secretary, M/o MSME, during its 
meeting on the issue on 15 th  April, 2014. The Secretary summarized the issue and stated : 
 
“the peculiar business cycle of the Khadi instituti on which needs to be recognised by the banks 
and once recognised it will lead to an agreed, adeq uate amount of working capital.  If the working 
capital is inadequate, the Khadi institutions will function in a very sub-optimal way, which is also 
happening at many places. We are not able to access  the loans.  This puts their sustainability into 
question and leads to a very vicious cycle in which  their further capability of raising loans and 
repaying loans is affected.  I think as the Committ ee has highlighted, the peculiar cycle of the 
Khadi institutions needs to be understood.  At the highest level, this agreement had actually taken 
place between the KVIC and the banks as to what wou ld be the requirement of working capital.  
But, in practice, the amount of working capital whi ch is being made available is less.  Over a 
period of time, because the working capital is less  even the margin money which is being provided 
for as per the budgetary exercise has also remained  stagnant.  So I think for breaking this vicious 
cycle we need to once again focus on the peculiarit y of the business cycle of the KVIC and the 
engagement between the KVIC and the RBI and the ban king institutions should be revived in a 
more meaningful way.” 
 
In this regard, the Committee recognizes that the G overnment has replaced the 
Seasonal rebate Scheme with Marketing Development A ssistance (MDA), to facilitate the 
Khadi institutions to sell their products year long  instead of during seasonal rebate period. 
The Committee believes that the MDA scheme should h ave reduced the business cycle to 
make it more compatible with Banking norms.   
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
The Committee concurs with the suggestions emerging  from the study.   The Committee 
particularly recommends that there was a need that the banking institutions appreciate the business 
cycle of khadi sector and the constraints faced by it.  There is a need for alignment of 
banking/financial norms with business cycle of khadi sector. 
(Para 14) 
 

-10- 
 
 
Action Taken 
 
 
There are already guidelines issued by RBI on credi t requirement of Khadi institutions, 
wherein, it was specifically mentioned that KVIC’s assessment may be accepted if it does not 
exceed the assessment made by the banks more than 1 0%. In case the KVIC’s assessment of 
working capital exceeds more that 10%, the quantum of working capital may be arrived at by 
mutual dialogue between the institutions/KVIC and finasncing bank. 
According to DFS, the sales of khadi are discount b ased/ rebate based/season based and 
festivals specific.  Accordingly, the production of  khadi is undertaken by the institutions.  
Moreover, this is a highly decentralized activity a s spinning, weaving, dying, printing, conversion 
into fabrics takes place at different places and th erefore, khadi completes only one business cycle 
in a year. As per recommendations of Standing Commi ttee, banks should not insist on maintaining 
higher stocks by the khadi institutions. DFS has so ught details of non-compliance so that 
consolidated instructions could be issued to all th e banks to agree the present business cycle for 
khadi based on the ISEC issued by KVIC.   
 
Further Recommendation/Observation  
 
The Committee may be apprised of the new consolidat ed instructions to be issued by 
Department of Financial Services. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
The Committee is inclined to accept the observation s made by the Chief  Advisor ( Cost). 
Still, the Committee hopes that the detailed norms should facilitate the KVI institutions to access 
the institutional finance at affordable rate. The C ommittee also observes that while the 
Government and RBI has put the sector under priority sector category, yet the terms and conditions 
are too stringent and defeat the entire purpose of placing them in the priority sector. The purpose 
of 'priority sector' is not merely to provide great er access to institutional credit, rather to provid e 
greater access to it at affordable terms.  While financing Khadi, the Banks should not look at it as a 
commodity, they should also look at the noble legacy and philosophy which sustain it. Howsoever  
 

-11- 
 
intangible it may be, Khadi remains a proud heritag e of freedom struggle invoking the ideals for 
which Mahatma Gandhi lived and sacrificed his life. 
(Para 16) 
Action Taken 
 
 
The study of Working capital formula under ISEC was earlier done by Chief Advisor, Cost, 
Ministry of Finance as decided by the Commission ba sed on the recommendation of Task Force 
Committee. The report of Chief Advisor, Cost was pl aced in Commission in its meeting 
March,2013, wherein, the Commission has formed a Re view Committee to study the issue for 
taking suitable decision. The observation and recom mendation of Review Committee was 
discussed in the Commission in its meeting held in June’ 2013 and thereby it was directed that 
detailed proposal acceptable to the banks regarding  working capital formula may be evolved with 
the help of Chartered Accountants . 
Accordingly, a committee of Officers was formed by KVIC under chairmanship of 
Financial Adviser, KVIC to discuss the issue with W estern Council of the Chartered Accounts of 
India. The meeting is proposed to be held shortly. DFS agreed with the observations of the 
Ministry of MSME. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
The Committee may be apprised of the outcome of the  new Committee set up by the 
KVIC.  The Committee also recognize that the Department of Financial Services to has  been 
 seeking the inputs from Bankers  on  this  Scheme.   Therefore  it  is  advisable  that  the  
Committee set  up  by  KVIC should be in sync with the Department of Financial Services so 
that the outcome should result in consensus.  The C ommittee set up by KVIC may include 
the Indian Bank Association. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

-12- 
 
 
III                                                  
Third Meeting

REPORT 
 
 The Action Taken Report of the Committee deals wit h the Action Taken by the 
Ministry of Civil Aviation on the recommendations c ontained in the Committee’s Two 
Hundred and Thirty- seventh Report on the Revival a nd Restructuring of Hotel 
Corporation of India Ltd. 
  
2. Action Taken Notes have been received from the M inistry of Civil Aviation in 
respect of the recommendations contained in the Rep ort. These have been categorized as 
follows: 
 
Chapter I -  The recommendations/observations which have been  accepted by the 
Ministry. 
 
 The Committee is pleased to observe that the Minis try has accepted its 
recommendations as mentioned in the Chapter – I of the Report. 
 
Chapter -II -  The recommendations/observations which the Commi ttee does not desire 
to pursue in view of the Government's replies. 
 
 In respect of these recommendations the Committee is convinced with the logic 
and explanations advanced by the Ministry and there fore do not want to pursue them for

Chapter -III -  The recommendations/observations in respect of w hich the Committee has

The Recommendations/observations, which have been accepted by the Ministry. 
 
Recommendation/observation 
 
Centaur Hotel, Delhi: 
 
 
 The Committee strongly recommends for substantial allocation of resources made 
available to the Air India for making the units wor king under the HCI more financially 
viable and sound.  The amount so released must be i n addition to Rs.11 crore earmarked 
in the outcome budget for renovation and upgradation of the Centaur Hotel, Delhi. 
Para No.9 
 
Action Taken Reply 
 
 Government has approved Rs.35.29 crore in 12 
th  Five Year Plan for carrying out 
renovation works in three Units of HCI located in D elhi and Srinagar. Out of which 
Rs.24.20 crore has been allocated for Centaur Hotel , Delhi and Chefair Flight Catering, 
Delhi. Rs. 10 crore was sanctioned during the finan cial year 2012-13 and Rs. 12 crore 
was sanctioned during the year 2013-14 for renovati on of HCI properties.  Based on this, 
unit-wise Project Report had also been prepared, al locating fund for repair/renovation of 
each Unit.  Accordingly, the work of Centaur Hotel, Delhi is in progress for repair of roof 
top terrace, replacement of leaking pipes in the du cts, up-gradation of kitchen 
equipments, service lifts, guest lifts, guest rooms , effluent treatment plant, DG sets with 
higher capacity etc.

Nil

CHAPTER–III 
 
Recommendations/Observations in respect of which the Committee has not accepted 
the replies of the Ministry and has asked the Ministry to review its replies. 
 
 
Recommendation/ observation 
 
Chefair Flight Catering, Delhi: 
  
  
 Commissioned in 1986 its capacity utilization is o nly 22 per cent.  This pathetic 
performance of the unit is attributed to lack of re novation of its kitchen infrastructure.  
Initially the capacity utilization ranged from 35 t o 40 per cent due to depreciation and 
normal wear and tear of the equipments installed.  The Committee takes note of the fact 
that rupees six crore have been allocated in the ou tcome budget 2012-13 of the Ministry 
for renovation and restoration of the facilities available for flight kitchen. 
Para No.19 
 
Action Taken Reply 
 
 Chefair Flight Catering Delhi was commissioned with  a capacity of 8000 meals 
per day.  Initially, the Unit was having total cate ring business of the erstwhile Indian 
Airlines/Air India. However, subsequently a policy decision was taken by Indian 
Airlines/Air India for bifurcating their catering c ontract amongst private players after 
which a major chunk of their catering business went to the private sector.  This led to loss 
of large volume of business to the Unit and thereby under-utilisation of its capacity. 
 
 A decision has been taken by Air India to reserve 30% of the total volume of its 
in-flight catering business for Chefair Flight Catering. 
 
 Also Government of India has approved the budgetar y support to renovate/repair 
the HCI properties located in Delhi and Srinagar. A fter the necessary up-gradation/ 
renovation in the Kitchen, it will able to tap the potential business from Airlines. 
 
Recommendation/ observation 
 
Chefair Flight Catering, Mumbai: 
 
 
 The Unit which started functioning in 1986 is able  to utilize 32 per cent of its 
installed capacity.  The same problem of lack of re novation which plagued the Centaur 
Hotels in the Chefair Flight Catering Delhi is plag uing the Chefair Flight Catering 
Mumbai.  Its problems have been further compounded because of the bifurcation of the 
catering contract by the Air India.  As a result, t his unit only caters to a few flights which 
is far below the target.  The Committee was informed that the area where the Chefair unit

of Mumbai was operating was taken away for expandin g the airport.  As a result, the 
Chefair was shifted and relocated.  The Committee u nderstood that the HCI is insisting 
for a fully developed infrastructure in the vicinit y of the airport to run the flight kitchen.  
The Committee takes note of the fact that work for this purpose is in progress.  The 
Committee also takes note of the fact that rupees t hree crore has been allocated in the 
outcome Budget for the year 2012-13 of the Ministry  for the renovation of the flight 
kitchen in Mumbai.  The HCI maintains that with the  new infrastructure to be made 
available to the flight kitchen in Mumbai and with the new budgetary provision for its 
renovation and upgradation the flight kitchen would  get adequate business not only from 
Air India but also from other airlines.  The turn-a round plan proposal for the 12 th  Plan 
period stated that Chefair Delhi and Chefair Mumbai  are expected to commence 
operations of Air India lounges at Terminal 3 Delhi (both domestic and international) and 
Air India Maharaja Lounge at Terminal 2C at Mumbai respectively to fulfill the 
requirements of Air India. 
Para No.20 
 
Action Taken Reply 
 
 At the time of commissioning, Chefair Flight Cater ing, Mumbai had a capacity to 
produce 10000 meals per day and was also catering t o erstwhile Air India and Indian 
Airlines besides other international airlines.  Lik e Delhi, Air India decided to shift 
majority of its catering business in Mumbai to priv ate caterers, which led to loss of 
business to the Unit.   
 
 It was proposed to relocate the Chefair facilities  at Mumbai and MIAL had 
proposed to relocate the existing facilities at its  cost on a piece of land to be made  
available by NACIL/Chef Air. Keeping in view the sa me, renovation work of Chefair 
unit at Mumbai was dropped from the proposal of ren ovation/repair of HCI units at 
Mumbai. However, in view of the discussion that the  Chefair Mumbai would be handed 
over to MIAL, repair work of Flight Kitchen Mumbai was dropped from the same. 
 
 However, it has now been confirmed by Air India th at 30% its total in-flight 
catering business will be given to Delhi and Mumbai Unit of Chefair. 
 
Further Recommendation/ observation  
 
 Chefair Flight catering, Delhi and Mumbai have to make the most of the 
30% reservation of the total volume of flight cater ing by Air India and the 
Budgetary support approved by the Government for th e 12 th  Five Year Plan.  They 
must keep in mind that in the long term their viabi lity will only be through catching 
up with the private catering operators and survivin g through competing with them. 
Chefair Flight catering should utilize the captive market provided by Air India and 
financial support to consolidate their business and  carve out a market share of their 
own in the flight catering field.

Recommendation/ observation 
 
 The Committee would like to see the Air India, the parent body of the HCIL, take 
measures so that at least some portion of amount is  released for its revival is utilized for 
HCIL. It will help the HCIL to improve its MoU perf ormance.  The Committee 
recommends that this amount must be at least Rs.100  crore which would be exclusive of 
Rs.25 crore already earmarked in the outcome budget s as mentioned in the earlier 
paragraphs. The involvement, dedication and commitm ent of the employees, 
management and the government are fundamental perqu isites for the maintenance, 
revival and success of any PSE like Centaur Hotel, Srinagar.  No tangible result would be 
achieved by pumping more money unless the employees and management of the Hotel do 
not qualitatively improve their performance.  In ad dition to the monetary or budgetary 
support there must be innovative and creative planning to revamp the infrastructure of the 
hotels and flight kitchens under the HCL and refurb ish their image for attracting tourists 
and passengers to its quality products and services. 
 
Para No.22 
 
Action Taken Reply 
 
 As Government has sanctioned the total amount of R s. 35.29 crore to HCI for the 
renovation / upgradation of its three Units i.e. Ch efair Flight Catering Delhi; Centaur 
Hotel, Delhi and Centaur Lake View Hotel Srinagar.  The work has already been 
entrusted to AAI and the progress of the work is re gularly being monitored by Ministry

work. Further, Air India have come forward and deci ded that 30% of its in-flight catering 
business shall be provided to Chef air unit at Delh i and Mumbai. MOU of HCI with Air 
India is also being signed for the year, 2014-15.

 The reply does not mention anything about steps ta ken to improve employee 
efficiency and quality of service in hotel like Cen taur Hotel, Srinagar. The 
Committee reiterates that Budgetary support alone c annot turn around a PSE, if all 
round qualitative improvement is ignored. Quality o f personnel, in the opinion of 
the Committee, is a deciding factor in the hospital ity business. It is, therefore, felt 
that HCL should choke out clearly defined capacity building programmes for 
improving its man power efficiency.

Evolution and Mandate  
The Government of India established the Ministry of  Small Scale Industries 
and Agro & Rural Industries (SSI & ARI) in October,  1999 as the nodal Ministry 
for formulation of policies and Central sector prog rammes/schemes, their 
implementation and related coordination and for sup plementing the efforts of the 
States/Union Territories for promotion and developm ent of small scale, agro and 
rural industries in the country.  Subsequently, in September, 2001 the Ministry of 
SSI and ARI was bifurcated into two separate Minist ries, namely, Ministry of 
Small Scale Industries and Ministry of Agro and Rur al Industries.  In 2006, 
“Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Ac t (MSMED) 2006” were 
enacted by the Parliament.  Pursuant to this enactm ent, the Ministry of Agro and 
Rural Industries and the Small Scale Industries were merged into a single Ministry, 
namely Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises. 
2. The Committee acknowledges that the Micro, Small  and Medium 
Enterprises (MSMEs) including Khadi and Village/Rural Enterprises, constitute an 
important segment of the Indian economy in terms of  their contribution to 
country's industrial production, exports, employmen t and creation of 
entrepreneurship base.  The Committee noted that th e primary responsibility for 
promotion and development of MSMEs lies with State Government.  However, the 
Government of India has always taken active interes t in supplementing the efforts 
of the State Governments.  The role of the Ministry  of MSME is mainly to assist 
the States in their efforts to promote growth and d evelopment of MSMEs.  In 
addition, the Ministry also attempts to address the  common concerns of these 
enterprises.  

-2- 
3.  Instead of assisting the State Government, the Min istry has devised its 
own Schemes and implements them through State agenc ies like KVIBs and 
DICs.  The Committee finds that though State Govern ments are involved in 
consultative process at apex level, and execution l evel, the Central and State 
agencies do not converge institutionally.  For exam ple in the KVIC act, there 
is no institutional arrangement for coordination be tween KVIC, State 
Directorate and KVIBs to execute KVIC programmes.  The Committee 
observes that with greater emphasis of cooperative federalism and setting up 
of Niti Ayog as consultative forum between Centre a nd State Governments,  
the role of the Ministry may be suitably recast with respect of formulation and 
implementation of the various programmes. 
Composition of the Ministry 
 
4. The formulation and implementation of policies a nd 
programmes/projects/schemes for MSME sector is undertaken by the Ministry with 
the assistance of its attached and autonomous organ izations, namely, Micro, Small 
and Medium Enterprises Development Organization (MS ME-DO) or O/o 
Development Commissioner (MSME), the National Small  Industries Corporation 
Limited (NSIC), the Khadi and Village Industries Co mmission (KVIC), the Coir 
Board and three National Level Entrepreneurship Dev elopment Institutes, viz., 
National Institute for Entrepreneurship and Small B usiness Development 
(NIESBUD), NOIDA (U.P.), National Institute for Mic ro, Small and Medium 
Enterprises (NI-MSME), Hyderabad and the Indian Ins titute of Entrepreneurship 
(IIE), Guwahati.  The Ministry of MSME is having tw o Divisions called Small & 
Medium Enterprises (SME) Division and Agro& Rural I ndustry (ARI) Division.  
The  SME Division  is  allocated  the work, inter –alia, of administration, vigilance  
 

-3- 
and administrative supervision of the National Smal l Industries Corporation 
(NSIC) Ltd., a public sector enterprise and the thr ee autonomous national level 
entrepreneurship development/training organizations .  The Division is also 
responsible for implementation of the schemes relat ing to marketing and export 
promotion.  The ARI Division looks after the admini stration of two statutory 
bodies called the Khadi and Village Industries Comm ission (KVIC), Coir Board 
and Mahatma Gandhi Institute of Rural Industrializa tion (MGIRI).  They are also 
supervising the implementation of the Prime Ministe r’s Employment Generation 
Programme (PMEGP).

and this gross budgetary support has been allocated  amongst the different wings of

funds by the Ministry in its Planned schemes.  Desp ite repeated observation

17. The Secretary, M/o MSME tried to rationalize th e pattern of expenditure:

Introduction 
 
In India, the Heavy Industries Sector encompasses H eavy Engineering, Machine 
Tools, Heavy Electrical, Construction Machinery and  the Automotive Industries.  The 
output of these industries permeates almost all sec tors of the economy including basic 
infrastructure like power, rural and road transport s industries and provide heavy 
machinery that are critical to other important sect ors like mining, refineries, 
petrochemicals, fertilizers, shipping, paper, cemen t, textiles etc.  The Department of 
Heavy Industry (DHI) which looks after this industrial sector is the part of the Ministry of 
Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises, which was created by the President’s

Committee finds that for the year 2015-16 too DHI h as been given lesser Plan funds 
compared to the Non Plan allocations. As per the current classification of funds, this 
trend points towards less asset creation activities  under DHI year after year. 
Accordingly, in view of the Committee, the activiti es of DHI are gradually tilting 
towards non creative activities like winding up of CPSEs, settling dues, managing 
VRS, etc.  Though there might be a contrary view th at winding up of sick CPSEs 
also contributes indirectly to asset creation and e fficient channelisation of available

count as a productive activity.   
 
10. Accordingly, the Committee expresses its concer n over the fact that the Plan 
activities of DHI are either stagnating or getting reduced.  This would also mean 
that the Department has largely been unable to come  up with schemes necessary to 
cater to the varying needs of the extremely important Heavy Industries Sector in the 
country.  In view of the above, the Committee obser ves that DHI should strive more 
to come up with Plan schemes in a proactive manner by gauging the needs of the 
Heavy Industries Sector. Such initiatives will faci litate business environment in the 
sector.

Indian economy, the Committee, during examination o f DFG (2015-16), heard some 
select Auto Associations.    
 
19. During the interaction, the Committee came acro ss the following issues and 
demands: 
 According to the Associations, while considering F TAs, the Government should

NATRiP 
 
 
21. The National Automotive Testing R & D Infrastru cture Project (NATRiP), 
approved by the Government in 2005, envisaged setti ng up of world-class automotive 
testing and homologation facilities in India with a  total investment of Rs.  1,718 crore. 
However, right from its inception, the execution of  the NATRiP has been badly delayed 
and has suffered cost escalation due to several rea sons.  The project got extended to 2012  
and thereafter, the Cabinet again extended the time  line for completion of the project up 
to 31 
st  December, 2014.  The revised cost of the project w hich was to be completed by 
December 2014 was Rs. 2288.06 crore. But the Commit tee notes with extreme concern 
that the completion of NATRiP still needed time.   
 
22. In reply to a question regarding reasons which necessitated further extension of 
time for completion and the cost escalation, DHI su bmitted that initially scheduled date 
of completion of NATRiP project was April, 2011, wh ich was extended to December, 
2012 and further to December, 2014.  The proposal f or further extension till December 
2017 was under process. The project had faced hurdl es in the initial stages on account of 
delays in acquisition of land at various sites, del ays in clearances, shifting of utilities, 
contractual complications, etc. First Revised Cost Estimate (RCE-I) of NATRIP was 
approved by CCEA in April, 2011 at Rs.2288.06 crore . During the implementation of the 
project as per RCE-I approval, it was observed that  the escalation for land cost and the 

increased cost of Civil and Infrastructure works fo r the project were captured only 
partially and there was also foreign exchange variation during the period including delays 
in implementation. The RCE-II proposal of NATRIP wi th proposed cost at Rs.3827.30 
crore with the revised date of completion of the pr oject as 31 st  December, 2017 is under 
the consideration and will be shortly submitted to CCEA for approval. 
  Main reasons for cost overrun were:  
• Increase due to price escalation (Rs.80.80 cr.),  
• Foreign exchange variation (Rs.115.09 cr.),  
• Change in scope (Rs.75.88 cr.),  
• Additions/deletions (Rs.247.23 cr.),  
• Under estimation of certain items in RCE-I (Rs.190.28 cr.),  
• Land acquisition (Rs.145.45 cr.) and  
• Other reasons (Rs.684.51 cr. mainly due to terminat ion of M/s. IVRCL 
contracts for non-performance at risk and cost basis.   
 
23. During 2014-15, an amount of Rs 241.91 crore was released to NATRIP till Oct. 
2014. Since the project completion date expired on 31.12.2014, further fund could not be 
released to NATRIP. As part of the examination of D FG 2015-16, the Department 
submitted before the Committee that Rs 300 Crore ha s been earmarked to NATRiP as 
loan during 2015-16. 
 
24. The Committee notes with apprehension that NATR iP, which was originally 
thought to be completed in 6 years from 2005, after  the expiry of two extensions 
spanning three years from 2012 to 2014, still needs  three more years, i.e., upto 2017, 
for completion.  Having taken cognizance of all sta ted reasons for delays, the 
Committee, still feels that even a flagship project  like NATRiP, which has delivered 
a lot of unprecedented results, could not escape ti me and cost overruns which are 
typical banes of the Indian administrative system.  The Committee is of the 
considered opinion that NATRiP sans the delays woul d have produced more 
spectacular results. Therefore, the Committee recom mends that every effort should 
be made to successfully wind up the project by the current period of extension being 
sought.  The details of the completion of NATRiP sh ould be presented to the 
Committee in the form of a comprehensive Status Report.

25. The Scheme for Testing Infrastructure and R & D  Projects for Electric Vehicles 
aims to achieve national fuel security by promoting  hybrid and electric vehicles in the

and electric vehicles to become the first choice fo r the purchasers so that these vehicles 
can replace the conventional vehicles and thus redu ce liquid fuel consumption in the 
country from the automobile sector. It is expected to save 9500 Million Liters of crude oil

Heavy Industry under National Electric Mobility Mission Plan (NEMMP) 2020 approved

st  April 2015 onwards. The Govt. has

implemented over a 2 year period, i.e, FY 2015-16 and FY 2016-17 commencing from 1 
st

Capital Goods Sector 
 
 
31. The Capital Goods Sector (CGS) provides the bas e for a strong, resilient and 
vibrant manufacturing sector.  An effective manufac turing sector is essential for the 
prudent economic growth of the country.  Basic infr astructure buildup is also dependent 
on the products of the CGS.  Besides, the sector al so creates a considerable amount of 
employment opportunities.  The performance of CGS i s vital for DHI as they overlook 
the sector in India and is also in administrative c ontrol of some of the largest CPSEs of 
India that are big stakeholder in the sector. The C GS in India saw a growth of 4.9% 
during April-November 2014-15 as compared to the gr owth of -0.1% during the 
corresponding period of the last year.  
 
32. As part of the DFG examination of DHI for the y ear 2015-16, the Committee 
sought the views of major Industry associations cat ering to the sector.  The interaction 
brought forth the concern and expectations of the v arious private players in the CGS.  
Their demands included efficient and expedient impl ementation of Scheme for 
Enhancement of Competitiveness in Capital Goods Ind ustry, Purchase Preference 
Mechanism by Government and Public Sector Enterpris es for Indian companies, creation 
of level playing field for the domestic CGS in the wake of FTAs, regulation of import of 
second hand equipment, development of manufacturing  cluster and zones, demand 

creation in the power sector through enhanced publi c and private investment.  Further, 
the need for Skill Development /Skilled manpower, rectification of inverted customs duty 
structure, making transfer of technology to Indian partner mandatory, in cases of large 
imports of machinery, setting up of Technology Acqu isition Fund and Centres of 
Excellences were also stressed as the requirements of the sector.  
 
33. Regarding the dynamics of the sector, in the ov erall economy, it was 
submitted to the Committee, that whenever an econom y undergoes a bit of 
recession, this sector was the first area to be eff ected and when there is a recovery, 
this is the sector which recovers last.  Considerin g this and the fact that the CGS is 
one of the most important contributors to national growth, the Committee 
recommends that DHI should explore the possibility of acting upon the suggestions 
made by the Industrial associations and provide a r eport to the Committee on the 
basis of a detailed feasibility examination.  
 
34. In this regard the Committee further recommends tha t along with skill 
Development, the Department should consider and pro mote the system of 
apprenticeship programmes on the lines of similar a pproaches being followed in 
nations like Japan and China.  Also, the establishm ent of Centers of Excellence with 
participation of Universities, so that small player s of the  industry sectors who 
cannot invest large sums of money on R&D can also be benefited with such facilities. 
 
Scheme for Enhancement of Competiveness in Capital Goods Industry 
 
 
35. The Scheme for Enhancement of Competitiveness i n the Capital Goods Sector 
aims to make the Indian Capital Goods sector global ly competitive by addressing the issues of 
lack of technology and innovation, lack of industry  academia connectivity for technology 
development, non-availability of adequate infrastru ctural facility on value chain in 
manufacturing, absence of test and certification ce ntres etc. The Scheme envisages 
infrastructural intervention through Scheme components like setting up of (i) Centre of 
Excellence for technology development, (ii) Integra ted industrial infrastructure centre, 

(iii) Common Engineering Facility centre   (iv) Tes t & Certification centre and (v) 
Technology Acquition Fund.  
 
36. The Scheme, with an outlay of Rs. 2360 crore wa s proposed to Planning 
Commission in 2012- 13, i.e, during the 1 
st  year of the 12 th  Five Year Plan (2012-17). 
DHI proposed a requirement of Rs.10, 600.26 crore a s Plan budgetary support including 
the scheme of capital goods.  However, Planning Com mission on 4.1.2013 allocated only 
Rs. 4680 crore to DHI for the 12 th  plan.  This led to a drastic reduction of Plan bud getary 
support for the scheme to Rs. 581.22 crore.  Howeve r, in January, 2015 the Planning 
Commission had approved the scheme in principle. 
 
37. Regarding the delay in the approval of the sche me, DHI submitted that the 
process for obtaining approval of the Expenditure F inance Committee (EFC) was 
initiated soon after the Planning Commission commun icated it’s ‘in principle approval’.  
In a review meeting chaired by the then Secretary, HI  on 20.3.2013 it was decided to 
visit Indian Institutes of Technology (Delhi, Mumba i and Madras) to explore the 
possibilities of their intervention for technology development in collaboration with the 
domestic capital goods industry.  After interaction s with Indian Institutes of Technology 
(IITs) and  Federation of Indian Chambers of Commer ce and Industry (FICCI) on 
Technology Acquisition Fund, a  draft memorandum fo r EFC was circulated on 5.9.2013 
to the concerned Ministries/ Departments / Organiza tions with approval of the then 
Minister of Heavy Industries & Public Enterprises. After receiving comments/ views 
from the concerned Ministries/ Departments/ Organiz ations note for EFC was finalized 
and sent to Ministry of Finance on 17.1.2014.  The EFC considered and approved the 
proposal in its meeting dated 26.2.2014.  However, minutes of the meeting was received 
in DHI only on 23.4.2014.  DHI agreed to comments/ recommendations of the EFC, with 
the exception that funding by GoI for Test and Cert ification Centre should be 100% as 
opposed to EFC recommendation of limiting governmen t contribution to 80% of the 
project cost. Since there has been a deviation  fro m EFC recommendations before 
approaching (CCEA), it was decided to circulate the  draft Cabinet Committee on 
Economic Affairs (CCEA) note to the concerned Minis tries/ Department/ Organizations 
inviting their comments/ views. After obtaining com ments and views the proposal on the 

scheme was sent to CCEA on 25.8.2014.  CCEA approve d the scheme with an outlay of 
Rs.930.96 crore (budgetary support Rs.581.22 crore and industry support Rs.349.74 
crore) on 15.9.2014.  The scheme was notified in the Gazette of India on 5.11.2014. 
 
38. For the current financial year, out of two proj ects approved by the Apex Committee 
formed under the scheme, 1 st  installment of Grant-in-Aid was likely to be paid to the project 
implementing authority. For infrastructural components, except technology &  
certification centre, Government funding will be li mited to 80% of the individual 
project cost. Test and Certification Centre for ear thmoving machinery will be fully 
funded by the Government. For technology acquisition fund programme, Governme nt 
contribution will be limited to 25% of the cost of acquisition/ transfer of technology subject to 
a maximum of Rs.10 crore in each case. 
 
39. During the oral evidence, when queried about th e scaling down of the originally 
conceived much larger allocation and provision of o nly a meager amount of Rs.25 crore 
for the year 2015-16, the Department submitted that  the scheme at present was a pilot 
scheme, but was initially conceived with a much wid er proposal.  It was also informed 
that there were several proposals under the scheme and DHI had chalked out a roadmap 
for obtaining proposal for incurring expenditure un der the scheme.  Further, it was also 
informed by DHI that a large number of Small & Medi um Enterprises (SMEs) in the 
private sector have come forward   enthusiastically, for the scheme.   
 
40. The Committee notes that though the scheme was originally proposed during 
2012-13, the final approval has come through only i n August, 2014.  Meanwhile, the 
original proposed outlay of Rs. 2360 crore has been  reduced to a Plan Budgetary 
support of only Rs. 581.22 crore.  This scaling dow n of fund indicates that the 
original span of activities planned under the schem e has also been shrunk.  In view 
of this, the Committee expresses its apprehension a bout the adequacy of the 
dispensation under the scheme.  Even so, the Commit tee recommends that DHI 
should work towards the effective implementation of  the scheme as approved now, 
without allowing the usual administrative and proce dural delays to creep in, 
resulting in under performance of scheme.  

 
R&D Project for “Development of Advanced Ultra Supe rcritical (Adv. USC) 
Technology for Thermal Power Plants”  
 
41. It has been submitted to the Committee that the  R&D Project for “Development 
of Advanced Ultra Supercritical (Adv. USC) Technolo gy for Thermal Power Plants” 
will be carried out jointly by BHEL, Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research and 
NTPC. The objective of the First Phase of the proje ct is to undertake R&D on all 
aspects of Adv.USC technology for thermal power pla nts in order to improve power 
plant efficiency, reduce carbon-dioxide emissions a nd reduce coal consumption per 
unit of power generated.  The Thermal efficiency of  Power Plant was expected to go 
up from 38% to 45% and it would reduce the CO2 emis sion per MW substantially. 
The proposed project would enable Indian industries  to design, manufacture and 
commission higher efficiency coal fired power plant s with indigenously developed 
technology and manufacturing process. The duration of the project is estimated to be 
of two and a half years from the date of approval. 
 
42. The Ministry of Finance has approved the propos al for providing one time 
budgetary support of Rs. 1100 Crore spread over a p eriod of three years, commencing 
from 2014-15, to be provided as plan Gross Budgetar y Support to BHEL for 
implementation of the R&D project for Development o f Advanced Ultra Supercritical 
(AUSC) Technology for Thermal Power Plants, on a Mi ssion Mode. Advanced copy of 
final CCEA Note, approved by Minister of Heavy Indu stries & Public Enterprises has 
been sent to PMO & Cabinet Secretariat on 26.02.201 5. Final CCEA Note would be sent 
to Cabinet Secretariat, for obtaining approval of C CEA, following the extant instructions 
in the matter. After final approval of CCEA, action  may be taken for implementation of 
the project.  
 
43. While examining the Budgetary allocation (2015- 16) to the scheme, the 
Committee sought explanation for the reduced allocations at RE (2014-15)  to Rs 13.23 
crore from Rs 100 crore at BE (2014-15) and also ab out the proposal of being allocated 
only Rs 50 crore at BE (2015-16), half of the amoun t of the previous BE. The 
Department replied that initially it was presumed t hat the approval of Cabinet 

Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA) for the projec t could be obtained in the 3 rd  
quarter and Rs.100 crore could be utilised for the project.  Therefore, in the BE 2014-
15 allocation of Rs.100 crore was made for the proj ect.  However, subsequently at the 
RE stage, it was felt that approval of CCEA for the  project could have been possible in 
the 4 th  quarter of financial year 2014-15. Hence, as per t he guidelines issued by the 
Ministry of Finance for utilisation of funds in the  4 th  quarter of the financial year, the 
allocation of funds for the project was reduced to Rs.13.23 crore in the RE 2014-15. 
For the year 2015-16, while the Department had soug ht an allocation of Rs 583 crore, 
the Ministry of Finance had allocated only Rs 50 crore. 
 
44. The Committee notes that Advance Ultra Supercri tical Technology is the 
technology of the future in thermal power generatio n.  Higher plant efficiency and 
lesser coal consumption along with reduced carbon f ootprints are its salient 
features.  The Committee is of the considered opini on that if developed quickly it 
can help BHEL acquire a definite advantage over its  competitors in the domestic as 
well as international markets. Accordingly, the Com mittee views this as an 
endeavour that can give a fillip to BHEL in it’s st rive for recapturing lost ground in 
terms of its core business of thermal power plants.   Indigenous development of this 
technology will also give the nation an impetus in its infrastructural development.  
But, being an advanced technology, its development will need financial support 
from the Government, along with quickened process of approvals. 
 
45. However, the Committee finds that the approval for the scheme is yet to 
come about and has already suffered procedural dela ys.  Further, the Committee 
also takes note of the fact that as the approvals is still pending, the fund allocation to 
the scheme for the year 2015-16, is only Rs.50 cror e, against the demand of Rs.583 
crore,.  Regarding cost escalation, the Committee n otes that there has been no cost 
escalation till March, 2015.  However, the Committe e apprehends that further delay 
might lead to cost overrun and will also diminish t he magnitude of advantage it can 
provide to BHEL.  In view of the above, the Committ ee recommends that DHI 
should try to secure the necessary approval for the scheme as soon as possible.  Also, 
the Ministry of Finance should be impressed upon fo r timely allocation of the 

required funds as the entire project has to be comp leted in Mission Mode within the 
set time frame of two and a half years from the date of approval.

also like to observe that earnest pursuit of the R& D project for Development of 
Advance Ultra Super Critical Technology for Thermal  Power Plants will also help 
BHEL to stay a cut above their competitors. The Com mittee also observes that DHI 
should extend maximum assistance to BHEL in this matter.  
 
 Also, the Committee is happy to observe that BHEL i s making use of the

 Jagdishpur Paper Mill 
 
 
65. Jagdishpur Paper Mills Ltd. (JPML) was incorpor ated during the year 2008 after 
CCEA approval, for setting up a modern paper mill t o manufacture 3,00,000 tonnes of 
quality Writing & Printing Paper. The estimated cost of setting up this plant was Rs. 3700 
crores. Since the date of incorporation, not much p hysical, tangible activity could be 
made as the land was not allotted by Govt. of U.P. Meanwhile, attempts were made to 
reconfigure the project keeping in view the raw mat erial availability as well as the 
infrastructure, by getting a revised DPR prepared t hrough a renowned consultant. After 

receipt of the DPR, a fresh proposal incorporating therein the usage of substitute raw 
material was made. CCEA approvals have been obtaine d during the financial year 2012-
13. After pursuing vigorously all these years for g etting the required land at Jagdishpur a 
breakthrough could finally be made only during the year 2013. Jagdishpur Paper Mill Ltd 
(JPML) was allotted 187.59 acres of land by UP Stat e Industrial Development 
Corporation (UPSIDC) at Industrial Area Utelwa, Jag dishpur, Amethi District, UP. 
Pursuant to the allotment order cited above, JPML h ad paid EMD of Rs.11.8 Crores, 
towards the allotment of 187.59 Acres of Land and a n MoU was signed on  14.12.13 
between  UPSIDC and JPML. 
 
66. Subsequently, it was learnt from UPSIDC that Ka mala Neheru Memorial Trust 
has filed writ petition before the Hon’ble High Cou rt Lucknow Bench against allotment 
of land and the Hon’ble High Court had passed an or der dt.27.11.13 which states as 
follows:- 
           “as a interim measure we direct the part ies to maintain status quo as it exists   
today. The respondents shall ensure no construction  is raised over the land in question by 
fresh allottee. Allotment made shall be subject to further orders passed by this court.”  
 
67. Considering that the matter regarding allotment  of land to JPM is sub- judice and 
was pending before the Hon’ble Supreme court and also the fact that the project itself had 
the CCEA approval in the year 2008, the Committee s ought to know the timeframe 
further required for the commencement of the Greenf ield Pulp and Paper project at 
Jagdishpur under HPC.  The Committee also wanted to  know the possibility of 
considering an alternate location for the Mill.  In  reply, the Department stated that it 
appears the even after the present  legal battle, t here was a likelihood of litigation in the 
future from the farmers cultivating the land and the encroachers of the allotted land as the 
same is not free from encumbrances as per the averm ents made by Kamala Nehru Trust 
(KNT).  
 
68. The present litigating parties i.e. Kamala Nehr u Trust and UPSIDC have been 
fighting the legal battle from the year 2007. Recen tly, UPSIDC has communicated an 
offer to procure land from farmers and allot to JPML, if JPML was agreeable to the offer. 

The said offer of acquisition of land and allotting  the same after acquisition also may not 
be free from litigation and also quite time consumi ng. Under the circumstances, DHI has 
informed that it was not be possible to give a defi nite time frame for settlement of 
litigation and acquisition of land without encumbrances in a case wherein JPML was only 
an impleaded party and as such the settlement of li tigation would much depend on the 
main litigation parties i.e. Kamala Nehru Trust and UPSIDC. Meanwhile, attempts to find 
alternate sites to locate the project duly consider ing the raw material availability, and 
other infrastructure, were being made. 
 
69. The Committee takes note of the fact that the Green field Pulp and Paper 
Mill project at Jagdishpur, estimated at Rs. 3700 crore in 2008, has not taken off the 
ground as on date due to litigation regarding allot ment of land for the project at the 
designated site. The matter being sub judice, the C ommittee refrains from making a 
comment in this regard. Nevertheless, the Committee  recommends that nothing 
should stop the Department from earnestly exploring  the possibility of establishing 
the Mill at an alternate location taking into accou nt factors like raw material 
availability and other linkages. The Committee is o f the considered opinion that it is 
unacceptable to let an important project worth Rs. 3700 crore linger on indefinitely 
without its operationalisation being expected in near future.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE-AT A 
GLANCE  
 
1. During the oral evidence in connection with the exa mination of Demands for 
Grants  (DFG) 2015-16, it was submitted before the Committe e that the problems 
related to Coal linkage, delayed environmental clea rness and low demand had a 
negative impact on the performance of CPSEs dealing  in Heavy Industries Sector.  
However, the Committee expects a better performance  from the CPSEs of DHI as 
the teething issues like coal availability which ha s been hampering the growth of the 
power sector is being resolved through successful c oal block allocations.  This 
coupled with the favorable initiatives like the ‘Ma ke in India’ campaign of the 
Government can be presumed to provide the CPSEs of DHI with a conducive 
environment to regain the lost ground. 
(Para No 5) 
2. Further, the Committee observes that NPPC has ha d ‘Nil’ performance for 
the past four years and is not expected to open its  account even in 2015-16.  
However, it has been submitted that BIFR has given the final approval for the 
Modified Draft Rehabilitation Scheme (MDRS) for NPP C and the Revival process 
of the company will be completed by November, 2016.   The Committee wants to be 
informed of the progress in this regard. 
(Para No 6) 
 
3. Continuing the trend that can be observed over t he last two years, the 
Committee finds that for the year 2015-16 too DHI h as been given lesser Plan funds 
compared to the Non Plan allocations. As per the current classification of funds, this 
trend points towards less asset creation activities  under DHI year after year. 
Accordingly, in view of the Committee, the activiti es of DHI are gradually tilting 
towards non creative activities like winding up of CPSEs, settling dues, managing 
VRS, etc.  Though there might be a contrary view th at winding up of sick CPSEs 
also contributes indirectly to asset creation and e fficient channelisation of available 
resources, as per extant classification of Plan and  Non Plan activities, it does not 
count as a productive activity.   
(Para No 9) 

 
4. Accordingly, the Committee expresses its concern  over the fact that the Plan 
activities of DHI are either stagnating or getting reduced.  This would also mean 
that the Department has largely been unable to come  up with schemes necessary to 
cater to the varying needs of the extremely important Heavy Industries Sector in the 
country.  In view of the above, the Committee obser ves that DHI should strive more 
to come up with Plan schemes in a proactive manner by gauging the needs of the 
Heavy Industries Sector. Such initiatives will faci litate business environment in the 
sector.  
(Para No 10) 
 
5. The Committee feels unhappy to note that the Pla n funds allocated for 
crucial input studies that could have benefited the  flagship schemes of DHI could 
not be undertaken due to ‘procedural formalities’.  The study and analysis could 
have shed more light on many major concerns of Capi tal Goods sector and Auto 
Component Industry. Taking the above into account a nd the fact that the Plan 
allocation to DHI has been observed to show a decre asing trend, the Committee 
recommends that the Department should take proactiv e steps to carryout the in-
depth study for critical analysis as well as impact  assessment of Capital Goods 
sector and Auto component Industry. The Committee i s also of the strong view that 
such studies should be done with more frequency, wh ich would in turn help DHI, 
the administrative Department of such crucial secto rs, to come up with innovative 
schemes and thus overcome the hurdles plaguing their sector.       
(Para No 13) 
 
 
6. The Committee observes that there is a persisten t delay in reimbursing the 
claims of CPM of HPC. Considering the fact that the  Mill is already facing financial 
difficulties arising out of logistical challenges, the Committee recommends that DHI 
should augment the process of settling the admissib le transportation cost of CPM in 
a more efficient manner without delay, keeping in m ind that the extra cost in 
transportation is being expected to end by Septembe r, 2016.  The Committee is of 
the view that the timely settlement of the liabilit y would help CPM to start afresh 

from October, 2016 onwards, without financial backl ogs. As a CPSE, with 
considerable presence in the NER, HPC should receiv e special attention of DHI in 
its efforts to operate CPM, effectively and profitably. 
(Para No 17) 
 
 
7.  The Committee noted that though many of the problem s faced by the auto 
sector have been lingering on, the representatives of the Auto associations were 
appreciative of the initiatives taken and support p rovided by DHI. Accordingly, the 
Committee observes that the Department should furth er their efforts in this 
direction and apprise the Committee on the feasibil ity and practicality of taking 
action on the various demands placed by the associations before it.  
(Para No 20) 
 
 
8. The Committee notes with apprehension that NATRi P, which was originally 
thought to be completed in 6 years from 2005, after  the expiry of two extensions 
spanning three years from 2012 to 2014, still needs  three more years, i.e., upto 2017, 
for completion.  Having taken cognizance of all sta ted reasons for delays, the 
Committee, still feels that even a flagship project  like NATRiP, which has delivered 
a lot of unprecedented results, could not escape ti me and cost overruns which are 
typical banes of the Indian administrative system.  The Committee is of the 
considered opinion that NATRiP sans the delays woul d have produced more 
spectacular results. Therefore, the Committee recom mends that every effort should 
be made to successfully wind up the project by the current period of extension being 
sought.  The details of the completion of NATRiP sh ould be presented to the 
Committee in the form of a comprehensive Status Report.  
(Para No 24) 
 
9. The Committee notes that Faster Adoption and Man ufacturing of Electric 
Vehicles in India (FAME-India) is an ambitious sche me that aims to cater to the 
future scenario in the Automotive Industry, when fo ssil fuels become less available 

and alternative propulsion systems become inevitabl e.  Hybrid and Electrical 
vehicles would eventually become the norm of the da y.  Further, the Ministry of 
Finance has directly put the onus of efficiently im plementing and running the 
scheme on DHI, by stating that the funds for the sc heme will be allocated depending 
on the utilization of the funds already given. In t his context, the Committee 
recommends that considering the possible positive i mpact the scheme can bring 
about in a variety of areas, DHI should make all ou t efforts for its fruitful and 
timely implementation, by taking along all stakehol ders. The Committee keenly 
awaits to be appraised of the performance of the scheme, periodically.  
(Para No 29) 
 
10. Further, while deliberating on the merits of th e scheme and its impact on the 
auto industry, it was pointed out that, the Automot ive Component industry, 
catering to conventional fuel vehicles can be adver sely affected by the advent of 
electric vehicles.  Accordingly, the Committee wants DHI to address the effect of the 
introduction of Hybrid/Electrical Vehicles on the A uto Component industry 
through an impact assessment study. The Committee a lso observes that 
development of Hybrid/Electrical Vehicles entail hi gh technology inputs. Cost 
intensive battery technology and charging infrastru cture are going to be extremely 
decisive factors in the successful attainment of th e objectives of the scheme.  
Accordingly, the Committee hopes DHI will be able t o secure enough funds to 
facilitate development of the requisite high-end technology required for the scheme.  
(Para No 30) 
 
 
11. Regarding the dynamics of the sector, in the ov erall economy, it was 
submitted to the Committee, that whenever an econom y undergoes a bit of 
recession, this sector was the first area to be eff ected and when there is a recovery, 
this is the sector which recovers last.  Considerin g this and the fact that the CGS is 
one of the most important contributors to national growth, the Committee 
recommends that DHI should explore the possibility of acting upon the suggestions 

made by the Industrial associations and provide a r eport to the Committee on the 
basis of a detailed feasibility examination.  
(Para No 33) 
 
12.  In this regard the Committee further recommends tha t along with skill 
Development, the Department should consider and pro mote the system of 
apprenticeship programmes on the lines of similar a pproaches being followed in 
nations like Japan and China.  Also, the establishm ent of Centers of Excellence with 
participation of Universities, so that small player s of the industry sectors who 
cannot invest large sums of money on R&D can also be benefited with such facilities. 
(Para No 34) 
 
13. The Committee notes that though the scheme was originally proposed during 
2012-13, the final approval has come through only i n August, 2014.  Meanwhile, the 
original proposed outlay of 2360 crore has been red uced to a Plan Budgetary 
support of only Rs. 581.22 crore.  This scaling dow n of fund indicates that the 
original span of activities planned under the schem e has also been shrunk.  In view 
of this, the Committee expresses its apprehension a bout the adequacy of the 
dispensation under the scheme.  Even so, the Commit tee recommends that DHI 
should work towards the effective implementation of  the scheme as approved now, 
without allowing the usual administrative and proce dural delays to creep in, 
resulting in under performance of scheme.  
(Para No 40) 
 
14. The Committee notes that Advance Ultra Supercri tical Technology is the 
technology of the future in thermal power generatio n.  Higher plant efficiency and 
lesser coal consumption along with reduced carbon f ootprints are its salient 
features.  The Committee is of the considered opini on that if developed quickly it 
can help BHEL acquire a definite advantage over its  competitors in the domestic as 
well as international markets. Accordingly, the Com mittee views this as an 
endeavour that can give a fillip to BHEL in it’s st rive for recapturing lost ground in 
terms of its core business of thermal power plants.   Indigenous development of this 

technology will also give the nation an impetus in its infrastructural development.  
But, being an advanced technology, its development will need financial support 
from the Government, along with quickened process of approvals. 
(Para No 44) 
15. However, the Committee finds that the approval for the scheme is yet to 
come about and has already suffered procedural dela ys.  Further, the Committee 
also takes note of the fact that as the approvals is still pending, the fund allocation to 
the scheme for the year 2015-16, is only Rs.50 cror e, against the demand of Rs.583 
crore,.  Regarding cost escalation, the Committee n otes that there has been no cost 
escalation till March, 2015.  However, the Committe e apprehends that further delay 
might lead to cost overrun and will also diminish t he magnitude of advantage it can 
provide to BHEL.  In view of the above, the Committ ee recommends that DHI 
should try to secure the necessary approval for the scheme as soon as possible.  Also, 
the Ministry of Finance should be impressed upon fo r timely allocation of the 
required funds as the entire project has to be comp leted in Mission Mode within the 
set time frame of two and a half years from the date of approval.  
(Para No 45) 
 
16. Drawing inference from the discussions and the facts placed before the 
Committee, it feels that favorable conditions of bu siness are ahead for BHEL.  
Accordingly, the Committee recommends that BHEL as a Maharatana company 
should be able to fully capitalize on the expected favorable market demand owing to 
improved coal availability and the Government's pro posal to set up 5 new ultra 
Mega Power Projects. The Committee also recommends that BHEL should more 
vigorously pursue its efforts towards consolidating  its diversified areas of business 
like solar energy, defence production, etc, so as t o countervail the similar possible 
slumps in future in their area of core competence. Further, the Committee would 
also like to observe that earnest pursuit of the R& D project for Development of 
Advance Ultra Super Critical Technology for Thermal  Power Plants will also help 
BHEL to stay a cut above their competitors. The Com mittee also observes that DHI 
should extend maximum assistance is to BHEL in this matter.  
(Para No 53) 

 
 Also, the Committee is happy to observe that BHEL i s also making use of the 
slogan “Make in India’ in Hanover to invite countri es like Germany to work in 
collaboration with India to boost the quantum of business of BHEL. 
(Para No 53) 
17. The Committee views the fall in the performance  of HEC and its pathetic 
state of affairs with extreme disappointment. In it s Report on DFG (2013-14), the 
Committee had recommended that HEC, which was a shi ning example of a CPSE 
turning around with the help of a revival package, should be extended all support in 
its modernization efforts.  However, the Committee finds that two years from then, 
HEC, though has managed to prepare a Modernization plan, is still far from its 
implementation. The Committee observes that HEC, fr om a turn around champion 
has been reduced to another victim of administrativ e lethargy and managerial 
ineptitude. In view of the above, the Committee rei terates its earlier 
recommendation of extending all possible support of  DHI to the Modernizations of 
HEC by helping them in securing the portion of fund s the Company has to raise 
through loans from financial institutions /banks.  In case, HEC is unable to secure 
the same on their own within a reasonable time limi t, DHI should even considering 
enhancing the budgetary assistance of Rs. 500 crore  appropriately.  The Committee 
is also not averse to resorting to foreign collabor ation for the Modernization of 
HEC.  However, the solution to the problems faced b y HEC has to come before the 
Company goes beyond the point of recovery. 
(Para No 58) 
18. Taking into account the present problems being face d by the company, the 
Target set by HEC for achievements during 2014-15, and 2015-16, the Committee is 
of the considered opinion that these are unreasonab ly high, especially, when during 
2014-15, they could attain only one fourth of the s et target. Therefore, the 
Committee recommends, that under the circumstance HEC should set only realistic, 
attainable targets for itself. 
(Para No 59) 

19. The Committee observes that R&C was referred to  the BIFR almost quarter 
a century ago, in 1992, but, now DHI has agreed tha t the latest revival plan of R&C 
can be implemented since it does not involve any cash assistance and the Company’s 
activities can be considered as the core activities of economy falling under the ‘Make 
in India’ campaign. In this context, the Committee recommends the DHI should 
expeditiously place the revival of R&C for approval  of the Cabinet and help the 
company in its road to revival.  
(Para No 64) 
 
20. The Committee takes note of the fact that the Green field Pulp and Paper 
Mill project at Jagdishpur, estimated at Rs. 3700 crore in 2008, has not taken off the 
ground as on date due to litigation regarding allot ment of land for the project at the 
designated site. The matter being sub judice, the C ommittee refrains from making a 
comment in this regard. Nevertheless, the Committee  recommends that nothing 
should stop the Department from earnestly exploring  the possibility of establishing 
the Mill at an alternate location taking into accou nt factors like raw material 
availability and other linkages. The Committee is o f the considered opinion that it is 
unacceptable to let an important project worth Rs. 3700 crore linger on indefinitely 
without its operationalisation being expected in near future. 
(Para No 69)
