Report  
 
 
Introduction 
 
 
 Public sector units are hailed as ‘the temples of modern India.’ Government of 
India has employed the public sector enterprises to  achieve various socio-economic 
objectives. The basic difference between private an d public ownership is the difference 
lies in their objectives, viz welfare maximization by the public sector and profi t 
maximization by the private sector. The Central Pub lic Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) 
comprise enterprises established by the Government of India (GOI) as Government 
companies under Section 617 of the Companies Act, a nd wherein the equity holding of 
the GOI is more than 50 per cent. It also includes statutory corporations constituted under 
specific statutes of the Parliament. The CPSEs do n ot, however, include departmental 
undertakings, banking institutions and enterprises where equity holding of the GOI is 
50% or less.  
 
2. As per the Public Enterprises Survey (2013-14), there were 290 Central Public 
Sector Enterprises consisting of 234 operating CPSE s and 56 CPSEs under construction 
as on 31.3.2014.  The turnover of all 234 operating  CPSEs during 2013-14 stood at Rs. 
20, 61,866 crore as compared to Rs. 19, 45,814 cror e of 230 operating CPSEs in the 
previous year. The list of 64 Schedule ‘A’, 68 Sche dule ‘B’, 46 Schedule ‘C’ and 4 
Schedule ‘D’ CPSEs is placed at Annexure-I.  Also, the list containing names of the  7  
Maharatna, 17 Navratna and 72 Miniratna CPSEs is kept at Annexure-II.  
 
Department of Public Enterprises (DPE)  
Mandate  
 
3. The DPE is the nodal department for all the Cent ral Public Sector Enterprises and 
formulates policy pertaining to CPSEs.  Mandate of DPE as submitted to the Committee, 
lays down policy guidelines on performance improvem ent and evaluation, autonomy and 
financial delegation  and personnel management in CPSEs. Furthermore, it  collects and 
maintains information on several areas in respect of CPSEs.  
 

4.         The Committee was also informed that as per Allocation of Business Rules of the 
Government, the following include the functions all ocated to the Department of Public 
Enterprises:- 
 
i) Bureau of Public Enterprises including Industria l Management Pool. 
 
ii)     Coordination of matters of general policy o f  non-financial  nature       
affecting all public sector industrial and commercial undertakings. 
 
iii)     Matters relating to Memorandum of Understa nding mechanism of 
improving the performance of public sector undertakings. 
 
iv)       Matters relating to Permanent Machinery o f Arbitration for the Public 
Sector Undertakings. 
 
v)        Counselling, Retraining and Rehabilitatio n of employees in Central Public 
Sector Undertakings under Voluntary Retirement Scheme. 
 
 
5. The Board for Reconstruction of Public Sector Enterprises (BRPSE) was set up in 
December, 2004 to consider inter-alia , Revival/Restructuring proposals of Sick/Loss 
making CPSEs and make suitable recommendations rela ted thereto. The DPE provides 
secretariat support to BRPSE. 
  
6. In fulfilling its role, the Department coordinat es with other Ministries, CPSEs and 
concerned organization.  Some of the important task s of the Department are listed as 
follows: 
 
i)  Co-ordination of matters of general policy of non-financial  nature relating 
to Public Sector Enterprises. 
 
ii)  Issue of Presidential Directives and Guidelines to Public Sector 
Enterprises. 
 
iii)  Publication of the annual survey of CPSEs known as Public Enterprises 
Survey. 
 
iv)  Memorandum of Understanding between the Public Sector Enterprises and 
the Administrative Ministries/Departments. 
 
v)  Formulation of policies pertaining to Public Sector  Enterprises in areas 
like Board Structures, Personnel Management, Performance Improvement, 

Financial Management , Wage Settlement and Vigilance management, 
etc.   
 
vi)  Matters relating to reservation of posts in the Pub lic sector Enterprises for 
certain classes of citizens. 
 
vii)  Policy relating to Voluntary Retirement Scheme in CPSEs. 
 
viii)  Matters relating to Counseling, Retraining and Rede ployment Scheme 
(CRR) for rationalized employees of CPSEs. 
 
ix)  Investiture and review of Maharatana / Navratana / Miniratna status to 
CPSEs. 
 
x)  Policy matters relating to composition of Board of Directors of CPSEs, 
Categorization of top posts Scheduling of CPSEs.  
 
xi)  Notification of Pay Scales of Board level executive s as well as below 
Board level personnel and unionized workers and the  DA admissible 
thereon at periodic intervals. 
 
xii)  Policy relating to deputation of Government officer s to Public Sector 
Enterprises. 
 
xiii)  Matters relating to reservation of posts in the Pub lic sector Enterprises for 
certain classes of citizens. 
 
xiv)  Settlement of disputes through Permanent Machinery of Arbitration 
(PMA) among Public Sector Enterprises and between P ublic Sector 
Enterprises and Government Departments except dispu tes relating to tax 
matters. 
 
xv)  Matters relating to International Centre for Promot ion of Enterprises 
(ICPE).  
 
xvi)  Matters relating to Standing Conference of Public Enterprises (SCOPE). 
 
xvii)  Matters relating to delegation of powers to Board of Directors.  
 
xviii)  Matters relating to Board for Reconstruction of Pub lic Sector Enterprises 
(BRPSE). 
 
7. The Committee notes that as per the Allocation o f Business Rules, the 
functions of DPE includes inter-alia  ` Coordination of matters of general policy of 
non-financial 
 nature affecting all public sector industrial and commercial 

undertakings'.  However, as per the submission made  before the Committee during 
the oral evidence relating to the examination of De mands for Grants (DFG)  (2015-
16), the functions of DPE includes laying down of p olicy guidelines on autonomy 
and financial  delegation.  Similar dichotomous position regarding  the mandate of 
DPE on financial matter is also reflected in the Ou tcome Budget of the Ministry of 
Heavy Industries & Public Enterprises.  This incong ruence was pointed out during 
the oral evidence of DPE and a clarification was so ught.  But DPE did not provide 
the requisite information either at the meeting or in their subsequent written replies 
to the queries raised during the meeting.   
 
8. In this context, the Committee recommends that t he ambiguity regarding the 
functions of DPE relating to whether the Department  is tasked to frame 
policies/guidelines relating to financial matters n eeds to be addressed immediately.  
Accordingly, the action taken in this direction sho uld be intimated to the 
Committee.  
 
Demand for Grants (DFG)

up of proposed Planned Revenue Expenditure and the Non-Planned Revenue Expenditure

11. The Committee notes that in the year 2013-14, t he Non Plan Allocation of DPE 
was only slightly lesser than their Plan allocation at the BE stage.  During the revision for 

the period, the Non Plan figures overtook the plan money.  While considering the Actual

utilized in its entirety, the Plan fund utilisation  was only Rs. 6.41 crore out of Rs. 8.25

crore and Rs. 9.82 crore, which at the RE stage is shown as Rs.5.00 crore and Rs.9.00 
crore, respectively. That is, though the Plan funds  were reduced by almost 40%, the Non 
Plan fund nearly remained the same.  For the curren t financial year, the Non Plan 
allocations have exceeded the Plan allocation, keeping the figures at Rs.10 crore and Rs.9

12. The Committee observes that during 2013-14, the Non  Plan allocation 
exceeded only at the RE stage.  Whereas in 2014-15 and 2015-16, the Non Plan 
allocations can be seen to exceed Plan allocation a t the BE stage, itself.  During 
2014-15, the Plan figures at BE which were already less than Non Plan figures, were 
drastically slashed at RE.  The Committee views thi s trend of Plan allocation being 
kept lower than Non Plan allocation as highly undes irable.  Especially when that 
Non Plan expenses of DPE almost entirely consist of  the expenses to run the 
Department.  Further, it is also not encouraging to  find that the Plan allocations of 
DPE have remained stagnant over the years.  From th is, the Committee infers that 
DPE has not been able to come up with enough new Pl an schemes, which would 
have had a facilitating impact in the realm of CPSEs in India.

the number of employees in CPSEs came down from 140 1519 in 2012-13 to 1351306 in

15. The effective reduction of number of employees was 50,213.  In this regard 
the Committee wants to know how the total number of employees has come down by

17. The salient policy initiatives/achievements of DPE during the 12 
th  FYP till now 
have been given below:- 
(i) Corporate Governance & Personnel Management:  DPE a fter consultation 
of stakeholders issued model role & responsibilitie s for non-official Directors of CPSEs. 
The Department has taken the initiative to conduct capacity building programmes for 
non-official and Government Directors of CPSEs in t he context of provisions of newly 
enacted Companies Act, 2013. DPE has also taken act ion to sensitise CPSEs regarding 
professionalization of below Board level management in CPSEs. 
 
(ii) MoU system: The Department after consideration of s uggestions received 
from administrative Ministries/Departments, CPSEs a nd recommendations of external 

studies/evaluation of the MoU system made significant changes in the MoU guidelines in 
2013. These include interalia greater flexibility t o CPSEs to select parameters suitable to 
their nature of operations, common format formulate d for CPSEs (except sick and loss 
making, Section 25 and under construction CPSEs), s ick & loss making CPSEs included 
in their domain syndicate, greater emphasis on CAPEX and project implementation etc.  
 
(iii) Corporate Social Responsibility: Department of Publ ic Enterprises (DPE) 
had issued first guidelines on Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) to the Central Public 
Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) in April, 2010, which were revised as Guidelines on CSR and 
Sustainability and issued to CPSEs in April, 2013. After the enactment of the Companies 
Act, 2013 and the coming into force of the provisio ns of Section 135 of Companies Act, 
2013 on CSR and rules framed there under by the M/o  Corporate Affairs, (MCA) DPE 
has issued Guidelines on Corporate Social Responsib ility (CSR) & Sustainability-2014 
for Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) in Oc tober, 2014. These Guidelines are 
aligned with the provisions of Companies Act, 2013 on CSR, the Companies (CSR 
Policy) Rules 2014 notified by M/o Corporate Affair s under the provisions of the Act, 
and Schedule-VII of the Act, and are intended to re inforce the complementarily of CSR 
and Sustainability and to advise the CPSEs not to o verlook the larger objective of

28. Realizing the need to have a safety net for the  separated employees, Government

st  March 2001. Since 2001-02,

29. The objective and scope of the CRR scheme is to  provide opportunities of to the 
separated employees who are rendered surplus as a r esult of modernization, technology 
upgradation and manpower restructuring in the PSEs.  The aim of retraining of the 
employees is to reorient them through short duratio n training programmes to enable them 

to adjust to the new environment and adopt new avocations after their separation from the 
PSEs due to VRS/VSS or retrenchment due to closure / restructuring of the enterprise.

interested; (ii) Extended duration of training from  20/30/40 days to 30/45/60 days with 
revised expenditure norms; and (iii) Dedicated amou nt earmarked in the expenditure 
norm for follow-up of trained VRS optees.

Board for Reconstruction of Public Sector Enterprises (BPRSE) 
 
 
45. The Government constituted BPRSE  vide  Resolution dated 6 th  December, 2004 as 
an advisory body to address the task of strengtheni ng, modernizing, reviving, and 

restructuring of CPSEs and to advise the Government  on strategies, measures and 
schemes related to them. 
 
46. Regarding the process of revival/ restructuring  of sick CPSEs it was earlier 
submitted before the Committee that proposals are f irst sent to BRPSE; they appraise 
them and make appropriate recommendations. The reco mmendation then, through the 
Department, goes to the Cabinet. Cabinet approves a  package to be presented before the 
Board for Industrial and Financial Reconstruction (BIFR). It is the BIFR award which has 
statutory force for all sick companies. So, BIFR is  the final body as far as sick companies 
are concerned. On this, the Committee, in its Repor t on Demands for Grants 2012-13, 
brought to the notice of the Department that the fu nctioning of BRPSE is adversely 
impacted by the fact that for every small thing the  sick companies have to approach 
BIFR. Further, recommendations of BIFR were given i mportance over the 
recommendations of BRPSE due to its statutory backi ng. Accordingly, this Committee 
recommended that when National Company Law Tribunal  (NCLT) was put in place of 
BIFR, its mandate should avoid any duplication of work with BRPSE. The Department in 
its Action Taken Note (ATN) assured the Committee t hat its recommendation would be 
represented appropriately at the time of constitution of the new body.  
 
47. During the examination of the DFG for 2015-16 o f DPE it was submitted that the 
NCLT has not been constituted yet as the matter is sub-judice in Supreme Court. Further, 
during the oral evidence of DFG 2015-16, when enqui red about the status of the proposal 
currently under the consideration of the Government  on the replacement of BRPSE with 
a new entity, DPE failed to respond.  
 
48 . The Committee understands that the BIFR and BRPSE, two pivotal 
organizations engaged in the process of revival / restructuring of CPSEs in India are 
reported to be replaced in the near future.  The Co mmittee views these proposed 
changes as a potential watershed in the area of revival /restructuring of CPSEs.  The 
Committee recalls that during their co-existence ti ll now, owing to certain overlaps 
and conflicts in the roles essayed by BIFR and BRPS E in approaching the revival 
/restructuring proposals of CPSEs, the cases of rev ival/restructuring suffered 

avoidable delays. Accordingly, in the backdrop of t he proposed replacement of 
BRPSE and BIFR, the Committee would like to further  reiterate its earlier stand 
and recommend that the every care should be taken t o avoid conflicts and overlaps 
in the role assigned to the new entity of BRPSE and  the NCLT which has been 
conceived to replacing BIFR. Further, the new agenc ies should be conceived in such 
a manner that the revival /restructuring of CPSEs s hall be completed in a 
prescribed timeframe without lingering for years.

justification of the amount being spent by the rele vant agency for the training, 
specifying whether such training can be provided at  a lesser cost domestically or in 
some other international institution.  
(Para No 43) 
14. Overall the Committee is apprehensive of the im pact of such expensive 
courses at ICPE.  The Committee seeks to know if it  is Department’s considered 
position that such specialised courses are not avai lable in the country at a much 
reasonable cost.  The Committee also notes that whi le States PSU executives are 
being trained at IIM and other national institution s the executives of CPSEs are 
being sent to much costlier ICPE.  The Committee ma y be informed of such 
distinctions in training of executives of CPSEs and  States PSEs is at all desirable.  
The Committee is of the firm view that Department m uch discontinue its 
subscriptions of ICPE unless there is a very pressing necessity.   
 (Para No 44) 
 
15 . The Committee understands that the BIFR and BRPSE, two pivotal 
organizations engaged in the process of revival / restructuring of CPSEs in India are 
reported to be replaced in the near future.  The Co mmittee views these proposed 
changes as a potential watershed in the area of revival /restructuring of CPSEs.  The 
Committee recalls that during their co-existence ti ll now, owing to certain overlaps 
and conflicts in the roles essayed by BIFR and BRPS E in approaching the revival 

/restructuring proposals of CPSEs, the cases of rev ival/restructuring suffered 
avoidable delays. Accordingly, in the backdrop of t he proposed replacement of 
BRPSE and BIFR, the Committee would like to further  reiterate its earlier stand 
and recommend that the every care should be taken t o avoid conflicts and overlaps 
in the role assigned to the new entity of BRPSE and  the NCLT which has been 
conceived to replacing BIFR. Further, the new agenc ies should be conceived in such 
a manner that the revival /restructuring of CPSEs s hall be completed in a 
prescribed timeframe without lingering for years. 
(Para No 48)

INTRODUCTION 
  
  
 I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliame ntary Standing 
Committee on Industry, having been authorized by th e Committee, hereby 
present this Two Hundred Sixty Seventh Report on Ac tion Taken Note 
furnished by the Ministry of Micro, Small and Mediu m Enterprises on the 
recommendations contained in the Committee’s Two Hu ndred Fifty Ninth 
Report on Review of the implementation of Khadi and  Village Industries 
Commission (KVIC) Act, 1956.  
 
2. I thank the Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises for 
furnishing the Action Taken Note on the recommendat ions contained in the 
Committee’s Two Hundred Fifty Ninth Report. 
  
3. The Committee in its meeting held on 30 
th  July, 2015 considered and 
adopted the report. 
 
  
 
  
K.C. Tyagi 
                          
Chairman                                                                                   
                Department -related Parliamentary  
                                                                     Standing  Committee   on    Industry  
 
New Delhi 
July, 2015 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
(ii) 
 

REPORT 
 
The Action Taken Report of the Committee deals with  the Action 
Taken by the Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium En terprises on the 
recommendations contained in the Committee’s Two Hu ndred Fifty Ninth 
Report on Review of the implementation of Khadi and  Village Industries 
Commission (KVIC) Act, 1956  pertaining to the Ministry of Micro, Small and 
Medium Enterprises. 
 
2.  Action Taken Notes have been received from the Ministry of Micro, 
Small and Medium Enterprises in respect of the reco mmendations contained 
in the Report. These have been categorized as follows:  
 
Chapter –I   The recommendations/observations, which have bee n accepted 
by the Ministry. 
 The Committee is pleased to observe that the Minis try has accepted its 
recommendations as mentioned in the Chapter – I of the Report. 
 
Chapter -II   The recommendations/observations which the Commit tee does 
not desire to pursue in view of the Government's replies. 
 In respect of these recommendations the Committee is convinced with 
the logic and explanations advanced by the Ministry and therefore do not want 
to pursue them for the present. 
 
Chapter -III    The recommendations/observations in respect of w hich the 
Committee has either not accepted replies of the Mi nistry or has asked the 
Ministry to review its reply. 
 The Committee expresses its concern over the non-i mplementation of 
recommendations contained in Chapter – III and desi res that the Ministry 
should furnish logical explanations therefor. 
 
Chapter -IV    The recommendations/observations in respect of wh ich final 
replies of the Ministry have not been received. 
 In respect of recommendations placed in Chapter-IV , the Ministry has 
either furnished the interim replies or couched its language in vague terms like 
noted for compliance/guidance, therefore, the Commi ttee desires that the 
Ministry should furnish Action Taken Notes in respe cts of recommendations 
categorized in Chapter-IV in detail and to the poin t, as per the intention and 
spirit of the recommendations of the Committee. 
 
3. The details of the ATR are being discussed in the succeeding pages. 
 
 

-2- 
 
CHAPTER-I 
 
Recommendations/observations, which have been accep ted by the 
Ministry  
       
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
The Committee also recommends that like MSME Develo pment Act, 
the definition of  ‘Fixed per Capita’ investment sh ould only include plant and 
machinery and not the cost of land, work shed etc. 
(Para 31) 
Action Taken  
 
Agreed. As per the MSMED Act, a micro enterprise  is an enterprise 
where investment in plant and machinery [original c ost excluding land and 
building and the items specified by the Ministry of Small Scale Industries vide 
its notification No. S.O. 1722(E) dated October 5, 2006 does not exceed Rs. 
25 lakh. The same provision may be replicated for t he ‘Fixed per Capita’ 
investment for PMEGP. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
The Committee found an anomalous situation exists i n the Act as 
powers of the Commission under Section 4(1) have be en delegated to the 
CEO under Sections 5 (1), (1A) of the same Act and not through any 
subordinate legislation.    
(Para 36) 
Action Taken  
 
Agreed. The proposed amendment of the KVIC Act would address the issue.  
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
The Committee is of the opinion that the intent of the Act and its 
provisions is abundantly clear. The power of genera l and not specific 
supervision is given to Commission in order to ensu re its administrative 
autonomy required to facilitate its mandate. As the  Commission meets once a 
month and by implication cannot supervise day-today  affairs of the 
Commission, the Act itself empowers the CEO to supervise the day to day  

 
-3- 
 
affairs. In view of Sections 4(1), 5(1) and (1A) an d Rules 10, 11 and 12 made 
by the Central Government under Section 26, the Com mittee feels that the 
demarcation is fairly clear that Commission is esse ntially a policy making 
body and powers bestowed on it are incidental. 
 
(Para 37) 
 
Action Taken 
 
 
Agreed. The proposed amendment of the KVIC Act woul d address the 
issue. 
 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
Section 27 of the Act prescribe the Commissions pow ers to frame 
regulations thereby setting broad parameters of adm inistrative policies in 
consonance of its objectives, financial and human r esources. The CEO is 
required to carry out the administration and superv ision as per the broad 
administrative policies determined by the Commissio n through Regulations.   
The Committee is of the view that general superinte ndence on the part of 
Commission in its day-today affairs as envisaged in  Section 4(1A) is 
oxymoron. Committee accordingly recommends that tha t word “day to day” 
should be deleted. Similarly, General Superintenden ce on the part of Chief 
Executive Officer under Section 5(1) too should be deleted and consequential 
changes be made in the Act. As part of general supe rintendence, the 
Commission though may seek information from the CEO  on general 
administrative matters. 
(Para 38) 
 
 
Action Taken 
 
 
Agreed. The proposed amendment of the KVIC Act woul d address the 
issue. 
 
 
 

 
 
-4- 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
The Committee noted the constraints in achieving th e financial 
autonomy and also observed the reluctance in attain ing it. It was stated that 
the KVIC is basically a promotional body and does n ot engage in any 
commercial activities, the question of attainment o f financial sustainability in 
the present set up is too remote.  Instead it was l eft to the planners of our 
country to consider whether to change the present r ole of KVIC from a 
promotional body to a commercial body. 
(Para 44) 
 
Action Taken 
 
 
Agreed. The Ministry agrees with the views of the C ommittee that role 
of KVIC should be changed from a promotional body t o a commercial body. 
The KVIC as of today is completely dependent on the  Government of India 
for operating the schemes of the Ministry through P lan funds and the entire 
salaries of KVIC are paid from the non-plan funds. However, KVIC should 
make efforts to raise resources and grow as a finan cial autonomous body, and 
to become a self-sustaining organization. 
 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
The Ministry should persuade KVIC to leverage its p osition with financial 
institutions like SIDBI, NABARD, National Backward Class Finance & 
Development Corporation, National SC Finance Corpor ation, National ST 
Finance Corporation, National Minorities Developmen t Finance Corporation, 
Rashtriya Mahila Kosh etc. to raise finances for it s schemes.  For which the 
KVIC will have to evolve a sound business model. Th e Committee 
recommends that Rules 32, 33 and 34 should be made more substantive.  
(Para 49) 
 
Action Taken  
 
Agreed and noted 
 

-5- 
 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
The Committee is of the view that despite pronounce d objective of the 
Act, the KVIC may not be able to attain full administrative autonomy unless it 
attains financial autonomy.  It must shed its reluc tance and evolve into a self- 
sustaining organization. 
(Para 50) 
 
Action Taken  
 
Agreed and noted 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
The Committee may remind that the Khadi as a concep t evolved 
independent of government support. It was a tool an d symbol of protest and 
not a captive vocation of Government.  To continue to make it dependent of 
grants from the Government will defeat the very pur pose and message of 
khadi. 
(Para 54) 
Action Taken  
 
Agreed and noted 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
The Committee expresses serious concern over the er osion of statutory 
institutions prescribed under the Act. The National  KVI Board does not meet 
as per the provisions of Act. The Zonal Committee a re not fully formed 
despite Committee’s recommendation that same should  be notified within 30 
days. The Committee is persuaded to wonder if these  bodies are superfluous 
or have been relegated to redundance. In absence of  representation of States 
and Khadi Institutions, the Zonal Committee cannot fulfill its mandate.  In this 
regard the Committee recalls that the initial propo sal in the Act did not 
include the Khadi Institution and it was only on Co mmittee’s 
recommendations that the Khadi Institutions were in cluded in the Act. 
However, despite, provision in the Act, the Government does not comply. 
 (Para 75) 

-6- 
 
 
Action Taken 
 
 
Based on the letter no. 6(3)/2012-KVI-II dated 27.0 2.2014 of Ministry 
of MSME: for six geographical zones, the Zonal comm ittees have been 
formed by   KVIC on 28.02.2014 (the addendum S.O. N o. 1716 dated 
31.07.2012) making the CEO/secretaries of State KVI Bs as the members in 
the Zonal Committees. 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
The Committee further recommends that the Ministry should include 
the details of the activities/meetings/ agenda of t he boards/ committees/other 
bodies created under this Act. The Annual Report sh ould also include the 
Rules and Regulation made under relevant Sections of this Act.   
(Para 78) 
 
Action Taken 
 
 
Every significant development and achievements of K VI sector are 
mentioned in the Annual Report of KVIC very coherently and cogently. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

-7- 
 
 
CHAPTER-II 
 
 
 
Recommendations/Observations which the Committee do es not desire to 
pursue in view of the Government’s replies  
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
The Committee takes note of the list of Village ind ustry included in the 
Schedule framed under Section 2 (h). The Committee is of the opinion that 
States should be given flexibility in deciding the Village Industry. This will 
facilitate greater coverage of the Village Industry  schemes and make them 
more relevant to local traditional crafts, skills and employment needs. 
(Para 32) 
Action Taken  
 
Even though the definition under the act is suffici ently flexible, 
however, the States may be given the option to incl ude more relevant and 
traditional crafts to make it more broad-based and far reaching. 
 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
The Committee is of the view that the KVIC has neit her been given the 
financial autonomy nor was in position to attain fi nancial autonomy despite 
provisions in the Act.  It has to seek approval fro m the Government at every 
stage. The Committee is of the view that KVIC shoul d be allowed to re-
appropriate funds from Khadi and Village Industry funds, under the intimation 
to the Ministry. KVIC should also be allowed to spe nd the resources 
generated by it. 
(Para 46) 
Action Taken  
 
Scheme-wise funds are allocated to KVIC in the Budg et Estimates of 
the Ministry as per the demand of KVIC and the fund s released to KVIC on 
quarterly basis after assessing the performance and according to the guidelines 
of Department of Expenditure, Ministry of Finance. Funds are also re-
appropriated in the last quarter according to the u tilization of funds and KVIC 
demand. KVIC allocates the funds schemes-wise and State/UTs-wise. 

-8- 
 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
 
The Committee is also of the view that the Governme nt should release 
the Funds in time, but it should be the obligation of the KVIC of keeping the 
Government informed of the expenditure out of annua l Budgetary Grants. 
However, it is essential that KVIC even as a promot ional organisation for a 
commercially viable vocation like Khadi and Village Industries, must leverage 
itself to generate its own finances. 
(Para 47) 
 
 
Action Taken  
 
The Ministry supports the proposal of the Committee . KVIC has been 
implementing Khadi Reform and Development Programme , wherein various 
activities have been envisaged for generation of re sources, and to make KVIC 
and the KVI institutions self-sustaining. 
 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
 
The Committee accepts the assertion that Section 16  of the Act does 
dilute the autonomous character of the KVIC to a great extent. The Committee 
also takes note  of an unprecedented arrangement un der Sections 10 and 11 
where 51 Member National KVI Board chaired by the M inister concern and 
largely consisting of Secretaries of relevant Ministries of Government of India 
will advise a 13 Member KVIC of which 10 Members are part-time Members. 
The Committee wonders if such an arrangement exists  anywhere in the 
Government where a larger body headed by the execut ive Minister renders 
advice to a smaller Commission under the administrative and financial control 
of that Ministry. 
 
(Para 59) 
 
 
 

-9- 
 
Action Taken  
 
(i) The Section 16 will be reviewed under the compr ehensive 
amendment of the KVIC Act. 
  
(ii) It is felt that the NKVIB being the advisory b ody should be 
involved in advising the Government rather than the KVI Commission. The  
suggestion of the Committee to reduce the size of t he NKVIB may be 
considered and the number of participants as members can be reduced suitably 
during the aforesaid amendment. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
The Committee wonders if the Minister, who discharg es executive 
functions could act in advisory capacity to another  body under its 
administrative control. Such an arrangement is furt her complemented by 
Section 16 of the Act which makes directions of the  Government obligatory 
upon the KVIC. The situation is indeed paradoxical if not oxymoron. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry must give time bound final approval 
to any administrative or financial proposal from the KVIC. 
(Para 60) 
Action Taken  
 
It is felt that the NKVIB being the advisory body s hould be involved in 
advising the Government rather than the KVI Commiss ion. The suggestion of 
the Committee to reduce the size of the NKVIB may b e considered and the 
number of participants as members can be reduced su itably during the 
aforesaid amendment. 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
Moreover, during the evidence, the Secretary inform ed the Committee 
that the National KVI Board has not been meeting re gularly as mandated in 
the Act. The Committee takes such state of affairs seriously. A statutory 
Board headed by Minister breaching the statutory ma ndate is indeed a serious 
issue. It only highlights the redundancy of such a superfluous arrangement. 
(Para 61) 
 
 

-10- 
 
 
Action Taken  
 
It is felt that the NKVIB being the advisory body s hould be involved in 
advising the Government rather than the KVI Commission. The  
suggestion of the Committee to reduce the size of t he NKVIB may be 
considered and the number of participants as members can be reduced suitably 
during the aforesaid amendment. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

-11- 
 
 
 
CHAPTER-III 
 
 
 
Recommendations/Observations in respect of which th e Committee has 
either not accepted the replies of the Ministry or has asked the Ministry 
to review its replies  
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
The Committee observed that the definitions of khad i and Poly-vastra 
are limited to cotton, woolen or silk yarns or mixt ure thereof. The definition 
does not include synthetic yarn. To that extent the  definition needs to be 
revised to include Poly-vastra. The definitions inc lude handspun fibre and 
handloom woven cloth. It does not include innovations like E-charkhas, which 
are meant to increase the productivity, which is on e of the objectives of the 
KVIC under Section 15 (2) (e). The Committee feels that the definition should 
be flexible enough to include technological advance s which are the mandate 
of the Commission. 
(Para 28) 
 
Action Taken  
 
The KVIC Act under Section 2 (d) defines: "khadi" m eans any cloth 
woven on handlooms in India from cotton, silk or wo ollen yarn handspun in 
India or from a mixture of any two or all of such y arns;”. However, “Poly-
vastra” is defined in the schedule under Section 2 (h) of the KVIC Act, the 
entry for “village industry”. Thus the two are diff erent set of products 
altogether. As far as the proposal to include synth etic yarn in the definition is 
concerned, it may be noted that as ‘Man-made-fibre’ is already included in the 
definition of ‘polyvastra’, which includes ‘synthetic yarn’ also. 
 
As regards introduction of e-charkha, all such tech nological 
advancements can be introduced for the products und er the category of 
“village industry”. This would maintain the purity and sanctity of khadi and 
would ensure the development of a niche market for it globally. The 
suggestion would be separately examined in consulta tion with main 
stakeholders. 
 

 
-12- 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
 The Committee found reply ingenious.   Poly Vastra  is a derivative 
of Khadi but has been categorized as Village Indust ry.  Similarly, the 
produce of E-charkha will not be considered as Khad i.  The Committee 
wonders whether incentives available to Khadi will also be available to   
E-charkha products.  The reply in one single stroke  junks the objective 
under Section 15(2)(e).  
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
The Committee notes that the Sections 2 (ff) pertai ning to ‘rural area’ 
and 2 (i) regarding village industry acknowledges t hat these are dynamic 
concepts and that the Government could change the p arameters by 
notifications. However, no notification has been is sued to change these 
definitions, ever since last amendment to the Act i n 2006.  The Committee 
recommends that the Ministry should change the defi nition in consultation 
with the KVIC through notification. 
(Para 30) 
 
Action Taken  
 
The definition of rural area is in line with the ce nsus definition and as 
such it would not be feasible to have a separate de finition under KVIC Act. 
However, the same will be examined. 
The definition of village industry needs to be chan ged taking into 
account inflation by increasing the per capita investment from Rs 1 lakh to Rs 
5 lakh for plain areas and Rs 1.5 lakh to Rs 7 lakh  for Hills, A &N Islands, 
NER regions. This will be incorporated under the pr oposed amendment of 
KVIC Act. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation  
 
 The Ministry contended that in the existing act th e definition of 
rural area was as per census.  While examining the issue, the Committee 
had sought the views of the Ministry regarding the need to amend the 
definition of ‘Rural area’ and the Ministry itself had suggested the need 
to change in definition.   

 
 
-13- 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
The Committee observes that no Rule has been framed  by the 
Government in this regard. The Committee is of the view that the terms and 
conditions for engagement of these two critical pos itions may be prescribed 
immediately. The terms of engagement should clearly specify the requirement 
of previous experience of prospective candidates in  the Khadi or Village 
Industries or associated fields. Also the choice of  candidates must not be 
limited to Government by deputation, instead should  be open to members of 
senior management of Banks, financial institutions and PSUs. The selection 
should be made through an independent body like Public Enterprises Selection 
Board. 
(Para 40) 
 
Action Taken 
 
 
The PESB is mandated to “evolve a sound managerial policy for the 
Central Public Sector Enterprises and, in particular, to advise Government on 
appointments to their top management posts”.  Thus the suggestion for 
selection for the post of CEO, KVIC through an inde pendent body like PESB 
may not be appropriate as KVIC is a Statutory Commi ssion created under the 
Government of India and operating on cent percent f inancial assistance from 
the Government. The current practice of selection t hrough the ACC may be 
continued. As far as application for the posts are concerned, suitable persons 
can always apply for it.  
 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 The reply obfuscates the issue raised by the Commi ttee in its 
report.  The Committee express its concern that the  rules for Selection/ 
appointment of the CEO and FA of KVIC have not been framed yet.  The 
Committee also reiterates its earlier recommendatio n that the selection 
by an independent body from a broader base as prescribed in the rules be 
framed immediately.  
  
 

 
-14- 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
The Committee also takes note of the composition of  the KVIC. The 
objective of the last Amendment of 2005 was to infu se greater 
professionalism to the KVIC. It provided for four e xperts as non-official part-
time Members of the Commission. The Committee is su rprised to note that 
despite having a specialized in-house body Mahatma Gandhi Institute for 
Rural Industrialization (MGIRI), the Act does not p rovide any scope for the 
Institute. The professional mandate of the Institut e almost coincides with the 
demands of the KVIC i.e to strengthen rural industr ialization, enhance rural 
employment in rural areas. The Institute is designe d as a ‘mechanism that 
would provide high quality of science, technology a nd management inputs 
and support in a comprehensive manner to KVI sector .” The Committee 
therefore recommends that the expert representative s of MGIRI may be 
included in the Commission under Section 4(2) (b) and existing part-time non-
government experts and also government representati ves may be involved 
with the KVIC as per requirement under Section 9 of  the Act. This will bring 
about a closer institutional linkage between KVIC and MGIRI.   
(Para 64) 
 
 
Action Taken 
 
 
Four Expert members from the fields of Science & Te chnology, 
Marketing, Rural Development and Technical Educatio n & Training are 
appointed to the Commission. MGIRI operates under t he guidance of General 
Council and Executive Council in which the Chairman  and CEO, KVIC are 
members of General Council and CEO & Director (S&T)  KVIC are the 
members of Executive Council of MGIRI. Such associa tions offer sufficient 
scope for interaction between KVIC and MGIRI on the  implementation of 
S&T programme in the sector and also to bring syner gy on the scientific 
approach of both organizations. The recommendation may be considered 
during comprehensive amendment of the KVIC Act. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
-15- 
 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
 
 The Committee strongly feels that in terms of econ omy, the KVIC 
would be saving its crucial resources by involving internal resources 
agency MGIRI instead of engaging part time experts,  who could be 
engaged as per requirements under Section 9 of the Act.  
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
The Committee is of the view that given the shortag e of manpower and 
resources faced by the State Directorates of KVIC a nd considering similar 
mandate of State KVIBs, the Ministry has not been a ble to justify the 
existence of State Directorates. Instead the KVIC m ust conserve its scarce 
resources for more useful purposes than deputing th em for similar 
assignments as State KVIBs. For this there is a nee d for institutional linkage 
between the KVIC and State KVIBs supported by expli cit statutory provision. 
The Zonal Committee could provide a forum where KVI C and State KVIBs 
converge to discuss the impact and shortcomings of KVIC schemes. 
(Para 69) 
 
Action Taken  
 
KVIC functions as a nodal agency for Non-farm micro  industry sector 
in the country. It assumes the supervisory and moni toring role of the sector 
specific centrally sponsored programme and scheme. Assignment of such 
functions warrants presence of KVIC in all state. H owever, KVIC enters into 
partnerships with appropriate institutions as per t he need and requirement of 
each scheme. The strength and outreach of KVIBs als o need to be looked into 
before assigning any responsibility to them. Also t he institutional linkage 
between the KVIC and State KVIBs need to be revisit ed in the light of the 
observations of the Committee.  
 
Further Recommendation/Observation  
 
 The Committee reiterates its recommendation in the  interest of 
economy.  KVIC which strives for financial autonomy  must not waste its 
resources on its establishment where parallel KVIBs  already have 
presence.  

 
 
-16- 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
Also the Committee is of the view that in order to reduce the unwieldy 
size of Zonal Committees, the representative of the  State KVIC Directorates 
should be excluded, as the Zonal Deputy CEO of the Commission is included 
in the Zonal Committee. The Committee recommends that Ministry and KVIC 
should consider the recommendation and make necessary changes. 
(Para 76) 
 
Action Taken 
 
 
State Directorates should be a part of the Zonal Co mmittees so that 
there can be effective monitoring and supervision b esides ensuring better 
implementation of the various schemes. 
 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
The Committee also recommends that the Government s hould set up a 
statutory functional linkage between KVIC and State KVIBs and till such time 
should revitalize the Zonal Committees. 
(Para 77) 
Action Taken  
 
KVIC functions as a nodal agency for Non-farm micro  industry sector 
in the country. It assumes the supervisory and moni toring role of the sector 
specific centrally sponsored programme and scheme. Assignment of such 
functions warrants presence of KVIC in all state. H owever, KVIC enters into 
partnerships with appropriate institutions as per t he need and requirement of 
each scheme. The strength and outreach of KVIBs als o need to be looked into 
before assigning any responsibility to them. Also t he institutional linkage 
between the KVIC and State KVIBs need to be revisit ed in the light of the 
observations of the Committee.  
 
Further Recommendation/Observation (Para 76 and 77) 
 
 The Committee reiterates its recommendation for th e sake of 
economy KVIC must deploy its scarce resources, judi cially to meet its 
mandate instead of spending the same on its establishment.   

 
-17- 
 
 
CHAPTER-IV 
 
 
 
Recommendations/Observations in respect of which fi nal replies of the 
Ministry have not been received 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
However, the Committee remains unconvinced of the statutory status of 
the KVIC Act. As per the reply of the Secretary and  the written reply, the Act 
was framed under Entry 97 of the Union List that ga ve the residuary powers 
which rest with the Union in 1956. However, with in clusion of Khadi and 
Village industries in the Eleventh Schedule enumera ting subjects under the 
powers and responsibilities of Panchayati Raj Insti tutions ( PRIs) read with 
the Article 243 (A), power of law making on the sub jects enlisted in the said 
Schedule including KVI sector, rests inter alia wit h the State legislature. And 
as such cannot be covered under the residuary power s of the Union in List I. 
Conversely, the State Government would not have the  legislative competence 
in respect of KVI sector regardless of Article 243 (A) as residuary powers are 
to be vested in the Union Government. The Committee  therefore recommends 
that the Ministry may review the statutory position  in consultation with 
relevant Ministry/agency to give KVIC firm statutory status. 
(Para 20) 
 
Action Taken  
 
The Ministry feels that the statutory status of KVI C has been 
decided already as KVIC has been formed by an Act o f Parliament. 
However, in the light of the specific recommendatio n of the committee 
to review the statutory status of KVIC, the same ma y be done by 
obtaining suitable opinion from the Law Ministry. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation  
 
The Committee may be apprised of the opinion of the Law Ministry 
in the matter.  
 
 
 

 
-18- 
  
Recommendation/Observation  
 
The Committee is of the view that the Government mu st 
ascertain the ways of devolution of funds to Panchayati Raj Institutions 
(PRIs) and monitor and audit their performance in i mplementing the 
Government schemes. In this regard the Committee al so emphasizes 
the need for an institutional linkage between KVIC and the State KVIBs 
supported by explicit statutory provisions instead of implicit Rules. 
 
(Para 24) 
Action Taken  
 
The recommendations of the Committee are noted and ways and means 
for the engagement with PRIs for devolution of fund s will be examined in 
consultation with the States. KVIC guidelines under  PMEGP already include 
PRIs as one of agencies to identify the beneficiari es. Under PMEGP scheme 
the representatives of PRIs are already involved in  the selection process of 
beneficiaries at District Level Task Force Committe es (DLTFCs) as per the 
scheme guidelines.  
As far as developing an institutional linkage betwe en the KVIC and 
KVIBs, the current status of existing KVIBs will be  examined separately. 
Opinion of the States will be elicited. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation  
 
 The Committee has sought the ways of devolution of  funds to 
Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs) instead of engag ing PRIs in certain 
Schemes.  
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
The Committee wonders that if KVIC could access the  funds like 
RIDF. The Ministry may explore if KVIC could avail institutional finances 
from Banks, as a Micro Finance Institution and from  RIDF. The Ministry 
should gradually promote KVIC as specialized resour ce agency and financial 
institution for village industries from being a pro motional organization. 
Sections 17, 17A and 21 give powers to KVIC to raise funds. 
(Para 48) 

 
-19- 
 
 
Action Taken 
 
 
The Ministry has written to KVIC to suggest and pro pose a road map 
for achieving financial autonomy. It may be stated that there is no bar on 
exploring institutional finance from banks and othe r financial institutions by 
KVIC with approval from the Ministry.  
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
 
The Committee would like to be apprised of the prop osal’s 
outcome.  
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
The Committee recommends that the Government’s powe rs under 
Section 16 too should be mitigated. Rules should be framed under this Section 
to limit the powers of Government to give direction . Powers should also be 
given to KVIC to discuss the issue and apprise the Government of its views. 
(Para 62) 
 
Action Taken  
 
Noted 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
The Ministry may inform the Committee of the outcom e of the 
Committee’s recommendation. 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
The Committee reiterates that the autonomy of KVIC is likely to remain 
constricted due to its continued reliance over Gove rnment for finances. It is 
the mandate given to KVIC to exercise autonomy and the Commission ought 
to generate resources independent of Government. Th ere are provisions in the 
Act to enable KVIC to generate resources provided K VIC formulates viable 
business case. 
(Para 63) 

 
-20- 
 
 
Action Taken 
 
 
The Ministry has written to KVIC to suggest and pro pose a road map for 
achieving financial autonomy. 
 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
 
 The Committee may be updated of the steps taken by KVIC.
