of the status and future of its Skill Development Program mes, in the wake of Finance 
Minister’s Budget announcement. However, in view of the indifferent performance of 
Ministry’s Skill Development Programme, the Committee is incli ned to recommend that 
these programmes may be made part of the overall Nation al Skill Development Mission 
and assets/institution  may be transferred  accordingly.     The Committee is also of the 
view that the Ministry should request the CAG to conduct Performance Audits under 
Audit Regulations, 2007 ( Chapter 7) of the CAG act, 19 71,  on the Skill 
Development Programmes being run by tool Rooms/Technology   Centres and National  
Level Entrepreneurship Development Institutes. 
 (Para 49) 
Action Taken  
 
Skill Development Programmes of the Ministry are part of the o verall targets set for 
the National Skill Development Mission.  Performance audit is being conducted by CAG 
empanelled auditors for all activities including Skill Developme nt Programmes being run 
by Tool Rooms/Technology Centres.  In respect of the oth er Institutes the CAG would be 
requested accordingly. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation  
 
 The Committee had specifically asked for Performan ce Audit as provided in 
Chapter 7 of the Audit Regulaltions, 2007. The Mini stry may share the outcome of 
the Performance Audit of Tool Rooms/Technical Centre. 
  
Recommendation/Observation  
 
The Committee is dismayed that after committing Plan outl ay of Rs. 800 crores for 
12th Plan for such important Scheme, the approval is render ed invalid on purely 
administrative issues.  Another Cabinet Note for an other Scheme is under circulation 
for inter-Ministerial consultation. The Committee finds it to be an illustration of attitude 
towards the MSME sector. 
 (Para 51) 

 
-33- 
 
Action Taken  
 
After the change in Government, the National Innovation C ouncil has ceased to 
exist and since the scheme was driven by that body, oper ationalization of the Scheme got 
delayed.  Presently, discussions are going on with vari ous stakeholders to sort out issues 
in order to operationalize the Scheme. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
 The Committee is dismayed at state of affairs wher e important Plan/Schemes 
with huge outlays are stopped with change in Govt.  While modifications/changes in 
schemes could have been done, but to stop an import ant scheme, just because of 
change in govt. is unacceptable.  The Committee is of the view that Govt. is a 
continuous and permanent institution.  The Committe e may be apprised of progress 
made on the new Cabinet note.  
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
The  Committee   noted  that  as  per  the  Outcome    Budget  till  31 st 
December, 2014, only about 60000 trainees were trai ned with Rs. 46 crores. Remaining 
40000 trainees were trained in next two months.  Wh ile Committee finds  serious  under-
utilization  of  fund  under  the  Scheme,  the  in tegrity  of figures as provided by the 
Ministry is doubtful. Despite drastic reduction in funds at RE stage the targets have not 
been revised. 
(Para 73) 
Action Taken  
 
The training targets were fixed at the beginning of  the financial year, taking into 
account the allocation made at the BE stage.  Even though the allocation was subsequently 
reduced at the RE stage, the targets already set we re not revised, since the courses had 
already commenced. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
 In BE 2013-14 with Rs. 117 crore, the target was t o train 1 lakh trainees.  
Eventually, 1.75 lakh were trained with same amount .  In 2014-15 allocation, Rs. 116 
crores was reduced to Rs. 77 crores.  Rs. 46 crores could be spent till December, 2014 
with 60,000 trainees trained against the target of 1.37 lakh.  However, by February, 
2015 the number grew to 1 lakh in two months. Again st targeted 5000 training 
programmes, 3400 training programmes were completed.  The Committee would like 
to be informed about the institutions that impart s uch training and what is their 
annual enrolment capacity.  The Ministry should monitor regularly, by whom? 
 
 

-34- 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
 The Committee finds it intriguing that while alloca tion was drastically reduced  
in  RE and utilization was only Rs 9 crores till the end o f III Quarter, yet achievement has 
been more than half the annual target. Despite such in credible  achievement  figures  the  
allocation  this  year  has  been  further pruned  to  o nly  Rs  3  crores.  This sums up the 
credence the  Government attaches to the performance under the scheme. The Committee 
finds the integrity of achievement figures doubtful or the  demands inflated. This has 
been borne out in the drastic reduction in BE 2015-16. 
 (Para 78) 
 
Action Taken 
 
 
The allocation for 2015-16 has been kept at Rs. 3.00 c rore as compared to the 
allocation made in the previous year, since the activities r elating to EDP/ESDP/MDP, 
being conducted by the MSME – Development Institutes have b een shifted to Tool 
Rooms.  The allocations for Tool Rooms have accordingly been enhanced for this 
purpose. 
 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation  
 
The Committee may be informed of the reason for shi fting activities relating to 
EDP/ESDP/MDP from Development Institute to Tool Roo ms.  What will be the 
mandate of Development Institutes now?  
 
Recommendation/Observation  
The Committee considers that no purpose is served if t hese courses lack 
employability.  Ministry’s reply is silent over e m p l o y a b i l i t y . The C o m m i t t e e  is 
not aware of the courses under the Scheme have recogni zed.   The Ministry must 
maintain the employability figure and furnish the same t o the Committee.   The 
Committee is also concerned over under-utilization of fu nds. The Committee reiterates 
that Ministry must get the performance audit of its ski ll and entrepreneurship 
development programme done by CAG. 
 (Para 79) 
 
Action Taken  
 
Steps have been initiated by the Ministry to maintain the employ ability figures.  The 
recommendation of the Committee on performance audit has  been noted for future 
compliance. 
 
 

-35- 
 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
 The Committee may be informed for further steps on  its recommendation.  The 
Committee specifically recommends Performance Audit  as per Chapter 7 of the 
Audit Regulations, 2007.  
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
The Committee is concerned over the employability o f trainees who undertake short 
term training at Technology Centres (TCs).  These cours es constitute the bulk of training 
programmes of TCs.   But no record of employability is kept.  To assess the efficiency of 
such courses, employment record must be maintained.  T he Committee reiterates its 
views that performance audit under Audit Regulations 2007 , (Chapter 7) of the CAG 
Act, 1971, of these TCs should be done by CAG.  The C ommittee may be apprised if 
these courses and institution will be transferred to Min istry of Skill Development as 
per Budget announcement. 
 
 (Para 86) 
Action Taken 
 
 
Technology Centres are conducting short term training progr ammes in the areas of 
Tool Engineering and related Upgradation of skills of the st udents who are 
pursuing/completed their degrees/diplomas/ITI trades in order to provide them hands on 
exposure.  These training programmes are also conducted for the employees of MSMEs to 
enhance their skills.  Technology Centres have observe d that most of the candidates 
undergoing short term training programmes (pursuing tech nical education or are already 
employed in the Industries) do not opt for placement.  How ever, the technology Centres 
have been advised to maintain placement records from the c urrent year onwards in respect 
of those candidates who opt for placement. 
 
Regarding performance audit by the CAG as 
 mphasized by the Committee, it is 
submitted that the accounts of the autonomous bodies are b eing audited by the CAG 
empanelled auditors, before the accounts are laid in both the Houses of Parliament. 
 
As regards the transfer of the training programmes and th e Institutions to the 
Ministry of Skill development, it is submitted that apart from conducting technical training 
programmes/skill development programmes, the Technology Centres are also engaged in a 
number of other important activities to facilitate promotion, de velopment as well as 
enhancing the competitiveness of Micro, small and Medium E nterprises as enshrined in 
the MSME Development Act, 2006.  As such, there is no pr oposal to transfer the training 
programmes and the Institutions to the Ministry of Skill Development. 
 
 

 
-36- 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
 The Committee may be informed of number of trainees  in short term and long 
term courses and about employability of trainees.  The Committee reiterates its 
recommendation to have performance audit as per Ch.  7 of the Audit Regulation 
(2007) and not merely audit of accounts. If any Per formance Audit has been done 
same may be provided to the Committee.  
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
Yet on certain parameters, the targets were met.   This shows either figures are 
doubtful or the Ministry had inflated demands. Clubbing such varied  schemes  under  one  
umbrella    allocation,  is  obviously  going  to  be difficult to monitor yet the BE 
allocation for financial year 2015-16 have been retained at same level as previous BE 
2014-15.  Government must benchmark actual utilization whi le allocating funds.  Also 
Ministry must take a hard look of achievement figures.   To say that there are demand 
driven schemes only justify   that a l l o c a t i o n    should   have b e e n    benchmarked   
against   actual utilization. 
 (Para 89) 
Action Taken  
 
The difference between target and achievement both in t he physical and financial 
aspects depends on receiving response from various exp ert organisations as well as 
individual MSME. Most of the proposals/claims submitted by ex pert 
organisation/individual unit do not fulfil the requisite criteria  as per the scheme guidelines 
within the stipulated period, resulting delay in actual payments/e xpenditure. However, 
efforts are always being taken to improve actual utilisat ion of fund as well as achievement 
figures. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation  
 
 The Ministry has not responded to Committee’s comm ents against clubbing up 
of different Schemes under one umbrella Scheme, making it difficult to monitor.  The 
Ministry may state the benefits of such clubbing co nsidering that there is serious 
under - utilization of allocation in each successive year yet, the BE remains the same.  
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
In every running Scheme, barring KRDP and new India Inn ovation 
Entrepreneurship and Agro Industry Fund, the BE (2015 -16) is lower than RE (2014-
15).  In both these Schemes the BE allocation were redu ced at RE stage and yet again 
they have been enhanced in BE (2015-16).   However, considering all other MSME 
Schemes the pattern is low BE which is enhanced at RE stage.  In the context of 
D.C.(MSME) Schemes the allocations have been enhanced  despite lower utilization, here  

-37- 
 
is case of KVIC, the budget 
allocation have  been  reduced  vis-a–vis  higher  RE.    The 
C o mm i t t e e   is  unable  to appreciate the reduction.   Th e Committee apprehends that 
such trend in allocation may force the  KVIC  to crow d its expenditure  towards  the  end  
of financial year.  KVIC is supposed to provide margin mo ney subsidy under PMEGP 
and Khadi Grant, the entire year, therefore its Budget allocation should be enhanced in 
the beginning of the financial year. 
 
 (Para 92) 
 
Action Taken 
 
 
For the year 2014-15, funds to the tune of Rs. 3327.00  crore were allocated for the 
Ministry.  Out of this, funds to the tune of Rs. 2042.00  crore with Rs. 1418.28 crore alone 
being allocated for PMEGP.  During 2015-16, funds amounti ng to Rs. 2612.51 crore were 
allocated to the Ministry, out of which Rs. 1050.00 crore w as earmarked for PMEGP.  
Since the allocation of funds for 2015-16 were lower than 2 014-15, the provision for 
PMEGP was accordingly reduced in comparison to 2014-15. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation  
 The Ministry has not informed as to why the Scheme s of DC(MSME) may get 
higher BE despite low utilization every successive year.  
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
The Committee has also failed to appreciate the rationa l of increasing budget 
allocation for Khadi Reform & Development Programme (K RDP) during 2015-16 as 
Rs. 66.50 crores when the scheme is not able to use the  money and allocation had to 
be reduced at RE stage. Acknowledging that the scheme is l argely funded by ADB 
assistance under certain conditions, the Committee also takes note of protests from Khadi 
Institutions against KRDP and the difficulties in getting the K hadi Institutions audited 
before availing the assistance under KRDP. 
 (Para 93) 
 
Action Taken 
 
 
Khadi Reform and Development Programme (KRDP) suggeste d various reform 
activities for total turn-around of the Khadi Sector.  Initially  the KIs were not coming 
forward seeking reform assistance. After conducting fi eld level sensitization programme, 
the hesitation of KIs is disappearing and the pace of the programme is gradually picking 
up.   
 
 
 
 
 

-38- 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
 The Committee may be apprised of suggested reform activities under this 
KRDP Programme and actual steps being taken under this Programme for total turn 
around of Khadi sector. Details of the terms and co nditions of ADB assistance and 
also the budget allocation for KRDP is being utilized be furnished to the Committee.  
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
The Committee notes that the allocation for Khadi I ndustries (Grants) hiked by 
almost double at RE stage in the year 2014-15.  The Ministr y state that it was done in 
view of increased midyear demand raised by KVIC.  The  Committee finds that this has 
been the pattern of allocation in previous years also.   The Committee wonders about the 
impact on Khadi Institution if grants are allocated within second half of the financial 
year.  It will force the KVIC to   release   Khadi   Gra nt   only   after   enhanced   
Revised   Estimates.   The Committee also wonder if only 57% of the BE was spent till 
the 3 rd quarter of financial year, why the allocation was enhan ced at RE stage.  The 
Committee therefore is of the view that Ministry must stagg er the release of grant 
in installments throughout the year. 
 
 (Para 99) 
 
Action Taken  
 
During 2015-16, adequate allocation of funds to the tune of Rs. 145.95 crore has 
been made in comparison to the previous year’s BE of Rs.  93.31 crore.  Thus, necessary 
action has been taken during 2015-16 while allocating budget under Khadi grant. 
 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
The Committee has not been informed about quarter-w ise release of allocation 
for the financial year 2015-16. The Ministry has in formed that it had used 90% of 
allocation by August, 2015.  The Committee may be i nformed if the funds were used to 
settle the dues of previous years.  If yes, has Min istry sought additional fund for 2015-
16.  
 
  Recommendation/Observation  
 
The  Committee  notes  that  MDA  scheme  was  devised   to  sustain  the Khadi 
institutions the year long instead of seasonal rebates. Ho wever, the purpose is defeated if 
MDA is released after the passage of Financial Year. Th e  Committee  therefore  
recommends  that  the  Ministry  must  devise  the schem e so as to ensure that MDA is 
staggered and is released to khadi institutions year lon g. The Committee noted that the  
khadi   institutions   were  working  on shrinking  marg ins and depleting capital.  Any  

 
-39- 
 
delay in 
releasing the  MDA  can  result  in  sickness  and  cons equent  
unemployment  among artisans.      The  Committee  stro ngly  recommends  that  the  
Ministry  must devise method and powers to transfer the K hadi   MDA Fund.   The 
Scheme was devised to replace annual rebate, so as  to  provide assistance throughout 
the  year.     However  current  expenditure  defeats  the  objective  of  MDA. Ministry  
must  ensure  regular  release  of  funds  at  any  sta ge  of  Khadi production. 
 (Para 100) 
 
Action Taken 
 
 
MDA is a component of Khadi Grant Head of Account.  Und er Khadi Grant BE 
2014-15 was Rs. 93.31 crore and BE 2015-16 has been  enhanced to Rs.145.95 crore.  Out 
of this Rs. 140.95 crore has been earmarked for MDA ( Khadi).  During 2015-16 (upto 
31.8.2015), funds amounted to Rs.127.38 crore had alr eady been released to KVIC for 
settlement of the MDA claims of Khadi Institutions.  Thus , more than 90% of the 
allocation has already been released during the current financial year. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation  
 
 The Ministry could utilize 90% of allocation by Au gust, 2015 whether it got 
additional allocation in supplementary demands to m eet the requirement for the 
remaining part of 2015-16.  
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
The C o m m i t t e e    noted  the  suggestion   by  represen tative   of  Khadi 
Artisans that the Janshree Bima Yojna be replaced with Rashtriya Swasthya Yojna, 
which has better medical benefits. Considering no expend iture under Janshree Bima 
Yojna due to delay in approval, the Committee recommends  the  Ministry  to  take  
appropriate  note  of  the  suggestion  given  by  the be neficiary artisans to replace 
Janshree Bima Yojna with Rashtriya Swasthya Bima Yojn a  and also inform the 
Committee of its view. 
 (Para 103) 
Action Taken  
 
The views of the Committee will help in providing health covera ge to the Khadi 
artisans.  
  
Further Recommendation/Observation  
 
 The Committee may be informed of the further actio n taken in this regard.  
 
 
 

 
 
-40- 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
The Committee noted that 800 clusters were proposed  to be developed during 
12 th    Plan.   71 cluster, majority of them Mini Clusters with less  than 500  artisans  
were  to  be  set  up  in  the  current  first  phase.    Guidelines of revamped SFURTI were 
issued only in August, 2014.  After complex and protra cted procedure only 17 proposals 
have  been shortlisted for preparation of  preparator y  project  report  and  other  
preliminary  survey  and documentation.  The Committee  in  convinced  that  going  by  
general performance of Ministry, it is highly improbable that 800 clusters could be set up 
during 1 2 t h  Plan period till 2017.  It appears that the Ministry due i t own complex 
processes, is severely constricted and hampered in a chieving its own targets. 
 
 (Para 117) 
 
Action Taken 
 
 
Seventeen Detailed Project Reports (DPRs) consisting of 9 p roposals from KVIC 
and 8 from Coir Board were presented before the Sche me Steering Committee (SSC) for 
obtaining final approval.  All 9 proposals from KVIC have been assigned ‘in principle’ 
approval of SSC in December 2014 and got revalidated in 1 5 th  Meeting of SSC on 
24.6.2015.  However, out of 8 proposals pertaining to Coir Board, 5 have been assigned ‘in 
principle’ approval of SSC in December 2014 and got rev alidated in 15 th  Meeting of SSC 
on 24.6.2015 and 3 proposal were put up for both ‘in p rinciple’ and final approval of the 
SSC. 
 
In the 16 
th  SSC held on 10.8.2015, 14 clusters (KVIC-9 & Coir-5) in volving an 
amount of Rs.2884.24 lakh worth of project cost and Rs. 2244.66 lakh as total assistance 
(including 50% of Soft Intervention, Technical Agency Cost and Implementing Agency 
Cost and 43% of Hard Intervention) under SFURTI has be en approved.  However, the 
releases have been restricted to Rs.968.911 lakh in resp ect of the final approvals of 
Detailed Project Reports (DPRs).  
 
As regards Detailed Study Report (DSR), 3 DSRs Coir cluster with one major cluster 
and two mini clusters have been approved in the 16 
th  SSC held on 10.8.2015.  10 proposals 
of KVIC for DSRs pertaining to different products and all in  mini category were approved 
by the SSC.  SSC also accorded financial approval of Rs. 107.21 lakhs for release to the 
Nodal Agencies in view of the ‘in principle’ approval of 13  clusters (KVIC-10 & coir-3) 
for total projects worth Rs.2530.70 lakh. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
-41- 
 
In order to achieve 800 Heritage clusters, Nodal Ag encies (NA) are also being 
increased and empanelled so that target are achieve d.  In addition to this, Asian 
Development Bank (ADB) fund was also being tied up.   
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
 Of the 800 proposed SFURTI clusters for 12 th  Plan, 71 were selected for 1 st  
phase, of which till August, 2015, detailed study r eports for 13 clusters (10 khadi and 
3 coir) have been approved by Scheme Steering Commi ttee after protracted and 
complex procedure.  Entire worth of these 13 projec ts Rs. 25 crores as against 
allocation of Rs. 45 crores allocated for SFURTI-KV IC for 2015-16.  However, the 
Scheme Steering Committee has given financial appro val for Rs. 1 crore only.  The 
Committee notes that all action is happening only at the level of Ministry and none at 
ground level even after passage of half the period of 12 th  Plan.  The Committee re-
affirms its apprehension about 800 clusters.  The C ommittee may be informed of 
purpose of assistance from ADB and terms and condit ions of such assistance.  Also 
provide the details of 13 approved clusters.  
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
The Committee observes that the level of Non-Planne d expenditure  must be 
reduced and   scarce resources should be used for pl anned schemes for the Sector and 
coir artisans. For this the Committee had recommended to dr astically reduce the size of 
Coir Board and its Committees. The Committee reiterates i ts recommendation and asks 
the Ministry to bring a comprehensive amendment to the Co ir Act, expeditiously. 
 (Para130) 
 
Action Taken 
 
 
Budgetary allocation for the financial year, 2015-16 unde r the head, Non-Plan 
Grants in aid is Rs.26.45 crore which consists of grant s in aid (Salary) and Grants in aid 
(General), Rs.22.20 crore and Rs.4.25 crore respectively.  The funds under the head Grants 
in aid (Salary) are utilized for the disbursement of salari es and allowances, pension and 
other staff entitlements.  All other establishment expenditure are met out of the funds 
under the head Grants in aid (General).  Allocation has be en made by the Ministry under 
Non-Plan head based on the annual requirement of the Bo ard in the light of scarcity of 
resources on the Non-Plan side.   
 
The proposal of comprehensive amendment to the Coir Industry Act for reducing the 
size of Coir Board and its Committees is under process f or obtaining the approval of the 
competent authority. 
 
 

-42- 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation  
 
 The Budget allocation for  Non-Planned expenditure of Coir Board belies the 
promised autonomy as envisaged in Coir Board Act.  It is therefore imperative that 
Govt. reviews the Coir Act comprehensively to minim ise overhead administrative 
expenditure like massive Board and also grant autonomy to coir Board to generate its 
own resources.  The Committee is also cognisant tha t the Coir Board has given its 
inputs to proposed amendments in Act,  in 2009.  Th e Committee wonders how much 
more time does the Ministry require to propose exte nsive amendments in view of 
emerging challenges before Coir Board and changes i n Coir Industry.  The 
Committee expects that the amendment should not be merely administrative and 
superficial.  The Govt. must bring the Amendment Bill expeditiously.  
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
The Committee has also learnt that domestic coir in dustries are facing shortage 
of raw material as coir is being exported to China at a  concessional duty  and  the  
finished  imported  Chinese  Coir  products  are  drivin g  the domestic producers out 
of competition in our own market. The Committee recommend s that the Government 
should address this duty imbalance. 
 (Para 131) 
Action Taken  
 
The reasons for the shortage of coir fibre faced by the domestic industry is the 
decline in production of coconuts due to the drought faced  by T.N State, the mite attack on 
coconut palm, and the exports of raw fibre to China.  Actually, the emergence of a strong 
defibering sector of coir industry is due to the high deman d of fibre from China.  The 
import of coir products from China to the tune of 35.80  lakhs in 2014-15 is found to be not 
significant.  So far the Chinese coir products are not rais ing any market threats, for Indian 
coir products, in India.  The fibre imported from India is mainly used by China for 
manufacturing boards which is used by them for manufacturing mattresses.    
Coir Board has already initiated steps for the conduct of a study on the scarcity of 
fibre.  On the basis of the outcome of study and the recommendations therein, suitable plan 
of action will be evolved and implemented to contain the present problem.    
 
Further Recommendation/Observation  
 
 The Committee may be informed of the outcome of st udy being done by Coir 
Board and recommendations thereon which should be a ppropriately reflected in 
proposed amendment. 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
The Committee is dismayed to note that its repeated reco mmendations seeking 
better  and  efficient  utilization  of  scarce  funds  f or as vital sector as MSME, have been  

-43- 
 
undermined by the Ministry despite its repeated 
assurance to   improve the performance.  
Every year the Ministry seeks ever higher allocation. Keeping in view the vast scope of 
the Sector, the Committee too would be inclined to support  the demand. But utilization of 
scarce fund defeats all the arguments in favour of enhan cing the allocation. The 
Committee recommends that Year-wise Budget Estimate , Revised Estimates and the 
Actual Expenditure should be provided on the Ministry’s w ebsite. Also, the Financial 
Advisor and Chief Controller of Ministry’s Accounts shoul d post Scheme-wise Planned 
and Non Planned expenditures for every Quarter of the F inancial Year. 
 (Para 135) 
Action Taken  
 
The Ministry has requested the Chief Controller of Accounts , M/o MSME for 
posting  the BE, RE and actual expenditure figures for the  last 3 years  on the Ministry's 
web portal.  Besides, we have also requested to post scheme-wise plan and non-plan 
expenditure figures, quarter-wise, from the current financial year onwards. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation  
 
 The Committee noted that expenditure only upto 1 
st  quarter of current 
Financial Year has been posted on the website.  Exp enditure for subsequent 
Quarters has not been posted.  Even in the 1 st  quarter, performance of Schemes run 
by NSIC and DC, MSME has not been up to the expecta tions. The Committee 
cautions the Ministry of possible sub optimal performance.  
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
In this Report, the Committee has made appraisal of the De mands of the Grants 
of Ministry of MSME and its previous performance in res pect of utilization of 
allocations.   The Committee inclined to suggest that Bud get Estimates should also take 
into account, the utilization of funds both Planned and  Non-Planned, during the previous 
years. 
 (Para 139) 
Action Taken  
 
The proforma for Detailed Demands for Grants (DDG) ha s been devised by the 
Ministry of Finance which is mandatorily applicable for a ll Central Ministries. However, 
DDG for the particular year contains the previous year's B E and RE for Plan and Non-plan 
and also actuals for last to last year. For reference of Hon'ble Committee, a copy of DDG 
for --- is being attached. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation  
 
 The Committee recommends that its observation on t his Report may be shared 
with Ministry of Finance.

Introduction
The Heavy Industries in India is dominated by the Capital Good Sector (CGS) and the Auto
Sector. The Indian Capital Goods Industry has enough potential but manufacturing capacity is
underutilized to the extent of 40%.  Two major hurdles faced by the sector are cheap imports and
technology gap. The Government has come up with many initiatives/schemes to make the sector
globally competitive. The Department of Heavy Industry (DHI) with a mission to achieve high
growth in Heavy Electricals and Capital Goods Industry have announced the National Capital Goods
Policy (NCGP) on 15
th February 2016 which is a landmark initiative in this regard and has been
reflected in the Budget 2016-17 by way of enhancement of Customs Duty on Heavy Electrical
equipments from 7.5 % to 10%, imposition of Countervailing Duty (CVD) on road construction
machinery and reduction of excise duty from 12.5% to 6% on parts of centrifugal pumps.  All
these measures are expected to help indigenous producers of Capital Goods to be more cost
competitive against imports.
2.. The Auto Sector contributes 45% to the Manufacturing Gross Domestic Product (GDP),
26% to the Industrial GDP and 7.1% to the National GDP hence it is evident that this sector is
critical to the manufacturing sector. The Auto sector provides 29 million job opportunities, both
direct and indirect and has made investments to the tune of  ` 70, 000 crores in the last five
Financial Years (FYs). Considering that the industry had a turnover of USD 124 billion during
2014-15 and assuming a growth rate of 10% during 2015-16, the Government expects it to achieve
around 94% of the target set for the industry in the Automobile Mission Plan (2006-16) by 2016.
An ambitious Scheme for Faster Adoption and Manufacturing of (Hybrid and) Electric Vehicles in
India (FAME-India) is being implemented by the Government to support the hybrid/electrical
vehicles industry and its manufacturing ecosystem to attain self-sustenance. In the Budget
2016-17, the Government announced measures aiming to invest big in infrastructure like outlay of
` 97,000 crore for road infrastructure,  `  200 crore to FAME-India scheme & National Automotive
Testing R&D Infrastructure Project (NATRiP), reduction in customs duty on raw materials for
catalytic converters from 7.5% to 5%, etc that are expected to provide fillip to the Auto sector
in the ensuing years.
Department of Heavy Industry (DHI)
3. The Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises, comprising the Department of
Heavy Industry (DHI) and the Department of Public Enterprises (DPE), was created as per the
Presidential Notification dated the 15
th October, 1999. DHI administers 31 operating Central Public
Sector Enterprises (CPSEs), including 12 subsidiary companies and 1 JV company i.e. NTPC-
BHEL Power Projects Pvt. Ltd. (NBBPL). The Department also administers the following
autonomous organizations:
(a) NATRiP Implementation Society (NATIS) set up in July 2005, for guiding the
1

2
implementation of the National Automotive Testing and R&D Infrastructure Project
(NATRiP);
(b) Fluid Control Research Institute (FCRI), Palakkad, Kerala which caters to the needs
of the flow industry for calibration;
(c) Automotive Research Association of India (ARAI), Pune, Maharashtra; and
(d) National Automotive Board (NAB).
DHI has also been allocated the following subjects/Industrial Sectors:
(a) Heavy Engineering Equipment and Machine Tools Industry.
(b) Heavy Electrical Engineering Industries.
(c) Automotive Industries, including tractors and earth moving equipment.
The 31 CPSEs administered by DHI can be categorized into 3 major groups namely,
Engineering Units, Non- Engineering Units and Consultancy/Contracting Units. The list of the
CPSEs is placed at Annexure I.
4. The main objectives of DHI are: -
(a) Optimum utilization of installed capacity of CPSEs under the Department;
(b) Management Development to ensure professional management and operations in the
CPSEs;
(c) Promotion of profitability, efficiency and productivity through restructuring,
modernization, technology up-gradation and optimal deployment of human and
material resources in the CPSEs;
(d) Closer co-ordination and interaction between the manufacturing and the user sectors;
(e) Development and growth of Sectors looked after by the Department; and
(f) Implementation of a national project in Auto sector for creating state-of-the-art
facilities for testing etc.
5. The enterprises under the Department produce wide range of products ranging from
machine tools, industrial machinery, boiler, gas/steam/hydro turbines, turbo generators, electrical
equipment, and railway traction equipment, pressure vessels, AC locomotives, prime movers,
agricultural tractors and consumer products such as watches, cement, paper, tyres and salts, etc.
The industries provide goods and services for almost all sectors of the economy including power,
rail and road transport. The Department also looks after the Machine Building Industry and caters
to the requirements of equipments for basic industries such as steel, non –ferrous metals,
fertilizers, refineries, petrochemicals, shipping, paper, cement, sugar etc.  Besides, it supports the
development of a wide range of intermediate engineering products like castings forgings, diesel
engines, industrial gears and gear boxes.
(I) Detailed Demand for Grants (DDG) 2016-17
6. The Demand for Grants (DFG) 2016-17 a

examination of Demands of DHI, explanation was sought regarding the changes made for the year
in comparison to the previous years and the rationale behind the changes.

7.  In their submission, DHI stated that as per the instructions of Ministry of Finance (MoF),
rationalization of existing plan/ non-plan schemes have been done. The aim is to rationalize all
programmes/schemes by merging the relatively small schemes into a logical large schematic
framework. Rationalized final set of schemes will lead to well defined measurable outcomes which
can be monitored. Schemes/sub-schemes reflected in the Detailed Demand for Grants are also to
be suitably merged /eliminated to yield a more compact framework for schemes/programmes,
which will help the Ministries/Departments gain more flexibility in execution of the schemes and
guard against spreading the resources too thin. MoF have stressed upon the need for rationalizing
Central Sector Schemes so as to ensure that schemes having small outlays could be done away
with or merged with bigger schemes, and the feasibility of achieving the intended objectives
through merger/clubbing could be explored.

(1) Development of Automobile Industry
22. Auto Industry has been an engine of growth in most developed countries and it is essaying

10
the same role in India too. Indian Automobile industry, which was at its nascent stage at the
beginning of the 21 st century, has now become a huge industry that contributes majorly to growth
and development of Indian Economy. The industry witnessed two difficult Financial Years (FYs)
2013 and 2014, in which the segments across the industry witnessed de-growth, carrying nearly
60% surplus production capacity. However, this situation was reversed in the first half of financial
year 2015-16. But it was submitted to the Committee that ban on registration of new Diesel
V ehicles with more than 2000 ml capacity, imposed by the Hon’ble Supreme Court for National
Capital Region (NCR) in Dec 2015, resulted in flattening of sales graph of such vehicles.
23. In the last few years, Government has taken many proactive steps for improvement of
safety and emission norms for the vehicles. About 60 mandatory safety requirements have been
duly notified by the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways.  Besides, Government has also
announced the introduction of BS VI compliant vehicles with effect from 1
st April, 2020.  One of
the major actions taken for controlling vehicular pollution is initiation of National Mission on
Electric Mobility. Under this mission, DHI has formulated a holistic scheme to promote electric and
hybrid vehicles along with necessary infrastructure development with Faster Adoption and
Manufacturing of Electric (& Hybrid) vehicles in India (FAME India).
(i) National Automotive Testing and R&D Infrastructure Project (NATRiP)
24. The aim of NATRiP is to create world-class automotive testing, validation, Research &
Development (R&D) and homologation facilities in line with emerging requirements of the National
Automotive Safety and Emission roadmap. These are being created in the three principal hubs of
North, West and South India. NA TRiP was approved by the GoI in 2005, with a total investment
of `  1,718 crore, which was revised to  `  2286.06  crore. The initial scheduled date of completion
of NATRiP project was April, 2011, which was first extended to December, 2012, then to

and manufacturing of full range of cleaner electric vehicles technologies that include mild hybrid,
full hybrid vehicles (HEVs), plug in Hybrids Vehicles (BEVs) (collectively termed as HEVs) thereby

industry and its eco-system in India.

(2) Development of Capital Goods Sector.
(i) National Capital Goods Policy, 2016 (NCGP).
34. The National Capital Goods Policy, 2016 was announced on 15
th February, 2016 in Mumbai.
Initially, a Joint Task Force (JTF) was put in place to prepare a base paper on Capital Goods Policy
and sought comments of various stakeholders on the same. Other than the base paper, three sub
groups were formed under JTF on Technology and depth, Demand creation and Trade and Export.
Based on the response on the draft paper and inputs from Sub Groups as well as regional
roundtables, JTF completed formulation of a draft policy by October, 2015. Thereafter, the same
uploaded in the DHI website with a view to seeking comments/ views on the same. An Inter-
Ministerial Meeting was held in November, 2015 and a draft Cabinet Note on the National Capital
Goods Policy was circulated to the Ministries/ Departments concerned in December, 2015. After
receiving comments/ views of the Ministries/ Departments concerned, the Note was sent to the
Cabinet on 8.2.2016. This was followed by a Supplementary Note on 10.2.2016. However, the
meeting of the Cabinet scheduled to be held on 10.2.2016 was postponed. Therefore, the case was
moved for seeking approval of Hon’ble Prime Minister under Rule 12 of the Transaction of
Business Rules with a view to launch the Policy during ‘Make in India week’ in Mumbai.
The National Capital Goods Policy 2016 is available on the website of the Department (dhi.nic.in) .
35. The policy has made various key recommendation such as (i) integration of major capital
goods sub-sectors as priority sectors to be envisaged under ‘Make in India’ initiative; (ii) creation
of an enabling scheme as a pilot for ‘Heavy Industry Export & Market Development Assistance
Scheme (HIEMDA)’ with a view to enhance the export of Indian made capital goods; (iii)

16
strengthening existing capital goods scheme by increasing the budgetary allocation & scope of the
present ‘Scheme on Enhancement of Competitiveness of Capital Goods’; (iv) launching a
Technology Development Fund under Public Private Partnership (PPP) model to fund technology
acquisition, transfer of technology, purchase of  Intellectual Property Rights (IPRs) designs &
drawings and for commercialization of such technologies; (v) creation of a ‘Start-up Center for
Capital Goods Sector’; (vi) mandatory standardization and (vii) up gradation of testing
infrastructure; (viii) skill development through a Scheme to develop existing training centers and
setting up 5 new State of the art skill development centers and; (ix) modernization of existing CG
Sector units especially in Small and Medium Enterprises segment through a scheme based on
capital subsidy to promote manufacturing of quality products.

(ii) R&D Projects – Development of Advanced Ultra Super Critical (Adv+- Ultra
Super Critical – Adv- USC) Technology for Thermal Power Plants ( AUSC).
41. The R&D Project for “Development of Advanced Ultra Supercritical (Adv. USC) Technology
for Thermal Power Plants” is to be carried out jointly by Bharat Heavy Electricals Ltd. (BHEL),
Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research (IGCAR) and National Thermal Power Corporation Ltd.
(NTPC). The objective of the First Phase of the project is to undertake R&D on all aspects of
Advanced Ultra Super Critical (Adv-USC) technology for thermal power plants in order to improve
power plant efficiency, reduce carbon-dioxide emissions and reduce coal consumption per unit of
power generated. The proposed project would enable Indian industries to design, manufacture and
commission higher efficiency coal fired power plants with indigenously developed technology and
manufacturing process. The duration of the project is estimated to be of two and a half years from
the date of approval. The Department informed the Committee that the fund of Rs 50 crore
allocated for the project in BE 2015-16 was surrendered because the project has yet not been
approved by the GoI. In the BE 2016-17 a token provision of Rs one lakh has been made for the
project. Further, the Department also updated the Committee on the progress made during 2015-
16 on the project.
42. DHI submitted that pursuant to the decision taken in a meeting held on 20-05-2015 under
the Chairmanship of Secretary, DHI, BHEL had committed to enhance its contribution for the
project from Rs 220 crore to Rs 270 crore. NTPC had confirmed the contribution of Rs 50 crore
for the project and IGCAR was to contribute Rs 234 crore for the project. The balance amount
of Rs 1000 crore was to be funded by GoI. Further, certain pre-project R&D activities were taken
up with funding of approx. Rs 25 Crore provided by the Office of Principal Scientific Advisor
(PSA), GoI, wherein two out of five small projects have been successfully completed and work
on the balance three is underway. However, the work on R&D Phase of the main project would
be taken up based only on the finalization of funding pattern. Final Note was sent to Cabinet
Secretariat on 3-3-2015 for obtaining approval of CCEA. However, the Cabinet Secretariat vide its
O.M dated 16-7-2015 returned the copies of CCEA Note with the direction that DHI may take
necessary action to finalize the note afresh as per Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) direction on the
issue.
43. The Principal Secretary to Prime Minister took a meeting on 20-08-2015 on the above
mentioned subject wherein the following were decided:
(1) NTPC and BHEL need to reconsider their commitment for financial support to the
project. Further, a suggestion was put forward that an amount of Rs 200 crore may
be contributed by the NTPC and Rs 400 Crore each by BHEL and IGCAR. The
remaining amount will be provided as support by the GoI.

19
(2) If the project is to be taken up, the funding of Phase-I & II needs to be finalized
upfront. The sharing pattern for phase-II should also be the same as for Phase-I.
Further, there needs to be a tight Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between
GoI, IGCAR, BHEL & NTPC, delineating their respective responsibilities clearly.
44. As part of their submission DHI also shared with the Committee the comments received on
this from BHEL, NTPC and IGCAR and Ministry of Power (MoP).
IGCAR has expressed its inability to contribute in Phase II and any additional amount in
Phase I.
NTPC has expressed its inability to contribute more than Rs 50 crore in R&D project in
the first phase. They further stated that Proposal for funding of phase-I and phase II must be
clubbed together. Phase-II of the project was expected to cost about Rs 8000 to 10000 crore. It
was, therefore, necessary to decide the modalities for funding of the Technology Demonstration
Plant (TDP) also before any commitments on the funding of R&D phase of the project.
Ministry of Power endorsed the views of NTPC.
However, BHEL is opposed to the clubbing of Phase I and II of the project. BHEL has also
expressed its inability to enhance the contribution from Rs 270 Crore for Phase I. They further
informed that in Phase II, the main objective was to manufacture, erect and commission a full size
800 MW demo power plant to be owned by NTPC, which would also sell the power generated
at this plant. BHEL as the equipment manufacturer would execute a commercial order from NTPC
for the equipment required for this plant on a nominated basis as the technology was being
developed by a consortium where both BHEL and NTPC were members. In Phase II, the need for
Government funding shall be only to NTPC and may be to the extent of the differential over and
above the cost of setting up of a Super Critical Power Plant of same capacity.
45. DHI has further informed that to resolve the issue of funding, a High Level meeting was
conducted at the level of Principal Scientific Adviser to the Government of India with the different
stakeholders, Member, Planning Commission, IGCAR, BHEL, NTPC, DHI, Ministry of Power,
Department of Science and Technology, and action is being taken to review the funding
requirements by the different stakeholders.
46. The Committee finds it extremely disappointing that the scheme originally conceived
in 2014-15 is yet to be operationalized, for want of requisite approvals. It is understood that
the latest impediment in the approval of the scheme has been disagreement on the funding
pattern. It is also understood that there was an initial agreement on the financial
contribution of the participants and the disagreement emerged after the direction from the
PMO to upscale their individual contributions. However, the participating entities BHEL,
NTPC, IGCAR have found it not possible to further increase their contribution to the
scheme.  In this scenario, the Committee observes that the finalization of the funding
patterns has to be taken up on a top priority by DHI.  Advanced Ultra Super Critical
Technology for Thermal Power Plants is a technology of future as it provides cleaner and
more efficient avenues of thermal power. Hence the development of the same getting
delayed because of indecision of funding pattern is disappointing. The Committee is of the
opinion that the onus of taking initiative to find a solution to this imbroglio lies with DHI

20
and recommends that the matter should be taken up at all reconciliatory fora including the
Cabinet, if needed.  The Committee wants DHI to come back to it with the progress made
in this regard.

Committee is aware that the Government has come up with a lot of new initiatives to

BHEL
57. BHEL, one of the largest CPSEs in India and is the only Maharatna under DHI.  It is
engaged in design, engineering manufacture, construction, commissioning and servicing of a wide
range of products and services for the core sectors of the economy viz. Power, Transmission,

24
Industry, Transportation, Renewable Energy and Oil & Gas.  BHEL has maintained a consistent
track record of growth, performance and profitability, since its inception more than five decades
ago. However, contrary to this claim, the status of BHEL has been indicated as ‘Weak’ as per
DHI’s classification of its CPSEs based on the new guidelines of DPE.
58. The Committee asked BHEL to present its case regarding the “Weak” categorization by its
administrative ministry, in the presence of the representatives of DHI. As part of their explanations,
both BHEL and DHI harped on reasons which had been placed before the Committee time and
again, which included dampened demand for products, both domestic and international, difficulties
in coal linkage, peculiarities in some of the provisioning in the balance sheet, stranded orders,
problems in securing environmental clearances, etc.  Hope was also expressed by BHEL that owing
to the impetus of the Government on power infrastructure through schemes like Ujjwal DISCOM
Assurance Yojana (UDAY), corrective action taken towards successful execution of orders with
better interaction with customers, diversification into areas including defence solar power and other
alternative energy options, etc, the performance of the company would pick up in the coming
years.  However, the Committee found it difficult to buy the reasons put forward for the poor
plight of BHEL.
59. DHI’s further submission to the Committee on the matter regarding BHEL being categorized
as a “Weak” CPSE stated that according to BHEL the yard-sticks/criteria formulated for the
classification did not factor the operating business environment and the severe competitive intensity
faced by the Company from both domestic and international players. As such, the DPE criteria on
the matter were made applicable for all CPSEs, irrespective of their type of operations/category/
sector which should not be the case.
60. The Committee notes that the performance of BHEL has slackened over the last two
to three years owing to a slew of reasons given by the Company viz. retarded demand,
delayed environmental clearances, stranded orders, etc. In the view of the Committee, the
reasons put forward by BHEL portrays an impression that these have been ‘beyond the
control’ of the company. Even while considering that BHEL might have taken steps to check
the slide in its performance, the fact remains that their performance seems to have dipped
despite these efforts. Accordingly, the Committee finds it difficult to isolate the reasons for
the lackluster performance of BHEL to those quoted by the company alone. Therefore, the
Committee’s conclusion is that there has been a delay on the part of BHEL in responding
to the challenges thrown to them by the market and other factors.  Though, the Committee
does not completely discount the reasons put forth by BHEL, it is the Committee’s firm
belief that BHEL’s current situation is the outcome of their poor performance in the area
of risk analysis and business foresight, both of which would have allowed the Company to
anticipate rough business weather and for effective and commensurate course correction.
61. In the area of diversification of business also the Committee finds that the efforts
taken by BHEL does not seem to be of the quality of the top most companies in India to
which BHEL belongs. Efficient and timely diversification could have acted as a buffer to
absorb the shocks in the core business. Since this has not happened it will not be out of
place to presume that the diversification initiatives of BHEL do not bring in the desired
results. And for DHI, the Committee opines that DHI should have pressed BHEL firmly for

25
implementation of timely corrective measures. Under these circumstances, the Committee
cannot but recommend strict measures to ensure accountability for lapses in business
decisions to the extent possible.  Accordingly, it is further recommended that a forensic
audit for BHEL shall be ordered with a view to identify instances of deficiencies in business
decisions and take suitable measure so that those are not repeated.

(v) Hindustan Newsprint Limited (HNL)
85. HNL which was incorporated as a wholly owned subsidiary of Hindustan Paper Corporation
in 1982 with the major objective of taking over the business of Kerala Newsprint Project is a unit
of HPC Limited. HNL has experienced a brief streak of three years (2013-2015) of losses and it
is expecting better results in the current FY . When queried about the reasons for the losses and
the steps taken to address them DHI submitted the following developments:
1. Forest Based Raw Materials:  Government of Kerala (GoK) is committed to HNL by
means of a long term agreement to supply 1,80,000 MT of Forest based raw
material every year for use in the process of manufacturing paper. The price of raw
material payable by HNL is however fixed by the Government every year.
However, in view of the losses incurred in the last three years, the company
represented to the Government for considering a concessional pricing of raw
material in order to improve the profitability and sustain its operations. Considering
the request, Government of Kerala has consented for concessional pricing of Forest
Based Raw Materials viz. Wood, Reed and Bamboo for the next six years with
effect from 2015-16. The GoK has agreed to reduce the price from the existing
level of  `  2,600/2,900 per MT to  `  1,000 per MT. This concession is expected to
reduce the cost by a significant amount.
2. To supplement the requirement of forest based raw materials, HNL has also forayed
into its own Captive Plantation. As on date, it has all together 2,670 hectares under
Captive Plantation of various species of pulpwood trees covering several districts of
the State. Since modern techniques of plantation like Clonal propagation are adopted
by HNL Forestry team, the yield per hectare is better than the average Government
plantation. Consequently, the cost of production of Raw material in HNL’s captive
plantation is much cheaper than that of the GoK supplies.
The GoK was originally committed to provide 5,600 Hectares of land on lease basis
for Captive plantation. However, it could only provide 2,670 hectares. Now, the

31
Govt. has also decided to allot the balance 3,000 Hectares in a time bound manner.
Out of which 1,500 hectare has already been identified for immediate allotment, and
the balance will be allotted in the course of another six months. With the allotment
of additional land under Captive plantation, HNL is expected to ensure continuous
supply of raw material at a cheaper cost.
3. Power Supply: In the FY 2014-15 the Company has started purchasing of Power
under the Open access trading portal of Power Trading Corporation. Under the
scheme, the company is able to bid for purchase of power at a price significantly
lower than that of the State Electricity Board. Even though, the price of traded
power may not always be cheaper than the State Board, it remains significantly
lower during winter and rainy season. The rates are also generally lower on holidays
and weekends. Taking advantage of the same phenomenon, the company is able to
save a significant sum of money on power cost. With the implementation of
purchase of power by trading from National Grid, the Company is expected to save
significantly in energy cost.
4. Cost Control Measures: In addition to the above, the Company has also started
different cost control measures like reduction of Employee cost by minimizing
Overtime Wage, streamlining the overhead costs by rationalizing manpower
requirement for factory maintenance, bulk tendering for Imported Coal for ensuring
better quality at a cheaper price, and overall monitoring of plant operations for
avoiding wastages of all sorts.
In view of the above positive developments and corrective measures undertaken by
the Company, it is expected that the cost of production will reduce significantly, and
Sales realization will also improve, which in turn will provide a competitive edge to
the Company. With the above the company is expected to turn around.
86. It was further submitted to the Committee that HNL proposes a Mill Development Plan with
an estimated project expenditure of ` 455 crore. On its implementation, there would be no qualms
so far quality of newsprint is concerned. The problem HNL is encountering is the realizable value
as Newsprint is in the Open General License and can be imported duty free, whereas HNL pays
Customs Duty on all its imports. Newsprint sold to the customers registered with Registrar of
Newspapers in India (RNI) is exempted from Excise Duty whereas manufacturers of Newsprint
have to invariably incur a heavy expenditure on paying Excise Duty on the inputs purchased and
Service Tax for services but the CENV AT credit is not available to them as the Newsprint itself
is free from Excise Duty. If these anomalies are removed specially imposition of Custom Duty on
import of Newsprint which used to be 10 % earlier is restored, HNL would be in a position to
substitute the imported newsprint, so far being dumped by the foreign manufacturers with cheaper
cost, and would be in a position to save lots of foreign currency for the Country.
87. The Committee notes that HNL has taken efficient and practical steps aimed at
revival of the Company. These proactive steps are expected to bring down the production
cost of newsprint and provide HNL a comparative advantage in the market.  The Committee
observes that the steps adopted by Government of Kerala are highly supportive of the cause
of HNL and the management of HNL would do well to make efficient use of it.  Further,

32
it is recommended that alongwith cost cutting measures, HNL should also revisit its
marketing strategies to be able to fully translate the benefits brought by the expected cost
advantage to tangible financial gains for the company.
88. As informed by DHI the Company is expected to turn around after a three-year
streak of losses.  In this regard, it is expected that DHI will monitor and guide HNL step
by step towards the turn around and provide all necessary support as expected from an
administrative ministry. The Committee further takes into cognizance the hardships faced

stage. This is also because IEBR of a company comprises of resources generated by
Company concerned through profit, loans, equity and other funds to be secured by the

(III)  Auto and Capital Goods Associations.
98. As part of the examination of Demands for Grants (2016-17) of DHI, the Committee heard
the representatives of select Auto Associations and Capital Goods Sectors in India.  The
Associations represented were ACMA, SIAM, ASDC, FICCI, ASSOCHAM, CII, IMTMA and
others.
99. In nutshell, the proposal placed before the Committee by these associations include
allocation of more funds for NEMMP 2020; more initiatives in investing in Charging Infrastructure
for electric vehicles; streamlining/eliminating inconsistencies in taxation of hybrid/electric vehicles
across various states in India; promotion of automobile skill development initiatives; impetus on
bridging technology gap in Machine Tool sector; measures to ensure level playing field to Indian
CGS companies in global tenders floated by major CPSEs; compulsory domestic value addition to

36
an appropriate percentage to be made part of all major CG imports, higher depreciation allowance
on Indian Machine Tools to generate greater demand and to heighten emphasis on technology
up-gradation, exclusion of Machine Tools and other Capital Goods from FTAs entered into
countries that have strong and surplus Capital Goods Sector; effective measures to counter fake
certificates of ‘Country of Origin’ under FTAs, Indian Embassies & High Commissions in different
countries to be allowed to promote India’s business interests with the help of Commercial Attaches,
Implementation of the Heavy Industry Export and Market Development Assistance Scheme
(HIEMDA), etc.
100. The Committee’s observation after hearing the representatives of Auto & Capital
Goods Sector associations is that the need of the hour is to focus more on urban & rural
infrastructure, road & highways, satellite cities, etc to generate demands at home in both
these sectors.  For auto industry, the Committee is of the opinion that they should start
looking for export markets in the face of saturating domestic arena while formulating
business expansion plans. Also, they should earnestly try and develop indigenous technology
in the field of electric vehicles. CG associations should come up with a concrete plan in tune
with the NCGP, 2016 objectives of the Government to triple the size of Indian CGS in a
decade.
101.  The Committee takes into account through the submission of DHI that they have
already taken into cognizance the areas put forth by the industry associations seeking
attention of the Government. Nevertheless, the Committee recommends that the
Government should look into the issues submitted by these associations before the
Committee and act upon them in best possible manner. This will encourage the private
sector to be more participative in the broader initiatives of nation building.

RECOMMENDA TIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE—A T A GLANCE
1. The Committee notes that the Demands for Grants (2016-17) for DHI has followed
a new pattern of depiction of allocation of funds when compared to the last year. On a quick
reference of Demands No. 44, the new pattern may appear difficult to comprehend due to
the absence of comparative details upfront. But, in reply to a query on this, the
Department has preferred to an explanation of bunching of smaller schemes under larger
umbrella schemes for the purpose of imparting more flexibility in the execution of schemes
and to guard against spending the resources too thin. The Committee finds reason in the
rational provided by DHI and appreciates the new initiative of the MoF.  It is expected that
the new system of Umbrella Schemes will result in timely implementation of schemes by
reallocating funds between sub schemes as per operational expediencies which should in
turn curb underutilization of funds as well. (Para No 10)
2. Regarding the allocation of funds to schemes under Development of Automobile
Industry, the Committee observes that funds for the same purpose has been allocated under
two different Heads, with one Head witnessing only a miniscule allocation and the other
reflecting majority of the funds.  The Department’s explanation for differential allocation
is that token allocations in two Heads have been made to cater to the possibility of funds
being allocated to NATRiP in the form of Grants–in-Aid as well as in the form of Loan, even
though the loan possibility is low. The Committee would have found it more appropriate if
the Government would have at least by now decided the manner in which funds to NATRiP
are to be provided, i.e. either as Loan or as Grants. Such uncertainties can affect the lucidity
of the Demand and the transparency with which allocations are made. (Para No 14)
3. The Committee takes note that under the Head, Grants to CPSEs, funds have been
reflected under two different Heads – on Depiction Head and on Operational Head. On this
duality of funds, it has been informed that funds under the Depiction Head will be
transferred to the Operational head for executing expenditure.  This arrangement has been
done under the directives of Government of India (GoI). Further, it is encouraging to take
into cognizance that DHI is one of the few Departments of the GoI where all fund transfers
are being made on-line through PFMS and under this system funds can be transferred only
to those Heads which atleast have some token allocation.  The Committee observes that the
PFMS will hasten up the release of funds and eliminate avoidable delays and
mismanagement. (Para No 18)
4. However, the Committee also wonders whether it is not ironical that while on the one
hand the Government is moving towards integration of small schemes under larger umbrella
schemes for the benefit of simplification of procedure and facilitating financial flexibility, on
the other hand it is complicating matters by adding more Heads for allocations and
expenditure of funds under a single umbrella scheme. (Para No 19)
37

38

of R&D Project Development of Advanced Ultra Super- Critical (Adv-USC) Technology for
Thermal Power Plants and Heavy Engineering Corporation Limited  (HEC) had to be
completely withdrawn at RE stage. As informed by the Department, such surrender of funds
had to be effected as the requisite approval from the final competent authority was not

which have not been approved by the final competent authority should not be reflected in
full as BE.  Instead, reflection of a token allocation will give a much realistic picture to the
Demands as funds can be sought at the RE stage when the final approval materializes
during the course of time. (Para No 21)

of NATRiP as submitted by the Department. It also notes the explanation given by the
Department on how it is to utilize the plan loan of  ` ` ` ` `  300 crore allocated to the project
during 2015-16 over a period of 3 years ending in 2017-18. In this regard, the Committee
recognizes that this spread of expenditure warrants yet another extension of NATRiP,
beyond currently extended period upto December, 2017.  The Committee express concerned
over the fact that a project which has already seen three extensions is looking for further
extension.  In the view of the Committee, this unending continuation of the flagship project

For an ambitious aim of tripling the size of the sector in a decade, there is a need for a
clear cut road map and commensurate funds. Further, in this venture, equal participation
of the Private Industry along with the Government will be a foregone conclusion. In view
of this, the Committee recommends that in tune with the objectives of NCGP, required
managerial and financial support ought to be provided to the sector through the Scheme for
Enhancement of Competitiveness in the Indian Capital Goods Sector and the components of

NTPC, IGCAR have found it not possible to further increase their contribution to the
scheme.  In this scenario, the Committee observes that the finalization of the funding

Technology for Thermal Power Plants is a technology of future as it provides cleaner and
more efficient avenues of thermal power. Hence the development of the same getting

11. The Committee notes with concern that none of the CPSEs under DHI have been
found to be operating in a healthy manner.  The status of CPSEs has been classified as
weak, incipient sick or sick.  In the case of DHI, even the prestigious Maharatna BHEL has
been termed as a ‘Weak’  CPSE. The Committee considers this as an extremely alarming
situation which calls for decisive intervention by DHI, the administrative department.  As
per the New Guidelines of DPE, the primary responsibility for ensuring profitable
functioning of CPSEs lies with the respective administrative ministries.  In this regard, the
Committee is aware that the Government has come up with a lot of new initiatives to
reshape the avenues for revival /restructure of CPSEs.  This includes the winding up of
Board for Industrial and Financial Reconstruction (BRPSE), constitution of National Council
of Law Tribunal (NCLT) and other similar measures.  The subject of revival /restructuring
of CPSEs have repeatedly attracted the attention of the Committee and every time the
Department comes up with some generalized reasons and solutions to the entire problem.
However, the Committee has found that the lack of foresight and timely action can be
termed as one of the main causes for the poor plight of the CPSEs. In this scenario, the
Committee would like to strongly recommend that DHI desperately needs some workable
roadmap on the performance of each of its 31 CPSEs regardless of their current
classification.  It is also recommended that some appropriate mechanism for fixing
responsibility with the management of the CPSEs for the distress of CPSE concerned has
to be drawn up. (Para No 54)

40
12. In this matter, the Committee is unanimous in its opinion and is in full support of
the view of the Department regarding disposal of assets of sick/loss incurring CPSEs that
the immovable assets, i.e., land and/or buildings of such CPSEs would be transferred only
to Central/State Government or Central /State Government entities/PSUs. Accordingly, the
Committee strongly recommends that the Government should retain the above stand as this
would avoid sell out of landed property of CPSEs to private persons. The Committee feels
that land/building of such CPSEs can be utilised to start ITI or other technical institutions
under the scheme “Skill India”. (Para No 56)
13. The Committee notes that the performance of BHEL has slackened over the last two
to three years owing to a slew of reasons given by the Company viz. retarded demand,
delayed environmental clearances, stranded orders, etc. In the view of the Committee, the
reasons put forward by BHEL portrays an impression that these have been ‘beyond the
control’ of the company. Even while considering that BHEL might have taken steps to check
the slide in its performance, the fact remains that their performance seems to have dipped
despite these efforts. Accordingly, the Committee finds it difficult to isolate the reasons for
the lackluster performance of BHEL to those quoted by the company alone. Therefore, the
Committee’s conclusion is that there has been a delay on the part of BHEL in responding
to the challenges thrown to them by the market and other factors.  Though, the Committee
does not completely discount the reasons put forth by BHEL, it is the Committee’s firm
belief that BHEL’s current situation is the outcome of their poor performance in the
area of risk analysis and business foresight, both of which would have allowed the
Company to anticipate rough business weather and for effective and commensurate course
correction. (Para No 60)
14. In the area of diversification of business also the Committee finds that the efforts
taken by BHEL does not seem to be of the quality of the top most companies in India to
which BHEL belongs. Efficient and timely diversification could have acted as a buffer to
absorb the shocks in the core business. Since this has not happened it will not be out of
place to presume that the diversification initiatives of BHEL do not bring in the desired
results. And for DHI, the Committee opines that DHI should have pressed BHEL firmly for
implementation of timely corrective measures. Under these circumstances, the Committee
cannot but recommend strict measures to ensure accountability for lapses in business
decisions to the extent possible.  Accordingly, it is further recommended that a forensic

primary responsibility regarding the health of its CPSEs. Accordingly, it is recommended
that DHI should take measures to properly guide the management of NPPC in the
implementation of the revival plan and see to that they steer clear of such lapses in the
times ahead. (Para No 84)
25. The Committee notes that HNL has taken efficient and practical steps aimed at
revival of the Company. These proactive steps are expected to bring down the production
cost of newsprint and provide HNL a comparative advantage in the market.  The Committee
observes that the steps adopted by Government of Kerala are highly supportive of the cause
of HNL and the management of HNL would do well to make efficient use of it.  Further,
it is recommended that alongwith cost cutting measures, HNL should also revisit its
marketing strategies to be able to fully translate the benefits brought by the expected cost
advantage to tangible financial gains for the company. (Para No 87)
26. As informed by DHI the Company is expected to turn around after a three-year
streak of losses.  In this regard, it is expected that DHI will monitor and guide HNL step
by  step towards the turn around and provide all necessary support as expected from an
administrative ministry. The Committee further takes into cognizance the hardships faced
by HNL due to customs and excise duty liabilities. HNL claims that restoration of 10 %
customs duty on imported prints would help the Company immensely and they would be in
a position to substitute imported material. In view of this, the Committee recommends that

43
DHI should proactively take up the duty rationalizations requested by HNL with the
appropriate agencies. (Para No 88)
27. As per the facts placed before the Committee it is noted that the RMDP of NEPA is
progressing reasonably well. The total Budgetary support of  ` ` ` ` `  157 crore approved to the
Company and as per DHI, an amount of  ` ` ` ` `  109.09 crore is purported to be utilized by March,
2016 in the form of 3 installments during the years, 2014-15. However, it is also noted that
NEPA has to secure a bank loan of  ` ` ` ` `  128 crore to complete the funds required for RMDP.
The Committee is made to understand that request for Bank guarantee has been pending
with MoF since September, 2015.  The Committee feels that it is high time a decision is
taken on the request, as the same is already badly delayed. It is therefore, recommended
that the execution of RMDP shall be expedited and all further delays are prevented. DHI
shall come back to the Committee on the progress made on the issue and efforts taken to
pursue the MoF for a decision on the above request. The Committee also wants DHI to
consider continuing the working capital support to NEPA Ltd as the company is so close to
standing on its own feet and might lose its way if support is withdrawn at this stage. As
already recommended in other similar cases, it will not be out of place to mention that DHI
should also ensure the responsibility of the management of NEPA in the timely execution
of RMDP and also in the follow up with the MoF. (Para No 95)
28. The Committee notes that in the Demands for Grants, the IEBR figures of CPSEs
portray a very unrealistic picture.  In most instances, the BE IEBR is greatly reduced or
even comes to naught at the RE stage. The explanation for such reductions provided by the
Government/ CPSEs range from deferred investments, decrease in profit, incurring of loss
by the companies, the companies being or becoming sick, reductions in tune with business
requirements, delay in securing loans, etc.  The Committee feels that though each variation
in IEBR figures are backed up with reasons by Government /CPSEs, it remains a fact that
the overall picture drawn while going through the Demands as such is confusing and borders
on misleading information as a considerable portion of the amount is disappearing at RE
stage. This is also because IEBR of a company comprises of resources generated by
Company concerned through profit, loans, equity and other funds to be secured by the
company, etc and in most cases these figures are assumptive. Accordingly, the Committee
observes that the Demand should contain an explanation to IEBR figures of each of the
CPSEs indicating the nature of the funds projected as IEBR. (Para No 97)
29. The Committee’s observation after hearing the representatives of Auto & Capital
Goods Sector associations is that the need of the hour is to focus more on urban & rural
infrastructure, road & highways, satellite cities, etc to generate demands at home in both
these sectors.  For auto industry, the Committee is of the opinion that they should start
looking for export markets in the face of saturating domestic arena while formulating
business expansion plans. Also, they should earnestly try and develop indigenous technology
in the field of electric vehicles. CG associations should come up with a concrete plan in tune
with the NCGP, 2016 objectives of the Government to triple the size of Indian CGS in a
decade. (Para No 100)

44
30.  The Committee takes into account through the submission of DHI that they have
already taken into cognizance the areas put forth by the industry associations seeking
attention of the Government. Nevertheless, the Committee recommends that the
Government should look into the issues submitted by these associations before the
Committee and act upon them in best possible manner. This will encourage the private
sector to be more participative in the broader initiatives of nation build ing. (Para No 101)
