REPORT
Public Sector Enterprises (PSEs) were set up to serve the broad macro-economic objective
of higher economic growth, self-sufficiency in production of goods and services, long term
equilibrium in balance of payment and low and stable prices besides meeting socio- economic
obligations. Performance of Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs), during the year 2014-15,
is summarized below:
(i) There were 298 Central Public Sector Enterprises (excluding 7 insurance companies)
under the administrative control of various Ministries/Departments as on 31.3.2015.
Out of these 298 CPSEs, 235 were in operation and 63 CPSEs have yet to
commence business. Schedules-wise list of the CPSEs and list of Maharatna,
Navratana and Miniratna CPSEs are placed at Annexure I and II, respectively.
Out of 235 operating CPSEs as many as 157 CPSEs showed profit and 77 CPSEs
incurred losses during 2014-15.
(ii) The cumulative investment (paid up capital plus long terms loans), which was
` 29 crores in 5 enterprises at the time of first Five Year Plan ( i.e. as on 31.3.1951),
has gone up to ` 10,96,057 crores in 298 CPSEs as on 31.3.2015. While the increase
in ‘investment’ in all the CPSEs went up by 10.48% in 2014-15 over 2013-14, the
increase in ‘capital employed’ went up by 7.40% during the same period.
(iii) The ‘net profit’ of 157 profit making CPSEs was ` 1,30,363 crores in 2014-15 as
against 164 profit making enterprises in 2013-14. The ‘net loss’ of 77 loss making
enterprise stood at ` 27,360 crores during the year as against 70 loss making
enterprises in 2013-14.
(iv) In comparison to 2013-14, the profitability ratios in terms of net profit to turnover/
revenue, net profit to capital employed, net profit to net worth, sales to capital
employed have declined, whereas interest to gross profit show an increase in
2014-15.
2. The Financial Year (FY) 2015-16 saw some important milestones in the realm of CPSEs in
India.  The revival/restructure/closure of sick CPSEs had evolved into a painful delayed process.
To address this, Department of Public Enterprises (DPE) brought out guidelines to “Streamlining
the mechanism for revival and restructuring of sick, incipient sick and weak Central Public Sector
Enterprises: General principles and mechanism of restructuring” in October, 2015. The guidelines
enumerated the criteria for identifying the CPSEs as sick, incipient sick and weak. Subsequently,
the formal closing down of Board for Reconstruction of Public Sector Enterprises (BRPSE), one
of the agencies involved in the revival/restructuring process of CPSEs, was announced in
November, 2015. After the closing down of BRPSE, the administrative Ministries/Departments were
put in charge of the primary responsibility of keeping watch over the health of CPSEs under them.
Further, the restructuring mechanism was also made time bound. The proposed National Council
1

2
of Law Tribunal (NCLT), as prescribed by Companies Act, 2013 was made the sole agency to
process the revival/restructure/closure of CPSEs in India thereby ending the hitherto existent multi
agency arrangement.
3. Further, in the Budget 2016-17, the Finance Minister announced that the assets of CPSEs
had to be leveraged for generation of resources for investment in new projects.  DPE has been
assigned the responsibility of monitoring Capital Expenditure (CAPEX) by CPSEs in infrastructural
projects. The Budget also contained an announcement that a comprehensive approach for efficient
management of Government investment in CPSEs would be adopted.  Regarding disinvestment/
strategic sale of CPSEs, the Government also had laid out a new method wherein the NITI Aayog
has been tasked with identifying the CPSEs for disinvestment, mode of sale, percentage of sale and
methods of evaluation.  DPE has been made part of the process of disinvestment at its different
stages and the same is in tune with the enhancement of the mandate of DPE carried out in the
second half of the year 2015.
Department of Public Enterprises- Mandate
4. In their 52
nd Report, the Estimates Committee of 3 rd Lok Sabha (1962-67) stressed the need
for setting up a centralized coordinating unit, which could also make continuous appraisal of the
performance of public enterprises which led to the setting up of the Bureau of Public Enterprises
(BPE) in 1965 in the Ministry of Finance.  Subsequently, as a result of the reorganization of the
Ministries/Departments of the Union Government in September, 1985, BPE was made part of the
Ministry of Industry.  In May, 1990, BPE was made a full-fledged Department known as the
Department of Public Enterprises (DPE).  Presently, it is part of the Ministry of Heavy Industries
and Public Enterprises.
5. The Department of Public Enterprises is the nodal department for all the Central Public
Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) and formulates policy pertaining to CPSEs. It lays down, in particular,
policy guidelines on performance improvement and evaluation, autonomy and financial delegation
and personnel management in CPSEs. It furthermore collects and maintains information in the form
of a Public Enterprises Survey on several areas in respect of CPSEs.
6. In fulfilling its role, the Department Coordinates with other Ministries, CPSEs and
concerned organizations. As per the Allocation of Business Rules of the Government, the following
subjects have been allocated to the DPE:
Residual work relating to erstwhile Bureau of Public Enterprises including Industrial
Management Pool.
Coordination of matters of general policy affecting all Public Sector Enterprises.
Evaluation and monitoring the performance of Public Sector Enterprises, including the
Memorandum of Understanding mechanism.
Matters relating to Permanent Machinery of Arbitration for the Public Sector Enterprises.
Counselling, training and rehabilitation of employees in Central Public Sector Undertakings
under V oluntary Retirement Scheme (VRS).

3
Review of capital projects and expenditure in Central Public Sector Enterprises.
Measures aimed at improving performance of Central Public Sector Enterprises and other
capacity building initiatives of Public Sector Enterprises.
Rendering advice relating to revival, restructuring or closure of Public Sector Enterprises,
including the mechanisms therefor.
Matters relating to Standing Conference of Public Enterprises.
Matters relating to International Center for Public Enterprises.
Categorization of Central Public Sector Enterprises, including conferring ‘Ratna’ status.
Survey of Public Enterprises.
The Department of Public Enterprises implements two Plan Schemes viz. (i) Scheme of
Counselling, Retraining and Redeployment (CRR) for the rationalised employees of CPSEs and (ii)
Scheme of Research, Development and Consultancies (RDC) on Generic issues related to Public
Sector Enterprises (CPSEs and SLPEs).
7. During the oral evidence as part of the examination of Demands for Grants (2016-17) of
DPE, the Committee pointed out that the mandate of the Department was significant and it had the
responsibility of overseeing the working of the CPSEs in India which had a cumulative turnover
of ` 22,00,000 crore. Further, the Committee also took into cognizance the expansion of the
mandate of the Department which now included evaluation of CPSEs, the monitoring of their
performance and the review of CAPEX by the CPSEs. Besides, DPE also had the responsibility of
running the PMA mechanism.
8. The Secretary, DPE while answering the queries of the Committee stated that-
“DPE has a chequered history. We started as a bureau and when we became a
Department, we were given certain responsibilities that have, sometimes, been changing.  At
one point of time, DPE was doing disinvestment, but some years back, the Department of
Disinvestment has been created.  So, that issue has been separated.  Just in August, we were
given the role of monitoring CAPEX and hon. Member has raised a point on that issue.
We are monitoring that from August last year only and we are trying to improve our system.
I do agree that there has been delay in projects.  But the delays in the projects of CPSEs
are being monitored now as closely as we can and we will keep on trying to improve the
system. There has also been a point made about the PMA mechanism.  The Departments
sometimes go to courts; the corporates also, sometimes, go to courts.  This issue has been
coming up again and again and we have had meetings at higher level in Cabinet
Secretariat and the Departments have been asked to desist from going to court and try to
settle it at the level of PMA. The pendency is there.  But, definitely, it has been a
mechanism that has helped us.  In certain issues which are not accepted by the parties
concerned, the appeal would lie with the Secretary, Law, and it is always settled within the
ambit of the Government without resorting to going to Courts.”

4
9. In their written replies to the queries of the Committee regarding the enhancement of
mandate, the Department submitted that the Amendment of Government of India (Allocation of
Business) Rules, 1961 has been done vide Presidential Notification in August, 2015 to enhance the
role of DPE in monitoring of performance of CPSEs and effective management of their assets by
allocating some additional subjects to DPE. These included review of capital projects and
expenditure in CPSEs, measures aimed at improving performance and rendering advice relating to
revival, restructuring or closure of Public Sector Enterprises including the mechanisms therefor.
DPE had accordingly initiated steps for monitoring the CAPEX projects of 33 CPSEs, Railway
Board and four other organizations. Similarly, for strengthening of performance evaluation process,
MoU guidelines for 2016-17 had been revised and parameter proposed were result oriented rather
than process oriented. Guidelines for Streamlining the mechanism for revival and restructuring of
sick/ incipient sick and weak CPSEs were issued on 29 October, 2015.
10. The Committee notes that the mandate of DPE has been augmented with the addition
of roles in monitoring of performance of CPSEs and effective management of their assets.
This has been done by addition of subjects to the Allocation of Business of DPE.  The
Committee is of the considered opinion that though the Budget allocation of DPE is small
compared to the major Ministries/Departments of the Government, the role to be essayed
by them is critical.  As the nodal Department of all CPSEs in India, their effective
evaluation and monitoring is going to be ‘humongous task.   The newly added responsibility
of CAPEX monitoring, measures to improve performance of CPSEs and other capacity
building initiatives and advice regarding revival/restructuring/closure of CPSEs will render
the working of DPE pivotal to the way CPSEs perform in the country.
11. Accordingly, the Committee observes that DPE should realize and imbibe the
magnitude and importance of the responsibilities that have been entrusted to them and take
more proactive measures to play out this role.  Rather them imagining themselves just as
a nodal coordinating agency, DPE should reinvent themselves as an arm of the Government
which can take decisive steps on its own or in coordination with other Ministries/
Departments   to create a facilitative milieu for CPSEs to perform to their potential.  The
Committee is of the firm view that DPE should not be restricting themselves to just issuing
guidelines and providing advice.  The new mandate gives them ample space to effectively
follow up the implementation of the advices rendered by them through their guidelines.
Accordingly, the Committee recommends that to be able to do this, DPE has to equip
themselves better and come out with measures implementable on ground and also
endeavour to create a coordinative platform involving the respective administrative
Ministries and other relevant Government agencies through which matters relating to the
working of CPSEs in the country can be resolved at a single stage avoiding time lag in
administrative decisions, the single most degenerative factor in case of decisions related to
CPSEs.
DPE during the Twelfth Plan Period (2012-17) till now.
12. When asked about to provide an overview of the CPSE ecosystem in the country during
the Twelfth Plan Period (2012-17) till now, and to bring out all major events/factors that made an
impact in the Sector by providing a brief outline of the initiatives of the Government during this

5
period, it was submitted by the Department that the global economic performance has been
subdued over the previous couple of years and the developing economies were struggling to cope
with the declining commodity prices, reduced capital inflows into their economies and increasing
financial volatility. The CPSEs in India were performing to the best of their abilities in the prevailing
economic scenario. Brief outline of the initiatives of the Government during this period were as
under:-
Amendment of Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961 has been
made vide Presidential Notification in August 2015 to enhance the role of DPE in

order to wider its scope and coverage.

23. When the Committee wanted to know about the outcome of the reviews of the scheme
undertaken by the nodal agencies and the modifications done in the CRR scheme after the review,
the DPE submitted that in the year 2012-13, National Institute of Entrepreneurship and Small
Business Development (NIESBUD), an autonomous body of the Ministry of Micro, Small and
Medium Enterprises was engaged to evaluate the CRR Scheme. Major findings and

10
recommendations had been circulated to Nodal agencies for compliance. Some of the key findings
and recommendations were as under:
Adoption of DPE’s strategic approach of mixing both private and Government sector
organisations as nodal agencies has paid dividend. With varied experience, these nodal
agencies have been able to infuse synergy for the furtherance of the CRR Scheme over
the years at grassroots.
The widening of the ambit of the scheme by involving dependents of separated employees
has proved to be beneficial. This provision has been continued while implementing the
scheme in the current year.
The analysis of quantitative data posted by VRS optees/dependents points towards greater
fulfilment of objectives and goals as outlined in the scheme.
Academic orientation of the training imparted by nodal agencies has market friendly ideology
with scope for self-employment in case of both Government and private agencies.
CRR Scheme necessitates involvement of State based Government organisations engaged in
skill development and livelihood promotion activities.
More stress is needed on follow-ups and redeployment after linking with micro credit/
finance. In this context, Nodal Agencies have already been directed to explore possibilities
of hand holding projects and linkages particularly in context with training to dependents
under CRR to enhance redeployment/self-employment opportunities.
The quality of mobilisation (motivation) by nodal agencies in relation to counselling of VRS
optees/dependents has been found to have moderate impact on (i) retention of expected
motivation during the training; and (ii) in the job employment or in self- employment
activities.
More stress is needed to explore the possibility of formation of Self Help Group (SHGs)
by the agencies. Nodal Agencies have been asked to form SHGs wherever feasible with
provision for creation of corpus funds. Nodal Agencies have also been advised to have
sessions on bankable projects and hand holdings with participation of financial institutions.
24. The Committee has always been appreciative of the objectives served by the CRR
scheme which basically offers a social security net to employees of CPSEs who optees for
VRS or get retrenched. The Committee takes into cognizance the fact that NIESBUD had
undertaken an evaluation of the scheme in 2012-13 and had recommended a host of
improvements. One of the major recommendations was the need to stress more on follow
ups and redeployment after linking with micro credit/finance. Handholding projects and
linkages were also recommended to enhance redeployment/self employment opportunities of
the former employees and their dependents trained under the scheme. DPE have submitted
that there recommendations had been circulated to the Nodal Agencies for compliance.
However, Committee finds that the number of people redeployed after being trained under
the scheme has always hovered around 50% or less of the total trained personnel. The

11
situation has continued even after the recommendations of NIESBUD made in 2012.
Accordingly, the Committee strongly recommends that the Department should take
appropriate measures expeditiously to improve the number of trainees who get redeployed
subsequent to the training under the scheme.  In this regard, the Committee also wants
DPE to consider focussed Skill Development under current impetus accorded to skill
development by the Government.  The Nodal Agencies under the Scheme should identify the
skill sets that are in demand in the local area in terms of employability and provide
training to people under the Scheme. To the Committee, this is one of the measures that
can be taken to improve the redeployment ratio. Further, this will also contribute towards
the efforts of the Government to address the huge skill deficit of the workforce in the
country in different spheres.

Revival/Restructuring of sick/loss incurring CPSEs.
32. As part of its examination of DFG 2016-17 of DPE, the Department was asked to explain,
step by step, the mechanism which was in place now and before i.e. , when Board for
Reconstruction of Public Sector Enterprises (BRPSE) was in existence (till November, 2015) for
revival/restructuring/closures of CPSEs while bring out the roles of each agency, i.e.  the
administrative Ministry, BRPSE, BIFR and various other approving authorities in the process. The
Department was also asked to make a comparison of the erstwhile process of dealing with a sick
CPSE with the process made effective beyond November, 2015 with the NCLT and the NITI Ayog,
as the authorities of approval.
33. In reply, DPE submitted that before the winding up of BRPSE, proposals relating to revival/
restructuring of sick CPSEs received in DPE from the administrative Ministries/Departments
concerned, were referred to BRPSE for its recommendations. BRPSE considered the restructuring
or revival plan of CPSEs and gave its recommendations. The recommendations were advisory in
nature. The administrative Ministry/Department concerned processed the recommendations of
BRPSE and obtained approval of the competent authority and thereafter implemented the
decisions.
34. Consequent upon the decision of the Government (on 7.10.2015) for winding up of BRPSE,
DPE issued guidelines on 29.10.2015 on “Streamlining the mechanism for revival and restructuring
of sick/incipient sick and weak Central Public Sector Enterprises”. The administrative Ministry/
Department concerned was now responsible to monitor the sickness of CPSEs functioning under
them and take timely redressal measures for revival/restructuring/disinvestment of sick/loss making
CPSEs with the approval of the competent authority.
35. Based on the information available in Public Enterprises Survey, 2014-15, DPE has prepared
a list of sick, incipient sick and weak CPSEs as on 31.3.2015 and has sent the list to the
concerned administrative Ministries/Departments of CPSEs on 10.2.2016 to confirm the
classification (identification of sick/incipient sick and weak CPSEs) for taking action as per the
DPE guidelines dated 29.10.2015 regarding revival and restructuring of sick and weak CPSEs.
36. Regarding the roles of different agencies involved in the process, DPE submitted that NCLT
and BIFR came under MoCA and Department of Financial Services, respectively. The role of DPE
was formulation of policy guidelines for dealing with sickness in CPSEs as per its guidelines issued
for revival/restructuring of sick CPSEs on 29.10.2015. The role of other agencies could be
explained by the administrative Ministries/Departments concerned. Further, the Department also
stated that the setting-up of NCLT is likely to replace BIFR. Ministry of MoCA was yet to notify
the setting-up of NCLT. In that case, BIFR would continue with its extant functions. DPE also
stated that the details regarding the setting-up of NCLT and the future of BIFR have been sought
from MoCA and Department of Financial Services, respectively.
37. During the oral evidence of DPE, the Committee further queried on the reasons behind
winding up of BRPSE for which the Department replied that the Government felt that the BRPSE

14
was an additional layer and needed to be removed.  In that process, the responsibility was given
to the administrative Ministry concerned to watch, to see and to review the performance. DPE has
prescribed a few things to do as part of this to the administrative Ministry. One of them was to
see whether they have become sick or they have become weak. If it falls in that category, DPE
instructed the administrative Ministry to keep a close watch and try to turn them around and do
mid-course correction and, wherever necessary, move for its restructuring or improving its
performance.  As per DPE guideline issued 29 th October, 2015 it had been always the role of the
administrative Ministry/Department concerned to address the issues of sick and weak CPSEs and
to take timely redressal measures for revival/restructuring/disinvestment of sick/loss making CPSEs
with the approval of the competent authority in a time bound manner.
38. During the oral evidence, the Committee asked DPE to submit in writing the salient features
of the guidelines of DPE issued on 29
th November, 2015 on streamlining the mechanism for revival/
restructuring of sick/incipient sick and week CPSEs in India, specially identifying the role of NCLT,
NITI Ayog, BIFR, DPE and the respective administrative Ministry in the case of such CPSEs.
39. Regarding the role of other agencies, it was submitted by DPE that the Companies Act,
2013 vide Section 407 to 434 (both inclusive), provide inter-alia  for setting-up of (a) the National
Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) and (b) the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT).
The Act provided for revival and rehabilitation of sick companies which were enumerated in
Section 253 to 269 of the Companies Act, 2013.  However, since these sections were yet to be
notified by MoCA, NCLT and NCLA T were yet to be operationalised. At present, the Board of
Industrial and Financial Reconstruction (BIFR)/Appellate Authority for Industrial and Financial
Reconstruction (AAIFR) were authorized in the Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act,
1965 for approval of revival and rehabilitation of Sick Companies, including CPSEs. DPE added
that MoCA had informed that the NCLT would replace (a) the existing Company Law Board;
(b) BIFR; (c) AAIFR and; (d) would also acquire the jurisdiction of the High Courts in the matter
where it was vested in the High Courts under the Act. Bodies referred at (b) and (c) would stand
abolished upon notification of the SICA (Repeal) Act, 2003.  MoCA has further informed that the
Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2015 had been introduced in the Parliament and it also proposed
to amend the Companies Act, 2013 with regard to insolvency (revival as well as winding up)
related provisions.
40. Firstly, the Committee notes with dissatisfaction the disowning by DPE of the subject
matter related to the agencies involved in the revival/restructure/closure of CPSEs in India.
The Committee is critical of the tendency of the Department to compartmentalise the
replies by contending that the roles of NCLT and BIFR would be explained by the respective
Ministry/Department concerned. As the nodal Department for the overseeing of all CPSEs
in the country, DPE is expected to provide a cogent reply to the Committee even if the
subject matter falls under the domain of other Ministries/Departments/Agencies. The
responsibility of action on the subject being with another Ministry/Department/Agency can
be justified, but that should not preclude the collection of information on the subject.
41. The Committee notes that the Government has come up with some important
initiatives in the area of revival/restructure/closure of CPSEs.  As the Committee gathers,
the earlier mechanism involved the administrative Ministry/Department, the BRPSE, the

15
BIFR and finally the approving authority, the Cabinet. This multiplicity of agencies involved
delay in granting approval to revival plans and most of the revival proposals when finally
approved would have already become redundant due to escalation of costs owing to the time
over run.  This vexed situation contributed to the further downfall of the sick/loss incurring
and weak CPSEs.
42. Now, as per the new system the respective administrative Ministry/Department will
oversee the performance of its CPSEs based on the guidelines for “Streamlining the
mechanism for revival and restructuring of sick/incipient sick and weak Central Public
Sector Enterprises: General principles and mechanism of restructuring” issued by DPE.
Further, the Government has done away with the BRPSE and BIFR and AAIFR and they
would stand abolished once the NCLT is constituted.  The NCLT, provided for in the
Companies Act, 2013, will henceforth be the sole entity to decide upon the revival/
restructure proposals of CPSEs. Also, the revival/restructure process has been rendered
time bound.  In this regard, the Committee observes that the step taken to put the
administrative Ministry/Department in-charge of the monitoring of the health of their
respective CPSEs is an appropriate decision as mid-course correction and other reformative
measures can be taken swiftly without any time lapse as no third party is getting involved.
The Committee expects that all the lacunae which plagued the earlier system will be
eliminated in the new mechanism.
43. Further, it is observed that now with the enhanced mandate, DPE can also have a
proactive role to play in the process. The NCLT has been envisaged for all type of companies
in India, not just CPSEs. In this scenario, the Committee recommends that DPE has to take
this into account and take appropriate measures in coordination with the MoCA to ensure
that the CPSEs, due to their particular requirements of meeting socio-economic obligations,
are not put at a disadvantaged position in their efforts to get revived/restructured as they
would be treated as per the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013.
New policy on management of Government investments in PSEs, including disinvestment
and strategic sale.
44. In his Budget speech, the Finance Minister announced that a new policy would be put in
place for management of Government investments in PSEs, including disinvestment and strategic
sale. In this regard, the Committee queried whether any road map has been put in place for the
same, the suggestions of DPE on framing the new policy and as to which nodal Ministry would
be responsible for formulating and implementing the policy.
45.  In reply, DPE submitted that the issue of disinvestment and strategic sale would be handled
by Department of Disinvestment. DPE also stated that the Government, on a proposal of
Department of Disinvestment, has decided for a multi-tier structure of decision making and
implementation of the decisions on strategic disinvestment/sale of CPSEs. As per the approved
structure, the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA) is at the apex level, then a Core
Group of Secretaries on Disinvestment (CGD), which would function as a supervisory and
recommendatory body, and there would be an Evaluation Committee (EC) for valuation and
suggesting a reserve price, opening financial bids and giving recommendations on price.

16
46. Further, DPE submitted that the Government has approved the following procedure and
mechanism for strategic disinvestment to be carried out by Department of Disinvestment, now
renamed as Department of Investment and Public Asset Management (DIPAM):
(i) The NITI Aayog would identify CPSEs for strategic disinvestment. NITI Aayog
would also advice the Government on mode of sale, and the percentage of shares
to be sold of the CPSEs and suggest methods for valuation of the CPSE.
(ii) Constitution of CGD and its functions: (a) consider the recommendations of the
NITI Aayog on strategic disinvestment and recommend to CCEA on mode and
quantum of disinvestment; (b) lay down guidelines for evaluation by Evaluation
Committee; (c) recommend to CCEA on the terms and conditions of sale, the price
of sale and the strategic partner; and (d) supervise and monitor the process of
implementation of CCEA decision on strategic disinvestment.
(iii) Constitution of Evaluation Committee (EC) for strategic disinvestment and its
functions: the recommendations of the Administrative Department/Ministry on
valuation will be considered by the EC, which will fix the reserve price, open and
evaluate financial bids and make its recommendations to CGD.
(iv) Appointment of Independent External Monitor (IEM) to vet the process and settle
grievances; and
(v) Authorizing Ministry of Finance to put in place an appropriate mechanism for
protection of strategic disinvestment.
Secretary, DPE is a member of the CGD while Joint Secretary, DPE is a member of
Evaluation Committee that would consider the recommendations of the administrative Ministries/
Departments on valuation of the Company for strategic disinvestment/sale. Also, the Institute of
Chartered Accountants of India has issued Accounting Standard (AS) 10 on “Accounting for Fixed
Assets”. This included accounting for land, including its re-valuation.
47. On 13
th January, 2016, the Department of Economic Affairs constituted a Committee under
the Chairmanship of Department of Economic Affairs for suggesting broad guidelines on the issues
relating to Procedure for Exchange, Transfer, Leasing and Sale of Land held by the Government,
Government Controlled Statutory Authorities and CPSEs. DPE has representation in the Committee.
The recommendation of the Committee may be reviewed by the Cabinet Secretary before
finalization and submission of the report of the Committee.
48. Having representatives in the CGD, and the EC, the Committee asked DPE to clarify the
stand/decision/policy of the Government regarding disposal of land assets of CPSEs, but the
Department was non-committal in their reply to the Committee. With a view to have a deeper
understanding of the new policy of disinvestment, the Committee wanted to know the role of NITI
Aayog in disinvestment of CPSEs and why DPE was not given the assignment. For which
Secretary, DPE replied that the NITI Aayog would be the authority to identify CPSEs in which
disinvestment would need to be carried out and also wherever there was a need for strategic
alliances or strategic sale, and perhaps even those which need to be closed down.  After the
recommendations were made, the responsibility would not vest with the DPE, but with the

17
Department of Disinvestment. The Department of Disinvestment would take it forward. DPE was
to give them information and other backups wherever it was required. As far as the policy for
disinvestment was concerned, there was a Committee in the Ministry of Finance (MoF) which was
working on the policy of sale and how to utilize the excess land or the disposable land or the land
not in use with the CPSEs and autonomous bodies.  The approach was being worked out by the
Committee and as per the present approach the land would be first offered to the Government and
then to the CPSEs for the Government schemes and programmes. As per DPE, the controversial
part was the sale to private people. It was further submitted in this regard that such type of policy
was being deliberated at the moment as to how the Government would approach that issue. The
Committee was looking into it and DPE as a member in that would be giving feedback on the
subject.
49. The Committee notes that the Finance Minister has made couple of important policy
pronouncements – first, regarding disinvestment of Government share in CPSEs and second,
on the disposal of fixed assets of the CPSEs identified for winding up/closure.  The
Department has submitted that a mechanism has been structured to look into the
operationalisation of the said announcements. The multi-tier structure has CCEA at the
summit, NITI Aayog would identify the CPSEs and the critical parameters for
disinvestments/strategic sale. The CGD is to function as supervisory and recommendatory
body and an EC to valuate the assets of CPSEs concerned. The Committee has taken
specific note of the submission of DPE that this entire subject falls under the purview of
the Department of Disinvestment. However, the Committee observes that the subject will
have a profound bearing on the CPSEs in the country and DPE should evince keen interest
in the way things shape up on this front. This is even more important considering that the
very mandate of DPE has been enhanced on these lines and, it being member in all the
relevant Committees of disinvestment, the Department has to make more holistic
interventions on the issues/policies pertaining to CPSEs.
50. Further, the Committee has always taken a firm stand that the fixed assets,
particularly land, of wound up CPSEs should be retained with the Government or its
agencies. It is apprehended that the sale of such land to private players might have the
potential to generate many unethical practices. Accordingly, the Committee is of the strong
and unanimous opinion that the land belonging to wound up CPSEs shall be retained with
the Central Government or State Government or other Government agencies. Since
Secretary, DPE is the member of CGD it is firmly recommended that this view of the
Committee should be emphatically placed before the CGD while formulating any policy in
this area, for the present or in future. The Secretary has agreed to place the view point
of this Committee before CGD, when they deliberate on the approaches to be followed for
disposal or usage of land which is in the hands of sick PSEs or autonomous bodies.  The
Committee sincerely hopes that the view point would be considered in CGD.

RECOMMENDA TIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE—A T A GLANCE
1. The Committee notes that the mandate of DPE has been augmented with the addition
of roles in monitoring of performance of CPSEs and effective management of their assets.
This has been done by addition of subjects to the Allocation of Business of DPE.  The
Committee is of the considered opinion that though the Budget allocation of DPE is small
compared to the major Ministries/Departments of the Government, the role to be essayed
by them is critical.  As the nodal Department of all CPSEs in India, their effective
evaluation and monitoring is going to be humongous task. The newly added responsibility
of CAPEX monitoring, measures to improve performance of CPSEs and other capacity
building initiatives and advice regarding revival/restructuring/closure of CPSEs will render
the working of DPE pivotal to the way CPSEs perform in the country. (Para 10)
2. Accordingly, the Committee observes that DPE should realize and imbibe the
magnitude and importance of the responsibilities that have been entrusted to them and take
more proactive measures to play out this role.  Rather them imagining themselves just as
a nodal coordinating agency DPE should reinvent themselves as an arm of the Government
which can take decisive steps on its own or in coordination with other Ministries/
Departments   to create a facilitative milieu for CPSEs to perform to their potential.  The
Committee is of the firm view that DPE should not be restricting themselves to just issuing
guidelines and providing advice.  The new mandate gives them ample space to effectively
follow up the implementation of the advices rendered by them through their guidelines.
Accordingly, the Committee recommends that to be able to do this, DPE has to equip
themselves better and come out with measures implementable on ground and also
endeavour to create a coordinative platform involving the respective administrative
Ministry and other relevant Government agencies through which matters relating to the
working of CPSEs in the country can be resolved at a single stage avoiding time lag in
administrative decisions, the single most degenerative factor in case of decisions related
to CPSEs. (Para 11)
3. The Committee notes that DPE claims that the CPSEs in India are performing to the
best of their abilities in the prevailing economic scenario of declining commodity prices,
reduced capital inflows into their economies and increasing financial volatility. Even while
taking the claim of DPE in its face value and acknowledging the fact that the Committee
is not in knowledge of the performance of all the CPSEs in India, the Committee cannot
but share its observation that the current status of all the 31 CPSEs under the Department
of Heavy Industry (DHI) is sick/incipient sick and weak as per DPEs guidelines for
“Streamlining the mechanism for revival and restructuring of sick/incipient sick and weak
Central Public Sector Enterprises: General principles and mechanism of restructuring”.
Accordingly, the Committee observes that the stand taken by DPE that CPSEs are
performing well under the given conditions as status-quoits and wants the Department to
adopt a new forward looking stance. (Para 13)

19

schemes during Twelfth Five Year Plan, the Department has restricted themselves by just
submitting that no review has been undertaken.  The Committee observes that the
Department while replying to the Committee should keep in mind that answers given to a
Parliamentary Committee should be holistic and self-contained.  In the absence of a round
reply, the Committee is precluded from comprehending the reason for not undertaking the
MTR.  This information has to be provided to the Committee. (Para 15)
5. Further, from the submission of the DPE, the Committee takes note that of the XII
Plan outlays for various schemes of DPE, three schemes have seen roughly around only
50% of utilization and one has seen only 20% of expenditure.  The money allocated for
Information Technology alone has seen a healthy utilization.  Here again, since a review of
the scheme has not been undertaken the reasons for the gross underperformance observed
in the plan schemes are alien to the Committee. Regardless of this, the Committee
expresses its dissatisfaction in the way the plan schemes of DPE have underperformed
during the Twelfth Plan period.  DPE should make themselves aware of the reasons behind
this situation and take necessary steps to prevent them from recurring and report the same
to the Committee. (Para 16)
6. The Committee notes that departing from the pattern of previous years, the
Department has only two plan schemes in Financial Year 2016-17 - Counselling, Retraining
and Redeployment of Rationalized Employees of CPSEs (CRR) and Research, Development
and Consultancy (RDC) on Generic issues related to Enterprises (CPSEs & SLPEs).  A
merger of schemes has been undertaken in the case of RDC making the current RDC
scheme more expansive containing more components than earlier.  The Committee expects
this measure to impart more financial and operational flexibility to DPE resulting in better
utilization of allocated funds.  Accordingly, the Committee observes that DPE should make
the most of the new initiative brought out by the Ministry of Finance and avoid deficient
utilization and curtailment of funds these schemes were prone to earlier. (Para 19)
7. The Committee has always been appreciative of the objectives served by the CRR
scheme which basically offers a social security net to employees of CPSEs who optees for
VRS or get retrenched.  The Committee takes into cognizance the fact that NIESBUD had
undertaken an evaluation of the scheme in 2012-13 and had recommended a host of
improvements.  One of the major recommendations was the need to stress more on follow
ups and redeployment after linking with micro credit/finance. Handholding projects and
linkages were also recommended to enhance redeployment/self employment opportunities of
the former employees and their dependents trained under the scheme. DPE have submitted
that there recommendations had been circulated to the Nodal Agencies for compliance.
However, Committee finds that the number of people redeployed after being trained under
the scheme has always hovered around 50% or less of the total trained personnel. The
situation has continued even after the recommendations of NIESBUD made in 2012.
Accordingly, the Committee strongly recommends that the Department should take
appropriate measures expeditiously to improve the number of trainees who get redeployed
subsequent to the training under the scheme. In this regard, the Committee also wants DPE

20
to consider focussed Skill Development under current impetus accorded to skill development
by the Government.  The Nodal Agencies under the Scheme should identify the skill sets
that are in demand in the local area in terms of employability and provide training to
people under the scheme. To the Committee, this is one of the measures that can be taken
to improve the redeployment ratio. Further, this will also contribute towards the efforts of
the Government to address the huge skill deficit of the workforce in the country in
different spheres. (Para 24)
8. The Committee note that during 2015-16, with only a fortnight left for the
completion of the Financial Y ear almost ````` 1 crore out of the total ````` 2.81 crore allocated to
the scheme at RE has been left unspent. The Committee  take exception to such
underutilization under an important initiative like RDC scheme.  However, the Committee
takes into account the hope expressed by DPE that from 2016-17 onwards the performance
of the scheme is expected to improve as it has seen broad basing of its objectives and new
components have been added as part of subsuming some other schemes into it.  Further,
the umbrella nature of the scheme is thought to provide more financial inter-
operationability.  This will also help the Department to tide over the earlier problem of last
quarter spending peculiar to the earlier RDC scheme for which the Ministry of Finance has
already granted an exemption from spending limits. (Para 28)
9. The Committee is happy to know that the Department has already initiated steps
to act on its recommendation regarding setting-up of a monitoring system to look into
CSR fund utilization by CPSEs. It is also appreciated that the matter has also been
taken up with the MoCA which administers the Companies Act, 2013. The Committee
observes that DPE should work in synchronisation with the MoCA in the matter relating
to the monitoring of the CSR fund utilization to ensure efficient internalisation of the
CSR culture by CPSEs, thereby setting an example for the private sector also to
emulate. (Para 31)
10. Firstly, the Committee n otes with dissatisfaction the disowning by DPE of the
subject matter related to the agencies involved in the revival/restructure/closure of CPSEs
in India.  The Committee is critical of the tendency of the Department to compartmentalise
the replies by contending that the roles of NCLT and BIFR would be explained by the
respective Ministry/Department concerned. As the nodal Department for the overseeing of
all CPSEs in the country, DPE is expected to provide a cogent reply to the Committee even
if the s ubject matter falls under the domain of other Ministries/Department/Ag encies. The
responsibility of action on the subject being with another Ministry/Department/
Agency can be justified, but that should not preclude the collection of information on the
subject. (Para 40)
11.    The Committee notes that the Government has come up with some important
initiatives in the area of revival/restructure/closure of CPSEs.  As the Committee gathers,
the earlier mechanism involved the administrative Ministry/Department, the BRPSE, the
BIFR and finally the approving authority, the Cabinet. This multiplicity of agencies involved
delay in granting approval to revival plans and most of the revival proposals when finally
approved would have already become redundant due to escalation of costs owing to the time

21
over run.  This vexed situation contributed to the further downfall of the sick/loss incurring
and weak CPSEs involved. (Para 41)

performance of its CPSEs based on the guidelines for “Streamlining the mechanism for
revival and restructuring of sick/incipient sick and weak Central Public Sector Enterprises:
General principles and mechanism of restructuring” issued by DPE. Further, the
Government has done away with the BRPSE and BIFR and AAIFR and they would stand
abolished once the NCLT is constituted.  The NCLT, provided for in the Companies Act,
2013, will henceforth be the sole entity to decide upon the revival/restructure proposals of

regard, the Committee observes that the step taken to put the administrative Ministry in
charge of the monitoring of the health of their respective CPSEs is an appropriate
decision as mid-course correction and other reformative measures can be taken swiftly
without any time lapse as no third party is getting involved.  The Committee e xpects
that all the lacunae which plagued the earlier system will be eliminated in the new
mechanism. (Para 42)

proactive role to play in the process. The NCLT has been envisaged for all type of companies

Report  
Evolution and Mandate  
The Government of India established the Ministry of  Small Scale Industries 
and Agro & Rural Industries (SSI & ARI) in October,  1999 as the nodal Ministry for 
formulation of policies and Central sector programm es/schemes, their 
implementation and related coordination and for sup plementing the efforts of the 
States/Union Territories for promotion and developm ent of small scale, agro and 
rural industries in the country.  Subsequently, in September, 2001 the Ministry of SSI 
and ARI was bifurcated into two separate Ministries, namely, Ministry of Small Scale 
Industries and Ministry of Agro and Rural Industrie s.  In 2006, “Micro, Small and 
Medium Enterprises Development Act (MSMED), 2006” w as enacted by the 
Parliament.  Pursuant to this enactment, the Minist ry of Agro and Rural Industries 
and the Small Scale Industries were merged into a s ingle Ministry, namely, Ministry 
of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises. 
Composition of the Ministry 
 
2. The Ministry of Micro Small & Medium Enterprises  is having two divisions 
called Small & Medium Enterprises (SME) Wing and Ag ro & Rural Industry (ARI) 
Wing.  The SME Wing is allocated the work, inter-al ia, of administration, vigilance 
and administrative supervision of the National Smal l Industries Corporation (NSIC) 
Ltd., a public sector enterprise and NIMESE an auto nomous national level 
entrepreneurship development/training organizations .  The Wing is also responsible 
for implementation of the schemes relating to Perfo rmance and Credit Rating, 
Assistance to Training Institutions and preparation  and monitoring of “Make in 
India” initiative among others.   
3. The ARI Wing looks after the administration of t wo statutory bodies viz. the 
Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC), Coi r Board and a society called 

2 
 
Mahatma Gandhi Institute of Rural Industrialisation  (MGIRI).  It also supervises the 
implementation of the Prime Minister’s Employment G eneration Programme 
(PMEGP).  Scheme of Fund for Regeneration of Traditional Industries (SFURTI) and 
A Scheme for Promoting Innovation, Rural Industry and Entrepreneurship (ASPIRE) 
4. The implementation of policies and various progr ammes/schemes for 
providing infrastructure and support services to MS MEs is undertaken through its 
attached office, namely the Office of the Developme nt Commissioner (O/o DC 
(MSME), National Small Industries Corporation (NSIC ), Khadi and Village 
Industries Commission (KVIC), the Coir Board and tr aining institutes viz., National 
Institute for Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises ( NI-MSME), Hyderabad and 
Mahatma Gandhi Institute for Rural Industrialisation (MGIRI), Wardha. 
5. The Committee was informed by the Financial Advi sor that this year, the 
Ministry had undertaken a major rationalization of its Schemes. All the Schemes 
have been re-grouped under seven major Plan Schemes as following:

6. The Committee was also informed that several Sch emes have been merged.  
 
(i) Workshed Scheme for Khadi Artisans and Strengthenin g Infrastructure of Existing Weak 
Khadi Institutions and Assistance for Marketing Inf rastructure have been clubbed under 
Khadi Grant Head.  
(ii) Marketing and Publicity components of VI Grant Head  have been merged under 
New/Modified Scheme titled “Market Promotion and Development Assistance”. 
(iii) Khadi (S&T), VI (S&T) and Plan (S&T) of Coir have b een clubbed/merged under one 
common budgetary head i.e., Khadi, VI and Coir (S&T). 
(iv) MDA scheme of KVIC has been modified as Market Promotion and Development Assistance 
scheme (MPDA). MPDA scheme is formulated as a unifi ed scheme by merging different 
schemes/sub-schemes/components of different Heads i mplemented in the 11 th  Plan, 
namely, Market Development Assistance, Publicity, M arketing and Market promotion. A 
new component of Infrastructure namely setting up o f Marketing Complexes/ Khadi 
Plazas has been added to expand the marketing network of Khadi & VI products.  
(v) Interest Subsidy (Khadi) & Interest Subsidy (VI) bu dgetary heads have been dropped in BE 
2016-17. 
 
7. The Committee feels that CLCSS and NMCP should b e separated. As per 
the current practice, the CLCSS which draws much la rger budget is clubbed 
with six components of NMCP that draw meager budget . CLCSS is essentially 
an interest subvention scheme like ISEC and should be kept as a credit support 
scheme whereas the NMCP is technology upgradation scheme.

Rooms that are essentially training institutions an d must not be clubbed with 
Office construction. Tool Rooms and Technology Cent ers can be clubbed with 
Skill Development Programmes. And the Cluster Devel opment may be clubbed 
with SFURTI.

Trade Receivables Discounting System ( TreDS) 
 

20 
 
42. TReDS was announced in the Budget Speech 2014 t o ease cash flow to MSME 
suppliers. TReDS is an institutional mechanism for facilitating the trade receivables 
of MSMEs from corporate and other buyers including Government Departments and 
PSUs through multiple financers. The RBI had announ ced broad guidelines on 3rd 
December, 2014. In its 271 st  Report, the Committee had asked M/o MSME to obtain  
inputs from M/o Finance regarding status and struct ure of TreDS. The Committee 
was concerned over steep discount rates charged on discounting may harm the 
interests of the MSME suppliers.   
43. The Ministry informed that to solve the problem  of delayed payment to 
MSMEs, RBI has come out with the guidelines for setting up and operating the Trade 
Receivables Discounting System (TReDS). The intenti on is to facilitate Electronic 
Bill Factoring Exchanges in the country, which coul d electronically accept and settle 
MSME bills so that MSMEs could convert their receivables without delay.  
44. Three entities viz. (i) NSE Strategic Investmen t Corporation Limited (NSICL) 
and Small Industries Development Bank of India (SID BI), Mumbai; (ii)  Axis Bank 
Limited, Mumbai; and (iii) Mynd Solutions Pvt. Ltd. , Gurgaon, Haryana have been 
given "in-principle" approval for setting up and op erating TReDS with the approval 
of Board for Payment and Settlement Systems vide  Press Release dated November 
24, 2015. These entities have a time of at least si x months to fulfill the conditions of 
authorisation and need to approach RBI for receivin g final authorization under 
Payment and Settlement System Act. 
 45. The Committee was informed that the discount r ates have not been stipulated. 
TReDS will only act as a facilitator for creating an electronic factoring platform.  The 
bankers joining the platform as financiers can offe r their bids/ discount rates against 
each factoring unit (invoice / bill of exchange) an d the MSME seller is free to accept 
any of the bids. Upon acceptance of the bid, the factoring unit will be financed by the 

21 
 
concerned banker/ financier.  It is expected that t his transparent form of bidding 
would facilitate competitive bidding of MSME receivables by financiers/ banks. 
46. The Committee was informed that the success of Electronic Bill Factoring 
Exchange set up under TReDS  will be measured again st the volume and value of 
trade receivables traded in the Exchange. 
47. The Committee apprehands that such a mechanism though facilitate 
urgent cash flow and liquidity to the MSME supplier s but will also expose them 
to speculative dynamics of money market. The Commit tee wonder afterall what 
will be the incentive for financers to acquire Bill s and invoices? They may  tend 
to seek deeper and predatory discounts to the peril  of hapless MSME supplier.  
The Committee may be informed of  success of this s cheme in terms of 
participation, volumes and value of trade receivabl es traded in the Exchange. 
The Committee also recommends the Ministry to evolv e a mechanism to 
monitor so that discounting rates do not become too  deep and perilously 
predatory and inform the Committee of such mechanism.

MUDRA Yojna  
53. The Committee noted that under the aegis of Pra dhan Mantri MUDRA Yojana 
(PMMY), MUDRA has already created its initial produ cts / schemes. The 
interventions have been named ‘Shishu’, ‘Kishor’ an d ‘Tarun’ to signify the stage of 
growth / development and funding needs of the benef iciary micro unit / entrepreneur 
and also to provide a reference point for the next phase of graduation / growth to look 
forward to. The financial limit for these schemes are :-  

23 
 
• Shishu : covering loans upto 50,000/-  
• Kishor :  covering loans above 50,000/- and upto 5 lakh 
• Tarun :  covering loans above 5 lakh to 10 lakh 
MUDRA’s delivery channel is conceived to be through  the route of refinance 
primarily to Banks/NBFCs/MFIs. Non–Corporate Small Business Segment (NCSB) 
comprising of millions of proprietorship / partners hip firms running as small 
manufacturing units, service sector units, shopkeep ers, fruits / vegetable vendors, 
truck operators, food-service units, repair shops, machine operators, small industries, 
artisans, food processors and others, in rural and urban areas are the target groups. 
54. The Committee has been monitoring the progress of this important scheme in 
different States and with different Banks. For year  2015-16 a target of Rs 1.22 lakh 
crores was set. Till the first week of February 201 6, loan amounting Rs 97000 crores 
to some 270 lakh borrowers was distributed of which  some 248 lakh were Shishu 
borrowers with Rs 50,000 and less.  
55. Though Committee recognized the progress made i n MUDRA Yojna, it 
found that lending Banks were not coming forward to  avail re-finance from

and need cheap and prompt refinance and should be n atural partners in 
MUDRA Yojna instead of cash-rich Banks whose RIDF forms the corpus for the 
MUDRA Yojna. Also, the Committee would like to know  the reasons for

perhaps Banks find the interest cap prescribed unde r re-financing conditions,

rate permissible for Scheduled Banks under Mudra Yo jna is at around 8-9% 
which was lower than the prevailing interest rate c harged by Banks. The

National Manufacturing Competitiveness Programme  
 
70. The National Manufacturing Competitiveness Prog ramme (NMCP) is the 
nodal programme of the Government to develop global  competitiveness among 
Indian MSMEs. Conceptualised by the National Manufa cturing Competitiveness 
Council (NMCC), the programme was initiated in the year 2007-08.  There are 
presentably nine components in operation under the NMCP targeted at enhancing the 
entire value chain of the MSME sector, out of which  6 components are placed under 
Quality of Technology Support Institutions and Prog rammes. The components of 
Schemes and their allocation during 12 th  Plan is as under:- 
(a) Lean Manufacturing Competitiveness Scheme for MSMEs  : Lean 
Technologies are important in achieving Zero defect  and Zero effect Manufacturing. 
The Lean Manufacturing Competitiveness Scheme (LMCS ), is basically a business 
initiative to enhance competitiveness of the manufa cturing sector, imbibing a culture 
of continuous improvement, inculcating good managem ent system resulted through 
increase in overall productivity, quality of the pr oduct, process improvement, cost 
reduction, scientific inventory management, improve d process flows, reduced 
engineering time and so on. The scheme was started as a pilot in 2009 for 100 Mini 
Clusters in 11 th  Five Year Plan. The scheme was up-scaled in Septem ber, 2013 
considering the recommendations of the evaluation r eport. The up-scaled Lean 
Manufacturing Competitiveness Scheme was approved w ith a Total Project Cost of 
Rs. 240.94 crore (GOI contribution Rs. 204.94 crore ) for the 12 th  Five Year Plan for 
500 Mini Clusters. 

30

and international markets. The broad activities pla nned under this component

through cloud computing.

holding with facilitation for funding through Finan cial Institutions to set up new 
enterprises mainly in rural and agro based vertical s. Other skill development and 
entrepreneurship development programmes focus only in isolation on development of 
different skill sets and entrepreneurial skills rel ating to different fields respectively. 
However, under LBI, the entire gamut of requirement s of skill, entrepreneurial 
ability, basic financial accounting, computer opera tion, project writing, exposure to 
banks and other credit agencies, and also the support under different existing schemes 
of the Ministry like PMEGP, CUY and others are prov ided as far as possible. It may 

61 
 
also submitted that, as of now, there is no plan to  connect all training institution with 
LBIs.  
 
153. The Committee further probed as to what does m entoring and handholding 
entail and whether any tenure has been decided for such handholding since it will 
entail a cost.  
 
154. The Ministry submitted that hand-holding and m entoring are in the nature of 
critical support to any incubation and innovation e co system. Mentoring entails 
constant guidance and monitoring by the LBIs and ha ndholding is about supporting 
the trainees as and when required with inputs to set up their own enterprises including 
sourcing of finance etc.  
 
155. Considering that incubation entails prolonged handholding and mentoring 
which involves cost, the Committee is surprised with the conceptual ambivalence 
of the Ministry on the critical issue of what const itutes incubation and 
handholding, what is the tenure of such mentoring a nd whether the Ministry in 
view of limited allocation, has fixed cost of incub ation and mentoring per 
entrepreneur. The Ministry also does not have any c onvincing clarity of 
difference between incubation and entrepreneurship development programmes. 
The two concept are used inter-changeably. The Comm ittee 
 thus recommends 
that Ministry must decide and define the contours a nd tenure of mentoring and 
accordingly calculate the cost of mentoring per incubate.

about the placement of 200 youths trained at Deoria  LBI, how many of them had set

157. The Ministry informed that out of the 243 yout h successfully passed out of the

158. The ASPIRE scheme was launched to mentor the e ntrepreneurs to set up 
their own business and become employment provider. However, having 
observed the performance of Deoria LBI where out of 243 passed out candidates 
only 31 have set up their own units and another 19 have taken up wage 
employment. More than half remain unemployed. There  is no information 
regarding the survivability of entreprises which were supposed to be mentored.  
 
159. The Committee apprehands that even the ASPIRE may meet the same 
fate as other entrepreurship development programmes  being run by the 
Ministry. The Committee notes that ASPIRE too is fo llowing the set stereotypes 
of considering MSMEs as low cost low technology ent erprises, that may not 
independently survive the market competition  in lo nger run. The Committee 
was surprised to note that as per the Fourth Census  of MSME  2006-07, out of 
the 15 lakh registered MSME units, about 5 lakh bec ame sick. And the trades 
that are offered under ASPIRE may not improve the situation. ASPIRE needs to 
break this stereotype and consider MSMEs as technol ogy intensive sector that 
can survive the market competition.  
  
160. The Committee recommends that Ministry must li nk ASPIRE with 
MUDRA Yojna and Start up India. The Committee also  recommends that 
Ministry must survey the skill market and include t rades with larger demand, 
and attract aspirational youth that strives for higher skilled job market. For this 

63

is essential that Ministry should avoid  stereotypi ng MSMEs as low cost low

comparable to minimum daily wages“. 
  
 The Committee on previous occasions during its study visits has interacted with

regardless of the structure of khadi sector, where artisans are employed

observed the performance of Deoria LBI where out of 243 passed out candidates 
only 31 have set up their own units and another 19 have taken up wage 
employment. More than half remain unemployed. There  is no information 
regarding the survivability of entreprises which were supposed to be mentored.  
(Para 158) 

111 
 
 
59. The Committee apprehands that even the ASPIRE m ay meet the same 
fate as other entrepreurship development programmes  being run by the 
Ministry. The Committee notes that ASPIRE too is fo llowing the set stereotypes 
of considering MSMEs as low cost low technology ent erprises, that may not 
independently survive the market competition  in lo nger run. The Committee 
was surprised to note that as per the Fourth Census  of MSME  2006-07, out of 
the 15 lakh registered MSME units, about 5 lakh bec ame sick. And the trades 
that are offered under ASPIRE may not improve the situation. ASPIRE needs to 
break this stereotype and consider MSMEs as technol ogy intensive sector that 
can survive the market competition.  
(Para 159)  
60. The Committee recommends that Ministry must lin k ASPIRE with 
MUDRA Yojna and Start up India. The Committee also  recommends that 
Ministry must survey the skill market and include t rades with larger demand, 
and attract aspirational youth that strives for higher skilled job market. For this 
the Ministry may align ASPIRE with the National Skill Development Mission. It 
is essential that Ministry should avoid  stereotypi ng MSMEs as low cost low 
technology sector.  
 
(Para 160) 
 
61. The Committee notes that despite BE being reduc ed by half in RE, the 
utilization till January 2016 was only Rs 65 crores which also included a transfer 
of Rs 60 crores to SIDBI for setting up Fund of Fun ds to provide quasi equity in 
prospective projects. Thereby in effect, only Rs 5 crores were spent on setting up 
the incubators. Instead of ambitious District-wise Network of Incubators and 
Accelerators as announced in the Budget speech, the  Ministry has moderated 
the target to setting up 80 LBIs and 30 TBIs by Mar ch 2017.  However till 
December 2015 only 3 LBIs and 2 TBIs were approved.  
(Para 161) 
 
62. The Committee is concerned over the fact that e ven after three years of 
Budget announcement, there is hardly any progress o n ground in this ambitious 
scheme. Going by the statement made by the then Secretary and the information 
provided by the Ministry, the Committee draws infer ence that the  Budget 
announcement of Rs 200 crores for District-wise Net work of Incubators and 
Accelerators was made without any in-depth planning  or survey. Despite 
Committee’s conviction and recommendations that the  Budget announcements 
are solemn assurance to the Parliament and should b e implemented within that 

112 
 
Financial Year, only broad guidelines could be fram ed by March 2015, 
obviously the stakeholders, mostly the State agenci es with resources, took half 
the FY 2015-16 to put 19 proposals. 
(Para 162) 
 
63. It is ironical the Ministry has set approval of  40 LBIs and 15 TBIs by 
March 2016 as the target.   The Committee wonders i f only approval of a 
project, could ever be a target for a Planned Schem e. The Committee 
apprehends that with this rate, Ministry is unlikel y to set up 80 LBIs and 30 
TBIs by the March 2017 as envisaged. The Committee also noted that by the end 
of March 2016 only 22 LBIs were approved as against  the  target of approving 
40 LBIs and 15 TBIs for which Rs 6 crores have been  released out of BE of Rs 
95 crores. The Committee may be informed by when re maining Incubators are 
likely to be commissioned.   
(Para 163) 
 
64. Considering that the Scheme is dealing with tra ditional craftsmen and 
artisans to facilitate them with ease of doing rewa rding business, the Committee 
had felt that the structure and procedures of the S cheme are complex and 
protracted. The Committee notes that there are at l east ten stakeholders 
agencies that are involved in the decision making a nd implementation of this 
Scheme. The Committee feels that for efficient implementation the structure and 
procedures  of the Scheme needs to be simplified. 
(Para 166) 
 
65. The Committee is distressed to note that the ut ilisation pattern of a 
running Planned Scheme, whose structure and procedu res though complicated, 
are settled. There was almost Nil utilisation in th e first quarter of the FY 2015-
16. While the M/o Finance does not permit more than  33% in the last Quarter 
and 15% of BE to be spent in the month of March, th e Ministry however spent 
only some Rs 20 crores in first three Quarters and proposes to spend Rs 20 
crores out  of the BE of Rs 50 crores in last twent y days of the FY against the 
ceiling prescribed by the M/o Finance. The Committe e may be informed the 
groundson which the Ministry proposes to breach the  M/o Finance’s prescribed 
ceiling.  The Committee may be informed the rationa le of retaining high RE 
2015-16 despite poor utilisation of funds during the first three quarters.  
 
(Para 169) 
 
 

113 
 
66. The Committee may also be informed as to how wa s the Budget allocation 
utilised in absence of any actual commissioning of SFURTI cluster.   
(Para 170) 
 
 
67. Regarding the actual achievement of Plan target s, the Committee was 
informed that so far KVIC got final approval of 12 SFURTI clusters and 
another 12 proposals got in-principle approval by S teering Committee.  In view 
of meager expenditure, the Committee notes  that no  cluster was actually 
commissioned during the year 2015-16. Despite serio us under utilization and 
uneven utilization of allocation, the Ministry soug ht Rs 100 crores for 2016-17 
and was allocated Rs 75 crores which was an enhance ment over 2015-16. The 
Committee may be explained the basis of seeking hig her BE despite dismal 
performance in the previous year. The Ministry coul d release on Rs 30 crores 
out of BE of Rs 50 crores till the first week of Ma rch 2016.  The Committee also 
asks how does the Ministry propose to spend the mon ey during financial year 
2016-17?  
(Para 171) 
68. The Ministry expects that all 71 SFURTI cluster s of the 1 st  phase will be 
completed shortly. The Committee requires the Minis try to report to it the up-
dated status of commissioned SFURTI clusters in res pect of interventions made 
and the cost of making such intervention and the nu mber of artisans benefitted, 
in its Action Taken Note on this Report.  
 (Para 176) 
69. The Committee noted that the Scheme has gone throug h series of time 
consuming modifications, merger/clubbing of smaller  schemes with SFURTI 
and splitting of SFURTI into KVIC and Coir. This ha s made the monitoring of 
scheme against set benchmarks, difficult. Every mod ification has taken time for 
approval and consequently derailed the time lines. As a result towards the end of 
12 th  Plan none of the 71 SFURTI Cluster are actually co mmissioned and 
operationalised. The Committee may be informed of annual Fund allocation and 
utilisation during the 12 th  Plan period.  
(Para 179) 
70. The Committee finds SFURTI to be a representati ve case of poor 
management and poor monotoring of any Planned Scheme of the Ministry.  
(Para 180) 
 
 
71. However, the Committee noted that in reply to R ajya Sabha Unstarred 
Question 878 (3.3.16), it was informed that for FY 2015-16 Rs 1265 crore were 

114 
 
allocated for PMEGP, upto 31.1.16 only Rs 658 crore s margin money was 
utilized. The Committee probed if this amount has b een sanctioned or actually 
disbursed. And with such low utilization of allocat ed funds in first 10 months of 
the FY, what was the need for seeking an additional  fund of Rs 811 crores in 
Supplementary Demands? 
(Para 185) 
  
72. The Committee notes that two sets of figures em erge from the discussion 
above. By January 2016, the Banks sanctioned PMEGP loans involving Margin 
Money worth 102% of BE but actual disbursal of Marg in Money by the KVIC 
was only 65% of BE. Similarly in February, 2016, the Banks sanctioned PMEGP 
loans involving Margin Money worth 116% of BE but a ctual disbursal was only 
71% of BE. Ministry has stated having disbursed Rs 725 crores by February, 
2016, that was short of BE allocation by some Rs 30 0 crores. Also, the 
Committee observed that by the end of February 2016 , the KVIC was left with 
Rs 525 crores ( inclusive of Supplementary Demand).  In addition to existing gap 
between sanctioned loan and the disbursed Margin mo ney,  further loans 
involving another Rs 200 crores of Margin money wou ld have been sanctioned 
by the Banks in March, 2016. The Committee observes  significant gap between 
the sanctioned loans and actual disbursal of Margin  money by the KVIC. The 
Committee may be explained the reasons for such hug e gap between the two 
figures and how does the Ministry cover this gap in  absence of additional funds 
from Supplementary Demands. It is also clear that w hile Banks have been 
meeting their target, the bottlenecks in disbursal of margin money occurs at the 
KVIC’s end in promptly disbursing the margin money.  The Committee noted 
there was time gap between sanctioning  and actuall y disbursing the margin 
money. The Committee recommends that this is a proc edural issue which 
impinges upon the clearer figures of quarter-wise u tilisation of funds. The 
Committee recommends that Ministry, KVIC and the Banks should address this 
issue immediately. To address this issue the Commit tee had recommended that 
DLTFC may be replaced with Committee of Banker headed by lead Bank which 
may streamline the disbursal process. The Committee  may be informed of the 
action taken in this regard.   
(Para 188) 
 
73. The Committee observes that lesser number of ap plications being 
sanctioned and actually disbursed by the Banks in t he  year 2015-16 as 
compared to previous year. In both the years the ga p between sanctioned 
Margin Money and its actual disbursal has been sign ificant. The Committee 

115 
 
may be informed as to how does the Ministry propose  to meet the shortfall in 
Margin Money for sanctioned loans. 
(Para 190)  
 
 
74. The Committee in its previous Reports too has r epeatedly remarked over 
low utilization of PMEGP funds and crowding of expe nditure towards last 
months of FY despite applications remaining un-proc essed. The Ministry too 
had acknowledged for action. The Committee noted th at still no progress has 
been made apart from usual requests and advises giv en by CEO, KVIC to the 
State agencies. The Committee had made suggestions regarding modifying the 
structure/architecture of the Scheme, yet no action  has been taken. The 
Committee sought the reasons for acknowledging the observations of the 
Committee and yet not acting to improve the performance.  
(Para 191) 
 
 75. Having observed the gap between sanctioned amo unt and actual disbursal 
of MM, the Committee does not completely agree with  the KVIC’s  blame on 
Banks. The bottleneck lies with KVIC as well and ne eds to be resolved. The 
Committee finds the steps taken by the KVIC to be g rossly inadequate. KVIC 
can only monitor the progress through on line syste m, it has to resolve the 
procedural bottlenecks that have been created by the structure and procedure of 
the Scheme itself. Therefore, KVIC must address the  structure of the Scheme, 
accordingly.  
 
(Para 193) 
 
76. It is observed that in terms of employment gene ration in years 2013-14 
and 2014-15, every State significantly underperform ed, while allocations 
remained under utilized till the last months of the respective FY. The Committee 
asked the Ministry to elaborate the trend of under- achievement of employment 
targets despite availability of Funds.  
(Para 197) 
 
 
 
77. The Committee finds the situation grossly unacc eptable where money 
remains unutilised for larger part of FY and employ ment targets are 
underachieved by most of States. The Committee also  finds that targets under 
PMEGP are set in terms of Margin Money utilisation.  Rather their should be a 

116 
 
matrix of margin money and employment on the basis of which State-wise 
targets should be fixed.  
(Para 201) 
78. The  Committee during its study visit(s) also n oted that most of State 
Governments had launched their own employment gener ation schemes that are 
flexible and offer better terms. As those Schemes a nd the PMEGP are 
implemented by the same State agencies, people find  State Schemes better, 
convenient and allow greater flexibility in terms of vocations, whereas KVIC has 
to depend on the State agencies to implement PMEGP. The Committee therefore 
wonders the relevance of having two parallel schemes run  implemented by same 
State agency.  
 
(Para 202) 
 
 
79. The Committee is dismayed to note that after ei ght years of being 
launched, despite setting ambitious target of 100 P MEGP units per District per 
year, the facts are disconcerting. 175 Districts in  the country do not have 
aggregate 100 PMEGP units ever since the scheme was  launched. In reduction 
of target per district to 75 units, the Committee f inds a candid admission of 
failure to meet even the modest targets. However, there were 359 Districts in the 
country who could set up only 50 PMEGP units in 201 4-15,. In previous year 
2013-14 the figure was 339. The Committee expresses  its serious reservation 
over such dismal performance where despite enhanced  annual targets and 
commensurate enhancement in allocation, the actual achievements are stark. 
The fact remains that half the Districts in country  could not set up even modest 
target of 75 PMEGP units.   The Committee seeks a d etailed comment from the 
Ministry on such dismal performance at the District level.  
 
(Para 206) 
 
80. During the study visits particularly to smaller  States and UTs like A&N 
and Puducherry, the Committee recognized that local  entrepreneurs felt 
constrained due to negative list prescribed in the PMEGP. The Committee is of 
opinion that the scheme should facilitate the entre preneurs to exercise their free 
choice of vocation depending upon local resources, skill sets, market 
opportunities, instead of unduly constraining them. That a similar scheme is run 
by another Ministry should not be a consideration w hile deciding the negative 
list. Accordingly agro based or para agro vocations  like floriculture, 
horticulture, fishery etc. should be allowed in the  Scheme. The Committee is 

117 
 
inclined to state that the negative list should be prepared after due consultation 
with the concerned State Government/ UT administration.  
(Para 208) 
 
81. The Committee was dismayed to learn that during  2014-15 and 2015-16 
(upto 14.03.2016), only 162 and 57 applications respectively have been disbursed 
within 100 days. The Committee expresses its reserv ations that the KVIC is not 
been able to meet its own deadlines and standards. The Committee wonders the 
plight of PMEGP entrepreneur at the local level who  despite the tall claims of 
KVIC about online-monitoring, has to endure the unc ertainty for months. 
Instead of facilitating ease of doing business, suc h delays are actually dis-
incentives for any entrepreneur to avail benefits o f Government Schemes. It is 
squarely the responsibility of the Ministry and the KVIC to protect and promote 
the reputation of initiatives initiated by the Gove rnment. And going by the facts 
above, the Ministry and the KVIC have repeatedly fa iled the Government’s 
initiatives. 
(Para 210) 
 
82. The Committee considers this to be a violation of norms prescribed by the 
Ministry of Finance, that money that should have be en spent evenly within that 
Financial Year, is allowed to remain unspent in the  subordinate offices and 
carried forward to next Financial year. The Committ ee may be informed 
whether the Ministry has informed the Ministry of F inance about this money 
and whether proper approval has been obtained to ca rry the money forward to 
next FY. The Committee would also like to have a co mment from the Financial 
Advisor and CCA of the Ministry in this regard.  
(Para 214) 
 
83. The Committee expresses its serious reservation  over current 
Performance Audit of PMEGP. The Committee feels tha t the concurrent 
performance audit of the scheme for a small part of  current Financial year 
cannot present the true and fair picture of the sta tus of the Scheme that was 
launched in 2008. The Committee wonders whether thi s is a standard audit 
practice to conduct performance audit for such a sh ort period of current FY. 
Accordingly, the Committee recommends the scope of Performance audit of the 
PMEGP should be expanded  since the beginning of 12
th  Plan.   
(Para 219) 
 
84. The Committee noted that in BE 2015-16, the Coi r Board was allocated 
Rs. 44 crores as Planned and Rs. 26.75 crores as No n-Planned allocation which 

118 
 
were reduced to Rs. 31 crores and Rs. 24 crores as Planned and Non-Planned 
allocations respectively in RE 2015-16. The Committ ee asked the reasons for 
reducing the allocation at RE stage. 
(Para 220) 
 
 
85. However, the Committee during its earlier study  visit in January 2016, to 
examine the Mid-term performance in utilization of funds by Coir Board, was 
informed about much better utilization of allocatio ns by Coir Board as 
compared to other divisions like DC-MSME whose allo cation has been 
increased. The Committee was informed the following  expenditure pattern of 
Coir Board by end of third quarter in December, 2015. 
(Para 222)
