86. The Committee therefore wonders that if the pre vious information given 
in January 2016, were true then what was the ground  for reducing allocation at 
RE (2015-16) stage. 
(Para 223) 
 
87. The Committee has been informed that Coir Board  had diverted Planned 
Funds meant for MDA to Non Planned Funds for paymen t of salaries. This was 
objected to by the audit team of the Ministry which  advised against release of 
Funds to Coir Board. The Committee takes it serious ly to divert the Planned 
Funds  to pay the salaries and that is why the Comm ittee has been arguing that 
the Ministry must make a realistic assessment of th e cost of implementing a 
scheme instead of making a lumpsum Non-Planned allo cation for salaries and 
other dues. However, in the instant case the Commit tee may be informed of the 
conditions that forced the Coir Board to divert Pla nned funds for the payments 
of salaries. Did the Coir Board ever raise the dema nd for more Non-Planned 
allocation to meet the salary dues. If yes, what steps did the Ministry take. 
(Para 227) 
 
88. The Committee is unconvinced with the reply abo ut under-utilisation of 
Non-Plan funds meant for committed liabilities like salaries, pensionary benefits 
etc. The Committee may be informed of the condition s where even such 
committed liabilities were under-utilised by the Co ir Board which inter alia 
warranted a reduction of Non-Planned allocation at RE stage.  
(Para 228) 
 
89. The Committee may be informed about actual proc edure of devolution of 
subsidy to CUY beneficiary and the time taken in ac tual disbursal of subsidized 
loan.  
(Para 230) 
90. The Committee may also be informed about the pu rpose of proposed 
modification in the CUY Scheme.   
(Para 231) 
 
91. The Committee may be informed as to how unspent  balance of CUY was 
allowed to be carried forward after FY 2014-15 ende d. Whether the M/o 
Finance norms were followed or the unspent money sh ould have been 
surrendered. Should not such unspent funds be re-ap propriated by the 
Parliament through a separate Appropriation Bill? T he Committee has always 

120 
 
cautioned against the Planned money being parked wi th subordinate 
offices/statutory organization even after the FY. A s a result of delayed partial 
release and consequent under-utilisation of allocat ed Funds in BE, the RE was 
substantially reduced. As a result the target of as sisting 825 units was grossly 
under achieved to mere 424 units. The Ministry has blamed Bank’s lukewarm 
response for underutilization of Funds of CUY. Instead the Ministry should look 
to its own financial mismanagement.   
(Para 235) 
 
92. The Committee having seen the fate of India Inc lusive Innovation Fund, is 
justifiably apprehensive of the fate of such Scheme s where no planning, 
discussion or guidelines have been done proper to m aking any allocation in the 
Budget. The Committee has repeatedly cautioned the Ministry against the 
practice of launching new schemes before details of  mandate, procedures, 
stakeholders and have been decided. However, there is a tendency of 
announcing multiple schemes without having clearer vision, structure to 
implement and capacity to monitor. As a result such  allocations remain idle for 
years before being dropped. The Committee therefore  recommends that the 
Ministry should ensure that the mandate, structure,  procedures and the cost of 
this MSME Fund may be decided expeditiously by the competent authority, so 
that the Fund become operationalised within the cur rent  FY 2016-17.  Also, the 
Committee may be informed if Ministry proposes to s eek further Funds in the 
Supplementary Demands or the scheme will be Funded by diverting the savings 
of other Schemes. 
(Para 239) 
 
93. The Committee appreciates that the new modified  MPDA scheme has 
enhanced the financial assistance to artisans to 40 % while reducing the share of 
producing and selling institutions. The Committee a pprehends if such reduction 
may become a dis-incentive for producing and selling units. The Committee may 
also be informed how does the Ministry calculate th e per day per artisan wage 
for the purposes of overall allocation for MPDA. Th e Committee also 
recommends that the Ministry must explore the ways to transfer the wages 
directly to the Bank accounts of the artisan throug h DBT as is being done in 
other DBT schemes like MNREGA. 
(Para 242) 
 
94. The Committee also refers to the reply to Rajya  Sabha Question 1189 
(30.7.15) wherein the Ministry has stated “ Khadi spinning and weaving is a 
subsidiary activity. The artisans associated with K hadi Institutions are self-employed 

121 
 
persons. They operate charkha/looms depending upon the free time available to 
them. The artisans are paid on piece rate basis i.e. number of hanks of yarn spun and 
meters of cloth woven. Hence, the wages of Khadi ar tisans are not strictly 
comparable to minimum daily wages“.   
 The Committee on previous occasions during its study visits has interacted with 
khadi artisans in presence of the representatives of KVIC and had witnessed the 
abject drudgery the female artisans had to endure p ractically for long hours 
daily, to earn an uncertain meager daily wage. The Committee is convinced that 
regardless of the structure of khadi sector, where artisans are employed 
casually, the artisans must be classified as skille d labourer for the purposes of 
wage and other benefits and thus recommends that to  enforce this earnestly, it 
should be made mandatory condition for the institut ions availing MPDA 
assistance to classify khadi artisans as skilled wo rker for the wage purposes and 
other benefits.  
(Para 243) 
 
 
 
95. The Committee while appreciates that more compr ehensive coverage 
would be available to khadi artisans under new soci al security schemes, it 
however notes that no Budgetary provision has been made in this year’s Budget. 
The Committee may be informed by when the modalitie s of new insurance 
scheme will be finalized and what will be the share  of premium borne by the 
Ministry and the insurance Companies. Whether the M inistry will seek 
supplementary demand for this purpose.  
 
(Para 245) 
 
  
96. The Committee reiterates its serious reservatio n over persistent lack of 
regard for allocations and targets by the Ministry and its organizations. The 
Ministry continues to disregard its own estimates.  
(Para 246) 
 
97. The Committee in this penultimate year of 12 
th  Plan has recommended the 
performance audit by the CAG of several flagship sc hemes like PMEGP, 
Training Institutions and Tool Room and the NMCP fo r the entire plan period 
till 2015-16. In addition, the Ministry should have  its other schemes internally 
audited. And the salient findings of these audits m ust be included in the Annual 
Report. The Committee’s Reports may become the reference for such an audit.  

122 
 
(Para 247) 
 
98. The Committee takes serious note of the observa tions made by the CAG in 
its Report (1 of 2015) on Financial Audit of Union Government Accounts 2013-
14. The CAG says that Ministry’s Budget is prepared  without adequate 
proposals from the prospective grantees. Grants are released without taking into 
account unspent balance. There is a deficient inter nal oversight. Contrary to 
General Financial Rules, the details of grants are not disclosed to Parliament 
through Annual Reports. And yet, the demand for all ocation keeps increasing 
every year.  The Committee notes that the Audit obs ervations were not duly 
reflected in the Annual Report ( 2015-16) of the Mi nistry. The Committee 
therefore requires that Ministry should include its  point wise reply/action taken 
note in the Annual Report.  
(Para 248) 
99. The Committee reiterates its recommendation con tained in its previous 
264 th  and 271 st  Reports regarding Performance Audit by CAG of its select 
Schemes.  The Committee also recommends that Minist ry may get the 
performance its remaining scheme for the 12 th  Plan period internally audited. 
(Para 249) 
100. The Committee is particularly concern over ser ious under utilization of 
funds under SCSP, TSP and NER meant for the margina lized sections of the 
society.  That the funds are underutilized due to l ack of demand from these 
sections, is an insensitive argument  by the Minist ry to hide its own 
shortcomings in reaching out to these sections. The  Committee wonders if 
MUDRA Yojna could be successful with these very sam e sections, how can the 
Ministry blame the lack of demand. The Committee on ce again recommends 
that Ministry needs to physically expand its outrea ch among these sections. The 
Committee though finds it ironical that the same Mi nistry which blames lack of 
demand, has been entrusted by the Government to imp lement the SC/ST Hub. 
The Committee proposes to closely monitor the progr ess and performance of 
this Hub. The Committee may be informed of the stru cture and processes of 
proposed SC/ST Hub and the benchmarks to monitor its performance.  
(Para 250)

CHAPTER – I 
 
The Recommendations/observations, which have been accepted by the Ministry 
 
Recommendation/ observation 
 The Committee notes that the Government has come up  with some important 
initiatives in the area of revival / restructure / closure of CPSEs. As the Committee 
gathers, the earlier mechanism involved the adminis trative Ministry / Department, the 
BRPSE, the BIFR and finally the approving authority , the Cabinet. This multiplicity of 
agencies involved delay in granting approval to rev ival plans and most of the revival 
proposals when finally approved would have already become redundant due to escalation 
of costs owing to the time over run. This vexed sit uation contributed to the further 
downfall of the sick / loss incurring and weak CPSEs involved.    
Para No 41 
 
Recommendation/ observation 
 Now, as per the new system the administrative Minis tries will oversee the 
performance of its CPSEs based on the guidelines fo r”streamlining the mechanism for 
revival and restructuring of sick / incipient sick and weak Central Public Sector 
Enterprises: General principles and mechanism of re structuring” issued by DPE. Further, 
the Government has done away with the BRPSE and BIF R and AAIFR and they would 
stand abolished once the NCLT is constituted. The NCLT, provided for in the Companies 
Act, 2013, will henceforth be the sole entity to de cide upon the revival / restructure 
proposals of CPSEs. Also, the revival / restructure process has been rendered time bound. 
In this regard, the Committee observes that the ste p taken to put the administrative 
Ministry in charge of the monitoring of the health of their respective CPSEs is an 
appropriate decision as mid-course correction and o ther reformative measures can be 
taken swiftly without any time lapse as no third pa rty is getting involved. The Committee 
expects that all the lacunae which plagued the earl ier system will be eliminated in the 
new mechanism.

Action Taken Replies

decision regarding acceptance of such recommendatio ns rested with the administrative 
Ministries/Departments. In order to streamline the multiple mechanism for revival of sick

Reconstruction of Public Enterprises (BRPSE). Accor dingly, the BRPSE was wound up 
vide notification dated 9

the health of CPSEs functioning under their control  and take timely redressal measures 
for revival/ restructuring/disinvestment of sick/lo ss making CPSEs with the approval of 
the competent authority in a time bound manner .

 The Committee notes with concern that none of the CPSEs under DHI have been

 As regards categorization of  BHEL as a “weak” CPS Es alongwith BHEL EML 
(Subsidiary of BHEL) the following background and factual position is placed before the 
Hon’ble Committee:- 
           
 (i) The reasons for decline in performance of CPSE s vary from enterprise to 
enterprise. The causes can be broadly classified in to two categories viz. (a) Internal 
causes, and (b) External causes. While ‘Internal ca uses’ are those which can be attributed 
to the management, the ‘External causes’ are those which are attributed to factors outside 
the purview / control of the management. The pace i s based on both internal and external 
factors. Some common issues associated with the dec line in performance and losses of 
CPSEs include old and obsolete plant and machinery,  outdated technology, low capacity 
utilization, excess manpower, weak marketing strate gies, stiff competition, dependence 
on Government orders, heavy interest burden, high i nput cost, resource crunch, change in 
Government policy, general economic conditions etc. As such, performance improvement 
of CPSEs with suitable interventions by the Governm ent is a continuous process, 
including facilitated by the Government Nominees an d Independent Directors on the 
Board of such CPSEs. Enterprise specific measures f or their turn around are taken and 
inter-alia include business restructuring, such as, formation of joint ventures, merger with 
another PSE, modernization and improved marketing s trategies, etc. Moreover, financial 
and non-financial targets for the CPSEs are fixed k eeping in view the prevailing business 
scenario through the mechanism of Memorandum of Und erstanding (MoU), which is a 
negotiated agreement signed between the Administrat ive Department/Ministry of the 
Government and the Management of the CPSEs. Achieve ment of targets is inter-alia 
dependent on sectoral business environment. Moreover, the performance of CPSEs under 
the administrative control of DHI is reviewed by the Department. 
 
 (ii) As regards BHEL being categorised as a “Weak”  CPSE as per the DPE 
Guidelines for “Streamlining the mechanism for revi val and restructuring of sick / 
incipient sick and weak Central Public Sector Enter prises: General principles and 
mechanism of restructuring” dated 29-10-2015, the y ard-sticks/criteria’s formulated do 
not factor the operating business environment and t he severe competitive intensity faced 
by the Company from both domestic and international  players. Moreover, the DPE 
criteria on the matter are made applicable for all CPSEs irrespective of their type of 
operations/ category/ sector. BHEL businesses being  a part of Capital Goods Industry 
have close linkages with growth of infrastructure i n the Country and is driven by 
investments in the economy. These investments are c yclic in nature and is currently 
subdued. This has been mainly due to slowdown in th e Indian power sector as well as 
quietude industrial activity influenced by a combin ation of factors prevailing since last 3 
- 4 years, such as factors associated with fuel lin kages/ environment clearances/ land and 
water availability, funding constraints from lendin g institutions, existing orders being put 
on hold etc., which places additional strain on cap acity utilization. Consequently, there is 
decrease in fresh executable orders maturing in the  market due to which there has been a

reduction in level of operations and hence decline in the financial performance of BHEL 
in the recent past. Further, the Company has to incur certain fixed costs also eg. personnel 
payments, expenditure towards running of establishm ent etc. which do not decrease with 
decline in turnover. 
 
 (iii) The fundamental, inherent and core capabilit ies of BHEL have not decreased 
over the years. The Company has adequate manufactur ing and managerial prowess and 
this aspect is not a constraint. The current status  of BHEL is only a transient period. 
Certain new policy initiatives have been taken by t he Government such as launching of

material for power transmission & distribution / sw itchyard for domestically funded 
power projects [of MoP or CPSUs or projects funded by PFC and REC or by State power 
Utilities] should be made from domestic / local man ufacturers through domestic 
competitive bidding. With these initiatives, the pe rformance of domestic electrical 
equipment manufacturing industry including BHEL is expected to improve in the 
medium term.  
 
 (iv) As BHEL is a “Maharatna” CPSE w.e.f. 01-02-20 13 (earlier it was a 
“Navratna” CPSE) having certain degree of autonomy as per guidelines issued by the

 05 Independent Directors have also been appointed on the Board of BHEL.

 (v) BHEL EML has been categorized as ‘Incipient’ C PSE as per the latest

Recommendation/ observation 
 The Committee notes that the performance of BHEL h as slackened over the last 
two to three years owing to a slew of reasons given  by the Company viz. retarded 
demand, delayed environmental clearances, stranded orders, etc. In the view of the 
Committee, the reasons put forward by BHEL portrays  an impression that these have 
been ‘beyond the control’ of the company. Even whil e considering that BHEL might 
have taken steps to check the slide in its performa nce, the fact remains that their 
performance seems to have dipped despite these effo rts. Accordingly, the Committee 
finds it difficult to isolate the reasons for the l acklustre performance of BHEL to those 
quoted by the company alone. Therefore, the Committ ee’s conclusion is that there has 
been a delay on the part of BHEL in responding to t he challenges thrown to them by the 
market and other factors.  Though, the Committee do es not completely discount the 
reasons put forth by BHEL, it is the Committee’s fi rm belief that BHEL’s current 
situation is the outcome of their poor performance in the area of risk analysis and 
business foresight, both of which would have allowe d the Company to anticipate rough 
business weather and for effective and commensurate course correction.

th  October, 2016 considered and adopted the

REPORT 
 
The Action Taken Report of the Committee deals with  the Action Taken by the 
Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises on the recommendations contained in the 
Committee’s Two Hundred Seventy Fifth Report on Dem ands for Grants (2016-17)  
pertaining to the Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises. 
 
2.  Action Taken Notes have been received from the Ministry of Micro, Small and 
Medium Enterprises in respect of the recommendation s contained in the Report. These have 
been categorized as follows:  
 
Chapter –I   The recommendations/observations, which have bee n accepted by the 
Ministry. 
 
 The Committee is pleased to observe that the Minis try has accepted its 
recommendations as mentioned in the Chapter – I of the Report. 
 
Chapter -II   The recommendations/observations which the Commit tee does not desire to 
pursue in view of the Government's replies. 
 
 In respect of these recommendations the Committee is convinced with the logic and 
explanations advanced by the Ministry and therefore  do not want to pursue them for the 
present. 
 
Chapter -III    The recommendations/observations in respect of w hich the Committee has 
either not accepted replies of the Ministry or has asked the Ministry to review its reply. 
 
 The Committee expresses its concern over the non-i mplementation of 
recommendations contained in Chapter – III and desi res that the Ministry should furnish 
logical explanations therefor. 
 
Chapter -IV    The recommendations/observations in respect of wh ich final replies of the 
Ministry have not been received. 
 
 In respect of recommendations placed in Chapter-IV , the Ministry has either 
furnished the interim replies or couched its langua ge in vague terms like noted for 
compliance/guidance, therefore, the Committee desir es that the Ministry should furnish 
Action Taken Notes in respects of recommendations c ategorized in Chapter-IV in detail and 
to the point, as per the intention and spirit of the recommendations of the Committee. 
 
3. The details of the ATR are being discussed in the succeeding pages. 
 
 
 
 
 

-2- 
 
CHAPTER-I 
 
Recommendations/observations, which have been accepted by the Ministry  
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
It  is  evident  that  every  year  since  2013-14  the  Planned  allocation  has 
remained significantly under utilized by every wing  of the Ministry. And 
considering the expenditure norms prescribed by the  Ministry of Finance that not 
more than 33% of BE can be spent in last quarter of  FY and not more than 15%  
of  BE  can  be  spent  in  the  month  of  March  of FY,  it is  unlikely  that 
Ministry can stick to these norms this year (2015-1 6) as well and, therefore, 
unlikely to utilize the available resources prudent ly.  In the financial year 2015-16 
too,  as  per  the E-lekha  of  Controller  General   of  Accounts,  only  67%  of 
Planned allocation was spent by the end of January 2016, however, as per the 
above information provided  by the Financial  Advis or of the Ministry, about 
96% of Planned BE was likely to be spent by the end  of FY 2015-16 and around 
29% of the Planned BE was spent in last two months.     
   
  (Para 14) 
Action Taken :  
 
  It is true that expenditure of Plan allocation was relatively less during 
the year 2015-16 but it has considerably improved in 2016-17. 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
The Committee considers these Schemes a reflection of inadequate planning 
and poor implementation. Norms of Schemes are delay ed and schemes are  
modified  the  mid-way  and  till  the  modified  n orms  are  finalized  and 
approved by the competent authority, the allocation  remains frozen. 
(Para 22) 
 
Action Taken :  
 
The observations of the Committee are noted. All th e schemes are 
implemented as per the schemes guidelines, which ar e reviewed from time to time. 
 
 
 

-3- 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
In view of 345 lakh unregistered units in the count ry as per Fourth Census 
conducted in 2006-07, registration of mere 4 lakh u nits is rather slow and tardy 
progress. The very fact that of 4 lakh registration s majority are micro and small 
entrepreneurs, shows great demand among these entre preneurs to register to 
avail of possible benefits of Government schemes.   It is also evident that in 
certain smaller, hill and remote States, the regist ration has not picked up. Even in 
larger States the progress in registration is slow compared to the scope and 
extent of this Sector. The Committee recommends tha t it will require a sustained 
campaign to register all the MSMEs under UAM and th at the registration must be 
linked with benefits.  
(Para 40) 
Action Taken:  
 
For utilization of the Udyog Aadhaar Programme, the  notifications issued in this 
regard has been uploaded in the website of this Min istry. A national web portal 
namely, http://udyogaadhaar.gov.in has also been la unched for enabling e-filing of 
Udyog Aadhar Memorandum.  States have been requeste d to issue instructions to 
the concerned Directors of industries and General M anagers of DIC for expeditious 
implementation of UAM.  In the regional meetings, S tates were requested to 
undertake steps to encourage UAM registration. The benefit of Udyog Aadhar 
Memorandum registration is ease in registering the unit and getting benefits from 
the scheme/programme run by the Government.  As of now, the registration has 
crossed 11 lakhs and, on an average, more than 4000  MSE units are getting 
registered every day. The process was, so far, slow  because of systemic  issues 
which technology has resolved.     
  
Recommendation/Observation  
The Committee apprehends that even the ASPIRE may m eet the same 
fate  as  other  entrepreneurship  development  pro grammes  being  run  by  the 
Ministry. The Committee notes that ASPIRE too is fo llowing the set stereotypes 
of considering MSMEs as low cost low technology ent erprises, that may not 
independently survive the market competition   in l onger run. The Committee 
was surprised to note that as per the Fourth Census  of MSME 2006-07, out of 
the 15 lakh registered MSME units, about 5 lakh bec ame sick. And the trades 
that are offered under ASPIRE may not improve the s ituation. ASPIRE needs to 
break this stereotype and consider MSMEs as technol ogy intensive sector that 
can survive the market competition. 
(Para 159) 
 

-4- 
 
Action Taken :  
 
 The suggestion is noted and would be followed up. However, it is the

Action Taken:   
 
SIDBI has formulated SMILE Scheme with an objective  to provide soft loan, 
in the nature of quasi-equity and term loan on rela tively soft terms to MSMEs to 
meet the required debt-equity ratio norm for new un its as also for pursuing 
opportunities for growth by existing MSMEs. The sch eme is to take forward GoI’s 
‘Make in India’ campaign and to help MSMEs take part in the campaign.  
• All new as well as existing MSME units covered unde r 25 sectors covered under 
‘Make In India’ Programme of Government of India an d few other sectors are 
eligible under SMILE. 
Special features of SMILE: 
• It is a project finance scheme; wherein, MSMEs are assisted by way of soft loan, 
which is a quasi-equity assistance to meet the requ ired debt-equity ratio and term 
loan on relatively soft terms.  
• Maximum eligible quantum under soft loan is 10% of the project cost subject to a 
maximum of Rs. 20 lakh. A higher soft loan of up to  15% of the project cost will 
be considered for the enterprises promoted by Sched uled Caste (SC) / Scheduled 
Tribe (ST) / Persons with Disabilities (PwD) and wo men, subject to a maximum 
of  Rs. 30 lakh.     

-8- 
 
• Minimum term loan size is Rs. 25 lakh.                     
• While the interest rates are fixed based on rating of the proposal, the scheme 
provides concession in interest rate during the fir st 3 years from the date of first 
disbursement. Presently, the applicable interest ra te for initial period of three 
years is 9.35% p.a. for soft loans and interest rat es for term loan under SMILE 
ranges from 9.45% to 9.95% p.a., depending on the i nternal rating of the 
borrower.  
• The soft loan is converted into term loan after 3 y ear period and would carry rate 
as per the internal credit rating of term loan assigned at the time of sanction.   
• Longer moratorium period of upto 2 years will be provided for soft loan. 
• The scheme had benefitted 419 MSMEs with cumulative  sanctions of Rs. 1323 
crore till May 31, 2016. 
1. SIDBI operates Startup Assistance Scheme out its ow n resources, wherein startup 
ventures with revenue traction of at least 6 months  and subject to compliance of 
the norms under the Scheme are extended financial assistance by way of loans. 
As on March 31, 2016, SIDBI has assisted 57 Startup s with aggregate sanctioned 
amount of  Rs. 57.48 Crore under Startup Assistance  Scheme. The Scheme does not 
cover PMEGP whereas ASPIRE is meant for rural startups by way of equity through 
AIFs. 
 
The objective of SMILE Scheme  of SIDBI is to provide soft loan, in the 
nature of quasi-equity, and term loan on relatively  soft terms to MSMEs to meet the 
required debt-equity ratio for establishment of an MSME as also for pursuing 
opportunities for growth for existing MSMEs.  The minimum term loan will be Rs.50 
lakh for new enterprise and Rs.25 for existing ente rprises going for additional 
investment.  The minimum contribution of the promot er is 15% of the project cost 
for projects upto Rs.1 crore and 20% for the rest.  Term loan will be 75% for 
enterprises with total project cost upto to Rs.1 crore and 2/3 of the project cost for the 
rest, Soft loan will be 10% of the project cost sub ject to a minimum of Rs.20 lakh 
and upto 15% for enterprises promoted by SC/ST/PwD and women subject to a 
maximum of Rs.30 lakhs.  
Whereas the objectives of PMEGP  is aimed at generating self-employment 
opportunities through establishment of micro-enterp rises in the non-farm sector by 
helping traditional artisans and unemployed youth. General category beneficiaries 
can avail of margin money subsidy of 25% of the pro ject cost in rural areas and 15% 
in urban areas. For beneficiaries belonging to spec ial categories such as scheduled 
caste/scheduled tribe /women the margin money subsidy is 35% in  rural  areas  and  

-9- 
 
25% in urban areas. The maximum cost of projects is  Rs.25 lakh in the 
manufacturing sector and Rs.10 lakh in the service sector.  The assistance under 
PMEGP scheme is available only to new projects. 
The objectives of ASPIRE  scheme is to accelerate entrepreneurship and to 
promote start-ups for innovation and entrepreneursh ip in agro-industry through 
setting up of Incubators by providing one-time gran t of cost of Plant & Machinery.  
Whereas SMILE is for promoting individual enterprises. 
 
Similarly, on comparing PMEGP with SMILE, following observations may be 
drawn: 
 
1. The project cost under SMILE is from Rs. 50-100 lak hs whereas under 
PMEGP the project cost is limited to Rs.25 lakh only. 
2. Under SMILE, assistance of Rs.25 lakh is available for existing enterprises for 
upgradation whereas PMEGP scheme is available for new enterprises. 
In view of the above, PMEGP, ASPIRE and SMILE schem es are catering to 
different segments and hence cannot be linked or inter-linked.

  The funds from nodal banks are transferred to fin ancing banks on receipt of

Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
The Committee feels that CLCSS and NMCP should be s eparated. As per the 
current practice, the CLCSS which draws much larger  budget is clubbed with 
six components of NMCP that draw meager budget. CLC SS is essentially an 
interest subvention scheme like ISEC and should be kept as a credit support scheme 
whereas the NMCP is technology upgradation scheme. 
(Para 7) 
Action Taken :  
 
 As per the budgetary provisions, CLCSS and NMCP ar e implemented as 
distinct Schemes/Programmes.  However, for the purp ose of grouping/classification, 
CLCSS and NMCP have been placed in one broad group named as “Technology 
Up-gradation and Quality Certification”.   It is further submitted that the purpose 
of CLCSS is to provide subsidy for technology up-gr adation of SMEs through credit 
support from banks/financial institutions. The obje ctive of the NMCP component is 
to enhance competitiveness of the MSMEs. However, e ach component of the NMCP 
has distinct objectives. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation  
 
 As funding under two Schemes is different, the allo cation too should be 
indicated separately even under same group of Tech.  Upgradation and Quality 
Certification.  Rather Committee has suggested that  all the six components of 
NMCP should be indicated as separate allocation for  better monitoring. The 
Committee reiterates its recommendation in view of dismal performance in all 
the six components.  
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
The Committee has always believed that multiplicity  of schemes scattered 
the allocated resources of the Ministry. The Commit tee is also of the view that in 
absence of specific Non-Planned allocations for the  respective schemes, it was 
difficult to assess the performance of the Scheme i n terms of funds allocated for a 
specific scheme.  As  per  practice, a lumpsum Non- Planned allocation is made  

-20- 
 
towards the implementing agency that may be impleme nting several other 
Schemes. For example the DC-MSME implements around 25 schemes but had a 
Non Planned allocation of Rs 21 crores only to impl ement these Schemes 
throughout the country, resulting which several Sch emes  repeatedly performed 
poorly in terms of under-utilisation of Plan Funds or crowding of Planned 
expenditure.  The Committee while supporting ration alization of Schemes also 
suggests that Ministry must see that Schemes which are clubbed together should 
get equal importance rather than to carrying one or  two Schemes at the cost of 
others.  
(Para 11) 
 
Action Taken :   
 
The multiplicity of schemes to some extent is requi red because of the types 
of industries the Ministry is dealing with.  There are several schemes and all are 
being monitored. Because DCMSME is one office and t herefore non-plan allocation 
is only made at one level and it cannot be segregated. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation  
 
 The allocation of Non-Planned expenditure for indi vidual Scheme 
indicates the cost of implementing a Scheme.  The C ommittee believes it to be 
essential for cost benefit analysis of any Scheme.  It is good management 
practice to work out cost of exceeding a Scheme. By  subsuming all the Non-
Planned expenditure in the Non-Planned allocation m ade to an agency 
implementing several Schemes defeats the very purpo se of budgeting Non-
Planned expenditure.  The Committee is convinced th at multiplicity of Schemes 
without commensurable budget previous to implement at grass root level, is the 
cause of poor performance of most of the Schemes.   
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
However, the Committee finds contrast in the expend iture of Non-Planned 
expenditure. While by January 2016 the Planned expe nditure was 67% of the 
BE, the Non Planned expenditure had reached 88%. Pa ttern of Quarter-wise Non-
Planned expenditure is also fairly even. The Commit tee do not appreciates the 
sluggish implementation of Planned schemes. The Com mittee considers it 
imperative that there should be proportionate incre ases both the expenditures to 
ensure the efficient use of money.  
(Para 16)

Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
 Scheme like India Inclusive Innovation Fund which w as launched towards 
beginning of current Five Year Plan with an  initia l corpus of Rs 500 crores to 
promote and finance grass root level innovations, w as allocated modest amount 
which remained unspent and now towards the end of F ive Year Plan, the Fund is 
being reconsidered. The Committee may be informed o f the reasons as to why this 
Scheme could not be operationalised throughout the current Five Year Plan and 
under what conditions it is being reconsidered.  Th e Ministry may also inform the 
Committee of efforts made by it to operationalise t he Scheme. 
(Para 21) 
Action Taken :   
 The Cabinet had approved the creation of an India I nclusive Innovation Fund 
(IIIF) Scheme in November-December, 2013. As per th e Cabinet decision, oversight 
of the Fund would be by a Governing Council (GC) an d an Asset Management 
Company (AMC). 
The Governing Council and Asset Management Company mainly constituted 
of members/experts from National Innovation Council  under erstwhile Planning 
Commission which ceases to exist and NITI Aayog is a “successor in interest” of 
Planning Commission and Department of Financial Ser vices (DFS). This  office  has 
requested on several occasions to both DFS and NITI  Aayog to nominate the 
members for GC and AMC, as per the decision of Cabi net. However, no nomination 
of members/experts has been made from both DFS and NITI Aayog. 
 

-25- 
In the meantime, NITI Aayog has obtained the approv al of the EFC for the 
Atal Innovation Mission (AIM) and Self Employment and Talent Utilisation (SETU). 
Also launch of other schemes like Start-up India, S tand-up India and the 
establishment of the Fund of Funds, being operated by SIDBI overshadowed the 
objectives of IIIF. In view of this, Ministry of Mi cro, Small, and Medium 
Enterprises, with the approval of Hon’ble Minister of MSME, has decided to close 
the IIIF Scheme. In this regard, a draft Cabinet No te, with the approval of Hon’ble 
Minister of MSME, has been circulated to related Mi nistries, for their views, on the 
13 th  July, 2016.   
Further Recommendation/Observation  
 
 The Committee expresses its serious reservation th at a promising Scheme 
with such large allocation was allowed to be wasted  due to lack of oversight by 
bodies. Subsequently, parallel Schemes emerged.  As  a result despite 
Committee’s repeated caution in previous reports, the Scheme was wasted

Action Taken:   
 
Availment of refinance by Banks, RRBs and MFIs had picked up in last part 
of FY 2016 viz. during February/March 2016.  As on March 31, 2016, MUDRA had 
sanctioned refinance assistance amounting to Rs. 37 83.20 crore, out of which 
Rs.3337.20 crore has been disbursed to 16 PSU Banks , 3 RRBs and 21 Micro 
Finance Institutions.  Although RBI has allowed exe mption from Credit 
Concentration norms in respect of refinance assista nce to Scheduled Commercial 
Banks, the same is not exempted in respect of other  partner institutions.  Hence, 
MUDRA’s refinance to MFIs/NBFCs are subject to sing le party exposure norm of 
15% of Owned Fund, which works out to Rs.112.50 cro re.  Similarly, MUDRA is 
also subject to group exposure norm of 25% of Owned  Fund, which works out to 
Rs. 187.50 crore.  Moreover, Rs.250 crore sanctione d to 3 NBFCs could not be 
disbursed, as  MUDRA’s  assistance  to  NBFCs  is  subject to an interest cap of 6%

than 3.5 per cent above MUDRA’s lending rate to the m. Also MUDRA refinance is 
not exempted for the purpose of computation of CRR and SLR and same will

Action Taken:  
 
 As per RBI guidelines on Priority Sector Lending an d Classification dated 
April 23, 2015 issued to Banks, in order to classif y an advance to MFIs as Priority

percent for MFIs, with loan portfolio exceeding Rs. 100 crore and 12 per cent for 
others, over and above their average cost of funds.    Further, interest rate on 
individual loans will not exceed the average of bas e rate of five largest commercial 
banks, by assets, multiplied by 2.75 per annum or c ost of funds plus margin cap,

Recommendation/ observation

community assets and maintaining them in partnershi p with community. However, in

/recommendation and issue supplementary guidelines for PSEs in addition to the

Recommendation/Observation

RECOMMENDATION (PARA NO. No. 4 AND 5) 
l. The major aspect of the demand for grants of the Ministry of Mines, which m the view 
of the Committee should call for concern is its relatively small magnitude. The !11inimy is 
responsible for the exploration, developmen t and exploitation of all minerals barring atomic 
minerals, coal, natural gas and crud e petroleum. The rich ness and variety of underground 
mincr31 wealth the country possesses boggle the imaginati on. That apa rt, the country is 
stated to be on the threshold of a vastly accelerated process of industrial growth . It ts at the 
same time endeavouring to enlarge ats export potenti al. These factors together ~hould have 
persu aded the Government, the Ministry of Mines and the Planning Commission 10 place. at 
this junct ure, maximum emphasis on a massive development of mining operations. In this 
area of activity, the long·term return on investment cannot but be exceptionally high. The 
need to reduce fiscal deficits is offered as justification for economizing on budgetary outlay for 
different Ministries, including for tbe Ministry of Mines, in tbe immediate period. Such 
economizing, in the view of the Commitlee, is somewhat irrational if a "ider time fram e is 
taken into account. Whether it is zinc. bauxite, chromite, gruph ite, gold or other precious 
metu ls or stones, the pos,~ibili ties of mineral-based industri al expan>~on in the country are 
indeed immense, provided adequate technological and infrastructural support does not lag 
behind. The validity of this point of view is illustrated by the strides madi> by the alwninium 
industry in recent yeilrS. Where such domestic processing of mineral products is not yet 
considered feasible, the scope for exports to countries hungry for receiving them is practically 
limitless. And yet, in the o'·erall scheme of thing, the explora tion and exploitation of minerals 
for contr ibuting toward the notion's prosperity appear s to occupy a very modest space. The 
prop osed budgetary allocation of less than Rs. 250 crore for the Ministry of Mines is an 
eloquent testimony to the miniature scale of official thinking. 
During the span of the past five decades the authorities have mostly cont inued to lean on 
the constricted , colonial edifices or the Geological Survey of India and the Bureau of Mines 
in the matter of mineral use and exploitation. The only addition to the twosome has been 
the Mineral Exploration Corporation. Eve n if the activities of the Corporation are 
considered togetherwith those of the other two bodies , the sum total of the thrust is most 
modest. On the Government's own reckon ing, the aggregate value of extraction of minerals 
corning under the purview of the Ministry of Mines exceeds Rupees 30.000 crorc per annum. 
This return is on the basis of an annual budgetary outlay of less than 1 per cent of this 
amount. The allocation for the Ministry, in the view of the Committee, should be doubled and 
tripl ed; in case this be done, the return to the nation is likely to incre ase not just pari passu, 
but five or six times higher than what It Is at present.

of GSI and the MECL subject to the overall budgetary constra ints of the Ministry of

While enhanced allocations are welcome, it is at the same time appreciated that these 
allocations will not be enough to meet the growing requirements fully. Induction of 
investible funds from outside the budget is necessary to step up the tempo of exploration 
and exploitation of minerals in this sector. To this end in view, a new mineral policy was 
announced in M:rrch, 1993 which envisaged induction of foreign technology and foreign 
panicipation in exploration and mining of high value and scarce minerals. To ensure 
generation of adequate interest in prospecting of new reserves by aerial surveys and other 
means, the area which can now be made available to any investor, domestic or foreign will

also envisage that foreign direct investment in the equity participation by investors can be

case basis. However, this limit of 50% would not apply to captive mining of any mineral 
processing industry. In keeping with the new policy, the FIPB has already approved 33 
projects worth Rs. 2312.31 crore.

16. A final matter, it is ent irely fair that even as the responsibility for economic and 
industrial growth in the country is shared evenly between the Union and State Governments , 
resources that enable the fulfilment of this objective is also shared in a just manner. The 
royalty on mining operations. which is a prerogative of State Governments, is supposed to 
be paid by the Centre to the States o n a regular basis and at rates that are adjustable from 
time to time. The Union Government reportedly has not been honouring this practice; the 
rates are not beiog adjusted every two yea.rs as per standing rules and there is also a certain 
reluctance to cross over to an ad-valorem system of royalty payments. The Committee feels 
that whatever is due to the States ~hould be paid in an equitable manner. The Committee 
further hopes that a part of the prOC«ds of royalty, once made available to the full 
satisfaction of the parties concerned, is made available for the welfare of the people in tile 
mining areas. It is equally important that payment to the villagers as compensation for their 
land taken over for mining activities is paid on immediate basis. The record in this respect is 
most dismal. 
Action Token 
Under Sections 9 of the MMRD Act, 1957' every holder of a mining lease is required to 
pay to the concerned State Government royalty in respect of the mineral removed or 
consumed by him at the rates specified in the Second Schedule tO the ACL ft may thus be 
seen that Royalty is not released by the Central Government to the States. It is collected by 
the States themselves at rates as notified under Sec.9 of MMRD Act, 1957 in the case of 
major minerals and at rates as decided by the State Government in case of minor minerals. 
Further Section 24A of the MMRD Act, 1957 requires the lessee to provide proper 
compensation to occupier of the surface of the land for any loss or damage which is likely lO -.. 
arise or has arisen as a consequence of mining operatio n. Compensation to be paid 01 the 
rehabilitation to be provided by the lessee is determined by the State Government as per 
Rule 72 & 73 of MCR, 1960. As regards ope n-cast mining projects, the displaced person~ 
are paid proper compensation as determined by the State Land Acquisition authorities in 
accordance with the Land Acquisition Act and Central Government Directives . Employment 
is also provided as far as possible to one of the members of the displaced families.

The MSME sector has been contributing to expansion of entrepreneurial culture through 
business innovations. The MSMEs are widely disperse d across various sectors of the economy, 
producing diverse range of products and services to  meet demands of local as well as global 
markets. As per the data available with Central Sta tistics Office (CSO), Ministry of Statistics & 
Programme Implementation, Government of India, the Ministry of MSME gave an approximation, 
based on the results of Annual Survey of Industries (ASI) and surveys on unorganized sector, which 
indicates the estimated contribution of the MSME se ctor to Gross Value Added (GVA), GDP and 
Manufacturing Output, during 2011-12 to 2015-16. The details are as under:-

2.  The Committee notes that contribution of MSMEs in manufacturing sector is almost 
stagnant but has been steadily increasing in Service sector. 
   

2 
 
3.  In view of the size of the MSME sector in the coun try, a Budget allocation of                  
Rs 6482 crores for Financial Year 2017-18, is just meager and needs to be utilized efficiently 
and judiciously. 
 
4.  It was informed that there were about 25.27 lakh M SMEs registered under Udyog 
Adhaar Memorandum (UAM) till 31.1.2017 of which 22 lakh were micro units. The 
Committee also noted the submission made by the Secretary of the Ministry that there was no 
realistic estimation of number and scope of MSME un its in the country.  The Secretary had 
submitted that the Ministry is in the process of de veloping an online census of statistical data 
of MSMEs.  The Committee believes that without real istic and updated information 
regarding scope and extent of MSMEs in the country,  no worthwhile policy or budgetary 
intervention can be made. 
 
5.  However, the Committee also noted that ever since 4 th  Census of MSMEs, the 
Government has not conducted the 5 th  census which is due.  Instead, it has been decided  to 
discontinue the process of census and look for othe r sources of collecting reliable data on 
MSMEs. The Committee feels that Census figures are an important reference point for any 
future policy formulation initiative as it provides baseline data to measure prospective trends. 
Every year, in DFG, a separate allocation is made t o strengthen the database, survey and 
research. The Ministry may consider using this allo cation for conducting 5 th  decennial census 
of MSMEs. Also, like annual Public Enterprises Surv ey, Ministry of MSME too should 
present an annual MSME Survey on the basis of NSS Rounds.      
 
Economic Survey on prospects and challenges of MSME sector  
 
6. The Committee was informed that the  Economic Survey expressed concerns regarding the 
rise in NPA’s in the second half of 2016, which cam e from mid-size corporate and MSMEs, as 
companies that had been suffering from poor sales a nd profitability for a number of years struggled 
and remained indebted. This trend is likely to cont inue into 2017. Real loan growth to MSMEs 
slowed significantly in 2014-15, and actually turned negative during the past two fiscal years. 
 
7.  The Committee feels that an assessment should be  made of the impact if any,  of 
demonetisation, on the credit-worthiness of MSMEs and whether it has led to greater NPAs in 
MSME sector. The Committee takes note of demands pu t forth by certain industry 

3 
 
associations that in view of possible adverse impac t of demonetization on the business and 
overall lack of liquidity in the economy, the time limit for NPA should be extended from 
present 90 days to 180 days.  The Committee views t his demand favourably and recommends 
the Ministry to take up the issue with Ministry of Finance and RBI and report to the 
Committee of its outcome. 
 
Evolution and Mandate of the Ministry 
 
  
8. The Government of India established the Ministry  of Small Scale Industries and Agro & 
Rural Industries (SSI & ARI) in October, 1999 as the nodal Ministry for formulation of policies and 
Central sector programmes/schemes, their implementa tion and related coordination and for 
supplementing the efforts of the States/Union Terri tories for promotion and development of small 
scale, agro and rural industries in the country.  S ubsequently, in September, 2001 the Ministry of 
SSI and ARI was bifurcated into two separate Minist ries, namely, Ministry of Small Scale 
Industries and Ministry of Agro and Rural Industrie s.  In 2006, “Micro, Small and Medium 
Enterprises Development Act (MSMED), 2006” was enac ted by the Parliament.  Pursuant to this 
enactment on 9 May, 2007, the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries and the Small Scale 
Industries were merged into a single Ministry, name ly, Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium 
Enterprises.  
 
Composition of the Ministry 
 
 
9. The Ministry of Micro Small & Medium Enterprises  is having two divisions called Small & 
Medium Enterprises (SME) Wing and Agro & Rural Indu stry (ARI) Wing, besides office of the 
Development Commissioner (MSME) and other organisat ions.  The SME Wing is allocated the 
work, inter-alia, of administration, vigilance and administrative supervision of the National Small 
Industries Corporation (NSIC) Ltd., a public sector  enterprise and National Institution of Micro, 
Small & Medium Enterprises (NIMESE) an autonomous n ational level entrepreneurship 
development/training organization.  The Wing is als o responsible for implementation of the 
schemes relating to Performance and Credit Rating, Assistance to Training Institutions and 
preparation and monitoring of “Make in India” initiative among others.    
 

4 
 
10. The ARI Wing looks after the administration of two statutory bodies viz. the Khadi and 
Village Industries Commission (KVIC), Coir Board an d a society called Mahatma Gandhi Institute 
of Rural Industrialization (MGIRI).  It also superv ises the implementation of the Prime Minister’s 
Employment Generation Programme (PMEGP).  Scheme of  Fund for Regeneration of Traditional 
Industries (SFURTI) and A Scheme for Promoting Innovation, Rural Industry and Entrepreneurship 
(ASPIRE).  
 
11. The implementation of policies and various prog rammes/schemes for providing 
infrastructure and support services to MSMEs is und ertaken through its attached office, namely the 
Office of the Development Commissioner (O/o DC (MSM E), National Small Industries 
Corporation (NSIC), Khadi and Village Industries Co mmission (KVIC), the Coir Board and 
training institutes viz., National Institute for Mi cro, Small and Medium Enterprises (NI-MSME), 
Hyderabad and Mahatma Gandhi Institute for Rural Industrialization (MGIRI), Wardha. 
 
12.  The Committee notes that unlike KVIC and Coir Boar d, whose allocation is made 
under ARI Division, the Office of DC-MSME though ha s same mandate and implements the 
same Schemes as SME Division, get separate allocati on in the annual Demands.  The 
Committee has been raising the issues of overlappin g and duplication of multiple Schemes of 
the Ministry.  Considering that SME Division and DC -MSME both have not been able to 
utilize their allocated funds during previous years , the Committee is inclined to recommend 
that two allocations may be merged so that the Sche mes are also consolidated with more 
money available for their implementation.  The Comm ittee recommends that like KVIC and 
Coir Board, the allocation for DC-MSME too should b e brought under SME Division for the 
efficient and economic utilization of available resources.

18. The Committee notes that against the Plan Outlay o f Rs. 24124 crores for 12 
th  Plan, 
total annual Budget allocation for the Plan period was Rs. 1475 crores which is only about 
61% of the Plan Outlay.  The Committee finds it par adoxical that a Plan outlay of such 
magnitude is not supported by Budget allocation.  T he Committee may be informed about the 
rationale given by Ministry of Finance on lower Budget allocation compared to Plan outlay.  
 
19. The Committee also notes that despite low Budget a llocation, the actual utilization of 
funds under major Schemes of SME Division and DC-MS ME has been very low, thereby 
denying the Ministry any ground to seek high alloca tion in BE.  The Ministry has often 
justified poor utilization on the ground that Schem es are demand driven.  If the Ministry is 
not sure of demand for such Schemes then rationale for seeking higher allocation every 

8 
 
successive year may be explained. The Committee may  be informed that beyond routine 
awareness programmes, of the steps taken to generat e demand in a sector that seeks  policy 
intervention.  
 
Budget Proposals 
 
 
20. The Committee sought Ministry’s comments on the  impact of Budget declaration and tax 
proposals on MSME sector.  
 
21. It was informed that in order to make MSMEs mor e viable and also to encourage firms to 
migrate to company format, Union Budget 2017-18 pro poses to reduce the income tax for smaller 
companies with annual turnover upto Rs. 50 crore to  25%. As per data of Assessment Year 2015-
16, there were 6.94 lakh companies filing returns o f which 6.67 lakh companies’ fall in this 
category and, therefore, percentage-wise, 96% of co mpanies will get the benefit of lower taxation. 
This will make the  MSME sector more competitive as compared to large companies. 
 
22. The Committee is not sure that reduction in income tax rate as proposed in the Budget 
will make the MSME more competitive.  
 
23. The Committee further asked if these concession s were available only to Companies and not 
to proprietorship/partnership firms which constitute the majority of Companies in MSME sector. 
 
24. It was informed that the MSME classification wa s based on the investment criteria and not 
on the ownership of the firms. So all the MSMEs whe ther they are Private Ltd. Companies or 
proprietorship/partnership companies are eligible for this benefit. 
 
25. However, a closer reading of Budget speech sugg ests that this initiative is essentially to 
encourage MSME firms to migrate to company format.  The Finance Minister had announced in 
Budget Speech “ In order to make MSME companies more viable and als o to encourage firms to 
migrate to company format, I propose to reduce the income tax for smaller companies with annual 
turnover upto Rs. 50 crore to 25%.”.   
 
26. The Committee notes the demand expressed by one of the industry associations to 
widen the scope of this concession to proprietorshi p/partnership firms which constitute the 

9 
 
majority in MSME sector. The Ministry must take up the issue with Ministry of Finance and 
inform the Committee of the response.  
 
27. The Committee noted the Finance Minister’s Budg et Speech which stated “As against 5.6 
crore informal sector individual enterprises and fi rms doing small business in India, the numbers of 
returns filed by this category are only 1.81 crore… ..”   The Committee accordingly sought from the 
Ministry the suggestions to address the situation. 
 
28. It was informed that  demonetisation is expected and designed to bring th eir actual income 
and expenses in digital mode and thus, the taxable income would come to the fore, making the 
taxnet wider. During the presentation of DFG, the Ministry informed the Committee that it has been 
imparting training in digital transactions to MSME entrepreneurs. 
 
29. The Committee expresses concern over narrow tax ba se among informal sector 
individual enterprises.  On the one hand MSME propr ietorship/partnership firms demand 
their inclusion into proposed tax concession to sma ll enterprises, on the other hand they do 
not even file tax returns. This is an unacceptable situation and the Committee recommends 
that the Ministry of MSME must take corrective but non-intrusive action in consultation with 
Ministry of Finance. The Committee suggests that Mi nistry must seek PAN and TIN/ GST 
details of the proprietors/partners in the UAM and,  in association with the Ministry of 
Finance, link these references for better tax monit oring through data networking of direct 
and indirect taxes.  
  
  
New Initiatives by the Ministry  during 2016-17 
 
 
30. It was informed that Ministry of MSME has taken  the following various initiatives for 
strengthening and enhancing the contribution of the MSMEs in the National Economy:- 
 
(i) 
National Scheduled Caste / Scheduled Tribe Hub  
 
 The Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprise s was given the work of 
operationalization of National SC / ST Hub to ensur e 4% procurement from SC/ ST entrepreneurs 

10 
 
in all Central Government Ministries and Central Pu blic Sector Enterprises (CPSEs).  The High 
Powered Monitoring Committee on SC / ST Hub has alr eady met twice, which has resulted into 
more than 5000 SC / ST enterprises getting register ed on the MSME portal, namely 
msmedatabank.in. 
 
(ii) Udyog Aadhaar Memorandum  
 
 In the ease-of-doing business, the registration of  MSMEs was simplified by launching of a 
one-page online Registration methodology.   Udyog A adhaar Memorandum (UAM) was notified 
and launched on 18.9.2015 and more than 25.27 lakh Udyog Aadhaar Memorandums have been 
registered till 31.1.2017.   
 
(iii) MSME Databank  
 
 An online Census of MSMEs has started with the lau nch of MSME Databank and Micro, 
Small and Medium Enterprises Development (Furnishin g of Information) Rules, 2016 have been 
notified to make it compulsory for MSMEs to give in formation on MSME Databank.  More than 
70,590 units have already given information on MSME Databank till 31.1.2017. 
(iv)  Web portal for Micro and Small Enterprises Facilit ation Councils (MSE-FCs ) 
 The Ministry of MSME has developed a web portal wh ich will enable the States to keep 
track of the cases filed in Micro and Small Enterpr ises Facilitation Councils (MSE-FCs) under the 
provisions of the Micro, Small and Medium Enterpris es Development Act, 2006.  Ministry has also 
circulated  Draft  Model MSE-FC Rules  for consideration to revise their  MSE-FC Rules. 
(v) MSME Fund 
In exercise of the powers conferred by section 12 o f the Micro, Small and Medium 
Enterprises Development Act, 2006 (27 of 2006), the  Government has established a fund vide 
Notification dated 28.10.2016 to be called the Micr o Small and Medium Enterprises Fund. The 
objective of the Fund shall be promotion, development and enhancing the competitiveness of micro, 
small and medium enterprises, particularly of the micro and small enterprises.  
(vi)  Credit Guarantee Fund Scheme for Micro and Small E nterprises (CGTMSE) 
The Scheme is implemented by Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and Small 
Enterprises (CGTMSE) set up jointly by the Ggovernm ent of India and SIDBI and covers collateral 

11 
 
free credit facility (term loan and/or working capi tal) extended by eligible lending institutions to 
new and existing Micro and Small Enterprises up to Rs. 200 lakh per borrowing unit.  The 
guarantee cover provided is up to 75% of the credit  facility up to Rs. 50 lakh (85% for loans up to 
Rs. 5 lakh provided to Micro Enterprises, 80% for M SEs owned/operated by women and all loans 
to NER), and uniform guarantee of 50% of the credit  exposure above Rs. 50 lakh and up to Rs. 200 
lakh.  A composite all in Annual Guarantee fee of 1 .0% p.a. of the credit facility sanctioned is now 
being charged. 
The Government has augmented the corpus of the Trus t of CGTMSE from the present level 
of Rs. 2500 crore to Rs. 7500 crore.  The increase of corpus by Rs. 5000 crore would be entirely 
contributed by Government of India.  Government has  increased the coverage of the loans covered 
under CGTMSE from Rs. 1 crore to Rs. 2 crore for th e loans to be disbursed w.e.f. 1.1.2017.  The 
loans which are being extended to Micro and Small E nterprises by National Banking Finance 
Corporations (NBFCs) have also been taken into the ambit of the Scheme.  
 (vii)  ZED (Zero Defect Zero Effect)  
 
 The ZED (Zero Defect Zero Effect) Scheme was launc hed in October, 2016 under which the 
Ministry plans to assess 22,000 units to get themse lves rated for Zero Defect Zero Effect.  ZED 
certification will be in five categories viz., Bron ze, Silver, Gold, Diamond and Platinum.  The rated 
SMEs will get better business opportunities. 
 The scheme envisages promotion of Zero Defects and  Zero Effect (ZED) manufacturing 
amongst MSMEs and ZED Assessment for their certification with the following objectives of: 
 
• Developing an Ecosystem for Zero Defects Manufacturing in MSMEs. 
• To promote adaptation of Quality tool/system and Energy Efficient manufacturing. 
• To enable MSMEs for manufacture of quality products. 
• To encourage MSMEs to constantly upgrade their qual ity standards in products 
 and processes. 
• To drive manufacturing with adoption of Zero Defect  production processes    and  without 
impacting the environment. 
• To support ‘Make in India’ campaign. 
• To develop professionals in the area of ZED manufacturing and certification. 
 

12 
 
(viii)  Technology Centre System Programme (TCSP) 
 
 The Ministry is presently running 18 Technology Ce ntres (10 Tool Rooms and 8 
Technology Development Centres) to provide technolo gical support to the micro, small and 
medium industries in the Country. Technology Centre s cater to the needs of industries located at 
those places.   
 
 To expand and upgrade the network of Technology Ce ntres in the country, the Government 
is implementing Technology Centre Systems Program (TCSP) at an estimated Projected Cost of Rs. 
2200/- crore including World Bank Loan assistance o f USD 200 million to establish 15 new 
Technology Centres (TCs) identified across the country. 
 
 13 new Technology Centres at Bhiwadi, Baddi, Rohta k, Bhopal, Durg, Kanpur, Greater 
Noida, Imphal, Vishakhapatnam, Ernakulam, Bangalore,  Sitarganj and Pudducherry are coming up 
with the assistance of the World Bank scheme.  More  than Rs.2000 crores is being spent on the

and is coming up with new Technology Centres at Shillong and Agartala. 
(ix)  Finance Facilitation Centres  
 
 To ensure availability of credit to the MSMEs, Nat ional Small Industries Corporation 
(NSIC) has already established seven Finance Facili tation Centres at Ludhiana, Jalandhar, 
Guwahati, Bangalore, Hyderabad, Chennai and Jaipur.   Applicants could file online application for 
loan to a financial institution through Finance Fac ilitation Portal. FFC facilitates obtaining credit 
from financial institutions. The NSIC has also redu ced the lending rates on raw material assistance 
by 1% on micro units and by 0.5% on small industrie s.  It has also reduced its rate of Single Point 
Registration Scheme by 40% in case of micro entrepreneurs 
 
(x) My MSME  
 
 My MSME mobile application is for all Micro, Small  & Medium Enterprises (MSME) in 
India and other stakeholders. This application acts as a source of all information related to MSME’s 
Policies, Registration, Services, Schemes, etc. 
 
Some of the features of My MSME mobile application are:

Market Promotion and Development Assistance scheme 
 
 
174. The Ministry informed that MDA scheme of KVIC has been modified as Market Promotion 
and Development Assistance Scheme (MPDA). MPDA sche me is formulated as a unified scheme 
by merging different schemes/sub-schemes/components  of different Heads implemented in the 11 th  
Plan, namely, Market Development Assistance, Public ity, Marketing and Market promotion. A new 
component of Infrastructure namely setting up of Ma rketing Complexes/ Khadi Plazas has been 
added to expand the marketing net worth of Khadi & VI products.  
175. Under the erstwhile MDA scheme financial assis tance was distributed amongst Producing 
Institutions (30%), Selling Institutions (45%) and Artisans (25%).  Under Modified MDA shall be 
calculated at 30% of the Prime Cost {cost of raw ma terial plus conversion charges up to grey cloth 
plus processing charges without margins [establishm ent expenditure (25%) and trading, insurance 
& bank interest (8%)]}. The Modified MDA shall be d istributed amongst producing institutions 
(40%), selling institutions (20%) and artisans (40%).   
 
176. The Khadi institutions submit their claims thr ough DBT portal, which is  scrutinized by 
field offices of KVIC and Central office before making payment. The benefits to Khadi artisans and 
Khadi institutions are passed on to their Aadhar seeded Bank account. 
 
177. The Committee has been pursuing the issue of l ow wage remuneration to Khadi artisans.  It 
asked if KVIC is ensuring that Khadi institutions a vailing assistance under MPDA are paying 
wages at par with skilled workers.  
 
178. The Ministry replied that  linking the Minimum Daily Wage rates to Khadi artis ans was not 
correct as Khadi spinning and weaving is a subsidia ry activity.  The artisans associated with Khadi 
Institutions are self-employed persons.  They opera te charkha/looms depending upon the free time 
available to them. The artisans are paid on piece r ate basis i.e. number of hanks of yarn spun and 

47 
 
meters of cloth woven. Hence, the wages of Khadi ar tisans are not strictly comparable to minimum 
daily wages. 
179. The Committee takes strong objection to the Minist ry’s stand in respect of wages of 
khadi artisans. Khadi was a tool of Father of the N ation for self reliance. It cannot be allowed 
to become a tool of drudgery and exploitation due t o technicalities. If KVIC is unable to 
determine the daily wage for khadi artisans, it must determine reasonable wages on piece rate 
basis. The Committee may be informed as to  how oft en the KVIC has determined the piece 
rate wages. The Committee may also be informed of t he parameters on which piece rate 
prices are fixed by the KVIC. The Committee may be informed of comparative piece rates 
determined by KVIC over last five years.  
180. If wages are to be determined on piece rate basis,  then steps must be taken to improve 
productivity of artisans without drudgery. KVIC mus t ensure production and supply of solar 
charkhas at reasonable rate and any other improved version that enhances productivity, for 
which the Khadi and VI Grant for S&T may be increas ed provided its utilization too is 
improved.  
181. The Committee also recommends that Khadi artisans m ay be covered under 
MNREGA for the purposes of wages. The Ministry may expeditiously take up the issue with 
Ministry of Rural Development in this regard to fin alise the modalities. The Ministry may 
also inform the Committee about the outcome of discussions.

General Over View  
 
268. The  MSME sector which is critical for the equitab le growth and employment and 
entrepreneurship in the economy, is a fact that can  hardly be overstated. Though the Budget 
allocation  for the Ministry of MSME is not proport ionate to the importance of this Sector, 
the Committee reiterates that the available resourc es need to be used efficiently for the 
targeted objectives. The Committee has often noted the excuse of Schemes being demand-
driven for the under-utilization of allocations. If  the Ministry is not convinced of demand, 
then it should not seek allocation. The Ministry ha s not been able to generate demand for its 
Schemes in a Sector which is wide spread over sever al sectors and is starved of any 
worthwhile policy intervention. With number of KIs reducing and low employability  of 
training courses the Committee wonders the quality of monitoring at Ministry’s level and 
efficacy of its institutional network in States and at grass root levels.  
269. The Committee observes that while utilization of f unds has increased during last two 
years, the achievement in physical target remains t epid.   The employability of training 
Schemes remains serious concern. 
270. KVIC acts as regulator, promoter and certification authority for the Khadi and 
Village Industry sector.  Its multiple rules may co me into conflict. The Committee is
