REPORT
The Action Taken Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Ministry of Heavy
Industries and Public Enterprises (Department of Public Enterprises) on the recommendations contained
in the Committee's Two Hundred Eighty-Second Report on the Demands for Grants (2017-18) pertaining
to Department of Public Enterprises.
2. Action Taken Notes have been received from the Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises
(Department of Public Enterprises) in respect of the recommendations contained in the Report. These
have been categorized as follows:
Chapter-I : The recommendations/observations, which have been accepted by the Ministry.
The Committee observes that the Ministry has accepted its recommendations as mentioned
in the Chapter - I of the Report.
Chapter-II : The recommendations/observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue in
view of the Government's replies.
In respect of recommendations contained in Chapter II of the Report, the Committee is
convinced with the explanations advanced by the Ministry and therefore does not want
to pursue them for the present.
Chapter-III : The recommendations/observations in respect of which the Committee has not accepted
replies of the Ministry and has asked the Ministry to review its reply.
The Committee expresses its concern over the non-acceptance of recommendations
contained in Chapter - III and desires that the Ministry should furnish logical explanations
therefor.
Chapter-IV : The recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the Ministry have
not been received.
In respect of recommendations placed in Chapter-IV, the Ministry has either furnished the interim
replies or couched its language in vague terms. Therefore; the Committee desires that the Ministry should
furnish Action Taken Notes in respects of recommendations categorized in Chapter-IV as per the
intention and spirit of the recommendations of the Committee.
3. The details of the ATR are being discussed in the succeeding pages.

2
CHAPTER-I
THE RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS, WHICH HA VE BEEN
ACCEPTED BY THE MINISTRY
Recommendation/Observation
The Committee notes that during 2015-16, the total number of CPSEs stood at 320, which was a
significant increase of 22 CPSEs, compared to 2014-15 when the total number was 298. At the same
time, the number of operating CPSEs rose only by 8 during the said period. Further, the Paid-Up
Capital, Capital Employed, Investment and Reserve & Surplus by the CPSEs rose steadily during the
XIIth Plan period. Similarly, the dividend paid and the contributions made to the exchequer also saw
an increase during the Plan period. The indicator that decreased the most in the XIIth Plan period was
the foreign exchange earnings by the CPSEs. Another factor that is obvious is the decline in the number
of people employed. As submitted by DPE, due to the decline in the number of permanent employees
over the years, CPSEs are now hiring employees on contract basis. (Para 5)
Action Taken
Due to increase in the total number of CPSEs and number of operating CPSEs the Paid-Up Capital,
Capital Employed, Investment and Reserves and Surplus, Dividend paid and contributions made to
exchequer has increased during the XIIth Plan period. Exports of goods & merchandise are the major
source of foreign exchange earnings of CPSEs. Its share in total foreign exchange earnings, decreased
from 81.60% in 2012-13 to 76.62% in 2015-16. With the advancement of technology and superannuation
etc., the numbers of permanent employees have declined over the years.
Recommendation/Observation
The Committee considers the fact that the role of CPSEs in India has undergone a lot of metamorphosis
since the beginning of planned mixed economy. After playing their part in nation building in a protected
environment till the advent of the New Economic Policy of 1991, the era of economic liberalization
dawned upon them. Now, the Government has done away with planned economy and has set priority areas
wherein it would continue to be engaged in business through CPSEs. In the remaining spheres, only
CPSEs who keep themselves afloat by being profitable are encouraged while closure or strategic
disinvestment, as decided by the NITI Aayog, is being used by the Government to exit loss-incurring
CPSEs in non-priority areas. This approach is expected to free up capital for investment in the social
and infrastructure sectors. In this regard, the Committee observes that one of the causes for which CPSEs
were envisaged, i.e., for equitable economic and social development - is still relevant to our country and
has to be kept in mind along with financial and business prudence while deciding the closure or strategic
disinvestment of CPSEs. The Committee is of the considered opinion that employment generation is one
factor that CPSEs can facilitate for some more time especially, in areas suffering from regional imbalances,
besides the North-Eastern Region. Accordingly, the Committee recommends that CPSEs should be
encouraged to provide permanent employment to people and may be desisted from hiring personnel on
contract basis. (Para 6)
2

3
Action Taken
The CPSEs operate in a competitive environment and the recruitment of employees below board
level is done as per the HR policy of CPSEs taking into account their business plans. Generally, only
the non-core activities would be outsourced or undertaken through contractual staff by CPSEs. As per
latest PE Survey 2015-16, the total number of workforce in 320 CPSEs is 15.21 lakh employees. Out
of these, 81% i.e., 12.34 lakh are regular employees and only about 19% are contractual or casual
worker employees. This indicates that CPSEs largely function through regular workforce and it would
only be the non-core activities in which the contractual or outsourced manpower is deployed.
Recommendation/Observation
The Committee had a detailed deliberation on the Guidelines regarding the utilization of CSR funds
by CPSEs. In this context, it was brought before the Committee that there were certain activities like the
construction of toilets which were undertaken as part of the Swachh Bharat activities, but funds/efforts
were not spared for their upkeep or maintenance. The Committee notes that in many areas where such
constructions were taking place were remote in nature and lack of upkeep rendered them useless and most
unhygienic within a short span of time. (Para 15)
Action Taken
The suggestions of the Committee regarding upkeep or maintenance of assets and construction of
toilets as Swachh Bharat activities under CSR have been noted. CPSEs have been sensitized about the
need for including provisions for maintenance of the assets created under CSR, including upkeep or
maintenance of toilets as part of Swachh Bharat activity.
Recommendation/ Observation
While going through the performances of the schemes of DPE during the XII Plan period, the
Committee finds that CRR and the SDP have underachieved in terms of funds, utilised roughly by 50%.
The spending for the NER has also been seriously below par. The only scheme that has utilized fund
effectively, even beyond the initial allocation, is the RDC scheme. This scenario has pulled down the
total fund utilization of the Department to only around 61% during the Plan period. Though the
Committee is aware of some of the reasons quoted by the DPE, during the earlier years, for
underperformance of the schemes, it observes that constant underperformance during a Five-Year Plan
period only points to deficient proactive measures in scheme management and restructuring. The Committee
reiterates that mid-term reviews of the schemes should be undertaken in a timely and planned manner
so as to ensure that funds allocated are utilized optimally. (Para 19)
Action Taken
Suggestions of the Committee have been noted and it would be endeavoured that in 2017-18, the
utilization of funds under CRR and RDC Scheme is to maximum possible extent as per the Budget
Estimates.

4
Recommendation/Observation
Regarding the revival/ restructuring or closure decisions of CPSEs, the Committee is of the considered
view that along with financial and business considerations, social obligations of the Government should
also be given equal weightage. The Committee holds this view owing to its assessment that stark regional
economic and developmental imbalances exist in our country even now. CPSEs can still play a relevant
remedial role in rectifying such imbalances. Having opined so, the Committee is clear that in this process
CPSEs should not be allowed to grow into white elephants eating into the very vitals of valuable
resources of the nation taking recourse to the plea that their existence is necessary for addressing social
causes. With respect to the disposal of land of CPSEs identified for closure or strategic disinvestment,
the Committee has always held the view that such landed property should remain with the Government
be it the Central, State or other Government agencies, to the extent possible. It should be ensured that
the land does not change hands to private entities without a properly assessed remunerative value
accruing to the public exchequer. The Committee reiterates this view and wants this to be followed in
letter and spirit. (Para 54)
Action Taken
The observations of the Committee are noted. The Government's primary objective in recommending
the revival, restructuring or closure decision of the CPSEs has been to recommend strategies for more
efficient and effective use of resources that the CPSEs already control and the likely additional resources
the government may need to pump in, if effective corrective measures are not taken in a speedy manner.
This principle is tempered by the consideration that some of these CPSEs serve social goals/objectives
which take precedence over profitability alone.
All efforts are being made to ensure that the land of the CPSEs, identified for closure, stay with
the Central Government, State Government or their bodies. The Department of Public Enterprises has
on 7th September 2016, issued guidelines on time bound closure of sick/loss making CPSEs and the
disposal of their movable & immovable assets after extensive consultation with other ministries. Efforts
are first made to transfer the assets to the holding company/administrative ministry for its own use at
book value. Next the freehold land is offered for sale at the current circle rates or the prevalent
acquisition cost (excluding the R&R cost) to the Central Government, Central Government bodies/
CPSEs, State Departments and State Government bodies/ State PSEs (in that order of priority). Only in
case no offer is received from the above organizations within six months, can the land be auctioned in
an open and transparent manner to a private entity.

5
CHAPTER-II
THE RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT DESIRE
TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE MINISTRY’S REPLIES
Recommendation/Observation
The Committee finds that the Department managed around 95% of fund utilization during
2015-16. The utilization figure for the current year stands at 81.26% as on January, 2017. These are
appreciable figures compared to the respective Revised Estimates. The allocation for 2017-18, has seen
only a slight increase to the tune of Rs.1.34 crore compared to the last year's RE. In this regard, for
the year 2017-18, the Committee notes that the Department sought Rs.23.85 cr . But, DPE has not
provided as to under which Head the increased allocation had been sought and the reasons stated by the
Ministry of Finance for the reduced allocation, even though this was sought by the Committee. Accordingly,
the Committee fails to take cognizance of the scenario and has to refrain from making effective
observations. (Para 22)
Action Taken
Enhancement in budget allocation in 2017-18 is attributed to enhanced expenditure under "Secretariat
Eco Services" due to the implementation of 7th Central Pay Commission and also due to enhancement
in likely expenditure on account of outsourced services such as Consultants, Data Entry Operators,
MTS, etc.
5

6
CHAPTER-III
THE RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH THE COMMITTEE
HAS OTHER NOT OR ACCEPTED THE REPLIES OF THE MINISTRY HAS ASKED
THE MINISTRY TO REVIEW ITS REPLIES
Recommendation/Observation
The Committee notes that during the oral evidence, while making a presentation to the Committee,
the Department submitted as part of the 'CPSE highlights 2015-16" that the total number of CPSEs in
the country to be 320, out of which 244 are operating and the remaining 76 are under construction. In
the ensuing discussion, attention was drawn to the General Performance of CPSEs and the areas wherein
CPSEs have excelled and the areas where they have failed. It was pointed out that the sectors where the
top ten profit making CPSEs of the country operating currently were in the spheres where CPSEs can
deliver and where they should venture more into by the Government. Likewise, when the top ten loss-
incurring CPSEs were analysed except BHEL, it was not difficult to find that they are operating in areas
where technological changes are frequent and the market fluctuation were rampant due to varying
factors. (Para 10)
Action Taken
The decision on setting up of CPSEs is taken by concerned administrative Ministry/ Departments
after due inter-Ministerial consultations. Various techno-economic and social considerations are taken into
account while making the above decision.
Further Recommendations/Observations
The Committee notes the reply of the Department of Public Enterprises (DPE). However, the
Committee wants its opinion to be conveyed to the relevant decision-making Ministries/
Departments and other agencies. DPE as the coordinating nodal department with regard to
CPSEs has to take the necessary initiative in this regard.
Recommendation/Observation
In view of the above, the Committee while observing the data relating to the profit making and
loss incurring CPSEs, finds that there are certain captive sectors in the industry which are conductive
for the Government to set up CPSEs in a profitable manner. In the opinion of the Committee, general
parameters of such areas might include stable technology, steady market, capital intensive nature and
judicious utilization of public assets, etc. The Government can keep these broad principles in mind while
identifying and setting up of CPSEs in the future in strategic and priority areas. Besides this, the
principles of social responsibilities of the Government should also be intertwined with the business
considerations. (Para 11)
6

7
Action Taken
The decision on setting up of CPSEs is taken by concerned administrative Ministry/Departments
based on the techno-economic, social considerations and in the interest of balanced regional development
in the country.
Further Recommendations/Observations
The Committee notes the reply of the DPE. However, the Committee wants its opinion, with
regard to more amenable spheres of operationalism for future CPSEs, to be conveyed to the
relevant decision-making Ministries/ Departments and other agencies who would be involved in
their setting up. DPE as the coordinating nodal department with regard to CPSEs has to take the
necessary initiative in this regard.
Further, the Committee also wants to have the data regarding new CPSEs incorporated/
constructed or/ under construction of the Government, since the last five years indicating their
areas of operation and details of the specific socio-economic and regional considerations that
have gone into the decision- making that has culminated in setting up of these CPSEs.
Recommendation/Observation
Accordingly, as a preparatory step in this direction, the Committee recommends that DPE being the
body in charge of the General Policy Framework for CPSEs, should conduct a well-organized
comprehensive research study to identify the areas of business wherein CPSEs can successfully/profitably
operate and grow. A policy of public investment in CPSEs can be based on the findings of such a
scientific study. This, in the opinion of the Committee should help to ensure that the 76 CPSEs that are
being newly set up by the Government operate in a profitable environment and are not doomed to be
shut due to extraneous factors like in case of their predecessors. (Para 12)
Action Taken
The observations of the Committee are noted. However, it may be mentioned that the public
investment policy of the government is shaped largely by the Ministry of Finance, NITI Aayog and the
concerned line ministries handling specific sectors of the economy. Based on an analysis of the ground
level realities and the emerging economic scenario, public investment decisions are taken by these
ministries.
As regards the 76 CPSEs that are in 'under construction' (UC)'stage, the concerned administrative
Ministries/Departments monitor the progress for their operationalisation/ commissioning keeping all
parameters under consideration.
Further Recommendations/Observations
The Committee recognizes that the Ministry of Finance (MoF) and the NITI Aayog have the
final say in case of the Public Investment Policy of the Government. However, the fact that DPE
is the coordinating nodal body in the realm of CPSEs in the country cannot be denied. Accordingly,

8
in the opinion of the Committee, DPE will be well within its mandate to carry out a study, may
be as part of its Research, Development and Consultancies (RDC) on Generic issues related to
Public Sector Enterprises Scheme regarding the area of business which have favorable attributes
for CPSEs to venture into and prosper. Such a study conducted by DPE, the cumulative domain
expert, can come up handy to MoF, NITI Aayog and the administrative ministries concerned in
their decision making regarding setting up of CPSEs. Similar involvements by DPE, right from
the inception stage of a CPSE would also give a more meaningful role for the Department in the
various aspects of CPSEs as well.
Recommendation/Observation
The Committee take note that DPE's latest advisory on CSR activities mentions only transparency,
selection and implementation of activities under CSR by CPSEs. However, based on the facts brought
before the Committee, it finds that there are activities under CSR that become redundant in the absence
of provisions for their maintenance by utilizing CSR funds. Accordingly, the Committee recommends that
DPE guidelines/ advisories on CSR should contain provisions/ instructions to ensure the maintenance of
constructed toilets and their related facilities under Swachh Bharat activities. This will also be in
synchronization with the similar provisions as contained in Swachh Bharat Kosh guidelines.
(Para 16)
Action Taken
The recommendations of the Committee on maintenance of facilities under Swachh Bharat have
been noted. As per Guidelines of M/o Corporate Affairs, maintenance of assets created under CSR is the
responsibility of the local community. As per these guidelines, this should form an integral part of the
project design and project cost of the company.
Further Recommendations/Observations
It is understood that as per the existing provisions of Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR),
maintenance of assets is the responsibility of the local community. But the Committee, from the
facts brought before it, is of the opinion that the inefficiency of the said provision is already
resulting frequently in the toilets built under CSR activities being rendered useless owing to lack
of up keeping. Further, it is the considered opinion of the Committee, that if the existing
provision does not allow proper maintenance of assets, it is time those are revisited in the light
of ground reality. Maintenance provisions could be introduced on specific, defined conditions
attached with clauses for fixing responsibility for non- maintenance followed by appropriate
punitive provisions. The Committee also recommends that DPE may include in its guidelines on
CSR, the provision that CPSEs should build toilets in consultation with District Administration,
Municipalities, Panchayat Raj Institutions, Schools, Hospitals, Railways and Transport authorities,
etc. and maintenance of toilets should be left to these institutions. DPE could set in motion such
initiatives in the CSR activities of CPSEs through its guidelines, paving way for Ministry of
Corporate Affairs to extend the same to the entire corporate world.

9
Recommendation/Observation
Regarding the operation of the CRR Scheme, the Committee has consistently taken the stand that
the scheme needs thorough refurbishing and constant review for fine tuning. The Committee is aware that
the Department has taken steps in this direction during 2007 by widening the scope of the scheme and
had made another attempt in 2012-13 by evaluating the Scheme through National Institute of
Entrepreneurship and Small Business Development (NIESBUD). However, the results have not been
encouraging, so far. Now it has been decided to run the scheme through NSDC to further augment it and
make it more effective through better training and certification thereby increasing the employment ratio.
Due to the fact that the Department has now decided to implement the scheme through the NSDC it has
been submitted that the actual training for the year has started only in February 2017. But, the
Committee also takes note that the Department is planning to have a further relook at the Scheme even
before the major steps taken in September 2016 to engage NSDC as facilitator, has begun to yield results.
The Committee observes that it would be better to wait to assess the effectiveness of the measures taken
by the Department for the CRR scheme till next year. As per the Committee's view, the single most
important indicator of the success of the new arrangement will be a marked improvement of redeployment
ratio under the scheme which has never touched the half way mark till now. To improve the redeployment
ratio, the Committee again reiterates that the nodal agencies under the CRR scheme may be asked to
identify works skills in demand in the local area in terms of employability and provide training to people
in such identified skills. This is especially needed in area such as the NER, where the Department has
claimed that there is non-availability of VRS/VSS optees resulting in funds earmarked for CRR in the
NER to be transferred to Non-Lapsable pool. Further the Committee recommends that DPE may explore
possibilities of using the funds from the pool for benefits of CPSEs in NER, who are in need of funds
for their revival. (Para 30)
Action Taken
The CRR scheme is being implemented from 2016-17 onwards through NSDC which will act as
facilitator for conducting skill training as per Qualification Pack (QP)/ National Occupational Standard
(NOS). The revised scheme also includes a provision for incentive to training providers for achieving
70% or more redeployment. Besides, a provision is also there for additional support to beneficiary in
special areas like North East & special groups like women, SC, ST, etc. All these measures would help
in achieving higher rate of redeployment under the Scheme.
Regarding use of funds from the Non-Lapsable Pool of NER for benefit of CPSEs in NER for their
revival, it is submitted that CPSEs are not under the administrative control of DPE, the revival of CPSEs
through use of funds from non-lapsable pool of NER is not under the mandate of this Department.
Further Recommendations/Observations
The Committee appreciates the measures taken under the Counselling, Retraining/
Redeployment (CRR) Scheme during 2016-17 by the Department to improve redeployment under
the scheme. Further, the Committee is optimistic that the result may be evident in the budget

10
figures for the ensuing year. However, the Committee finds that the reply of the Government
does not mention anything about further relook at the scheme, DPE plans to undertake. On the
benefits of the scheme, the Committee recommends that DPE should ensure that ground reality
checks are conducted on the results projected as part of the scheme.
Regarding the use of funds from the Non-Lapsable Pool for benefit of CPSEs in NER for
their revival, it has come to the notice of the Committee that CPSEs located in the NER can
benefit from the Non-Lapsable Pool of NER. Under such conditions, considering that most of the
CPSEs or their units located in NER are facing persistent losses, sickness, the Department
should try and play the role of a facilitator in reviving and restructuring the beleaguered CPSEs,
struggling for their very survival. Many CPSEs are setting up their projects in North East and
are looking for skilled technician, DPE may try and convince Ministry of DoNER to utilize the
unutilized funds to impart skill to the local manpower as well.
Recommendation/Observation
The Committee finds that the Government has set up a well-defined time bound institutional and
procedural mechanism for the revival / restructuring and closure of CPSEs in the Country. While the role
of DPE in the process is restricted to the issue of general facilitative guidelines to be followed by
administrative Ministries/ Departments in this regard, the NITI Aayog has a decisive role in giving the
final recommendation on the revival/ restructuring or closure of CPSEs. The administrative Ministries/
Departments have been entrusted with the responsibility of the execution of the decision after the
approval of CCEA. (Para 53)
Action Taken
Noted.
Further Recommendations/Observations
In reply to Committee's observations in para 23, the Department sought to justify higher
allocation for Secretariat Economic Services on the grounds that it provided advice on revival,
restructuring or closure of CPSEs. However, its reply to Para 53, suggests that DPE is in
agreement to the Committee's observation that it has only a limited role of issuing general
facilities guidelines in cases of revival, restructuring or closure of CPSEs. There is blatant
contradiction in these two replies of DPE.

CHAPTER-IV
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH FINAL REPLIES OF THE
MINISTRY HA VE NOT BEEN RECEIVED
Recommendation/Observation
While examining the Head wise budgetary provisions for 2017-18, it is seen that the Head that has
attracted the largest allocation is 'Secretariat Economic Services'. Out of the total allocated funds of
Rs.19.38 crore to the Department, Rs.10.98 cr has been given to this non-scheme Head. The scheme
allocation is only Rs.8.00 cr. In view of this, the Committee observes that the expenditure to maintain
the establishment exceeds the schemes that it administers. (Para 23)
Action Taken
Besides, implementation of the two Plan Schemes, there are numerous other important activities
undertaken by Department, the expenditure in respect of which is required to be incurred from Non-
Scheme allocation side. These include Permanent Machinery of Arbitration (PMA), formulation of Wage
and other general policy guidelines of CPSEs, categorization of CPSEs including conferring Ratna Status,
rendering advise on revival, restructuring or closure of CPSEs, monitoring of capital expenditure projects
of CPSEs etc. Hence, the establishment cost of the Department has to cater to the above-mentioned
functions also which do not fall under the ambit of the two Plan Schemes.
Further Recommendations/Observations
The Committee would like the Department to provide the breakup of Non schemes allocation
for Secretariat Economic Services for last 3 years.
Recommendation/Observation
The Committee notes that the RDC scheme introduced in 2007-08 has been plagued by under-
utilisation of funds over the years. However, it is understood that the scheme has gone revision in
February 2016 to make it more comprehensive and need based. The activities have been designed to be
spread out better. Also, some schemes have been merged into the RDC scheme during the year at the
instance of MoF . The Committee expects that these remedial measures would help the scheme to be more
effective and facilitate fund utilisation more effectively. Having observed this, the Committee also
observes the fact that the utilisation during 2016-017 is around 70% with two months remaining in the
year . (Para 37)
Action Taken
Observations of the Committee with regard to proper utilisation of funds under the RDC scheme
have been duly noted.
11

12
Further Recommendations/Observations
The Committee would like to be apprised of the total utilization of funds under RDC scheme
for the year 2016-17.
Recommendation/Observation
As regards to the activities conducted under the Scheme, the Committee finds that awareness and
other related training activities about mandatory/regulatory/legal requirements of CPSEs like CSR, Corporate
Governance, MoU, etc. are covered therein. The Committee is appreciative of this fact and wants DPE
to persist with such programmes as it will help the employees of CPSEs to keep abreast of the operational
features of the said requirements. In this regard, the Committee recommends the inclusion of awareness
programmes relating to the statutory provisions made under the Public Procurement Policy issued by
Ministry of MSME prescribing 20% procurement from SMEs and Vendor Development within the ambit
of the RDC scheme. (Para 38)
Action Taken
The recommendation made by the Committee regarding inclusion of awareness programmes relating
to statutory provisions made under the Public Procurement Policy issued by Ministry of Micro, Small

noted for compliance. DPE has conducted a full day Workshop on "Capacity Building of CPSEs on
procurement policy of M/o MSME" in collaboration with the Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium

sensitize them about the procurement policy issued by Ministry of MSME. The workshop was attended
by senior officers from Administrative Ministries / Departments and Board level officers from CPSEs.
The workshop was organized under the RDC Scheme of DPE.
Further Recommendations/Observations
The Committee notes the reply, however, would like DPE to conduct more such workshops
and monitor the effect of such sensitization in procurement from SMEs as per the Procurement
Policy and update the same to the Committee.
Recommendation/Observation
The Committee further takes note that under the Scheme, a provision of Rs. 1 crore has been made
towards subscription to the annual ICPE contribution of the country. In its earlier DFG reports (2015-
16), the Committee had recommended the Department to review this allocation. Accordingly, the Committee
reiterates its earlier recommendation on the issues and wants DPE to look into the possibilities of
exploring indigenous alternatives for the courses offered by ICPE, Ljubljana, Slovenia for addressing
the needs of the CPSE employees. The Committee may be informed of the rationale of continuing costly
subscription of ICPE when domestic alternatives are available in the country (Para 39)

India is a founder member of ICPE, Slovenia and has been attending its Council and Assembly
Sessions regularly. The amount of US$ 1, 50,000 (equivalent to Rs. 1.00 crore approx.) payable towards

13
Govt. of India's Membership to ICPE has been decided with the approval of Department of Expenditure,
M/o Finance.
Regarding training needs of executives of Indian public sector enterprises, it is mentioned that
CPSEs design their own human resource development programmes to upgrade skills and knowledge of
middle and senior level executives by giving them training through their own management institutes or
outsourcing their training needs to premier management training institutions in the country and abroad.
Recently, DPE has organized a meeting with the Indian institutes which have been sponsoring

Based on their feedback and a review of the financial health of ICPE, including their infrastructure

The Committee would like to be apprised of the details of the meeting of DPE with the
Indian institutes and the follow up decision taken/proposed to be taken in consultation with MEA

Recommendation/Observation
The Committee notes that DPE has initiated measures aimed at carrying out the responsibilities
under its new mandate of monitoring CAPEX by CPSEs. The Committee observes that if the Department
continues this important monitoring activity it can help encourage CPSEs to utilize their locked up
capital towards their own business expansion, modernisation and diversification which in turn would
contribute to the overall economic development of the nation. (Para 41)
Action Taken
Noted.
Further Recommendations/Observations
The Committee would like to be furnished with the feedback obtained by DPE regarding
CAPEX by CPSEs from the time, the Department started monitoring this parameter.
Recommendation/Observation
MoU is seen by the Committee as an instrument to assess the financial and physical performance
and social obligations of CPSEs in the Country. Evaluation of CPSEs through the MoU system is one
of the core responsibilities of DPE. During the last year and the current year, the Committee finds that
the targeted number of MoUs to be signed could not be met. Further, regarding the mechanism of MoU,
the Committee takes into account that during 2016-17 there have been some notable changes in the
system. Introduction of result oriented parameters and increased weightage for CAPEX are some of them.
The Parameters recently set forth by the Department for MoU evaluation like CSR and 20% Public
Procurement Policy compliance and CAPEX are socially and economically very relevant. Accordingly,

14
the Committee is of the opinion that MoU, currently being the single mechanism under DPE to monitor
such relevant and crucial factors, should be effective to act as a deterrent for deviant CPSEs in matters
of compliance. Therefore, the Committee recommends that DPE should strive to evolve the instrument
of MoU to help calibrate the functioning of CPSEs to be in unison with the priorities of the nation.
The Committee also recommends that all out efforts be made by the Department to ensure that the
targeted numbers of MoUs to be signed are met. (Para 46)
Action Taken
Noted.
Further Recommendations/Observations.
The specific measures adopted by DPE during the current fiscal year in tune with the
recommendations of the Committee may be submitted. Also, the details of CPSEs with whom

REPORT
The Action Taken Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Ministry of Micro,
Small and Medium Enterprises on the recommendations contained in the Committee's Two Hundred Eightieth
Report on Demands for Grants (2017-18) pertaining to the Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises.
2. Action Taken Notes received from the Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises in respect of
the recommendations contained in the 280th Report have been categorized as follows:-
Chapter-I The recommendations/observations, which have been accepted by the Ministry.
The Committee notes that the Ministry has accepted its recommendations as mentioned
in the Chapter -1 of the Report.
Chapter-II The recommendations/observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue
further in view of the Government's replies.
In respect of these recommendations, the Committee is convinced with the logic and
explanations advanced by the Ministry and therefore does not want to pursue them
further for the present.
Chapter-III The recommendations/observations in respect of which the Committee has not
accepted replies of the Ministry and desires the Ministry to review their reply.
The Committee is not convinced with the replies of the Ministry in respect of
recommendations contained in Chapter-Ill and desires that the Ministry in the light of
further recommendations/observations of the Committee furnish explanations thereof.
Chapter-IV The recommendations/observations in respect of which the Committee desire further
comments of the Ministry.
In respect of recommendations placed in Chapter-IV, the Ministry has either furnished the interim
replies, therefore, the Committee desires that the Ministry may furnish Action Taken Notes in respect of
recommendations categorized in Chapter-IV in detail and to the point, as per the intention and spirit of the
recommendations of the Committee.
3. The details of the ATR of the Ministry and recommendations/observations of the Committee thereon
are given in the succeeding pages.

2
CHAPTER-I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS, WHICH HA VE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE MINISTRY
Recommendation/Observation
The Committee expresses concern over narrow tax base among informal sector individual enterprises.
On the one hand MSME proprietorship/partnership firms demand their inclusion into proposed tax concession
to small enterprises; on the other hand they do not even file tax returns. This is an unacceptable situation
and the Committee recommends that the Ministry of MSME must take corrective but non-intrusive action in
consultation with Ministry of Finance. The Committee suggests that Ministry must seek PAN and TIN/ GST
details of the proprietors/partners in the UAM and, in association with the Ministry of Finance, link these
references for better tax monitoring through data networking of direct and indirect taxes. (Para 29)
Action Taken
As per the Udyog Aadhaar Memorandum (UAM), Permanent Account Number (PAN) of the organization
alongwith Aadhaar Number of the authorized signatory shall be required for filling UAM in case of a Company
or limited liability partnership or a cooperative society or a society or a trust. However, the suggestion of the
Committee to link the data with M/o Finance for better tax monitoring has been noted.
Recommendation/Observation
The Committee takes note that Scheme-wise cost of implementation has not been indicated despite
Ministry's agreement with Committee's earlier recommendation to this effect. In this regard the Committee
takes note of C AG's earlier Report (1 of 2015) wherein the national auditor has commented on lax monitoring
of utilization of Grants-in -Aids which constitute more than 90% of the Ministry's expenditure. The Ministry
depends on these agencies outside the Ministry's control for outreach and delivery of most of its schemes at
ground level. The Committee may be informed about the institutional, administrative and financial linkage
between the Ministry and the State agencies to implement Ministry's schemes considering that most of States
have parallel schemes that are primarily the responsibility of the State agencies. The Committee therefore
finds it imperative that the Ministry should run only those Schemes that it can monitor effectively on regular
basis through the institutions directly under its control or have an institutional MoU with the State agencies
to implement its Schemes. The Committee recommends that the Ministry must consolidate its Schemes which
is essential for better implementation and monitoring which is essential for efficient implementation of
Schemes. (Para 54)
Action Taken
The observation of the Committee is noted. However, Ministry is continuously making efforts to
streamline and rationalize various Plan schemes and monitors the implementation of these schemes regularly.
Recommendation/Observation
The Ministry may also consider putting the SCSP at the disposal of SC/ST Hub which has elaborate
implementing and monitoring infrastructure under the Chairmanship of the Minister. (Para 58)
2

3
Action Taken
The observation of the Committee is noted.
Recommendation/ Observation
The Committee also recommends that ASPIRE must be closely linked up with MUDRA, Stand Up and
Start Up schemes to provide financial assistance to the entrepreneurs. The LBIs should tie up with SHGs and
women organizations, ITIs and skill development institutions. (Para 88)
Action Taken
The observation of the Committee has been noted.
Recommendation/Observation
The Committee also recommends that Ministry should frame a time bound programme to make all its
courses National Skill Qualification Framework (NSQF) compliant and should also start a special campaign
to enroll skilled artisans from unorganized sector for these programmes as NSQF is essentially for these
artisans. The Ministry must inform the Committee about such Scheme. (Para 121)
Action Taken
The observation of the Committee is noted. However, Ministry has already taken steps in this regard by
issuing directions to various implementing agencies to make their training courses NSQF compliant. The
courses conducted by LBIs have been designed to be NSQF compliant from the beginning. However, for
KVIC and Coir Board, efforts are on to make the courses on board as per NSQF. Out of 13 courses
shortlisted by KVIC, only 4 could be shortlisted for placing those before the Skill Committee. As regards the
ATI Scheme, all the implementing agencies viz. NIMSME, NSIC and CTRL have already been directed to
make all their training courses NSQF compliant.
Recommendation/Observation
The Committee recommends that Ministry should launch special drive for traditionally skilled craftsman
who do not possess any formal qualification. Training them is the objective of NSQF. (Para 138)
Action Taken
Tool Rooms are being advised to call traditional skilled craftsman for providing training in NSQF
compliant courses, which are within the frame work of Tool Room and can be beneficial to such craftsman.
54 programmes have been approved as NSQF compliance. More 55 programmes are proposed for NSQF
compliance.
Recommendation/Observation
The Committee takes note of recent CAG Report (11 of 2016) on the Ministry of MSME which has
serious comments on the working of the eight sample SFURTI Clusters, maintenance of records of their
assets, enhancement of remuneration of artisans, ownership of Common Facility Centers and relationship
between Implementing Agency and the artisans. The Committee may be informed of the Ministry's reply and
compliance to the CAGs observations. (Para 152)

4
Recommendation/Observation
The Committee also takes serious note that the Ministry has not included such serious Audit observations
of SFURTI by the CAG , in its Annual Report. The Committee recommends that Audit Observations and
compliance thereon should be included in the Ministry's Annual Report. (Para 153)
Recommendation/Observation
In view of recent CAG observations, the Committee reiterates its recommendation that SFURTI may be
Performance Audited by the CAG for the entire 12th Plan period at the conclusion of current Plan. Findings
of the Audit and the compliance thereon may be informed to the Committee. (Para 154)
Action Taken on Paras 152, 153 & 154)
Reply to the C&AG's Para No. 12.2 of Report No. 11 of 2016 has been uploaded on the Audit Para
Monitoring System (APMS) web portal on 7.4.2017. Further, Audit Observations and compliance thereon
will be included in the Ministry's Annual Report for the year 2017-18.
Recommendation/Observation
The Committee is inclined to suggest that the KVIC should sign MoU with State Education Departments
to develop at least one Government school in every district as Khadi institution under skill development
programme in schools. For this the KVIC could dovetail its schemes with those of Ministry of Skill Development
and Department of School Education of States. The Ministry must design such Scheme and begin negotiations
with M/o Skill Development and D/o School Education and also inform the Committee of its outcome.
(Para 192)
Action Taken
The observation of the Committee has been noted.
Recommendation/Observation
The Committee also noted that HS Code is presently not allotted for Khadi & Village Industry products
which are presently categorized as handicraft items. This makes it difficult to identify and track the exports
of Khadi & Village Industry products. The Committee recommends that Ministry should take up the issue
with Department of Commerce to allot HS Code for Khadi & Village Industry products. The Ministry may
inform what are the pre-requisites for getting HS code for Khadi and steps taken to fulfill them as well as the
outcome of their efforts in this regard. (Para 212)
Action Taken
Chairman, KVIC has written a letter to Smt. Nirmala Sitharaman, Hon'ble Minister of State (Independent
Charge), Ministry of Commerce and Industry on this issue of allotting separate HS Code for Khadi & V .I.
products so that intensive efforts could be undertaken for boosting exports of KVI products.
Recommendation/Observation
The Committee also recommends that Indian High Commissions and Indian Embassy abroad may use
Khadi & Village Industry products in their office as well as for Gifts and presentations. They may also
support Export Promotion of Khadi & Village Industry products by displaying Khadi & Village Industry
products and literature through a showroom/show case in their office. (Para 213)

5
Action Taken
The issue of providing exclusive KVI products to Indian Missions/Consulates abroad for gifting to
their foreign hosts has already been taken up with the concerned authority vide KVIC's communication Mkt/
Consulates/2016-17 dated 01.11.2016.
Recommendation/Observation
As Khadi is promoted as the Indian heritage, the Ministry/KVIC must use the Indian Council for
Cultural Relations' centers abroad to promote Khadi products. Master artisans may be sponsored to display
their craft in those countries by ICCR. Our Missions and ICCR centers abroad must maintain an exhaustive
database of khadi exporting institutions to help potential foreign customers. (Para 214)
Action Taken
The suggestion of the Committee has been noted.
Recommendation/Observation
KVIC should also host online the data base of khadi exporters. KVIC should tie up with E-commerce
companies to promote khadi exports. The Ministry and KVIC should communicate with Ministry of External
Affairs and ICCR in this regard and apprise the Committee of the outcome. (Para 215)
Action Taken
The suggestion of the Committee has been noted.
Recommendation/Observation
The Committee noted that more and more Government institutions and PSUs are placing bulk orders
for khadi products. As the KVIC do not produce khadi themselves, the Committee wonders how are the khadi
vendors/suppliers selected. The Committee recommends that the KVIC should formulate a transparent method
of devolving bulk orders to khadi institutions in consultation with such institutions. KVIC should also
encourage and train such Khadi Institutions with 'Khadi Mark' certification, to directly register with DG
S&D and with the PSUs. (Para 216)
Action Taken
The suggestion of the Committee is welcomed and KVIC will be advised to put in place a suitable
transparent mechanism for the same.
Recommendation/Observation
However, the Committee notes that the Ministry had demanded only ` 41 crores for 2017-18 (BE) but
was allocated ` 50 crores. Yet, the Committee recommends that the Ministry may look into the issue so that
paucity of funds may not hamper the operations of CVY. (Para 220)
Action Taken
To meet out the requirement of funds under Coir Vikas Yojana scheme, additionally over and above BE
2017-18 will be sought in the first batch of Supplementary Demand for Grants for 2017-18.

6
Recommendation/Observation
The Committee acknowledged the issue of complicated process of registration of vendors by respective
MSMEs. The Committee recommends that Ministry in coordination with DPE and other administrative
Ministries should evolve a uniform process of registration of MSE vendors. (Para 250)
Action Taken
Different CPS Us follows different procedure for registration of Vendors in their programme based on
their own policy, items to be procured and its required quantity. The matter will be placed in the Review
Committee for providing guidance/methodology for adopting the suggestion of the Committee
Recommendation/Observation
The Ministry must also conduct regular awareness programmes with the Administrative Ministries/
DPE and the CPSEs regarding the provisions and new amendments in the Public Procurement Policy. The
Ministry should also take steps to popularize the Governments e-marketing platform. (Para 254)
Action Taken
The meeting of the Review Committee is held at regular intervals wherein representatives from all the
Ministries are invited and briefed about the effective implementation of the Policy. In addition, DPE has also
organised "Workshop for effective implementation of the PP Policy" on 15th March, 2017. The workshop
was attended by Secretary (MSME) / AS&DC (MSME), wherein the representatives of procuring agencies
were briefed about mandatory provisions of the Policy. All the amendments made in the Policy are uploaded
on the website of this office for the convenience of the stakeholders. Ministry of Railways/Petroleum &
Natural Gas has also organised the similar workshop which was attended by the representatives from the
Ministry of MSME.
Recommendation/Observation
The Committee noted that there was suggestion of Sectoral registration of MSE vendors or Single
Point Empanelment Registration Scheme of NSIC which could be used by the sectoral PSEs for locating
relevant MSE vendors. (Para 255)
Action Taken
MSE registered under Single Point Registration Scheme of NSIC are availing the benefit of PP Policy
and are participating in the procurement process of sectoral PSEs as well as in the tenders floated by
procuring agency throughout the country. NSIC is maintaining the data bank of the MSE and the same is
shared with the CPSUs as and when asked by them.

7
CHAPTER-II
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT DESIRE TO
PURSUE FURTHER IN VIEW OF THE GOVERNMENT'S REPLIES
Recommendation/Observation
The Committee notes that contribution of MSMEs in manufacturing sector is almost stagnant but has
been steadily increasing in Service sector. (Para 2)

and surveys on unorganized sector, which indicates the estimated contribution of the MSME sector to
Gross Value Added (GVA), GDP and Manufacturing Output, during 2011-12 to 2015-16. The details are as
under:-

is increasing year on year basis in absolute terms. The stagnancy in the share of MSME manufacturing does

Recommendation/Observation
The Committee notes that against the Plan Outlay of 
` 24124 crores for 12th Plan, total annual
Budget allocation for the Plan period was ` 1475 crores which is only about 61% of the Plan Outlay. The
Committee finds it paradoxical that a Plan outlay of such magnitude is not supported by Budget allocation.
The Committee may be informed about the rationale given by Ministry of Finance on lower Budget allocation
compared to Plan outlay. (Para 18)
Action Taken
It is submitted that against the Plan Outlay of ` 24,124 crores for 12th Plan, total annual Budget
allocation for the Plan period was ` 14721.51 crores which is only about 61% of the Plan Outlay. On the
basis of overall budgetary resources and due to ways and means position, M/o Finance allocated less funds
than requested. The 12th Plan outlay has been under-funded and, therefore, the demand for higher outlay by
the Ministry has to be seen in the context of lesser than planned outlays being provided year on year.
Accordingly, the schemes were implemented within the allocated budget.
In the first, Second and Third year of 12th Five year Plan for the Year 2012-13, 2013-14 and 2014-15,
the Ministry of MSME had demanded Fund Allocations of ` 6720.40 crore, ` 5263.61 crore, ` 6066.96
crore, respectively whereas Finance Ministry allocated ` 3155.66 crore, `3289.71 crore and `3702.28
crore, respectively. Whenever this Ministry had asked for respective allocation, it provided all the rationale
for the same. This Ministry repeatedly raised issues with the Ministry of Finance about the need for higher
budget allocation, with special reference to CLCSS, PCRA and also for raising the corpus of the CGTMSE.
The Government has kindly agreed to raise the corpus from ` 2500.00 crore to ` 7500.00 crore. This year,
an amount of ` 3002.00 crore has been allotted for the contribution to the purpose. But we need ` 1000.00

9
cr. additional for CLCSS and this, too, has been communicated to Hon'ble Finance Minister by Hon'ble
Union Minister of MSME.
Recommendation/Observation
The Committee is not sure that reduction in income tax rate as proposed in the Budget will make the
MSME more competitive. (Para 22)
Action Taken
In Union Budget 2017-18 Government has proposed to reduce the tax rate of MSMEs reporting turnover
of less than ` 50 crore to 25% from the existing 30%. The Government has also provided the statistics that
this benefit covers 96% of the total companies in India that are filing tax returns. This initiative will further
boost the Make in India Programme and growth of MSMEs in across the country.
Recommendation/Observation
The Committee having observed the indifferent performance of other components on NMCP over last
5 years of 12th Plan seeks to know Ministry's roadmap for implementing ZED Scheme. Whether the Ministry
has any sector wise database of such technologies and its suppliers. The Committee finds sweeping
generalisation in broad objectives without much detail about availability of technological resources,
institutional architecture and financial resources that will be required for implementation. The Committee
would like to know the parameters fixed for selection of the intended beneficiaries. (Para 33)
Action Taken
The ZED scheme is an extensive drive to create proper awareness in MSMEs about ZED manufacturing
and motivate them for assessment of their enterprise for ZED (Bronze-Silver-Gold-Diamond-Platinum)
(from lower to higher) and support them. After ZED assessment, MSMEs can reduce wastages substantially,
increase productivity, expand their market as IOPs, become vendors to CPSUs, have more IPRs, develop
new products and processes etc. The core activity under the scheme is Assessment / Rating by empanelled
Credit Rating Agencies/ other Agencies. Under this 22222 MSMEs will be given financial assistance for
opting ZED assessment and certification. The assessment process consists of three stages as under:
(i) Online (e-Platform) self assessment
(ii) Desk Top assessment
(iii) Complete assessment
The ZED (Zero Defect Zero Effect) Scheme was launched by the Prime Minister on 18th October,
2016. Under ZED the MSMEs can get themselves rated for Zero Defect Zero Effect. ZED certification will
be in five categories viz., Bronze, Silver, Gold, Diamond and Platinum. The rated SMEs will get better
business opportunities.

"Financial Support to MSMEs in ZED Certification Scheme" is a voluntary scheme for MSMEs engaged
in manufacturing. The main intent of this scheme is to enhance global competitiveness of Indian MSMEs on
quality and environment related parameters of its systems and processes. ZED is a Maturity Assessment
Model that lays down parameters on various process and outcome based disciplines which assess, rate and
certify an MSME and provide a roadmap for improvement. The scheme provides an opportunity to an
MSME to adopt the ZED model, get itself assessed and avail handholding services. The key resources of
this scheme are the 'assessors' and the 'consultants'. The scheme has provisioned rigorous training of
eligible assessors and consultants who will carry out these activities through accredited rating agencies and
empanelled consulting organisations/consultants.
Objectives of the scheme: The scheme envisages promotion of Zero Defect and Zero Effect (ZED)
manufacturing amongst MSMEs and ZED Assessment for their certification so as to:
• Develop an Ecosystem for Zero Defect Manufacturing in MSMEs.
• Promote adaptation of Quality tools/systems and Energy Efficient manufacturing.
• Enable MSMEs for manufacturing of quality products.
• Encourage MSMEs to constantly upgrade their quality standards in products and processes.
• Drive manufacturing with adoption of Zero Defect production processes and without impacting
the environment.
• Support 'Make in India' campaign.
• Develop professionals in the area of ZED manufacturing and certification.
These objectives are holistic in nature and the scheme provisions institutional & financial support to
activities that support all these objectives. Some of the important activities are:
• Industry Awareness Programmes,
• Training Programmes,
• Development of e-Platform,
• Assessment, Rating & Certification,
• Gap Analysis and Handholding,
• International Benchmarking.
Through above activities the necessary wherewithal is being established to create an ecosystem of
Zero Defect Zero Effect manufacturing. This is an ongoing process. The Quality Council of India (QCI) has
been nominated as the National Monitoring and Implementing Unit for the scheme and financial support to
MSMEs for obtaining ZED certification are provided by the O/o DC(MSME) as per scheme guidelines. As
per the guidelines of the scheme, the only resources required to be created out of the scheme finances are
a pool of qualified Assessors, Consultants, Master Trainers and tools viz., e-platform, e-learning modules
and on line service support, domestically to achieve the objectives of the ZED scheme.

ZED rating / assessment: There are 50 parameters on which the MSME will be assessed and rated
under ZED. The MSME applicant is required to comply with identified 20 essential parameters and at least

15
10 other parameters which will differ as per the MSME/s domain competency, i.e. sector of operation and
type of industry. Hence, the MSME will be rated on a minimum of 30 paramete ` MSMEs may seek ZED
rating on more than 30 parameters as per the processes and systems available at the MSME. Accreditation
of rating/assessment agencies and training of their resources throughout the country is being carried out to
ensure availability of resources pan India. The assessment process consists of three stages as under:
(i) Online (e-Platform) self assessment: Nil Fee
(ii) Desk Top assessment: Rs 10,000/-per MSME
(iii) Complete assessment: (a) Rs 80,000/- for ZED rating per MSME; (b) Rs 40,000/-for additional
ZED Defence rating; (c) Rs 40,000/- for Re-rating
Above rating costs will include cost of Rs 10,000/- as certification cost by QCI.
Subsidy for Micro, Small & Medium Enterprises will be 80%, 60% and 50% respectively by the
Ministry of MSME. However, preference will be given to small enterprises to enable them to grow bigger
because of competition and to get reasonable economy of scale. The number of micro enterprises shall not
be more than 50%. There will be special emphasis on SC/ST entrepreneurs.
Additional rating for Defence angle i.e. ZED-Defence by empanelled Credit Rating Agencies/
other Agencies:There is a need of certification for MSMEs having interest and competencies for becoming
defence vendors and Indian Offset Partners (IOPs). Accordingly, interested MSMEs will be given financial
support for ZED-Defence assessment and certification. Apart from 50 assessment parameters there would
additional 25 defence parameters for assessing ZED-Defence certification. ZED Defence certification can
be additionally acquired by MSMEs if needed.

time as well as part-time, when there is no agricultural work in villages. The wages of artisans are enhanced

in the region. The spinning and weaving wages were revised in the past as follows:
(A) Spinning wages from `3/- per hank to `4/- per hank and weaving wages by 5% to 10% w.e.f.

Recommendation/Observation
The Committee also notes that despite low Budget allocation, the actual utilization of funds under
major Schemes of SME Division and DC-MSME has been very low, thereby denying the Ministry any
ground to seek high allocation in BE. The Ministry has often justified poor utilization on the ground that
Schemes are demand driven. If the Ministry is not sure of demand for such Schemes then rationale for
seeking higher allocation every successive year may be explained. The Committee may be informed, that
beyond routine awareness programmes, of the steps taken to generate demand in a sector that seeks policy
intervention. (Para 19)
Action Taken
The low utilization of funds in some of the schemes is because the schemes are demand driven. In
some of the schemes like CLCSS, there are pending claims under general category of applicants because
enough budgets are not allocated to meet the demand. Also, there is no claim from SC/ST/NER components
and the amount disbursed is negligible therein and hence the funds earmarked under these components
remain unutilized. Ministry has been taking various steps to generate demand under various schemes, for all
components/sub components. These, inter-alia, include awareness programmes, discussions with stake
holders at apex level in regional conclaves, meetings with Ministers/Secretaries of all States/UTs, discussion
in meeting of National Board for MSME and at other forums, simplification/redesigning/merger/restructuring
of the schemes.
But the apparent fallacy of higher demand for allocation along with lower utilization year-after-year
continues because of the simple reason that funds allocated under certain components do not get spend
whereas there are demand in other (General) components that are not matched by allocations.
As regards the DRPSC's query about the steps taken to generate demand beyond routine awareness
programmes, the following may kindly be noted.
The Ministry of MSME has regular consultation process with stakeholders in the sector in the form of
meetings of the National Board for MSMEs. The last such meeting was held on 27th April, 2017. Again, in
view of the present Government's emphasis on the true spirit of cooperative federalism, there was another
consultation, with the Stale Governments, on the 28th April, 2017. It was for the first time in many years
that such an initiative of consultation with the State Government was undertaken as per the kind instructions
of Hon'ble Minister of MSME. In these two meeting, the following important discussions had taken place:
1. Each State should have (a) a separate department for MSMEs (b) a Directorate of MSMEs with
a formal channel of interaction with the DICs, (c) a separate policy for promotion of MSMEs and
(d) a road for job creation in the MSME for the State.

2. It was also proposed that the Public Procurement Policy which was hitherto applicable only to
the Central Public Sector Undertakings should be applicable also to state Public Sector Undertakings
and awareness should be created in favour of purchase from the MSME sector so that the
Government market is open to the MSMEs. However, for this, too, the state Government concerned
would have to come forward to adopt such policies by appropriate enactment/notification.
In addition, the MyMSME mobile app on http://my.msme.gov.in also launched by Shri. M. Venkaiah
Naidu, provides information on all schemes implemented by the Ministry of MSME at one place. The

Union Minister of States for MSME Shri Haribhai Chaudhary stated that the Ministry has embarked on

There were demands to make Facilitation Councils (FCs) more effective by making their decisions

Action Taken
The Micro and Small Enterprises Facilitation Council (MSEFC) is a quasi judicial body established by
the State Governments/UTs as per the provisions of section 20, 21 & 30 of MSMED Act, 2006. The
MSEFC has been empowered for taking decisions regarding reference made with it. This Ministry cannot
intervene in the matter of MSEFC. It is clarified that State Governments/UTs were required to frame rules
under the provisions of the MSES Act, 2006 in respect of Micro and Small Enterprises Facilitation Council
(MSEFC). M/o MSME have sent model rules to the State Government and have repeatedly requested them
for framing of rules in respect of their States. While all the State/UT Government/Administrations have
framed the rules, the two States i.e. Arunachal Pradesh and Assam are yet to frame their Rules and the last

30
communication to these two States was issued on 12th January, 2017. However, it depends on the State
Governments when they would like to frame/notify their rules. The Micro and Small Enterprises Facilitation
Council (MSEFC) portal on http://msefc.msme.gov.in has been launched on 27 April, 2017, by Shri M.
Venkaiah Naidu. Hon'ble Union Minister, on the occasion of the 15th meeting on the NBMSME. This portal
would facilitate implementation of the delayed payment provision of the MSMED Act, 2006 and also assist
in monitoring of delayed payment cases. This online platform is expected to be significant step in the
direction of digital India from the prospective of the MSME Sector in the country. With the access to this
platform, micro and small enterprise would be able to file their delayed payment related grievances online.
The grievance filed would be communicated through email and SMS to the parties involved. It would also
help officer of the Ministry of MSME as well as the State Government concerned in monitoring the progress
of cases both at the State and National levels. He also informed that most of the States have already uploaded
the information regarding delayed payment cases on MSEFC portal. As on 30.03.2017, 3690 cases involving
an amount of ` 1660 crore are being considered by various MSEFCs. In fact, the online portal would be of
great help to start-ups since delayed payment is probably the single biggest problem for start-ups. The
number of cases resolved during 2016-17 is 701.

Recommendation/Observation
The Committee noted that Non Banking Finance Companies (NBFCs), who together are significant
lenders to MSME sector, have been covered under CGTMSE scheme. The Committee raised the issue of high
rate of interest being charged by the NBFCs on the MSME loans. The Committee may be informed if the
CGTMSE has designed separate guidelines and conditions for the NBFCs to become partners in the scheme.
(Para 35)
Action Taken
NBFCs seeking coverage under CGTMSE have been asked to cap interest rates at 18%. In this regard,
a circular has been issued which contains guidelines and conditions for NBFCs to become partners in the
scheme which includes:
(a) Guarantee fee for each NBFC will be determined based on the 'Average Expected Loss' (Exposure
at default; Probability of Default; Loss Given Default) of the NBFC based on precious loan
recovery date for the asset class being covered. The same will remain unchanged for a given
portfolio and will be re-assessed at the time of annual sanction of limit.
(b) Pay-out caps would be fixed depending upon the 'Average Expected Loss' data and will be worked
out as portfolio guarantee of the loss (upto x times of average expected loss based on the data of
each NBFC depending upon repayment and other account data, overall target coverage under the
programme/other considerations like corpus availability, etc.) Such cap would be specified by
CGTMSE at the time of approval of annual limit. After assessing loss data and other parameters.
(c) No-claim bonus features may be worked out as a part of the fee package based on experience of
portfolio.
(d) The guarantee cover will be limited to a maximum extent of 50% of 'Amount in Default' for
individual accounts covered in the portfolio (of such other percentage as may be specified by
CGTMSE form time to time) settled on a pro-rata basis. However, claims will not exceed the
amount worked out as per overall cap as described above.
(e) Effective interest rate inclusive of cost of guarantee over not exceed 18% p.a. for all MSP, loans
of as may be specified by CGTMSR Board from time to time.
(f) For the purpose of claims, loss for the portfolio will be determined for such loans which have
turned NPA as per RBI norms and subject to MLI initiating legal against such loans.
The payment of guarantee claim by CGTMSE to the lending institution does not in any way take away
the responsibility of the lending institution to recover the entire outstanding amount of the credit from the
borrower with applicable interest. The lending institution shall exercise all the necessary precautions and

33
maintain its recourse to the borrower for entire amount of loan owed to it and initiate such necessary actions
for recovery of the outstanding amount, including such action as may be advised by CGTMSE.

Scheme.

The BE for Credit Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme (CLCSS) in Financial Year 2016-17 was ` 298.0
crore. At RE stage allocation was enhanced to ` 565.52 crore. There were pending claims of ` 874.00 crore

at RE level.
For CLCSS, although there was no demand from SC/ST/NER components under the scheme but in

Action Taken/Comments
TEQUP scheme is one of the components of NMCP. The basic objective of this scheme is to sensitize
the manufacturing MSME sector to the use of Energy Efficient Technologies in Manufacturing Process to
reduce the cost of production. It also encourages MSMEs to adopt Product Certification licenses from
National/International bodies in respect of their product to become globally competitive.
MSME acquiring Energy Efficient Technologies (EET) are provided financial assistance upto ` 10.00
lakh through TEQUP scheme. Till 2016-17, 438 MSME units acquiring EET have been benefited.
Further MSME acquiring Product Certification from National/International certifications are provided
financial assistance upto ` 1.501akh/2.00 lakh respectively. Till 2016-17, 1342 MSME units acquiring Product
Certification have been benefited.
In order to sensitize MSMEs for above activities, Awareness Programme are conducted throughout the
country. It may be seen that adoption of EET involves considerable investment by the units over and above
the subsidy. It may also entail reengineering of the process. This is a big effort and needs time to fructify.
However, our efforts are being to bear fruit as may be seen from the fact that reimbursement under EFT at
` 17.008 crore in FY 2016-17 was highest ever since inception of the scheme.
Further Recommendation/Observation
The Committee is not satisfied over the slow pace of performance of TEQUP Scheme that can
not only enhance competition between domestic industries but also enable them to meet infrastructure
obligation on energy conservation. The Ministry must step up its efforts so that more and more
MSMEs are encouraged to adopt Energy Efficient Technologies and also become globally competitive
by acquiring product certification licences from National/International bodies.

by the Banks too. It has been Committee's experience that a large number of applications forwarded by the
DLTFCs are rejected by the Banks too. The Committee also takes note of Ministry's admission that

achieving the intended objective. In such a scenario, the Ministry by its own admission is not able to
disburse money till the end of FY due to technicalities involved in the Scheme and these have not been

for disbursement despite availability of funds. These had to be carried over to the next financial
