assistance under PMEGP.
59. The Committee observes that to implement PMEGP successfully pattern of project report
should be simplified, long drawn process of selection of beneficiaries and banks* should be
further reduced, introduction of Entrepreneurs Development Programme (EDP) at block level,
Evaluation of EDP training programme before issue of certificate, Innovations in EDP training
be in the form of product or services, cost reducing process improvements and innovative
business models & methods should be followed.
60. The Committee further feels that a detailed study should be undertaken to ascertain the
number of PMEGP units if any, affected by demonetization and implementation of the GST.

Interest Subsidy Eligibility Certificate (ISEC) Scheme
68. The Ministry apprised the Committee that ISEC Scheme was introduced in May, 1977 to mobilize
the funds from banking institutions in order to bridge the gap in the actual fund requirement and its
availability from budgetary source. KVIC extends financial assistance to cotton khadi, silk khadi, woolen
khadi and polyvastra as per Pattern of Assistance. For this, an interest Subsidy Eligibility Certificate is
issued to Khadi Institutions (KIs). It strengthens the FCIs to avail the bank finance for the shortfall in
working capital. It is also supported to achieve additional productions and sales target in the khadi field.
Under the Scheme 4% is to be borne by the KIs and the interest differential is provided by the
Government of India. KVIC has issued ISEC for the last three years as per details given below:

69. Further, the Committee was informed about the details of SWOT analysis of the scheme is given
below:
• The ISEC scheme strengthens the KIs to avail the Bank Finance for the shortfall in working
capital. KIs can fulfil their requirement of funds to achieve the approved productions and sales
target during the prescribed time limit.
• The weakness of the scheme is that the flow of funds from Bank is delayed due to the lending
norms prescribed by banks. Therefore, the shortfall in their working capital leads to their
under performance.

18
• The ISEC scheme has given opportunity to the KIs for availing of shortfall in funds to meet
out required working capital. It is also supported to achieve additional productions and sales
target in the Khadi field.
• There is a wide gap between the ISEC issued and funds availed by KIs through banks. KVIC
takes a longer working cycle of 18 months while the Banks normally apply turnover formula
and consider one working cycle of maximum of 90 days. This is effectively comes to 25%
of annual turnover of SSI units. This is the main reason for the gap between ISEC issued by
KVIC and Bank Finance sanctioned by Bank.
• KVIC follows Debt Equity Ratio (DER) of 1:10 and Banks normally adopt 1:4. The flow of
credit to Khadi sector under ISEC is not at the desired level. This creates gap in working
capital requirement and actual fund availability. The KVI sector faces set back in its performance
due to shortage of fund.
70. Under the ISEC scheme, the certificate is issued to the extent of shortfall in working capital for
the financial year concerned. For the next financial year, ISEC is issued to the extent of shortfall assessed
based on previous year's performance. In this case, the ISEC shall cover bank finance already availed
and additional eligibility arrived.

Scheme of Funds for Regeneration of Traditional Industries (SFURTI)
77. The Ministry of MS&ME informed the Committee that KVIC is implementing a Revamped Scheme
of Funds for Regeneration of Traditional Industries which is a cluster based Scheme for enhancing
competitiveness of Traditional Industries and artisan cluste ` Under SFURTI a major cluster receives
` 5 crore and a mini cluster receives ` 3 crore. Till date, 72 clusters have been approved and 32 clusters
have been completed. Further, 60 additional clusters in Khadi, VI and Coir sectors are to be set up and
over 60000 artisans are to be covered.

20
78. Further, the Ministry informed the Committee that the Budget Estimate of ` 75 crore for SFURTI
during 2017-18 was reduced to ` 10 crore at RE stage in view of the targets having been completed
for the 12th Five Year Plan. It was also informed that an enhanced allocation of ` 125 crore has been
requested for in BE. 2018-19 for developing 60 clusters as the EFC has been completed and there are
about 80 projects in various stages for approval.
79. The Committee is of the opinion that the main objective of the SFURTI Scheme is to
encourage Traditional Industries and Artisan clusters of the country. This scheme is likely to
complete 10 years of its inception and, by now every district of the country should have had at
least one project, but the fact is that the scheme could not make its presence felt even in 10%
districts of the country. The Ministry of MSME as well as KVIC and Coir Board appear to have
failed on this front. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should come out with the
specific targets so that each district of the country will have at least one SFURTI project.
80. In a recent Study Visit, The Committee came to know about the payment of low wages to the
workers in SFURTI cluster in Andhra Pradesh. The Committee therefore feels that derivation of
cost norms for job creation vis-a-vis investment and maintenance should be more realistic as
minimum wages to support the livelihood is a basic requirement. It appears that what the
Government spends on Khadi units/VI units for the benefit of artisans is not reaching them for
their financial upliftment. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the payment of wages
to the un-skilled, semi-skilled and skilled workers with Full Time Employment (FTE) in KVIC
in different pockets should be looked into properly.

Coir-Board
92. "Coir" is the native name of fibre extracted from coconut husk, the fibrous mass surrounding
coconut, which is a perennial plant cultivated extensively in tropics. Coir Industry plays a very significant
role in economic structure of the country as a source of employment, income and foreign exchange
earnings. The U.S., China, Netherland and South Korea are main buyers of coir products from India.
93. The Coir Board is a statutory body established under the Coir Board Industry Act, 1953 for
promoting overall development of the coir industry and improving the living conditions of the workers
engaged in this traditional industry. The activities of the Board for development of coir industries, inter-
alia include undertaking scientific, technological and economic research and development activities;
collecting statistics relating to exports and internal consumption of coir and coir products; developing
new products and designs; organizing publicity for promotion of exports and internal sales; marketing
of coir and coir products in India and abroad; preventing unfair competition between producers and
exporters; assisting the establishment of units for manufacture of the products; promoting co-operative
organization among producers of husks, coir fibre, coir yarn and manufactures of coir products;
ensuring remunerative returns to producers and manufacturers, etc. The following are major Scheme and
Programmes am under the Coir Board:
(a) Coir Udyami Yojana
(b) Coir Vikas Yojana
(c) Mahila Coir Yojana

under the new Scheme. A total of numbers of 7343 coir units have been assisted under the Scheme since
its inception. Due to the establishment of 7343 coir units, 32883 employment opportunities have been
created in the major coconut growing states in the country.

Potential use of coir geotextiles and Coir compreg boards for applications in railways for

Corporation have approved the coir wood.
• The future of the industry depends on innovative eco friendly consumer acceptable products
and coir wood shall bring immediate changes to the life of people especially in the building
and furnishing sector. The demand is increasing for Coir wood, made using coir fibre bonded
with thermosetting adhesive, which is a replacement foq wood and plywood. The coir fibre

corrosive, water resistant, long durability, low cost etc.

103. The Ministry of MS&ME informed the Committee that the Coir wood is made using coir fibre
bonded with thermosetting adhesive, which is a replacement for wood and plywood. Coir wood is highly
suitable for building and construction for door, furniture and other joinery work and transportation
application for cost effective replacement to wood and timber. This will preserve the natural forests and
saves the trees from cutting for wood. Coir composite board has to compete with products of wood
panel industry for a place in the market.
104. The Ministry further informed that the Coir wood composite boards are going to be the next trend
in the market. As the market is maturing to eco-friendly products, coir and other natural fibres have a
big role to play. The market is well tuned for such eco-friendly furnishing and building material. The eco-
friendly products are well received by the market and the current trend is for such products. As per the
Market Study Analysis of Composite boards, both the builder community and the vendors are really
positive on the market acceptance of the coir wood composite board.
105. The Ministry apprised the Committee that the market is having a high regard for eco-friendly natural
fibre based products and is found to be very much encouraging. Coir based furnishing and building
products are rated highly by the market, which indicates a good future for coir based innovative
products. The demand of eco-friendly products from international market and the laws against felling
of trees gives immense scope for coir wood industries. The boom in the construction industry also adds
up to the demand for coir composite industries. Presently there are only 10 units manufacturing MDF
Boards and 30 Units manufacturing Panicle Boards in India. The additional approved capacity for Particle
Board wood is 2.82,500 TPA and for MDFB it is 3,50,000 TPA. The annual demand on the wood based
panel industry is expected to go much beyond 3,00,000 TPA. But the capacity of the industry to cater
to this huge demand is limited.
106. Deforestation is one of the major threats for the maintenance of ecological balance. The
Committee, in order to avoid grave threats which are endangering the climatic conditions and

26
human life, recommends that the production of substitutes for wood, such as coir wood, has to
be encouraged and more coir clusters under SFURTI have to be established to meet the demands
of coir based furnishings and building materials from the domestic as well as international
market. To achieve this, more funds should be allocated by the Ministry of MS&ME to the Coir
Board with proper monitoring and utilization of allocated funds.

promotion of coir and its by products for aiding in multifarious activities such as soil erosion
control, landscaping, river embankment etc., establishment of overseas offices of the Coir Board
may be considered. This way, the Coir Industry would also grow internationally side by side with
the Khadi Industry.

heavily on the Banks and other financial institutions for funds. Natural calamities like tsunami/cyclones
etc. which are beyond the control of human being, sometimes badly effects the coir industries destroying

28
them seriously. The Committee therefore, recommends that in such cases, the coir sector should
be supported financially in order provide some relief to the affected artisans/units and, for the
purpose, a corpus fund specifically, for Coir Board may be a good solution and could be considered
positively.

raw material available cheaply in the coconut producing areas. Actually, it is a process of making value
added products from the waste, otherwise it would have been a threat to the environment. The Committee
is of the opinion that the GST imposed on coir and coir products may be reduced further for
encouraging the traditional coir industry in which livelihood of about 7 lakhs people is based in
rural sector. The matter may be taken up with Ministry of Finance.
119. The Committee is of the opinion that the skill required by the artisans in Coir sector can
be acquired easily and similarly, the amount of investment required is negligible vis-a-vis other
similar village industries. Also the employment generated in the coir sector during the last

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS — AT A GLANCE
The Committee observes that the allocations of the Ministry were either reduced or enhanced
at the R.E. stage, but the actual expenditure incurred most of the time is less than the Revised
Estimate. The Committee is therefore, of the opinion that adequate steps should be taken to
monitor the output of various Schemes, including individual components so that the output
targets are achieved timely. (Para 11)
The Ministry of MSME submitted during the examination of Demands 2018-19, that the
budget under certain Schemes could not be utilised properly as the schemes are demand driven.
The Committee therefore suggests that proper assessment regarding financial requirement of
the demand driven Schemes should be made by the Ministry before sending the Budget proposals.
Hence, it should be ensured in future that the budget allocation made is utilised properly and
overrated demands are not projected by any of the organization /Institution under its jurisdiction.
(Para 17)
It is observed that the allocation and utilisation of funds under the plan schemes of the
Ministry during the last three years have been almost equal. The Committee is of the view that
the funds for meeting the salaries and pensions should be considered suitably without affecting
the funds for the development schemes. The Committee also desires that the Ministry may
follow-up with the Ministry of Finance for release of funds on timely basis. (Para 18)
In the opinion of the Committee, most of the MSMEs are not paid timely by the Government
organisations and PSUs for their supply as a result of which MSMEs face serious financial crunch
and it becomes very difficult for them to survive in the market. On the other hand they have
to dole out a high rate of interest to the Banks against their loans for delayed repayment.
Further, procurement from SC/ST Enterprises has also not received adequate attention under the
Public Procurement Policy. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of MS&ME should
take immediate measures with the concerned Ministries/Departments to sort out these issues to
dispel the apprehensions of MSME sector. (Para 20)
The Committee reiterates its recommendation that the long lasting problem of delayed
payment to SMEs, although, resolved to a certain extent by introduction of a few portals for
MSME sector, yet, it should be settled effectively and a time limit for defaulting large Companies
be fixed along with some penal provisions for making delayed payments to MSME units so that
both Large and Small units are enable to flourish, side by side. (Para 21)
The Committee is of the opinion that Micro Entrepreneurs in Indian Society finance their
business through borrowings, credit from friends or through their own resource generation and
are away from access to the Capital whereas the big and powerful entrepreneurs in business
sector take advantage of loopholes in the Financial Institutions. It, therefore, desires that the
entire Industrial sector should ponder over the ways to check the slippages in the financial
42

43
Institution to make the system foolproof so that the Micro Entrepreneurs can also avail the
benefit. (Para 22)
The Committee observes that Micro and Small Enterprises Facilitation Council (MSEFC)
constituted under MSMED Act, 2006 to resolve the delayed payment issue for MSEs have not yet
been set up in all states. There is a wide gap in the number of cases settled and reported to it.
MSEFCs have not yet met the success due to lack of any legal power for enforcing its decision.
The Committee recommends that the Ministry should take steps to constitute MSEFCs in all the
States so that the issue of delayed payments is resolved expeditiously. (Para 23)
The Committee further observes that MSME Exchange gives them the opportunity to raise
equity through an IPO and then get listed on the exchange. There are more than 300 companies
listed on BSE and NSE. Efficient SME platforms could prove to be a vital source of Capital for
MSMEs, but the two platforms are far behind in expansion, the way it were envisaged. It,
therefore, recommends that requirement of presence of a company in the market for three years
could be considered for reduction to a shorter period by SEBI. Tax exemption to the investors
in SMEs could add to the growth of MSME sector. (Para 24)
The Committee heard the Industry and MSME Associations representing enterprises from
various sectors in the country and is of the opinion that rising input cost is affecting the
competitiveness of the products of MSME sector especially, Micro and Small Enterprises, in
Domestic as well as International Market. This sector finds it very difficult to pass on the extra
cost to its consumers due to which margins of Micro and Small units decline and thus making
productions unviable for them. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of MS&ME should
raise the issue with Ministry of Finance and persuade them to address it at appropriate level so
that the input cost for SMEs remain within their reach and they are not forced to take loan at
exorbitant rates. (Para 25)
The Committee observes that in the present scenario of digitalisation IT professionals are
in high demand and they are getting placement with reputed MNCs and other big establishments
in different sectors. Many employees in Micro and Small sector start from ground level after
working for many years they attain a certain level of expertise. These employees may not be IT
literate and often have high resistance to the rapid changes in the working process that they are
comfortable with after many years. (Para 27)
The Committee is of the opinion that smart manufacturing is now making its place in the
market which is dependent on industrial automation including breath taking innovation viz. use
of robots and machine intelligence, smart material self learning systems etc. MSME sector
requires integration of work force and digital manufacturing and production processes for better
performance. (Para 28)
The Committee observes that implementation of some bigger scale IT project especially
after the introduction of GST and changes in tax structure involving business process across
different Departments which requires large amount of data entries requiring human resource

44
during implementation. The SMEs are often in shortage of manpower and thus it becomes
difficult for them to carry out implementation as it is always conflicting to run business on day
to day basis with limited manpower and do the extra implementations work. This affects the
business enterprises in the nascent stage and forcing them to close the establishment many a
times. (Para 29)
The Committee is of the opinion that to fight with bankruptcy and insolvency, modern codes
in this area are need of the hour in the competitive markets and uncertainties in globalization
so that if an entrepreneur is encouraged to take risk and the creditors should also have an
assurance of disposal of case quickly and repossession of assets after the failure of business.
(Para 30)
The Committee observes that MSME sector having limited financial resources lags far
behind in adoption and acquisition of globally available expensive advanced technology and thus
fails to stand firmly in competitive and qualitative market. The Committee, therefore, recommends
that a Global Technology Acquisition Fund should be set up to enable the Indian Industries to
acquire high-end technology with its support to enhance their competitiveness globally and value
addition. (Para 32)
The Committee recommends that R&D and Technology related support facilities and services
including training and skill development programme should cover optimum educated unemployed
youths of the country having qualification and talent along with inclination through IITs, ITIs,
NITs and other research laboratories. The facilities available need to be modernized and should
be fine tuned and tailored as per the need and requirement of the MSME sector. (Para 34)
The Committee feels that there is an urgent need to evaluate the Research and Development
system to make it more effective and beneficial to the MSME sector which is crawling far behind
in technology adoption in comparison to MSMEs of developed countries. The Committee recommends
that Ministry of MS&ME being the protector of the units in this sector should allocate more
funds for R&D and qualified people working in the field be motivated and encouraged through
the best possible ways and means. (Para 35)
The Committee further recommends that technological and innovative preparedness of the
MSME sector need to be studied constantly and a mechanism is required to be evolved urgently
to fill the gaps or constraints being faced by MSME sector in view of various trade agreements
at International level including economic cooperation agreements. (Para 36)
MSMEs engaged in International business have developed co-operation, partnerships, linkages
and network with foreign companies and institutions. By way of import and export MSME
enterprises boost their efficiencies capabilities, competitiveness and their vision. FDI thus play
a prominent role for internationalization of MSMEs. Today FDI is being attracted and invited
which would certainly have catalyzing effect on technology flow and investment consequently
posing challenges and opportunity to MSME sector. The Committee recommends that the Ministry
of MS&ME in view of this should take careful steps in co-ordination with Ministry of Commerce

45
and Industry (Department of Industrial Policy and Promotion) to fine tune the FDI Policy to take
its full advantage, international aid and support to make the MSMEs growth oriented with
innovative capacities and internationalization. (Para 37)
The Committee recommends that there is an urgent and immediate need for strong innovation
and policy to develop technology with proper legalities for implementation to fulfil the demand
and need of the MSME sector. (Para 38)
The Committee feels that although a lot has been done for providing relief to the MSME
sector in the form of technological up-gradation and financial support but there is a need that
the Ministry of MS&ME should make further efforts in co-ordination with other Ministries/
Departments to provide linkage between Large, Small and Micro Enterprises so that the Large
Enterprises owning technological advancement share their technology with Small and Micro
Enterprises to improve the standard and quality of their products. (Para 40)
The Committee recommends that with the emerging of Fourth Industrial Revolution where
human robot co-operation is growing, a policy should be framed with the joint effort of the
Ministry of MS&ME, Schools, Colleges, Universities and Industry Association's to develop such
curriculum at various levels to make the country technologically advanced by sharpening the
skills under 'Skill India' and for faster growth, productivity and competitiveness in industrial
sector including MSME. (Para 42)
The Committee feels that still there is a lot to be done at the level of Ministry of MS&ME
by ensuring that every State/Zone of the country is benefited by its policies, programmes and
Schemes along with uniform and stable development of MSMEs. This would not only provide
employment opportunities to the people but also check migration from rural pockets to big cities
in search of job opportunities. (Para 43)
The Committee while hearing the Associations in the MSME sector was apprised of the poor
Credit Rating done by the Banks while extending credit facility to MSME units. The Committee
desires that the issue of parameters fixed for credit rating should be raised at the appropriate
level, including the Department of Financial Services, by the Ministry of MSME and a suitable
solution be made to address the financial requirement of MSMEs. (Para 46)
The Committee desires that the details of inadequate credit disbursement by Banks to
MSMEs and particularly to Medium Enterprises which has shown negative growth rate may be
informed to the Committee after consultation with Reserve Bank of India and Ministry of
Finance. (Para 47)
The Committee notes that the constraint faced by KVIC/KVIB is mainly due to procedural
delays, inadequate technology up-gradation, improper utilisation of funds etc. Despite providing
technical guidance to the units in KVI, the problems of the units remain inadequately addressed.
This is one of the reason for sub optimal functioning of institutions/units and high drop outs
among new entrants, low employment generation. The Committee, therefore, recommends that
KVIC in view of the expansion of its area of operation in every nook and corner of the country,

46
should come forward with a more holistic and unified policy in co-ordination with the Ministry
of MS&MEs and other stakeholders as regards the successful operation of the units is concerned.
Proper planning, monitoring and implementation in each scheme is required to meet the primary
objective of employment generation along with proper utilisation of the budgetary support in view
of year on year enhancement in it. (Para 49)
The Committee feels that in face of stiff competition in the market from organised industries
KVIs should concentrate more on its technology improvement and products upgradation. It
therefore recommends that regular training by efficient staff having experience and expertise
should be imparted to the artisans through its network of training institutions. A regular study
on the functioning of the training institutions should be conducted as the present methods and
practices may be outdated and not be that much effective. The Committee recommends that the
process of revamping and reorientation of KVIs should also be done wherever required so that
it helps in productivity and development of Khadi and Village Industries. (Para 50)
The Committee observes that the training in some cases is also imparted through NGOs who
take the training very casually and moreover, theoretical training is imparted as they lack
practical modules. (Para 51)
The Committee was apprised about the availability of Khadi Fabrics in private retail stores
at competitive price. The Committee observes that opening up of Khadi retailing to private
players are good initiative in this regard for enhancing and expanding the market of Khadi
fabrics among the customers. Though, the issue of "Khadi" brand under unfair trade practices
by private players is reported to be legally entangled. The Committee would like that the issue
should be sorted out congenially so that private players also contribute in promoting Khadi
products. (Para 52)
The recent innovative step to bring in fashion designer of repute to design Khadi fabrics is
a welcome move and it needs to be continued by bringing in more such steps. The Committee
therefore recommends that this along with good market techniques like frequent awareness
campaigns among the youth and introduction of Khadi in Schools, Hospitals and railways could
be good recourse which will surely increase the demand for Khadi products. Along with this,
premier showrooms known as Khadi lounge should be opened in all the States capitals and
Airports to market designer Khadi products. (Para 53)
The Committee is of the view that the economic empowerment of the poor artisans can be
enhanced by more intervention by KVIC by allowing the spinners and weavers need to be allowed
to work with the private designers without the approval of KVIC so that they could earn more
wages directly from these designers. (Para 54)
The Committee observes that the urban youths are not inclined to work in this sector due
to low wages and the hardships involved in it. The Committee recommends that the issue of low
wages of unskilled, semi skilled artisans needs to be addressed on priority as the availability of
more willing workers will bring in more quality outcome in Khadi sector. This would help in
increasing the benefits to the artisans. (Para 55)

47
The Committee observes that to implement PMEGP successfully pattern of project report
should be simplified, long drawn process of selection of beneficiaries and banks should be further
reduced, introduction of Entrepreneurs Development Programme (EDP) at block level, Evaluation
of EDP training programme before issue of certificate, Innovations in EDP training be in the
form of product or services, cost reducing process improvements and innovative business models
and methods should be followed. (Para 59)
The Committee further feels that a detailed study should be undertaken to ascertain the
number of PMEGP units if any, affected by demonetization and implementation of the GST.
(Para 60)
The Committee is of the opinion that the minimum educational qualification prescribed
under the PMEGP and absence of the option of regional language in publicity/procedural formality
may be the probable reasons hampering the proper implementation of the flagship scheme as a
potential entrepreneur with low education profile may be prone to face difficulties in completion
of all procedural formalities including filling up of form. In this regard, necessary steps should
be taken to address the problem. (Para 66)
The Committee also observes that only half the targeted projects set up by KVIC have been
approved/disbursed by the Banks which does not portray a rosy scenario. The Committee desires
that the Ministry may step in to resolve the problems in consultation with KVIC and financial
institutions so that targets set forth are achieved. (Para 67)
The Committee observes that the actual ISEC issued and funds released by Banks is not
very encouraging and creates gap in working capital requirement and actual fund availability as
a result the KIs fails to achieve the desired level performance. It also feels that norms for
turnover formula on one working cycle differs both at KVIC and Bank level, which appears to
be one of the lacunas for the gap existing between ISEC issued and Bank finance which needs
to be addressed at the appropriate level. (Para 74)
In fact this matter had also come up for discussion during the Committee's visit to Mumbai
and Ahmedabad in August, 2017, wherein the Committee had desires that the Ministry, KVIC
and the financial institutions may together hold talks with RBI and come up with a workable
solution. (Para 75)
The Committee observes that KVIC is not working impressively in North Eastern Region
and has a very small set up in these areas. The number of ISEC issued under Khadi and
Polyvastra is almost negligible except in Assam and Manipur in the last financial year. The
Committee desires that the reasons for the same other than the hardships faced due to hilly
terrain should be placed before it. (Para 76)
The Committee is of the opinion that the main objective of the SFURTI Scheme is to
encourage Traditional Industries and Artisan clusters of the country. This scheme is likely to
complete 10 years of its inception and, by now every district of the country should have had at
least one project, but the fact is that the scheme could not make its presence felt even in 10%

48
districts of the country. The Ministry of MSME as well as KVIC and Coir Board appear to have
failed on this front. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should come out with the
specific targets so that each district of the country will have at least one SFURTI project.
(Para 79)
In a recent Study Visit, The Committee came to know about the payment of low wages to
the workers in SFURTI cluster in Andhra Pradesh. The Committee therefore feels that derivation
of cost norms for job creation vis-a-vis investment and maintenance should be more realistic as
minimum wages to support the livelihood is a basic requirement. It appears that what the
Government spends on Khadi units/VI units for the benefit of artisans is not reaching them for
their financial upliftment. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the payment of wages
to the un-skilled, semi-skilled and skilled workers with Full Time Employment (FTE) in KVIC
in different pockets should be looked into properly. (Para 80)
The Committee is the opinion that KVIC which is mandated for providing employment
opportunities across the country must come out with a comprehensive plan considering the local
need for the Khadi as well as for village industries sector along with developing a marketing
network for rural Khadi artisans. (Para 86)
Since the majority of rural habitants are illiterate and/or not technically qualified, there is
as such a need for creating employment opportunities in the rural area. Khadi, being a sector
that required low investment, must be vigorously persuaded in the rural areas. Although, the
Government has emphasized on every occasion, the need of support to this sector, however
budget allocation for this sector shows a very notional increase in the last 3 years. The Committee
recommends that the reasons of slow progress in Khadi programme should be evaluated properly
and appropriate measures be taken for its development. (Para 87)
The Committee observes that first and foremost requirement is overhauling of the marketing
strategy for KVI products. Product development and marketing need a professional approach.
Even the attempts to boost sales using Khadi as brand name is unlikely to succeed unless some
fundamental changes are introduced. Bringing in, the private sector for marketing and product
development may be a good attempt and may be initiated as a pilot project. KVIC and M/o
MS&ME should think over the cost cutting and stoppage of rebate on sale. The Committee
desires that an enhanced B.E. of ````` 65 crores under MPDA for 2018-19 may be utilised judiciously
for organising Trade Fairs, Vendor Development Programmes etc. at domestic and international
levels so that a need to bring down the funds drastically at the RE stage does not arise.
(Para 90)
The Committee is of the opinion that MSMEs are an integral part of the economic development
of the country and therefore their growth and survival is vital for the Government. Hence, it
recommends that more and more MSME exposition, MSME Haats and MSME National/International
trade fairs/Exhibitions should be organised, including at District level, with the participation of
people's representatives, to enhance the market accessibility of MSMEs. (Para 91)

49
The Committee feels that one of the most important objective of the implementation of
various Schemes under Coir Board is the employment generation especially in rural areas. For
this, organisations like Coir Board is providing training on various aspects of production and
development of new/innovative products. The Committee recommends that Ministry of MS&ME
should give a consideration for recognition of such training courses/training institutions so that
more younger generation will be attracted to such training and the status of such training will
be elevated to the next level. (Para 100)
The Committee also desires that the Ministry in consultation with the Coir Board should
make all out efforts to reach out to the Coir Udyami Yojna applicants whose accounts are
frequently turning to NPAs resulting in Banks showing reluctance to sanction loans under the
Scheme. The Ministry of MSME should make efforts to ascertain the root cause of increasing
rate of NPAs under the Scheme. (Para 101)
Deforestation is one of the major threats for the maintenance of ecological balance. The
Committee, in order to avoid grave threats which are endangering the climatic conditions and
human life, recommends that the production of substitutes for wood, such as coir wood, has to
be encouraged and more coir clusters under SFURTI have to be established to meet the demands
of coir based furnishings and building materials from the domestic as well as international
market. To achieve this, more funds should be allocated by the Ministry of MS&ME to the Coir
Board with proper monitoring and utilisation of allocated funds. (Para 106)
The Committee is of the firm opinion that in order to have a better co-ordination of export
promotion of coir and its by products for aiding in multifarious activities such as soil erosion
control, landscaping, river embankment etc., establishment of overseas offices of the Coir Board
may be considered. This way, the Coir Industry would also grow internationally side by side with
the Khadi Industry. (Para 107)
The Coir Board is implementing multifarious developmental and promotional activities when
in turn is providing employment to a large number of people mostly in the rural areas of the
country. Sufficient manpower is however required for implementation and monitoring the
programmes and for providing research data/statistics in time for MIS. Hence, the Committee
recommends that in view of the increased activities of the Board, the necessary qualified manpower
should be provided to the Board for its smooth functioning. (Para 108)
The Committee is aware that there are various other schemes implemented by the
Government under which technology developed is transferred to the beneficiaries without any
charges. The Committee is therefore is of the view that the technology developed by the Coir
Board should be transferred to entrepreneurs, traders, clusters etc. free of cost to encourage
potential entrepreneurs to get into the coir sector. Besides, steps should also be taken to explore
the potential overseas markets for export of coir products particularly innovative coir products.
Also, 100% modernization of coir industry has to be encouraged with high funding support to
popularize the innovative coir products in domestic market as well. (Para 115)

50
The Committee is also of the opinion that Buyer Seller meets and Vendor Development
Programmes may be organized overseas to popularize coir products and to tap the virgin overseas
markets. (Para 116)
A maximum numbers of coir industries are in Micro and Small category and these are
dependant heavily on the Banks and other financial institutions for funds. Natural calamities like
tsunami/cyclones etc. which are beyond the control of human being, sometimes badly effects the
coir industries destroying them seriously. The Committee therefore, recommends that in such
cases, the coir sector should be supported financially in order to provide some relief to the
affected artisans/units and, for the purpose, a corpus fund specifically, for Coir Board may be a
good solution and could be considered positively. (Para 117)
Coir Industry is a traditional industry (at the same time an export oriented one also) and
using the raw material available cheaply in the coconut producing areas. Actually, it is a process
of making value added products from the waste, otherwise it would have been a threat to the
environment. The Committee is of the opinion that the GST imposed on coir and coir products
may be reduced further for encouraging the traditional coir industry in which livelihood of about
7 lakhs people is based in rural sector. The matter may be taken up with Ministry of Finance.
(Para 118)
The Committee is of the opinion that the skill required by the artisans in Coir sector can
be acquired easily and similarly the amount of investment required is negligible vis-a-vis other
similar village industries. Also the employment generated in the coir sector during the last
2-3 years is very negligible in view of the vast potential available in the sector. The Committee
recommends that more Entrepreneur Development Programmes (EDPs) should be organised so
that potential entrepreneurs are motivated for setting up of their own units as a result employment
opportunity are created for rural youth. (Para 119)
The Committee was informed about the Solar Charkha Mission for which an allocation of
````` 50 crores has been made for the first time during 2018-19. Though the Solar Charkha mode
will surely remove drudgery, the Committee is of the view that the KVIC should ensure that
there is no conflict in the definition of Khadi which originally was totally 'hand spun', but with
the introduction of Solar Charkha, it would become 'motorised'. (Para 121)
The Committee observes that the funds released to MGIRI during the last three years is
always less than the Revised Estimate for the respective years. The requirement of fund and its
utilisation for an Institution engaged in rural upliftment should be monitored properly by the
Ministry of MS&ME so that the targets are achieved timely. If there is any grey area, the
Ministry should take initiative to address it immediately. (Para 125)
The Committee notes that the MGIRI is the only Institution under the Ministry of MSME
which is working on empowerment of traditional artisans through R&D projects for alternative
technology using local resources and it has given excellent results, especially, with regard to the
project based on cow urine and waste human hair producing Amino acid as a plant growth

51
promoter. The Committee observes that the success of this pilot project would go a long way in
increasing employment generation in the rural areas of the country. The Committee is of the
view that there should not be any shortage of funds for the institution rather it should be
promoted and motivated. (Para 126)
The Committee is of the view that Joint Plant Committee which is looking after the
procurement and distribution of metals, coal etc. should ensure unhampered supply to NSIC and
see that allocation order is released by the respective Ministries in time so that there is no
dearth of raw material supply to MSME sector. (Para 139)
The Committee is of the view that the Ministry of MS&ME should consider other available
options to provide necessary raw materials required by the MSMEs and for this, the other
concerned Ministries/Departments be persuaded for allocation of raw materials like, aluminum,
copper, paraffin wax, cement and bitumen etc. to fulfil the requirement of MSME sector.
(Para 140)
The Committee is of the considered opinion that the Incubation Centres run by NSIC
provide training to the prospective entrepreneurs by imparting training in the manufacturing as
well as service sector for skill development. In view of the huge skill demand existing in the
country, the Committee recommends that more Incubation Centres should be established in co-
ordination with State Government so that training in conventional trade as well as hi-tech areas
are imparted to entrepreneurs to accure skill in all areas of business operation for gainful
employment. (Para 141)
The Committee observes that NSIC through its Vendor Development Programme sensitize
and facilitate MSEs, including SC/ST MSEs, to become qualified vendors to public sector units and
other Government Departments as per the provision, of 20% mandatory procurement under
Public Procurement Policy. Of this, 4% should be from SC/ST MSEs. While the PSUs and
Government procurement from MSEs has been gradually improving, procurement from SC/ST
units is still very low. Therefore, the Committee recommends that there should be more VDPs
organised to publicise Public Procurement Policy among MSEs including SC/ST units.
(Para 142)
The Committee observes that as per reply furnished by the Ministry under the Single Point
Registration Scheme (SPRS), there are 527 MSMEs registered upto 15th February, 2018. However,
as per the Annual Report, 2017-18, there were 21922 cumulative number of units registered
under SPRS upto 31st December, 2017. The Committee desires that mismatch between the
figures should be clarified and placed before the Committee. (Para 143)
The Committee is pleased to note that the launch of the UAM has proved to be a stepping
stone for the ease of doing Business by the MSMEs. However, at the same time it also observes
that the online filing system under UAM based on self declared information shows an uneven
geographical distribution of UAMs across all Indian States and Union Territories. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that the Ministry should take the required steps to encourage MSMEs,

52
especially, the Small and Medium Enterprises to register under UAM. In this direction, the
stakeholders from the States/UT Governments, Industry Associations and Public at large should
also be encouraged to contribute significantly for the purpose, especially in the NER, in order to
afford ease of doing business in the MSME sector. (Para 148)
The Committee feels that use of standard raw material consistently; possible design
development, process and product development including planning for maximum output, maximum
efficiency, better finishing with accuracy can sharpen the competitiveness in manufacturing and
production sector. MSMEs face competition from developing countries due to globalization and
increased international trade but most of the Micro and Small Enterprises do not see financial
competition as major deterring factor but tend to face stiff competition in quality rather than
prices. (Para 152)
To enhance the marketing, targeted advertising through social network sites may prove a
right platform to reach out to prospective customers. The Committee feels that Ministry of
MS&ME should emphasize on setting up of more LBIs and TBIs with modern practice and
procedure for skill up-gradation of MSMEs. (Para 153)
The Committee feels that despite the efforts, the problem of unemployment, poverty, drudgery
and migration still exists in rural economy. The one of solutions to address these problems is
creation of employment opportunities in rural areas by setting up of Small Enterprises in Agro
based sector as nearly 56% of the population is still dependent on Agriculture. There is always
a scope for innovation, value addition and entrepreneurship development in this sector. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that the skill up-gradation, handholding, credit support and
incubation aiming rural zones should be considered to provide employment in rural areas.
(Para 157)
The Committee would also like the Ministry of MSME to expedite the sanctioning and
setting up of the targeted number of LBIs and TBIs and also make the States and other
organisations in world, aware of usefulness of the Incubation Centres by holding talks with them
from time to time. In this way, the States would be encouraged to furnish more and more
proposal for setting up of Incubation Centres. (Para 158)
The Committee finds that there is a tangible gap in subsidy claims received and settled
every year. There is also a declining trend in the number of MSEs benefited. The Committee is
constrained to note the decreasing trend in subsidy claim amount. The Committee recommends
that the Ministry of MS&ME should come out with a concrete plan to get sufficient allocation
from the Ministry of Finance for clearance of subsidy claims. (Para 164)
The Committee observes that benefits under CLCSS are extended to the beneficiaries only
through 11 Banks. The Committee recommends that more Banks should be added to the list of
banks. Moreover, the list of 51 subsectors should be increased in consultation with Industry
Associations and GTAB. The Ministry of MS&ME should also ensure release of timely payment
to scheduled Banks. (Para 165)

53
The Committee in its Action Taken Report on 280th Report of the Committee on Demands
for Grants (2017-18) expressed its dismay over the utilisation and lack of performance of Schemes
in NER. The Committee observes and again reiterates that the Ministry should make concerted
efforts for industrialization in NER region, be it in the field of traditional art, craft and artisan
work. It should try to utilise the fund allocated to the full extent as the Committee is not
convinced with the reason given by the Ministry regarding the lack of industrialization and
demands in NER. (Para 170)
The Committee expresses its reservation over low employability under PMEGP during
2017-18 and feels that without raising the employability, the Scheme would be a wastage of
resources. The Committee expects the Ministry to inform it about the concrete steps taken to
improve employability in NER. (Para 172)

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry,
having been authorized by the Committee, hereby present this Two Hundred and Eighty Ninth
Report on the Credit Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme (CLCSS) pertaining to the Ministry of Micro,
Small and Medium Enterprises.
2. The Committee took up the subject for detailed examination and as part of its examination, in a series
of meetings, the Committee heard the views/suggestions of Secretaries of M/o MS&ME, Department of
Financial Services (M/o Finance) and representatives from SIDBI, CII, ASSOCHAM, FISME, CIMSME,
CWEI, DICCI etc.
3. The Committee while drafting the report has mainly relied upon the following documents:- (i) Background
Notes from the M/o Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises; (ii) Views/suggestions from Industrial Associations
and Nodal Agencies like SIDBI, CII, ASSOCHAM, FISME, CIMSME, CWEI, DICCI etc. taken during the
course of meetings; (iii) Oral presentation made before the Committee by the M/o MSME and various
Industrial Associations; and (iv) Replies furnished by M/o MS&ME on the points/issues raised by the Members
during the meetings of the Committee and to the questionnaire sent by the Secretariat.
4. I, thank the M/o Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises and various Industrial Associations for furnishing
Background notes, written replies and their inputs during the meetings.
5. The Committee in its meeting held on the 6th August, 2018 considered and adopted the Report.

REPORT
Micro, Small and Medium Enterprise is the pillar of economic growth in many developed and developing
countries in the world. Often rightly termed as “the engine of growth” for India, MSME has played a
prominent role in the economic development of the country in terms of creating employment opportunities,
scaling manufacturing capabilities, curtailing regional disparities, balancing the distribution of wealth, and
contributing to the GDP. It is the biggest employer after the agriculture sector and presently, nearly 120
million people are employed under this sector. Though India is still facing infrastructural problems, lack of
proper market linkages, and challenges in terms of flow of institutional credit, it has seen a tremendous
growth in this sector.
2. The advantage of this sector is that it requires less investment, thus creating employment on a large
scale, and reducing the underemployment problems. However, the sector faces stiff challenges too and one
of the biggest challenges is technology adoption and technology upgradation. Further, the adoption of modern
technologies is itself dependent on availability of finance and is a major challenge for MSEs as regards to
competition from large enterprises and MNCs and Increasing exports as well as global footprints. Moreover,
this sector has survived almost all threats emerging out of technology upgradation and adoption from both
domestic and international market.
3. To tackle these problems Ministry of MSME implements the following three Schemes/Programmes:
a) Credit Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme (CLCSS)
b) National Manufacturing Competitiveness Programme (NMCP)
c) Tool Rooms and Technology Centres
4. In order to promote the adoption and up-gradation of technology in the MSE sector, the Government
of India through the Ministry of MSME implements a capital subsidy scheme called the Credit Linked
Capital Subsidy Scheme (CLCSS).
5. The Scheme aims at supporting technology up-gradation of Micro and Small Enterprises (MSEs) by
providing up front capital subsidy to MSE units, including khadi, village and coir industrial units, on institutional
finance (credit) availed of by them for modernisation of their production equipment (plant and machinery)
and techniques.
6. Under the Scheme, subsidy is provided for induction of well-established and improved technologies.
It provides 150/0 (subject to maximum of `15.00 lakhs) up front subsidy on capital investment for technology
up-gradation to micro and small enterprises for modernization of their production equipment. The above
scheme was launched in October, 2000 and has been revised w.e.f. 29
th September, 2005. As per the
guidelines of the scheme, technology up-gradation means induction of state-of-the-art or near state-of-the-
art technology. In other words, technology up-gradation would mean a significant step up from the present
technology level to a substantially higher one resulting in improved productivity, and/or improvement in
the quality of products and/or improved environmental conditions including work environment for the
unit. It would also include improved packaging techniques as well as anti-pollution measures and energy
conservation machinery. Furthermore, the units in need of introducing facilities for in-house testing and
inline quality control equipments would qualify for assistance, as the same are considered technology up-
gradation.

7. For implementation of CLCSS the eligible PLI (All scheduled Commercial Banks, Scheduled co-
operative Banks, RRBs State Financial Corporations and North East Development Finance Institute (NEDFI),
will execute a general agreement for availing capital subsidy under the scheme with any of the nodal agencies
i.e., SIDBI and NABARD. However, the PLIs will have to produce an undertaking to either of nodal agency
that subsidy claimed in respect of beneficiary unit has not been claimed from other nodal agency. The PLIs
will also execute an agreement on behalf of the Government of India with Micro or Small units, as the case
may be. The information on subsidy would be furnished on quarterly basis through Head Office of the PLIs
to Regional Office/Branch Office of the nodal agencies located in the region. The subsidy forecast information
for each quarter would be published on 1st of the preceding month in respect of the quarter for which it is
claimed i.e., on or before 1st March for April-June quarter and so on. The PLIs would ensure furnishing of
details of release of subsidy on quarterly basis and this would be ensured by nodal agencies on receipt of
complete details of subsidy released to beneficiary units.
8. As per the information given by the Ministry of MS&ME to the Committee, Online application and
tracking system was introduced from October, 2013. To claim subsidy under CLCSS eligible MSEs are
required to apply online through PLIs from where MSEs can avail term loan. The completed application is
being uploaded by PLI through Online Application and Tracking System to the attached Nodal Agency,
which, in turn, recommends the application online to Office of DC (MSME) for release of subsidy. After
processing of application and subject to availability of funds, due approval is accorded by competent authority
after obtaining concurrence of Internal Finance Wing, after which funds are released to Nodal Agencies.
Funds are then transferred by the Nodal Agencies to the PLIs where the account of the MSE is operated.
9. The Ministry of MS&ME informed the Committee that as is the case with MSE sector in general, the
SC/ST owned MSEs in particular continue with outdated technology and plant/machinery and due to lack of
awareness and inadequate finance, the problem gets further compounded and puts them in a disadvantageous
position as they lose out on economy of scale. In view of this, the existing CLCSS has been able to benefit
only a negligible number of SC/ST MSEs. Although it aims at facilitating purchase/upgradation of plant and
machinery by providing 25 per cent upfront capital subsidy to the existing as well as new SC/ST owned
MSEs on institutional finance availed of by them. Sole Proprietorships (In case of proprietary MSE, proprietor
shall be SC/ST), Partnerships (In case of partnership MSE, the SC/ST partners shall be holding at least 51
% shares in the unit), Co-operative societies, Private and Public limited companies (In case of private limited
companies, at least 51 % shares shall be held by SC/ST promoters) owned by SC/ST Entrepreneurs of
Micro Small Enterprises sector engaged in the manufacturing activities are eligible for seeking assistance
under this scheme. The existing enterprises should have obtained registration under Udyog Aadhar
Memorandum as well as have enrolled in MSME Data Bank.
10. The objective of this scheme is to promote new enterprises and support the existing enterprises in
their expansion for enhanced participation in the public procurement. However, the Public Procurement
Policy mandates each Central Ministry/Departments/PSUs to procure atleast 4 per cent (out of the 20
per cent quota) of the total annual procurement required from SC/ST MSMEs.
11. Regarding the utilization of Government assistance i.e., subsidy, the Committee was apprised that it
cannot be utilized for the purpose other than for which it has been sanctioned, no deviation is allowed in this
regard. In case a beneficiary unit is found to have availed the subsidy on false information, action would be
taken against the unit and the unit would have to refund the capital subsidy availed with penal interest on

3
prime lending rate from the date of disbursal to the date of refund. A suitable condition to this effect has to
be ensured by PLIs in their documents for agreement with MSE units. The Committee took note that online
onus of credit risk would be with PLIs and it has to make its own judgment at the time of appraising the
project and decision of PLIs would be final in this regard.
12. The Committee was also informed that the proposal covered under CLCSS need not get any sanction
from Government of India and also that there is no such binding obligation on the Nodal Banks/Agencies for
the purpose. However Nodal agencies i.e., SIDBI and NABARD may always inspect the books and accounts
of PLIs and call for any information including amount of capital subsidy in respect of assessee as required
by the Government of India from time to time if it is found that there is a deviation from policies, procedures
and guidelines laid down under CLCSS. A beneficiary unit has to remain in commercial production for a
period of at least three years after installation of eligible plant and machinery on which subsidy under CLCSS
has been awarded.
13. Further, the Committee was informed that under the pre-revised Scheme, 12 per cent capital subsidy
used to be provided to Small Scale Industrial units, including tiny units, on institutional finance availed of by
them for induction of well-established and improved technology in selected sub-sectors/products approved
under the Scheme. The eligible amount of subsidy calculated under the pre-revised scheme was based on
the actual loan amount not exceeding `40 lakh. The Scheme was revised with a 15 per cent upfront subsidy
up to a subsidy cap of `15 lakh (up to total cost of plant & machinery of ` 1 crore) with effect from the 29
th
September, 2005.

18. The Committee is concerned to note that there has been the steep fall in the number of MSEs
benefitted under CLCSS from the Financial Year 2014-15 onwards which is mainly on account of
lack of adequate budgetary resources allocated under the scheme. The Committee accordingly
desires that adequate budget allocations should be made under the Scheme to cover more MSEs
under the Scheme.
19. The Committee heard the Ministry of MS&ME and various associations working for MSME sector
viz. Confederation of Indian Industry, Confederation of Indian Micro Small and Medium Enterprises,
Consortium of Women Enterpreneurs of India, Dalit Indian Chamber of Commerce and Industry, Federation
of Indian Micro and Small Enterprises on the issues related to CLCSS and their suggestions on the Scheme.
The representatives from the Ministry also supported the views of all associations for sustainable growth of
the MSME sector. The representatives from DICCI submitted that the computation of the eligible cost
should be calculated for capital invested on the fixed assets such as land, building and machinery in the
project as per the rates certified by chartered engineer. On the basis of the information, the representative of
the Ministry of MS&ME explained various issues and clarified almost all queries raised by the Committee
and the representatives of various associations of industries.
20. On a query raised by the Committee as to what strategy is being adopted by the Ministry to step up
the outreach of the Scheme to the 115 aspirational districts, identified by the NITI Aayog, the Ministry
clarified that officials of its Ministry and Nodal officers from NSIC, KVIC, Coir Board and MSME-DIs
visit the aspirational districts for close co-ordination with State Governments and concerned district
authorities.

21. The Ministry of MS&ME informed the Committee that MSEs are lacking information and awareness
on quality standards and access to newer technology. In this regard, the Committee wanted to know as to
how the Government is planning to spread awareness about technology up-gradation and also about the
features of the CLCS Scheme among the MSEs.
22. The Committee desires that the outcome of such visits may be disclosed to the Committee
and whether the visits have had any lasting impact the percolating the benefits of the Scheme to
the grass root levels in these Aspirational Districts or not.
23. Further, the Committee desires that Ministry of MSME should works in tandem with the
State Governments of the more populous States, where there is less off take of the CLCSS to
encourage more and more promising entrepreneurs to set up industries and also to take part in the
scheme for technical upgradation.
24. The Committee appreciated the efforts/measures being taken by the Ministry of MSME to
step up the penetration of CLCS Scheme to the underprivileged sections (SC, ST and Women), 115
Aspirational Districts identified by NITI Ayog, and also the NE Region.
25. Further, the Committee was of the opinion that the M/o MS&ME should utilised the UAM data of
entrepreneurs to create awareness, in every nook and corner of the country regarding the scheme by using
the available mobile numbers with them.
26. The Committee after discussions with various associations In the MSE sector, observed that M/o
MS&ME should give a serious thought on erasing the cost ceiling on the Machines as it appears impractical
without any prescribed specification and listed plant and machinery supplier. The Committee felt that
requirement of each and every Micro and Small Entrepreneur may vary in different sectors and products.
27. In order to popularize the scheme, the representatives from CII suggested that the Ministry of MS&ME,
if it deems fit, may consider propagation of scheme through Non Banking Finance Companies and Fintech
Companies. Even the private sector may be asked to come forward to give impetus and benefit to more and
more people under the CLCSS.
28. The Committee noted the reply of the AS&DC of the M/o MS&ME on coverage of all sectors under
the CLCS scheme along with pending liability which is to the tune of `829 crores requiring liquidation on
priority. Against the budgetary allocation of `326 crores in 2018-19, `155.75 crores were released and
utilized. It was also informed that the M/o MSME is making all out effort to ensure proper utilization of
funds under the scheme by introducing flexibility in the Listed Sectors for SC/ST, women and NER
Entrepreneurs by removing the cap of 51 Sectors/Sub-Sectors or Technologies, keeping in view the
requirement of specific technology for them. Regarding the expansion of 51 Sectors/Sub-sectors, the
Committee was also apprised by the Ministry that these Sectors are not limited or restrictive as prima facie
it appears. There are numerous technologies available under the sectors. The Committee is of the opinion
that the Ministry of MSME has to ensure that in future, appropriate/measures should be taken for
induction of more sectors/Sub-Sectors/technologies under the CLCS scheme in addition to the
existing 51 Sectors/Sub-Sectors for all categories of entrepreneurs.
29. The Committee is of the opinion that the CLCS scheme should be made applicable for all
sectors (including plant and machinery) for subsidy under CLCSS. The Committee, therefore is of

6
the view that the M/o MS&ME should also ask the Ministry of Finance for more budgetary allocation
for betterment of MSE sector as a whole as well as to liquidate pending liabilities under the
scheme.
30. On the enhancement of subsidy limit, some of the associations favored increase in the limit of term
loan from `1 crore to `5 crore. In response the M/o MS&ME informed the Committee that most of the
enterprises fail to touch even the prescribed subsidy limit of ` 15 lakh ( i.e. 15%) since MSEs are small
entrepreneurs and their needs are limited rather they need timely disbursement for availment of loan or
subsidy amount. It has been the experience of the Ministry that at the most MSEs touch `6.4 lakh as subsidy
under the scheme. Even the loan amount has not crossed a maximum of `52 lakh as of now. During the

31. In this connection, the Committee undertook a study visit to Bengaluru, Tirupati and Chennai from
15
th to 19th January, 2018 to examine the issue of the overall performance and applicability of Credit Linked
Capital Subsidy Scheme (CLCSS) in the MSE sector. During the discussion, the Committee desired to know
the mechanism adopted by PLIs/Banks/Nodal Agencies while appraising the applications for release of
subsidy by Office of the DC(MSME). The Members of the Committee also asked about the return of the
loan amount to PLIs/Banks. The Committee further raised the query about the how the Scheme has benefitted
the Coir units in modernization process etc. and the status of revision in the Scheme. In this regard, the
Committee was informed about the technologies under the Scheme.
32. The Committee observed from the presentation given that the performance of NABARD is not very
encouraging in these States as far as the number of units benefitted and subsidy released is concerned. The
representatives from the banks informed the Committee that they have not been able to process the applications
because of paucity of funds under the scheme. The Committee was also apprised that thrust of the scheme
has been the more coverage of MSEs with reasonable subsidy per unit within the overall budgetary limits. It
was informed to the Committee by some of the Associations that CLCSS is available only to micro and small
entrepreneurs for whom modernization is the biggest challenge, unlike the other technology upgradation
schemes like TUFS of the Ministry of Textiles. Besides, it is available only for projection up to a cost of ` 1
crore. So it is really serving the enterprises under the bottom of the manufacturing pyramid. When the
Government is continuing with TUFS scheme under which even large corporates are given subsidy up to 25
per cent of the project cost for modernization of textile and apparel units, the reason for throttling this
scheme for the MSEs only who are the largest employer is not justified. However, the Committee was
informed by the Ministry that the objectives of both the schemes are different. TUFS is to achieve the vision
of employment generation and promotion of export through ‘Make in India’ with zero effect and zero
defects in manufacturing of Textile sector and is open to all including large scale industries whereas CLCSS
aims to facilitate technology upgradation by providing capital subsidy on institutional finance availed by
MSEs.
33. The Committee is of the considered view that taking into account the rate of inflati on, the
M/o MSME should gradually consider to enhance the limit of subsidy i.e., from `````15 lakh to `````25 lakh
inprescribed sectors/sub-sectors which would prove to be more helpful for MSEs to cater to their
needs for upgradation of machinery and plants.

34. The Committee was informed by some of the Associations that the scheme is linked with credit
facility availed by the entrepreneurs in MSE sector which should not be a binding obligation on the Micro
and Small entrepreneurs as availment of credit sometimes take time. The scheme therefore should be available
even for the expenditure made by the entrepreneurs out of their own savings if they do not want to avail
credit facility under the scheme. However, the Ministry of MSME apprised the Committee that this could
only add to liabilities and fiscal imbalance. One of the suggestion from the associations present during the
meeting was regarding the Third Party Evaluation of the Plant and Machinery genuinely required by the
entrepreneur; to which the Ministry of MSME responded that aggregation of plant and machinery at their
level as suggested by one of the MSME associations would only lead to a kind of indirect licensing and may
attract allegations and criticism.
35. The Committee after hearing the Ministry of MSME is of the view that M/o MSME taking the
practical aspect into consideration may ensure or ascertain the genuineness of the claim by MSEs
for subsidy against the purchase of machines or requirement of the machines for technology up-
gradation, the M/o MSME may consider about the possibility of a Third Party Evaluation by some
rating agency or NSIC or SIDBI who can report directly to the M/o MSME in this regard and
thereafter the Ministry may take necessary action without delaying the process.
36. The Committee further noted that in the North East Region, there is considerable proliferation of the
NEIP Scheme, which offers a subsidy of 30%. More and more people prefer the NEIP Scheme due to the
larger subsidy involved. The Committee observes that less intake under CLCSS in NER is perhaps
due to the existence of the NEIP scheme offering more subsidy vis-a-vis CLCSS.
37. The Committee accordingly desires that Ministry may chalk out measures to make the CLCSS
more attractive by perhaps increasing the subsidy in order to woo the NE entrepreneurs.
38. The Committee is of the view that the Ministry of MSME should regularly monitor the progress
in the matter in co-ordination with State Governments so that the Scheme reaches out to more
entrepre neurs. The Committee also suggests that subsidy for women entrepreneurs of all
categories should be raised to 25 per cent as is the case of SC/ST entrepreneurs after exploring
the feasibility.
39. The Ministry of MSME informed the Committee that during the implementation of the scheme, the
performance of the MSE increased in terms of productivity turnover, energy efficiency, profits etc. whereas
the pollution reduced substantially. About 88.9% and 98.4% of MSE units from Eastern and Western regions
reported that CLCSS technology has helped to improve their quality of products. In other regions, all MSE
units have reported in favour of improvement of quality of products owing to CLCSS. About 88.3 % of
beneficiaries reported that the listed technology under CLCSS is very effective.
40. An independent Third Party Evaluation of Credit Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme (CLCSS) was carried
out by National Institute of Labour Economics Research and Development (NILERD) an Autonomous
Institute under NITI Aayog, Government of India in 2016-17 which submitted its Report in August, 2017.
In the evaluation report the continuation of the Scheme further beyond the Twelfth Five Year Plan Period has
been recommended.
41. The Committee took note of the status of implementation of the CLCS scheme in NER and amongst
women entrepreneurs along with the pattern of utilization of maximum subsidy benefit by few selected

8
States. It also observes that there is a general complaint of lack of awareness about the scheme among the
PLIs and even the Micro and Small entrepreneurs.
42. The Committee therefore is of the view that serious efforts with practical approach and result
oriented goals should be made to dispel the confusion and lack of awareness about the scheme in
MSE sector as well as among the PLIs and Financial Institutes. Technology Exhibitions may be one
of the measures to create awareness. However, there must be a unified attempt by the Ministry of
MS&ME and different Industrial Associations to create awareness among the MSEs about the Schemes.
The M/o MSME should make all out efforts for the growth of the MSEs on a uniform pattern across
the country for the overall development resulting in creation of various job opportunities for the
masses and dispelling the geographical imbalance of industrial set up. Therefore, there is a need of
continuance of the scheme for a longer period.
43. The Committee observes that to popularize the CLCS Scheme it should be discussed at
appropriate levels i.e., SLBC, Districts Heads, DIC, industry associations and grass root level etc.
for better off take under the scheme.
44. The Committee observed during the course of the presentations that the scheme is beneficial, good
and has been acclaimed across all MSE Sector. However, the Committee noted that the women entrepreneurs
availing this scheme is negligible.
45. The Committee was of the view that when a woman entrepreneur is eligible in any sector, the
benefit of subsidy should be credited to her individual account or account of the enterprise, as the
case may be without any delay. The subsidy should be extended as margin money rather than
granting it at the completion of 3 years.
46. The Committee notes that the CLCS scheme is still devoid of service sector under its umbrella. It also
observed that the EFC had already given its approval to include the service Sector under the CLCSS.
However, it is still awaiting the approval of the Cabinet. The Committee took note of the issue of shifting of
the small and medium industries to far away locations from their present premises due to energy and
environment related issues as these sectors have not been able to avail the benefits of subsidies as compared
to large industries.
47. The Committee is of the opinion that if the SMEs are shifted from their present location on
the plea of energy or environmental pollution, adequate infrastructural facility viz. power, road,
easy labour etc. should be provided to them before shifting them.
48. The Committee desires that M/o MSME may pursue the matter and the Committee may be
apprised as soon as Cabinet approval is accorded.
49. The Committee recommends that the timeline for application process and disbursement of
subsidy should be reduced by the M/o MS&ME by co-ordinated effort with the Department of Financial
Services.
50. The Committee is of the considered opinion that besides Technology up gradation before granting
subsidy the basic difficulties being faced by the MSEs viz., land, power, -water, communication and
road facilities etc should also be taken care of appropriately to make the MSEs globally competitive
and grow in a hindrance free environment.

51. The Committee was constrained to note the pathetic picture of subsidy utilization under CLCSS in
Eastern Zone (only 2%), Northeastern States (only 0.l %) and worst case of Jammu and Kashmir where
only one Unit is availing the subsidy even after 17 years of the implementation of the scheme.
52. The Committee is of the opinion that the Ministry of MS&ME should conduct a study in all
States to know as to how the awareness could be created to get the optimum out of the Scheme. The
Ministry may also undertake a research study to know the reason as to how five States achieved a
stupendous target of 77% while the rest of India lagged behind.
53. The Committee noted the fact that budget under the scheme allocated for SC/ST category/NER
remain unutilised whereas for general category the budget is entirely exhausted. On being inquired as to
what steps are being taken by the Ministry to resolve the problem of the benefits of the Scheme not percolating
to the SC/ST and probable entrepreneurs from the North East Region, it was informed that the norms for
eligibility under the Scheme are being revised. It was also informed that a proposal is in the anvil to make
subsidy admissible to the aforecited categories for investment in technological up-gradation on acquisition/
replacement of plant and machinery etc.
54. The Committee desires that it may be apprised of as soon as norms of the Scheme are revised.
55. The Committee therefore, is of the view that M/o MSME should approach the M/o Finance for
diversion of allocated budget from other schemes and allocate this fund for benefit of Micro and
Small Enterprises under CLCSS at last quarter of the financial year. The Committee also feels that
delays in release of budget under the scheme delay the process of disbursement of subsidy which
should be taken up with M/o Finance for timely allocation.
56. During the course of discussions, the Secretary, Department of Financial Services informed the
Committee that GeM platform has been initiated by the Government to onboard all MSMEs so as to ensure

57. The Committee also took cognizance of the fact that under SIDBI there are 109 PLIs which included
Public Sector banks too and it has released `1648 crores towards subsidy. The-online application and

58. The Industry Associations have informed the Committee that sometimes MSEs suffer due to the delay
in submission of their cases by respective banks i.e. PLI and Nodal Agency, thereby leading to rejection of
their cases by the Ministry of MSME.
59. The Committee is of the view that subsidy should be released to MSEs in such cases where the
delay in submission of cases occurs on the part of PLls and Nodal Agency. Further, the Ministry

10
should develop an online mechanism to monitor the applications and identify whether delay occurred

60. The Committee desired to know whether the eligible technology/machinery under all approved sub-
sectors fulfilled the intended objective of the CLCS Scheme. The Committee was informed that overall

61. The Committee while hearing the presentation from industrial associations found that there were

62. The Committee is of the opinion that to provide smooth corridor for the betterment of MSEs
for having a flourishing business, there is always a need for concerted efforts at every level. On the

63. In the opinion of the Committee, the Ministry may consider setting up of a Grievance

technical upgradation. (Para No. 23)
